0.title: The Letter to the Ephesians
0.overview:
Paul wrote this letter from a Roman prison, around AD 60–62, awaiting trial before Caesar. He was chained to a guard. And from that cell he wrote what has often been called the most majestic letter Paul ever penned — a letter so vast in its theological vision, so soaring in its doxology, that it feels less like correspondence and more like a window thrown open onto eternity.

The letter may have been circular — several early manuscripts omit the words “in Ephesus” from 1:1, suggesting it was passed between the churches of Asia Minor. Tychicus carried it personally (6:21). Whether it reached one church or many, it was written for the whole church in every age — including yours.

Did Paul really write it? Many modern scholars think a follower wrote it in his name, pointing to its long sentences and unusual vocabulary, its close overlap with Colossians, and phrases such as his holy apostles and prophets (3:5) that they take to look back on an earlier generation. But the letter names Paul twice (1:1; 3:1), the early church received it as his without dissent, and the differences are well explained by its subject and setting: a letter of praise and teaching rather than controversy, written at the same time as Colossians and carried by the same man (6:21; Col 4:7). A letter claiming to be Paul’s that was not would be a forgery, and the church of that day rejected such letters. The more likely conclusion is that Paul wrote it.

The heartbeat phrase is in Christ, appearing over thirty times. Everything God has done, is doing, and will do for his people is located in the person of his Son. Chosen in him. Redeemed in him. Raised with him. Seated with him. Built together in him. The letter is not primarily about what Christians must do; it is about who Christians already are — and the doing flows from the being.

The grand theme is God’s eternal purpose to unite all things in Christ — things in heaven and things on earth (1:10). The church is not a human institution that God blesses; it is the centrepiece of his cosmic plan, the body through which the manifold wisdom of God is displayed to the watching principalities and powers (3:10). To be part of this church is to be enrolled in the most significant project in the universe.

The structure is clean and powerful. Chapters 1–3 are the great indicative: what God has done in Christ from before the foundation of the world to the present moment. Chapters 4–6 are the great imperative: how the people of God now walk, in every relationship and in every spiritual battle. The hinge is the word “therefore” in 4:1 — one of the most consequential words in Christian ethics. The imperative is always grounded in the indicative. We do not obey in order to be accepted; we obey because we already are.

Preach this letter and you will give your congregation the full panorama of God’s saving purpose, from the eternal counsel of the Trinity before creation to the armour for the battle they face this week. There is nothing higher in Paul. There may be nothing higher in Scripture.

1.title: Grace, Election, and Prayer
1.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, To the saints who are in Ephesus, and are faithful in Christ Jesus: <sup>2</sup>Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>3</sup>Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, <sup>4</sup>even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him. In love <sup>5</sup>he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will, <sup>6</sup>to the praise of his glorious grace, with which he has blessed us in the Beloved. <sup>7</sup>In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace, <sup>8</sup>which he lavished upon us, in all wisdom and insight <sup>9</sup>making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ <sup>10</sup>as a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth in him. <sup>11</sup>In him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, <sup>12</sup>so that we who were the first to hope in Christ might be to the praise of his glory. <sup>13</sup>In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, <sup>14</sup>who is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it, to the praise of his glory. <sup>15</sup>For this reason, because I have heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints, <sup>16</sup>I do not cease to give thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers, <sup>17</sup>that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him, <sup>18</sup>having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you, what are the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints, <sup>19</sup>and what is the immeasurable greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of his great might <sup>20</sup>that he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, <sup>21</sup>far above all rule and authority and power and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come. <sup>22</sup>And he put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the church, <sup>23</sup>which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — Every Spiritual Blessing in Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul greets the saints with grace and peace, then blesses God for every spiritual blessing in Christ. Before the world was made, the Father chose his people in Christ to be holy, and in love destined them to be his adopted children, for the praise of his grace given in the Beloved. In Christ they have redemption by his blood and the forgiveness of sins, poured out generously, and God has made known his plan to bring everything in heaven and earth together under Christ. In him believers have received an inheritance by the purpose of the God who works all things by his will: first Jewish believers, then Gentiles who heard the gospel and believed, sealed with the promised Spirit as the guarantee of their inheritance until God’s possession is fully redeemed. Everything leads to the praise of his glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
Election, Grace, and the Glory of God

These twelve verses are the biblical locus classicus of the Reformed doctrine of election. "He chose us in him before the foundation of the world" (v.4) — the election is personal, particular, and prior to anything in us. It is not based on foreseen faith; it is the ground of faith. God chose us before we existed, before we believed, before we had done anything good or bad (Romans 9:11). The choice was made in eternity, rooted in the sovereign good pleasure of his will (v.5), and directed toward the praise of the glory of his grace (v.6).

The purpose of election is not merely the salvation of individuals; it is the display of grace. "So that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus" (2:7). We are saved so that the universe — angels, principalities, and powers — might see what grace looks like. The church is God's exhibit A: the living demonstration that mercy triumphs over judgment, that the undeserving can be made heirs, that the dead can be raised.

John Calvin wrote that the knowledge of election is not given to breed pride or speculation but to ground assurance. The believer who knows they were chosen before the foundation of the world — not because of what they would become but because of God's sovereign love — has a security that no circumstance can shake. This is the pastoral gold of Ephesians 1: your standing before God does not depend on your spiritual performance today. It was settled in eternity, sealed by the Spirit, and guaranteed by the inheritance that awaits.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian Christians lived in the shadow of the great temple of Artemis — one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, a monument to a goddess who offered fertility, protection, and blessing to her devotees. The mystery religions of Ephesus promised spiritual elevation through initiation rites, secret knowledge, and ritual participation. Against all of this, Paul announces something infinitely more magnificent: you already possess every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places — not through ritual, not through initiation, not through any human achievement, but through your union with Christ. You have been chosen, adopted, redeemed, forgiven, enlightened, and sealed. The goddess in the marble temple has nothing to offer you. You are already heirs of the universe.

Now: We live in an age of spiritual seeking. The bookshops are full of self-help and spirituality. People curate their own spiritual experiences, their own moral codes, their own pathways to meaning and blessing. Against all of this noise, Ephesians 1 speaks with clarifying force: every spiritual blessing is in Christ, and in Christ alone. The person who has Christ has everything. The person who lacks Christ lacks everything that ultimately matters, however enriched their life may appear. The church's task is not to offer a slightly better version of what the world already has, but to announce that in Christ, the one thing that actually satisfies every longing of the human heart is freely and fully given.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, to the saints who are in Ephesus, and are faithful in Christ Jesus:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, to the saints who are in Ephesus, and are faithful in Christ Jesus:

Meaning first. Ephesians 1 has two parts. Verses 3–14 are one long outburst of praise, a single sentence in Greek, celebrating every blessing God has given his people in Christ: the Father chose them before creation and adopted them as his children (vv. 4–6); the Son redeemed them by his blood and revealed God’s plan to bring everything together under Christ (vv. 7–12); and the Spirit, received when they believed, seals them as God’s own and guarantees their future inheritance (vv. 13–14). Verses 15–23 turn that praise into prayer: Paul asks God to open their eyes to know him better, to grasp the hope he has called them to, how precious they are to him, and the power at work for them, the same power that raised Christ from the dead and set him above every power in the universe as head over all things for the church. The chapter tells believers who they are and what they have, before the rest of the letter tells them how to live.

Setting and background. Paul writes from prison, probably in Rome about AD 60–62, chained to a soldier (3:1; 4:1; 6:20). Ephesus was the great city of the province of Asia (western Turkey): a busy port, home of the vast temple of the goddess Artemis, one of the seven wonders of the world, and famous for magic and spells (Acts 19:19). Paul had spent nearly three years there (Acts 20:31). Most of the believers were Gentiles who had come out of that world of idols, magic and fear of spiritual powers. Much of the letter answers that fear: Christ is above every power (1:21), and his people are safe in him.

Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus. An apostle (apostolos, one sent) was an official envoy carrying the full authority of the one who sent him. Paul was one of those personally commissioned by the risen Christ to lay the church’s foundation (2:20; Galatians 1:1). His words carry Christ’s authority; that is why this letter is Scripture.

By the will of God. This is not a modest disclaimer; it is the only possible explanation for his being an apostle at all, and we know exactly how it happened. Paul’s apostleship did not begin with a sense of calling or a period of discernment. It began on a road, with letters in his pocket authorising the arrest of Christians, while he was breathing threats and murder against the very people he would spend the rest of his life serving (Acts 9:1–2). He was not recruited from among the interested. He was intercepted mid-crime. That is why he can begin a letter of this size without a trace of hesitation. A man who talked himself into a ministry can be talked out of it. A man who was stopped in the road by the risen Christ cannot. And it sets the tone of everything that follows: in this letter, everything begins with the will of God.

To the saints. English has quietly emptied this word. Say saint today and people picture either an exceptionally good person, or a figure in a stained-glass window, declared holy long after death by a committee that examined the evidence. In both cases the word describes an achievement, and in both cases it belongs to a small minority. Paul uses it (hagioi, holy ones) as the ordinary name for every Christian in the city.

Feel the force of that. Before he finishes this letter he will have to tell some of these same people to stop stealing (4:28), to stop lying to each other (4:25), to deal with their anger before sundown (4:26), and to get rid of bitterness and slander (4:31). These are the saints. The word is not his verdict on how they are getting on; it is his statement of who owns them. “Holy” means set apart, like a vessel in the temple. A temple bowl was not holy because it was beautiful or unusually clean, but because of whose it was and what it was now reserved for. Its holiness was given to it from outside, on the day it was set apart. So it is with you. If you are in Christ, “saint” is not a title you have to earn; it is the name on your post.

And are faithful in Christ Jesus. “Faithful” (pistois) here means believing, trusting: the same people described from another angle, those who trust Christ.

In Christ. The key phrase of Ephesians, used about thirty-five times in different forms (in him, in the Beloved). It means union with Christ: believers are joined to him, so that what is true of him becomes true of them. Every blessing in this chapter comes in him. And notice the two addresses on this one line: the saints who are in Ephesus, faithful in Christ Jesus. A settled identity in Christ, and a difficult postcode on earth, a city built around the temple of Artemis and so given to magic that the converts burned books of spells worth fifty thousand pieces of silver (Acts 19:19). That is the tension every Christian lives in, stated before a single doctrine is taught. Put your own town in place of Ephesus. The letter is written to you at both addresses.

Textual note. Some of the earliest manuscripts (P46, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) omit “in Ephesus”. The letter has no personal greetings, though Paul spent three years there. Verdict: probably a circular letter to the churches of Asia, carried by Tychicus (6:21), with Ephesus as its chief destination. This does not lessen its authority; it widens its reach.

Where Christians differ: did Paul write it? Many modern scholars think a follower wrote it, citing its style and its overlap with Colossians. Verdict: Paul is the author. The letter claims Paul twice (1:1; 3:1), the early church received it without dispute, and its differences fit a letter of praise written at the same time as Colossians.

What it does not mean. Calling every believer a saint does not mean that how we live does not matter. Paul will spend half the letter calling saints to live like saints (4:1). But the order is everything: first who you are, then how to live.

In a sentence. From Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus because God willed it, to God’s holy people in Ephesus, who trust in Christ Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Could you say, without flinching, “I am a saint”? Most of us reach for a softener: well, not really, not like some people. But the flinch is a claim about your record, and the word was never about your record. You are a saint because you are in Christ. Live up to your name.

For worship. Blessed be the God whose will stands at the head of this letter, and of every Christian life. He did not wait for Saul of Tarsus to become suitable; he took a persecutor and made him a herald, and took idol-worshippers in a city of spells and called them his holy ones. Holiness flows from God and not from us: he sets apart, he owns, he names. And all of it is in Christ, in whom the Father has placed his people so securely that his Son’s standing becomes theirs wherever they live. Ephesus or anywhere, the address that counts is in him, and he never moves.
verseByVerse.note: Paul wrote from prison, probably in Rome around AD 60–62. The ESV notes that some early manuscripts omit “in Ephesus”; the letter may have been meant to circulate among several churches of the region.

verseByVerse.quote: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Grace to you. The ordinary Greek greeting at the head of a letter was chairein, greetings. Paul bends it into a word that sounds like it and means far more: charis, grace, God’s free, undeserved favour, kindness given to people who deserve the opposite (2:8–9). It is the source of everything in this letter.

And peace. Eirēnē translates the Hebrew shalom, the Jewish greeting. So the greeting itself is a Greek word and a Jewish word standing together in one breath, which is exactly what Paul will explain in chapter 2, where Christ makes Jew and Gentile one and breaks down the dividing wall (2:14–16). The argument of the letter is being made in its first line.

We have shrunk the word peace. We use it of an atmosphere: a peaceful evening, a quiet room. Shalom is not a mood but wholeness, everything in its right relation and working as it was made to work. That is why a Christian can have it in a hospital bed, and a man can be entirely without it on a beach. The question is not how much pressure is on you, but whether the central relationship of your life is in order. First peace with God, since we were once under his wrath (2:3), and then peace between people once divided (2:14–17).

The order. Always grace first, then peace, in every letter Paul wrote, and never reversed, because one produces the other. Grace is what God does; peace is what results. Many people want the second without the first: the calm, the untroubled conscience, and they would rather reach it by managing their lives well enough to deserve it. It cannot be done in that direction. Peace is the state of a person against whom nothing is any longer held, and only grace can produce that. Having been justified by faith, we have peace with God (Romans 5:1). First the gift, then the quiet.

From God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. One source, two persons. Paul puts Jesus beside the Father as the giver of the gifts only God can give, something no Jew would ever say of a mere man: a quiet witness to Christ’s deity, two verses into the letter. And notice the word our. Paul does not hold himself at a respectful distance from his readers. An apostle and a congregation of former idolaters and thieves address the same Father in the same sentence. Two words in, and the family has already been named.

What it does not mean. Not a polite formula. There is no verb in the Greek: not “I hope you receive”, but simply grace to you and peace. It is closer to a blessing pronounced over them, as Aaron was told to put the LORD’s name on Israel (Numbers 6:24–27).

In a sentence. May God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ give you their undeserved kindness and the peace it brings.

For worship. Before you have done anything today, this is spoken over you: grace, and then peace, from the Father and the Son.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places.

One great sentence. Verses 3–14 are a single sentence in Greek, the longest in the New Testament, written by a man so caught up in praise that he cannot find a place to stop. It is shaped by the Trinity: the Father chooses and adopts (vv. 4–6), the Son redeems (vv. 7–12), the Spirit seals (vv. 13–14). Three times it ends with the same refrain, to the praise of his glory (vv. 6, 12, 14). Verse 3 is the headline; everything after it is the itemised list.

Blessed be God … who has blessed us. To bless (eulogeō, literally to speak well of) means two very different things depending on who is speaking. When we bless God, we cannot add one thing to the one who already holds all good in himself; our blessing can only be praise, the glad acknowledgement of who he is. When God blesses us, his word is never mere breath. For God, to speak good over someone is to do good to them. His blessing does not merely wish us well; it makes us well, giving the very thing it names. It was so from the first page: God blessed them and said, Be fruitful (Genesis 1:28). So the sentence swings on a hinge: we bless God with our lips because he has first blessed us with his hand.

The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is known as the Father of Jesus. We know him truly only through his Son.

Every spiritual blessing. Every: not some, not the ones we have earned, but the whole treasury. A believer is not waiting for some further blessing to make him complete in Christ. And spiritual (pneumatikē) does not mean wispy, private or unreal, the thing a person means when he says he is spiritual but not religious. It means belonging to the Holy Spirit, given and applied by him (the Spirit is named in v. 13). These are not thin blessings as against solid ones. Your salary is temporary and your health is on loan; your adoption is not.

That collides with what “blessed” has come to mean. In common speech a blessing is a circumstance that has gone well: the promotion, the clean scan, the parking space. But run that definition through this letter and it falls apart. The man writing this sentence is under arrest and will die in custody. His readers include slaves, and within a generation some of them will be killed for the name. If blessing meant circumstances going well, Paul would be an unblessed man writing to unblessed people about how blessed they all are. He is not being ironic. Read the list that follows and notice what is not on it. Chosen, adopted, graced, redeemed, forgiven, given wisdom, let into the secret of his will, given an inheritance, sealed with the Spirit. Not one item is a circumstance. Not one can be lost in a redundancy, a diagnosis or a bad year.

In the heavenly places. The phrase (en tois epouraniois) appears five times in Ephesians and nowhere else in Paul, and the five uses explain it. It cannot simply mean heaven as the home of the redeemed, because in 6:12 Paul places the spiritual forces of evil there, and there are no demons in paradise. It means the unseen realm of spiritual reality, where God, Christ, the angels and the hostile powers all act, lying not far above us but immediately behind everything we can see. Read the five in order and they make an argument. Every spiritual blessing is there (1:3): that is where the treasury is kept. Christ is seated there, far above every power (1:20): that is where the throne is. You are seated there with him (2:6): that is where your position is. God’s wisdom is displayed there to the rulers and authorities (3:10): that is who is watching. And your real struggle is there (6:12): that is where the battle is. Treasury, throne, seat, audience, battlefield: five things that shape your life, all in a realm you have never seen.

For the Ephesians, people who had spent their lives and money trying to manage unseen powers with amulets and spells, this was not an abstraction. Paul does not tell them the unseen world is imaginary. He tells them who is enthroned there, that every power is under his feet, and that they themselves are seated with him above everything they used to fear. And having taken us into the heavenly places, he ends the letter with telling the truth, honest work, and not exasperating your children. The most cosmic letter in the New Testament ends in the kitchen. Knowing where the throne is does not lift you out of your Tuesday; it tells you who is over it.

In Christ. Every blessing comes only in union with him. Outside Christ, none; in Christ, all.

Has blessed. Past tense (eulogēsas): already given, done, with nothing outstanding. Much is still to be enjoyed in full (vv. 14, 18), but it is already ours. So the prayer “Lord, bless me”, offered as though the cupboard were bare and might be filled if we are earnest enough, misunderstands where we are standing. The Christian is not a beggar hoping the door will open. He is an heir who has not yet read the inventory. Your problem this morning is almost certainly not that God has withheld something. It is that you do not know what you already have. Paul opens the inventory in the next eleven verses so that nobody has to wonder.

What it does not mean. Not a promise of earthly comfort, health or wealth. Paul writes this in chains. And not that the blessings are vague: the Spirit is not only the one who delivers them, he is himself the down payment of them (v. 14). The Giver has moved in with the gift.

In a sentence. Praise the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who, by joining us to Christ, has already given us every blessing his Spirit brings, kept safe where Christ reigns.

On a Tuesday. When someone asks how you are on a bad day, you may say honestly that the day is hard, and that you are blessed. Both are true, and the second is the deeper one.

For worship. The God who needs nothing has emptied his treasury into your hands in Christ. Blessed be the God who has blessed you.
verseByVerse.note: Verses 3–14 are a single long sentence of praise in the Greek. “The heavenly places” is the unseen realm where Christ reigns.

verseByVerse.quote: Even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him.

Even as he chose us. “Even as” (kathōs, just as, because) ties this verse to the last: here is the first blessing, and it explains all the others. They come to us because God chose us. “Chose” (exelexato, picked out for himself) is in the middle voice: God chose for his own sake, to be his. This is election, God’s free decision to save particular people, and it is personal: us.

In him. Election is never apart from Christ. Christ is himself the Chosen One: behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights (Isaiah 42:1). God chose a people in his Son, as their head and Saviour, so that his standing becomes theirs. That changes where you must look for assurance. The question “am I chosen?” is not answered by peering back into eternity, where you were never invited and cannot see. It is answered by looking at Christ: all whom the Father gives him will come to him, and whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37).

Before the foundation of the world. Stand where the verse puts you. Before the light was made. Before there was anything to look at, and ages before there was a you to inspect. That settles what God’s love could have been based on, because at the moment it was set on you there was nothing about you to see: no faith yet, no obedience, no promise of improvement, not even existence (Romans 9:11; 2 Timothy 1:9). And that is the most secure thing that could be said about it. A love that began before you were anything cannot be ended by your turning out to be something disappointing. Your worst week did not alter the basis of it, because the basis was never you. God’s love for his people is older than the universe.

That we should be holy and blameless before him. “Holy” (hagious): set apart for God and pure. “Blameless” (amōmous): without blemish, the word for a sacrifice fit to be offered. This is the purpose of election: God chose us for holiness, not because of it. Does Paul mean sinless perfection? Many read these words and feel condemned instead of called. He means two things at once. Now, in Christ, you are already counted holy and blameless in God’s sight, not on your record but clothed in Christ’s (Colossians 1:22). And one day God will finish what he began, presenting you without fault before his glory (5:27; Jude 24). The standing gives you your footing: God sees me in Christ; I am not disqualified. The goal gives you your direction: this is where he is taking me; I am not finished. So the believer who sinned badly this week does not come back to God with a smaller holiness, because it was never measured by this week. That is not permission to sin (Romans 6:1–2); it is the mercy that makes repentance possible.

Where Christians differ: why did God choose? Arminians hold that God chose those he foresaw would believe (citing Romans 8:29; 1 Peter 1:2). Verdict: unconditional election (Westminster Confession 3.5). Paul roots the choice in God’s love, will and purpose (vv. 5, 9, 11), never in anything foreseen in us; and he says we were chosen to be holy, which would make no sense if God chose us because he foresaw our holiness. Faith is the result of election (Acts 13:48), not its cause. Is it unfair? The question assumes we were owed a choosing, and we were not. Left to justice, every one of us would be passed by (Romans 3:23). The wonder of this verse is not that some are not chosen, but that any are: that grace should reach into a mass of the justly condemned and lift out a people who deserved what the rest received. No one perishes who wanted Christ and was refused.

Where Christians differ: chosen as individuals, or as a group? Some (following Karl Barth, and some Arminian scholars) hold that God chose Christ, and that the church is elect only as a group, in him; individuals become elect when they join themselves to Christ by faith. Verdict: God did choose a people, the church, and he chose them in Christ; but the people are made up of persons. Paul says he chose us, and v. 5 says he predestined us for adoption, which is personal. Elsewhere election is clearly of individuals: Jacob, not Esau (Romans 9:11–13); names written in the book of life (Revelation 13:8). The corporate and the personal belong together.

Common questions. If God has chosen, why preach the gospel? Because God chose the means as well as the end: the chosen come to faith through hearing the gospel (v. 13; Romans 10:14). Far from killing mission, election is the reason it cannot fail. To a discouraged evangelist in a hostile city the Lord said, I have many in this city who are my people (Acts 18:9–10). We preach to all, freely and urgently, because he has a people to gather, and not one will be missed. What about my own choice? Scripture holds both truths, and so must we. The same letter that says you were chosen before the world began pleads with you to walk worthy of your calling (4:1). You heard and believed, and your believing was truly your own (v. 13); God’s sovereignty runs underneath your choice, not instead of it. Where the two meet is a depth we are not given to sound (Deuteronomy 29:29; Romans 9:20). How can I know I am chosen? Not by looking for a secret sign, but by trusting Christ and seeing the fruit of holiness he produces (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5; 2 Peter 1:10).

Is there any point praying for my unbelieving son or daughter, if God has already chosen? Yes, every point. The God who chose the end also chose the means, and prayer is one of them. No one believed in election more firmly than Paul, and he wrote that his heart’s desire and prayer to God was for his unbelieving people to be saved (Romans 10:1). Election does not make your prayers pointless; it makes them hopeful, because you are not asking God to overcome a will he cannot reach. You are asking the God who raises the dead (2:5) to do the very thing he delights to do. You do not know who is chosen, and you are not meant to. So pray by name, keep loving, keep speaking of Christ, and leave the timing with him. Augustine’s mother prayed for him for years before he was converted.

Textual note. “In love” may end verse 4 (holy and blameless in love) or begin verse 5 (in love he predestined us). The ESV links it with verse 5, which fits Paul’s stress on God’s motive.

What it does not mean. Not fatalism, as if it does not matter what we do. Nor a reason for pride: election leaves no room for boasting (2:9). And it is not given to make anyone anxious. Scripture teaches it to comfort believers that their salvation rests on God, not on themselves.

In a sentence. For before the world was made, God chose us to belong to Christ, so that we would stand before him holy and without fault.

On a Tuesday. If you sinned badly this week, you are not less chosen. You can come back without first making yourself presentable, because Christ has already made you so. Repent, and go on in the holiness you were chosen for.

For worship. Before there was a sun to rise or a world to rule, the Father had set his heart on a people and given them to his Son. Election is not a cold decree; it is the Father’s free delight, resting on nothing in us and everything in Christ. And it has a face: the Chosen One, in whom the Father is well pleased and in whom we are found. Praise the God who did not discover his people but decided them, and who will present them holy and blameless because he purposed it before the foundations were laid. What he began in eternity, he does not abandon in time.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “in love” may go with verse 4: “holy and blameless before him in love.”

verseByVerse.quote: In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will.

In love. The motive behind election is not cold decree but love (see the textual note on v. 4). Predestination is the Father’s affectionate purpose to have children, and the warmth of the next word confirms it.

He predestined us. “Predestined” (proorisas, marked out beforehand, set a boundary in advance; our word horizon comes from the same root). Election (v. 4) is God choosing whom; predestination is God deciding what he would make of them, and here Paul names it: his children. In Scripture, predestination is almost always spoken of to comfort believers about their destiny, not to make them speculate about others.

Did God also predestine some people to hell? Scripture speaks of the two very differently, and so must we. Those God saves, he actively chose, predestined and brought to life; their salvation is entirely his work. Those who are lost, God passed by, leaving them in the sin they love, and they are condemned for their sin, never for want of being chosen (Westminster 3.7). No one in hell will be able to say that he wanted Christ and was kept from him. Paul marks the difference even in his wording: God himself prepared the vessels of mercy beforehand for glory, while the vessels of wrath are simply said to be prepared for destruction (Romans 9:22–23). God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11), and the gospel is offered freely to all. The question for you is not what God decreed about others, but whether you will come to Christ today.

For adoption to himself as sons. “Adoption” (huiothesia, placing as a son) was a Roman legal act. An adopted son received a new father and a new name, had his old debts cancelled, and gained full rights of inheritance, equal to a natural son; the adoption could not be undone, and the past could not reclaim him. Wealthy Romans adopted adult heirs to carry their name. We were by nature children of wrath (2:3), outsiders; God brings us into his family as heirs (Galatians 4:4–7; Romans 8:15–17). And notice: to himself. Not merely to a status, but to belong to him.

Why adoption, and not only forgiveness? God could have pardoned us and left us as forgiven servants, standing at the kitchen door. Instead he makes us his children, seated at his table. Forgiveness deals with our guilt; adoption gives us a Father, a family, a home and an inheritance. The Westminster Shorter Catechism (Q. 34) calls it an act of God’s free grace, whereby we are received into the number, and have a right to all the privileges, of the sons of God. The Judge who acquits us steps down from the bench and takes us home.

As sons. In that world sons inherited. The word includes daughters: every believer, man or woman, receives the full inheritance of a son (Galatians 3:26–28).

Through Jesus Christ. God has one eternal Son by nature; we become children by grace, through union with him. We share his sonship as we share his life.

According to the purpose of his will. Literally the good pleasure (eudokian) of his will. God delighted to do it. It was not reluctant; it made him glad. Nothing outside God moved him to it, and that is exactly why it is permanent. A choice that rested on something in us could be undone by something in us. This rests on his good pleasure alone.

What it does not mean. Not that all people are God’s children in this sense. All are his creatures and his offspring as their Creator (Acts 17:28), but adoption comes through Christ, received by faith (John 1:12).

In a sentence. In love he decided beforehand that, through Jesus Christ, we would be adopted as his own children, because this was what he gladly willed.

For worship. The God who owes you nothing has given you his name, his table and his inheritance, and he was glad to do it. When you say Our Father today, remember what it cost to make it true.
verseByVerse.note: In Roman law an adopted son received the full rights and inheritance of a natural son.

verseByVerse.quote: To the praise of his glorious grace, with which he has blessed us in the Beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the praise of his glorious grace, with which he has blessed us in the Beloved.

To the praise of his glorious grace. The first of three refrains (vv. 6, 12, 14), each closing the work of one person of the Trinity. Salvation has a goal beyond the saved: that God’s grace be seen and celebrated. “Glory” (doxa) is God’s weight, his splendour made visible, and his grace is glorious because it shows how great and good he is.

Is that not vanity? A modern reader feels the question even if he never asks it aloud. We do not admire a man who arranges every conversation to end in applause for himself. Why is it admirable in God? C. S. Lewis was troubled by exactly this, and what opened it for him was noticing what praise actually is. We spontaneously praise whatever we enjoy, a piece of music, a landscape, a friend’s cooking, not because we have been asked to, but because delight overflows into speech. The enjoyment is not complete until it is spoken: the finest view is only half enjoyed until you say to someone, look at that. Praise is not payment extracted from us; it is enjoyment reaching its full form. Now put that together with who God is. If there is a being of infinite goodness, then calling creatures to praise him is not vanity but honesty, telling them the truth about the most valuable thing there is. And it is kindness, because it points them to their own deepest joy. A father who tells his son to come and look at the sunrise is not fishing for compliments on his taste. He wants the boy to see it.

With which he has blessed us. Literally which he graced us with (echaritōsen, a verb made from the word grace). It appears only once elsewhere in the New Testament. The angel Gabriel says it to a girl in Nazareth: greetings, O favoured one (Luke 1:28). She had done nothing to deserve it; she was simply the object of God’s free favour, and the whole course of her life ran from that word. That is the verb Paul now uses of ordinary believers in Ephesus: dockworkers, slaves, tradesmen. Whatever was true of Mary in being singled out by sheer favour is true of you.

In the Beloved. Paul could have said “in Christ” again. He chooses instead the title the Father spoke from heaven over his Son: this is my beloved Son (Matthew 3:17). That means the love that falls on you is not a second-class affection God worked up for sinners as a separate exercise. You are inside the Beloved, and so the love that has always passed between the Father and the Son runs over you too. It is exactly what Jesus prayed on the last night: that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me (John 17:23). Read that slowly. Not somewhat as you loved me. Even as.

What it does not mean. Not that God saved us because he needed praise. He lacks nothing (Acts 17:25). He shows his grace because it is good, and we flourish by seeing and enjoying it. His glory and our joy are not rivals.

In a sentence. He did this so that his glorious grace would be praised, the grace he freely gave us by uniting us to his beloved Son.

For worship. The Father loves you with the love he has for his Son, because you are in the Son. Even as. Praise the glorious grace that put you there.
verseByVerse.note: “The Beloved” is Christ, echoing the Father’s voice at his baptism.

verseByVerse.quote: In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace.

In him we have. Present tense: a possession now, held on the worst day of your life as securely as on the best.

Redemption. “Redemption” (apolytrōsis, release by payment of a ransom) is the language of the slave market and of the exodus, and both pictures should be seen, not only named. Stand in the slave market. A man is on the block, and whatever he was before, today he is property. He cannot buy himself, because he does not own himself. Then someone else comes with the price, pays it in full, and the man walks out with nothing to repay, having contributed nothing but his chains. Now stand in Egypt on the last night. A household is under sentence, and what stands between them and the destroyer is not their character, their record or their remorse. It is blood on a doorpost (Exodus 12). In both scenes the freedom is real, it is total, and it is entirely someone else’s doing. We were slaves to sin and under its penalty (2:1–3); Christ bought our freedom.

Through his blood. “Blood” means his life given in a violent, sacrificial death (Leviticus 17:11). The price was not silver or gold, but the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish (1 Peter 1:18–19).

Why blood? Why can God not simply forgive? To a modern ear blood sounds primitive, and the question underneath is fair: he tells us to forgive freely; why does he require a death before he does it himself? The answer is that nobody ever forgives a real wrong without cost. Suppose someone smashes something of yours. There are only two possibilities. He pays, and then nothing has been forgiven; it has been settled. Or you forgive him, which means you absorb the loss: the thing stays broken and you carry it. There is no third option in which the damage simply evaporates. That is why forgiving a real injury hurts, and why we find it so hard: to forgive is to agree to bear the cost yourself instead of taking it from the one who caused it. So when God forgives, he is not shrugging off a small debt. Real wrong has been done to a holy God by every one of us, and it has to go somewhere. A God who ignored it would not be gracious but indifferent, and a judge who dismissed every case would not be loving but corrupt. What this verse says is that God did what every true forgiver does, at a scale beyond measuring: he absorbed it himself. The blood is the measure of what it cost him.

The forgiveness of our trespasses. “Forgiveness” (aphesis, release, sending away). “Trespasses” (paraptōmatōn, false steps, crossing God’s boundaries). Not sin in the abstract, but actual missteps, plural and particular. God did not issue a vague general amnesty. The account that was cancelled had your name at the top and your own specific items listed beneath it, including the one you have never told anyone, and the one you did again last week. Those. Paid for, by blood, and gone.

If I am forgiven, why do I still feel guilty? Because feelings are slow to catch up with facts, and because you have an accuser who works on them (Revelation 12:10). First, ask whether the guilt is pointing at something specific you have not yet brought to God or put right with someone. If so, confess it plainly, and where you have wronged a person, go to them; God is faithful and just to forgive those who confess (1 John 1:9). If the sin is already confessed, the guilt is not God’s voice but an echo, and the answer is not more penance but the cross. There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). Tell yourself what is true: Christ died for that sin, God has sent it away, and he does not bring it up again. If the feeling will not lift, talk to your pastor. Sometimes the gospel needs a friend to say it aloud.

Where Christians differ: how does the cross save? Some modern writers deny that Christ’s death was a substitute bearing our penalty, seeing it only as an example of love or a victory over evil. Verdict: penal substitution is central to the atonement: Christ bore the punishment our sins deserved, in our place. Scripture joins blood, redemption and forgiveness: a price paid, a penalty borne (Romans 3:24–25; Galatians 3:13; Hebrews 9:22). His victory over evil (Colossians 2:15) and his example of love (5:2) belong with it, not instead of it.

According to the riches of his grace. Not measured by our need but by his wealth: not the minimum, not the barely adequate, but proportioned to the riches of God himself. No sin is too great for riches like these.

What it does not mean. Not that the ransom was paid to Satan, as some early writers suggested. It satisfied the justice of God himself, who in love provided the payment (Romans 3:25–26).

In a sentence. In Christ we have been set free at the cost of his blood, and our sins are forgiven, as fully as God’s rich grace can forgive.

On a Tuesday. This is the pattern the letter will ask of you: forgive as God in Christ forgave you (4:32), which means bearing the cost of a wrong instead of passing it on. Is there a debt someone owes you that you could carry today?

For worship. Name a sin you have been forgiven, and thank him for the blood that paid for it. It is gone, and it is not coming back.
verseByVerse.note: Redemption was the word for buying a slave’s freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: Which he lavished upon us, in all wisdom and insight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which he lavished upon us, in all wisdom and insight.

Which he lavished upon us. “Lavished” (eperisseusen, made it overflow, more than enough). God did not measure out grace carefully, exactly what was sufficient. He poured. Grace is not rationed.

In all wisdom and insight. The two words are not the same. “Wisdom” (sophia) is the deep grasp of how things truly are, of God and his purposes. “Insight” (phronēsis) is its practical cousin: discernment, the working out of that grasp in real decisions. One sees; the other knows what to do on Monday morning.

Whose wisdom? It may describe God’s wisdom in planning salvation, or the wisdom he gives us to understand it. Probably the second. The nearest parallel prays that believers may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding (Colossians 1:9); Paul prays for this very wisdom a few verses later (v. 17); and the sentence runs straight on, making known to us the mystery of his will (v. 9). A mystery cannot be made known to someone who has not been given the eyes to receive it. Nothing is lost if a reader takes it the other way, for God’s plan is supremely wise (3:10). But the point is this: the grace that saves you does not rescue you and then leave you baffled about what has happened. He gives the gift, and then he gives the eyes to see the gift. That is why this letter can spend three chapters on the eternal purposes of God and still expect slaves and dockworkers in Ephesus to follow every word.

In a sentence. He poured this grace out on us in abundance, and with it gave us wisdom and understanding.

On a Tuesday. Ask God for wisdom when you open Scripture. He gives generously to all without reproach (James 1:5).

For worship. How like God to pour where we would have measured. The grace that forgave us at the cost of the Son’s blood (1:7) did not stop at pardon; it overflowed into understanding, as if the Father could not bear for his children to be rescued and remain bewildered. He is a God who explains himself to beggars. The wisdom that planned redemption before the ages now stoops to open the eyes of slaves and dockworkers, so that the saved may see their Saviour and adore him. Every glimmer of light you have ever had on his word was one more drop of that lavish grace.

verseByVerse.quote: making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ as a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ as a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth in him.

Making known. God has told us what he is doing; it is not hidden from his people.

The mystery of his will. In Paul a mystery (mystērion) is not a puzzle or something unknowable, but a truth once hidden in God and now revealed (3:3–6; Romans 16:25–26). The Old Testament gave hints; in Christ the plan is laid open.

According to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ. Christ is the centre of God’s plan from the beginning. History is not a series of accidents with Christ added at some point; it was planned around him.

As a plan for the fullness of time. “Plan” (oikonomia, the management of a household; our word economy comes from it): God administers history like a wise steward running an estate. “The fullness of time” is the moment history reaches its goal. It began with Christ’s coming (Galatians 4:4) and will be completed at his return.

To unite all things in him. One towering Greek verb (anakephalaiōsasthai): to sum up, to bring together under one head. An ancient writer added a column of figures and put the total at the top. Christ is the sum and head of everything. Sin broke the universe apart: people from God, people from each other (Jews and Gentiles in chapter 2), creation into frustration (Romans 8:20–22), spiritual powers into rebellion. God’s plan, purposed before creation, is to bring it all back into order and harmony under its true head. And Paul says all things (ta panta), not only all people. Salvation is bigger than the rescue of individual souls out of a ruined world; it is the restoration of everything to its right relation with Christ. The material creation is not discarded but renewed (Revelation 21:1–5).

What would it look like? Let it come down to the ground. A world under one head is a world where the ground no longer throws up thorns and the body no longer grows tumours; where there are no funerals, because there is nothing left to bury. A world with no armies, because there is nothing left to defend against; where families are not quietly divided by something said twenty years ago. A world in which you are no longer divided against yourself, where the person you want to be and the person you are have at last become the same (Romans 7:19). And a world where heaven and earth are no longer two addresses. Now we pray, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven (Matthew 6:10), a prayer that admits a gap. Then the gap closes: behold, the dwelling place of God is with man (Revelation 21:3). And nothing good is lost on the way: the glory and honour of the nations are brought into it (Revelation 21:24–26). Everything you have ever loved is kept; everything that spoiled it is gone. That homesickness you feel under the best music and the worst news, for a world that holds together, is not a defect in you. It is the memory of what the world was made for, and Paul gives it a name: not a system or a golden age, but a Person, under whom everything finally fits.

Already, and not yet. Already, Christ has been raised and seated above every power (1:20–22), and the powers were disarmed at the cross (Colossians 2:15). The gathering has begun, and it has a visible address. When a Jew and a Gentile sat down at one table in Ephesus, that was not good community relations; it was the future arriving early (2:14–16; 3:10). Not yet: at present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see him, Jesus (Hebrews 2:8–9). That is the honest Christian position, and it is enough to go on with.

Things in heaven and things on earth. The whole created order, seen and unseen. The uniting is not an end in itself. The fall was at root a dishonouring of God, creatures setting up rival thrones in their Maker’s world. The summing up of all things under Christ ends every rival throne, until every knee bows and every tongue confesses that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:10–11). That is why the refrain keeps returning: to the praise of his glory.

How this shapes the letter. Chapter 2 shows it happening now: Jews and Gentiles made one in Christ. Chapter 3 says the church displays it to the heavenly powers (3:10). Chapter 4 calls the church to live in that unity.

Where Christians differ: will everyone and everything finally be saved? Some, from Origen in the third century to modern universalists, read uniting all things as a promise that every person, and even the devil and fallen angels, will finally be reconciled to God. Verdict: no. To unite under one head means to bring everything under Christ’s rule, not that everything will be saved. In the same letter Paul warns that the immoral have no inheritance in the kingdom and that God’s wrath comes on the disobedient (5:5–6). Some will bow in joyful worship, and others in defeat (1 Corinthians 15:24–28; Philippians 2:10–11). Everything will be put in order; not everything will be saved.

In a sentence. He has let us in on the secret of his plan, which he purposed in Christ to carry out when history reaches its goal: to bring everything in heaven and on earth together under Christ as its one head.

On a Tuesday. Your fractured world, family, nation or church, has a future in Christ. Every genuine reconciliation you work for now is a small patch of that future showing through.

For worship. Here is the end of all things, and it is a Person. The Father has not made Christ one part of his plan; he has made him its centre, its head and its sum. Every broken thing in heaven and on earth is heading home to him, and every rival throne will fall before his. What a Saviour, that the universe should find its meaning in the one who was crucified outside a city wall. And what a God, that he should tell us his secret, letting sinners in on the purpose of the ages before it is complete, so that we may begin the praise now that creation will one day sing together.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

verseByVerse.quote: In him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we who were the first to hope in Christ might be to the praise of his glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we who were the first to hope in Christ might be to the praise of his glory.

In him we have obtained an inheritance. Everything in this sentence has hung on two small words: in him. Chosen in him (v. 4), adopted through him (v. 5), graced in the Beloved (v. 6), redeemed in him (v. 7), and now given an inheritance in him. “Obtained an inheritance” (eklērōthēmen, were allotted a share) recalls the land being divided by lot among Israel’s tribes (Joshua 14:1–2). The Greek can mean we were given an inheritance, or we were made God’s inheritance. Both are true (v. 18; Deuteronomy 32:9).

God himself is the portion. Picture the day the land was divided. The other tribes walk away holding a map: this valley, that ridge, the olive terraces, the well. Levi is handed nothing. No acres, no boundary stones, no deed. To any watching eye the priestly tribe has been cheated, and then God says the sentence that explains everything: I am your portion and your inheritance among the people of Israel (Numbers 18:20). The other tribes were given things God had made. Levi was given God. Test it on yourself. Suppose you were given everything you have ever wanted, your health back, every broken relationship mended, the people you have buried returned, and God himself were not there. Would that be heaven? Every Christian who thinks honestly knows the answer is no. Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you (Psalm 73:25). And if you had him and nothing else, you would still be rich. Everything else you own can be taken by a diagnosis, a market, a war, or simply time. A portion that is God cannot be repossessed.

And the glory to come. The inheritance is also given real content in Scripture, and it should not be left vague. A body, raised imperishable and made like his glorious body (1 Corinthians 15:42–44; Philippians 3:21). A world: new heavens and a new earth, which the meek will inherit (Matthew 5:5; Revelation 21:1–5). A face: they will see his face (Revelation 22:4), the one thing Moses asked for and was not given. A likeness: we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). And the measure of it all: we are heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17). Not a small plot at the edge of the estate. Whatever belongs to the Son is being settled on you.

Having been predestined. As in v. 5: decided beforehand by God. Note the tense of the main verb again: we have obtained. The allotment is already made and the deed already signed in the blood of the Son; only the delivery is outstanding.

According to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will. “Works” (energountos, is actively at work in, carries out). “All things” (ta panta): not some things, not most, but all. “Counsel” (boulēn, deliberate decision). God is not reacting to history; he is carrying it out, every event, according to his own wise decision (Romans 8:28; Proverbs 16:33). And the God who works all things is the God who has promised you the inheritance. He is the executor of the will. It will be delivered.

Where Christians differ: does God govern all things, or only some? Many Christians hold that God sets the overall direction of history but leaves most events to human free choices, which he foresees and responds to. Open theists go further and say God does not know free choices in advance. Verdict: Paul says God works all things according to his will: not most things, not the big things only. Scripture shows God governing the fall of a sparrow (Matthew 10:29), the roll of dice (Proverbs 16:33), the decisions of kings (Proverbs 21:1) and even the wicked acts that crucified Christ (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). This does not make human choices unreal. Joseph’s brothers chose freely and sinned, and God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). God works through our choices, not around them; how both are true is beyond us, but Scripture teaches both, and the cross proves them both at once. It is the deepest comfort a believer has: nothing in your life is outside his purpose.

We who were the first to hope in Christ. “First to hope” (proēlpikotas, hoped beforehand). Probably Jewish believers, Paul included, who had hoped for the Messiah and believed in Jesus first; verse 13 then turns to you also, the Gentiles, and the two are brought together in one people (2:11–22). Some take it as all believers, who hope now before Christ’s return; but the switch from “we” to “you” in v. 13 favours the first reading.

To the praise of his glory. The second refrain.

What it does not mean. Not that God is the author of sin. He governs evil without doing evil or approving it, and turns it to good, as at the cross (Genesis 50:20; Acts 2:23). Every person remains responsible for what he chooses (James 1:13).

In a sentence. In Christ we too were given a share in God’s inheritance, as God decided beforehand, the God who carries out everything according to his own will, so that we Jewish believers, who were the first to put our hope in Christ, might bring praise to his glory.

On a Tuesday. Whatever happens today, the God who works all things is working in it, for his glory and your good. The poorest believer reading this is, at this moment, an heir of God.

For worship. The God who works all things is not a distant clerk of history but a Father settling an estate on his children, and the estate is himself. Every event bends to his counsel; nothing slips through his hands, not even the sins that nailed his Son to a cross. That is his glory: he rules without rival and turns the worst of human choices into the means of grace. Praise him that the inheritance was secured by Christ, the true Heir, who shares with his brothers what is his by right, so that his people exist, now and for ever, to the praise of his glory.

verseByVerse.quote: In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it, to the praise of his glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it, to the praise of his glory.

In him you also. Now the Gentiles. You who were outsiders share fully in everything just described: the same election, the same redemption, the same seal (2:11–22).

When you heard … and believed. This is how God’s eternal choice becomes real in history: through ordinary preaching and real faith (Romans 10:14–17). Election never bypasses the gospel; it works through it. You heard, you believed, you were sealed: one moment, not three stages.

The word of truth, the gospel of your salvation. The gospel is true and it saves. “Gospel” (euangelion) means good news: the announcement of what God has done in Christ.

Were sealed. Put the word back on the dock at Ephesus. A merchant’s cargo is loaded and bound, and before the ship sails he presses his signet ring into hot wax across the bindings (esphragisthēte, sealed). Every man on that quay could read what the mark meant, and it said three things at once. This is mine: ownership, hands off. This is genuine: the real consignment, not a substitute swapped in on the way. And this is protected: the cargo now crosses hostile water, and to break that seal is not to quarrel with a crate but to answer to the man whose ring made the mark. Now hear what God has stamped on you. Not wax, and not a certificate. The seal is a Person. God’s answer to the question of whether you will arrive is to place himself on you (4:30).

With the promised Holy Spirit. Promised by the prophets (Ezekiel 36:26–27; Joel 2:28) and by Jesus (Acts 1:4–5).

Who is the guarantee of our inheritance. “Guarantee” (arrabōn) was a business word: a down payment, the first instalment that legally commits the giver to pay the rest. In modern Greek the word means an engagement ring. And a deposit is not a sample of some different substance; it is the first portion of the very same thing. So what you have of the Spirit now is not a lesser thing than heaven. It is heaven’s first payment, in heaven’s own currency. That peace that came when nothing in your circumstances explained it; the joy that caught you in a hymn; the love you find you have for people you would never have chosen: that is not preparation for the inheritance. It is the inheritance, in instalments. And it explains why the Christian life feels the way it does. You hold the deposit, not the estate, so the ache is not a sign that something has gone wrong. The deposit was designed to make you homesick. A man with an engagement ring is not less eager for the wedding than a man without one; he is far more eager, and far more certain.

Until we acquire possession of it. Literally until the redemption of the possession: until God fully takes possession of his people at the resurrection, and they possess their inheritance. And note who would lose if that day never came: the one who paid the deposit. God has put down a pledge he does not intend to forfeit.

To the praise of his glory. The third refrain closes the great sentence. Three times, each after a different Person has done his work: the Father choosing, the Son redeeming, the Spirit sealing. One salvation, three hands, one refrain.

Where Christians differ: when are believers sealed? Some Pentecostal teaching, and some Reformed writers such as Martyn Lloyd-Jones, treat the sealing as a further experience after conversion, an overwhelming assurance to be sought. They read it out of a real hunger for more of God, which is nothing to despise. Verdict: the text ties it to believing: having heard and believed, you were sealed. The Greek participle describes what happened together with believing, not a later stage. Every believer is sealed with the Spirit at conversion (Romans 8:9). Believers may still seek to be filled afresh (5:18), and God may give special seasons of assurance; but no Christian is unsealed. You can check it, not by hunting for a feeling, but by looking for the marks the Spirit leaves: that you call God Father and mean it (Romans 8:15–16), that sin now grieves you, that Christ has become precious to you and not merely true.

Where Christians differ: can a sealed believer be lost? Those who hold that true believers can finally fall away read the seal as a mark that can be broken, and point to the warnings of Hebrews (Hebrews 6:4–6). Those warnings are real and must be heard. Verdict: the seal is God’s, set until the day of redemption (4:30), and the guarantee pledges the full inheritance. A pledge God gives is not withdrawn. Jesus says of his sheep, they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28). Those who abandon Christ show they were never truly his (1 John 2:19); the warnings are among the means God uses to keep the people he has sealed.

What it does not mean. Not that the seal depends on feeling the Spirit. It is God’s act, whether felt strongly or not.

In a sentence. And you Gentiles too, when you heard the true message, the good news that saves you, and believed in Christ, were marked as God’s own with the Holy Spirit he had promised, who is the down payment guaranteeing our full inheritance until God completes the redemption of his people, so that his glory is praised.

For worship. God has not handed you a receipt for the inheritance and left you to wait. He has given you the first instalment of it, and the first instalment is himself.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership and security. The “guarantee” was a first instalment, pledging full payment later.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Having heard of their faith and love, Paul never stops thanking God for them and praying that the Father of glory will give them the Spirit of wisdom and revelation to know him better. He prays that the eyes of their hearts will be opened to grasp the hope of God’s call, the wealth of his inheritance in his people, and the vast power at work for believers. That power is the strength God exerted when he raised Christ from the dead and seated him at his right hand, above every ruler and name in this age and the next, putting all things under his feet and giving him as head over all things to the church, his body, the fullness of the one who fills everything.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit of Wisdom and Revelation

Paul prays for "the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him" (v.17). This single phrase encapsulates the Reformed understanding of how divine truth moves from the page to the heart. The Spirit who inspired the Scripture is also required to illuminate the reader of Scripture. Without the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit, the words of God remain external — true, but not transforming; known about, but not known. Calvin devoted a famous section of the Institutes to this: the Scripture needs no external proof of its authority, because the Spirit who produced it also produces the certainty of it in the heart of the believer.

The practical implication is that Bible reading and prayer are inseparable disciplines. To open the Scripture without asking the Spirit to open our eyes to it is to work without our most essential tool. The Puritans understood this, and habitually prayed for illumination before they opened the book. The eyes of the heart do not open themselves. This prayer of Paul's is therefore not only a prayer about the Ephesians — it is a prayer for every reader of Scripture in every age who wants not merely to know about God but to know God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul writes this prayer from prison. He cannot visit the Ephesians; he cannot lay hands on them; he cannot preach to them in person. What he can do is pray — and his prayer from chains is not for his own release but for their illumination. This is one of the most searching things in the letter: the imprisoned apostle, whose situation would seem to give him every right to focus on his own needs, pours his intercession entirely outward, toward the people he loves. His joy is in their knowledge of Christ, not in his own circumstances. This is the mind of Christ (Philippians 2:5) applied to prayer.

Now: We live in an age of unprecedented access to biblical content. More sermons, commentaries, podcasts, and Bible apps exist today than at any point in history. And yet spiritual blindness remains our greatest problem. We have more information about God than any previous generation, and arguably less experiential knowledge of him. Paul's prayer cuts through all of this: what we need is not more content but opened eyes — the Spirit of wisdom and revelation, granting us not information but encounter. The Ephesians had Paul's letter. We have the whole Bible. Both of us need the same thing: the Spirit who makes the word alive.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason, because I have heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints, I do not cease to give thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this reason, because I have heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints, I do not cease to give thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers,

For this reason. Because of everything in vv. 3–14. The man who has just spent twelve verses gazing at the riches of grace can do nothing else but fall to his knees. Doctrine leads to prayer. Knowing God’s purposes does not make prayer unnecessary; it gives prayer its confidence.

Because I have heard. Stand where Paul is standing as he writes. He is in Rome under guard, probably chained to a soldier (Acts 28:16, 20). He has no freedom to travel, no money to send, no way to step in and sort anything out in Ephesus, and a real possibility that he will never see these people again. Someone has come up the road with a report about them. He cannot get to them. So he does the only thing left to him, and it turns out to be the greatest thing one person can do for another: he carries them to God. Prison did not reduce his ministry to prayer. Prison showed that prayer had always been the larger half of it. And notice how he knows anything at all: someone talked. A traveller mentioned a church where people believed in Jesus and looked after each other, and the news reached a cell in Rome. Your quiet faith is being reported somewhere too, usually to people you will never meet.

Your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints. The two marks of genuine Christianity, always together: trust towards Christ and love towards his people. Faith looks up to Christ; love looks sideways at the people he died for and calls them family (Galatians 5:6; 1 John 3:14). And do not slide past the word all. Ephesus was a room containing Jews and Gentiles together, people raised to regard each other as unclean, who now passed the same cup. This is not warmth towards the agreeable. It is love towards the whole awkward set of them, the ones you would cross the street to avoid included, which is the only kind of love that proves anything.

Textual note. Some early manuscripts omit “your love”, reading “faith … toward all the saints”. The longer text is probably original (compare Colossians 1:4).

I do not cease to give thanks for you. Paul thanks God, not the believers, for their faith and love, because these are God’s gifts. And he begins with thanks. He has plenty to correct, and he will get to it; but the first thing out of his mouth about this church is gratitude for what God has already done in them.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul prayed every moment without stopping. He prayed regularly and often for them, and they were never left out.

In a sentence. That is why, since I heard of your trust in the Lord Jesus and your love for all God’s people, I keep thanking God for you and mentioning you when I pray.

On a Tuesday. Think of a Christian, or a church, with a long way still to go. Thank God for what he has already done in them, and then tell them.

For worship. Every word of thanks in this verse is aimed at God, because faith and love are things only he can make. A traveller brought news of people who trusted Jesus and loved each other across the oldest divide in their world, and Paul recognised the fingerprints at once. The Lord Jesus, who once prayed for all who would believe through his apostles’ word (John 17:20), was answering that prayer in a port city of idols. Glory to the Christ who still gathers a people to himself and knits them together in love, quietly at work in churches no one in Rome has ever seen.

verseByVerse.quote: That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him.

The God of our Lord Jesus Christ. As a man, Jesus worshipped and prayed to the Father (John 20:17). Paul prays to the God Jesus prayed to.

The Father of glory. Take the word glory down off the shelf for a moment, because it has become a church word and began as an ordinary one. The Hebrew kābôd means weight: heaviness, substance, the thing solid enough to matter. That reverses how we usually rank the world. The things that feel most solid to us are the things we can bank, insure and put on a CV. Scripture calls those the lightweight things, chaff that the wind drives away (Psalm 1:4). God is the heavy thing, the most real being there is, and everything else has weight only as it reflects him. To call him the Father of glory is to say that this weight is not something he sometimes carries. It is what he is. Paul worships before he asks a thing.

May give you the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation. Notice something easy to miss. Paul has just written the most magnificent twelve verses in the New Testament. The words are inspired; the doctrine is flawless. And he does not assume for a moment that this will be enough. He stops and prays, because he knows he can put the truth in front of their minds and still not get it into their hearts. Only God can open eyes. Every preacher and every parent learns this: you can explain something perfectly and watch it not land. So the greatest teacher in the church turns at once into an intercessor. “Wisdom” (sophias): seeing things as God sees them, reading your own suffering in the frame of his purpose, seeing the cross, an apparent defeat, as the turning point of history. “Revelation” (apokalypseōs, unveiling): the curtain drawn back on what is already given.

Where Christians differ: the Holy Spirit, or a spirit of wisdom? Some translations read “a spirit of wisdom”, meaning a wise attitude or disposition. Verdict: the Holy Spirit. Wisdom and revelation are his work (Isaiah 11:2; 1 Corinthians 2:10–12), and only God can give revelation. But they already have the Spirit (v. 13), so Paul is not praying for them to receive him again; he is praying for the Spirit’s ongoing work in their understanding.

Revelation without new revelation. “Revelation” here means God opening their eyes to what he has already revealed in Christ, not new truths beyond Scripture. The canon is complete; but every believer still needs the Spirit to make what is written clear and real to the heart (1 Corinthians 2:14).

In the knowledge of him. “Knowledge” (epignōsei): full, personal knowledge. Not knowledge about God, but knowledge of him (John 17:3; Philippians 3:10). You can read the commentaries, take the course, learn the Greek, and still not know him, in the same way you can know a man’s birthday, his job, his home town and the name of his dog, and never have met him. So run the test honestly: is God someone you know a great deal about, or someone you know? The two feel similar from the inside for a long time, and they are not the same.

How do I come to know God, and not only know about him? In the same way you come to know anyone: by spending time in his company, listening when he speaks, and answering him. He speaks in Scripture, so read it as a letter from someone, asking each time, what does this show me about him? Then answer him: pray back what you have read in your own words, with thanks for what he has done, confession where the passage finds you out, and requests where it makes promises. Do it with other believers, because you know a person better through the eyes of friends who also know him. And obey, because Jesus promised to show himself to the one who keeps his commandments (John 14:21). Knowing God is not a technique, and it grows slowly, like any friendship. But no one who seeks him with all his heart is left a stranger (Jeremiah 29:13).
