Why this prayer? They have every blessing (v. 3), but they need to see what they have. A man who does not know he has inherited a fortune lives like a pauper. Paul could have prayed that their circumstances would ease or their numbers grow. He asked instead that they would know God, because the one who truly knows him is equipped for anything that is coming, and the one who does not is unequipped for everything, however well life is currently going.

What it does not mean. Not a request for secret knowledge or private visions, the kind of thing Ephesian magic offered. It is understanding of the God revealed in Christ.

In a sentence. I ask that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the glorious Father, will give you his Spirit, who brings wisdom and opens your eyes, so that you come to know him better.

On a Tuesday. You cannot manufacture this; you can ask for it. Pray Paul’s words for yourself before you open your Bible this week, and for one other person by name.

For worship. The God to whom Paul prays is the God to whom Jesus prayed, and that alone is a wonder: in Christ we are brought into the very fellowship the Son has with his Father. He is the Father of glory, and he does not keep his glory sealed away. He gives his Spirit, so that creatures of dust may know the eternal God, not by rumour but in the face of his Son (2 Corinthians 4:6). There is no higher gift than this, and none more like him: the God who is worth knowing above all things wants to be known.

parallels.desc: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding

verseByVerse.quote: Having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you, what are the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you, what are the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints.

Having the eyes of your hearts enlightened. In Scripture the heart (kardia) is the centre of the whole person, thinking, willing and feeling, not only emotion, and it has its own eyes. “Enlightened” (pephōtismenous): flooded with light. Every Christian knows the moment when a verse he has read a hundred times, and could have quoted on any of those occasions, suddenly opens, and he finds himself sitting very still over words that did nothing to him last year. Nothing changed in the text. The lights came on in the room. That is what Paul is asking God for, and it is why he prays instead of only explaining himself more clearly. He can raise the standard of the teaching; he cannot reach in and turn on the light. Only God can: the God who said, Let light shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts (2 Corinthians 4:6).

What if I read the Bible and the lights never seem to come on? Keep reading, and keep asking. Seasons of dryness are normal, even for mature believers, and they are not proof that God has stopped speaking. Much of what Scripture does in us is quiet: like meals you cannot remember, it has fed you even on days when nothing felt memorable. A few practical things help. Read smaller portions, slowly, instead of racing through chapters. Read with two questions: what does this show me about God, and what does it ask of me? Pray before you start, with the psalmist: Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18). And read with others, because a friend will often see what you missed. The light comes in God’s time, and often when you have stopped straining for it.

The hope to which he has called you. Christian hope (elpis) is not wishful thinking but certain expectation of what God has promised: the resurrection of the body, Christ’s return, the renewal of all things, life with God face to face, all guaranteed because Jesus rose. Scripture’s picture for it is an anchor (Hebrews 6:19), and an anchor does not work as we tend to imagine. It is not dropped behind the ship to hold her where she has been. It is thrown out ahead, grips ground the crew cannot see, and steadies them in the water they are in now. Whether you have truly seen this hope tends to show up in three very ordinary places: what happens inside you when money goes, what happens inside you at a graveside, and whether the thought of your own death is a horror or a door.

The riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints. Whose inheritance is meant: ours, or God’s?

Where Christians differ: our inheritance, or God’s? Some read this as the inheritance believers receive, kept among the saints. Verdict: most likely God’s own inheritance, which is his people. Paul says his inheritance, and the Old Testament calls Israel the LORD’s portion and inheritance (Deuteronomy 32:9; Exodus 19:5; Malachi 3:17). Both truths are biblical (v. 14 speaks of our inheritance), but here the wonder is that they are God’s treasure.

God’s treasure is his people. Sit with what that must mean. He already owns everything. The galaxies are not his estate but his handiwork, and he could speak a thousand more into being. So what does the God who owns it all count as treasure, what did he go out and buy at cost? Not the stars. His people. Jesus told of a man who found treasure hidden in a field, and in his joy sold all that he had and bought that field (Matthew 13:44). Read it once with God as the buyer. And any treasure is priced by what the buyer paid. Peter gives the figure: not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18–19). For Gentiles who had been without hope and without God (2:12), this was astonishing. So when you are tempted, as most believers are by about Tuesday, to think of yourself as someone God barely tolerates for Jesus’ sake, this verse stands in the way. You are not what he puts up with. You are what he is inheriting.

What it does not mean. Not that God gains something he lacked. He chooses to treasure his people, and he will not lose what he has paid for.

In a sentence. I pray that the eyes of your heart will be opened, so that you know the sure hope God has called you to, and how rich and glorious a treasure he has in his people.

For worship. The God who made the stars calls his people his treasure, and he paid for them with the blood of his Son. Look up, and let him be praised.

verseByVerse.quote: and what is the immeasurable greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of his great might that he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places,
verseByVerse.commentary:
and what is the immeasurable greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of his great might that he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places,

The immeasurable greatness of his power. “Immeasurable” (hyperballon, surpassing, beyond measuring). This is the third thing Paul prays they will see, and it meets the objection every honest reader has been forming since verse 18: that people like us are far too weak to make it to the end.

Four words for power. Paul piles them up like a man describing something beyond description: power (dynamis, ability), working (energeia, power in action), great (kratos, strength that prevails) and might (ischys, inherent strength). And then he anchors the whole pile to one event.

According to the working of his great might that he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead. Read the measurement carefully, because it is the most extraordinary thing in the sentence. Paul does not say God’s power for us is like resurrection power, or a scaled-down household version of it. He says it is the same exertion, now aimed at you. Look at what it had to do the first time. This was not a man revived a few minutes after his heart stopped. Jesus had been executed in public by professionals who did not make mistakes about death. He had been taken down, wrapped, carried and sealed in. The stone was in place, the guard posted, and his friends had gone home to grieve, not to wait for Sunday. Death had won completely, with witnesses. And then God exerted himself, and the strongest power in this world, the one that has never lost an argument with anybody, gave way.

Now set your own situation beside that. The habit you have failed to break for twenty years. The person you cannot forgive. The fear you have reasoned with a hundred times and never beaten. The prayer you have carried so long that you no longer expect an answer. Ask the question this verse is built to make you ask: is any of it harder than a corpse? Whatever still holds out in you is not stronger than death, and death is precisely what this power has already beaten, once, in the open.

Toward us who believe. Toward is a direction, not a vault. This power is not locked away until you fill in the right form; it is aimed at you and already in motion. And it is toward us who believe, not us who believe flawlessly. I believe; help my unbelief! cried a desperate father, and Jesus acted (Mark 9:24). The power does not grow with the strength of your faith, but with the strength of God, received by any faith, however weak, fixed on the right object. And it has already been used on you. Even when we were dead in our trespasses, God made us alive together with Christ (2:5). You were not merely helped. You were raised.

Power for what? Not mostly for spectacle. Power to believe and keep believing (Philippians 2:13). Power over sin, since the strength that broke death can break the grip of an old habit (Romans 6:4–6). Power to endure: the long marriage, the chronic illness, the prayer carried for years, strengthened with all power … for all endurance and patience with joy (Colossians 1:11). Power to love the difficult (3:16–17). And power in weakness, made perfect exactly when human strength runs out (2 Corinthians 12:9).

And seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places. The right hand is the place of supreme honour and authority beside a king: The LORD says to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool (Psalm 110:1). It is not a physical location, as if the Father had a body with a right side; it means Christ shares God’s throne and rule. He sits because his saving work is finished (Hebrews 10:12). And believers are seated there with him (2:6).

What it does not mean. Not that believers will always feel powerful or see miracles, or that hardship will be removed. The man writing this prayer is in chains; his power was given for endurance, not escape. Its aim is not to make your outer life spectacular, but to make your inner life like the Son’s.

In a sentence. And that you may know how immeasurably great is his power for us who believe, the same mighty power he used when he raised Christ from the dead and enthroned him at his right hand in heaven.

On a Tuesday. The habit you think you cannot break, the grief you think you cannot bear: is it harder than a sealed tomb? The power that emptied it is at work in you.

For worship. On the third day the Father put forth his might, and the grave that had never given anything back gave up the Son. Christ rose not as a man revived but as the firstborn of the new creation, and ascended to the throne he had left for our sakes. Worship the Lord who went down into death and came up its conqueror, and who now sits because his work is done. His empty tomb is the measure of God’s power, and his throne is the pledge that the same power will finish what it has begun in us. The God who raised Jesus has never once been overmatched.

parallels.desc: sit at my right hand

verseByVerse.quote: Far above all rule and authority and power and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Far above all rule and authority and power and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come.

Far above. Paul does not simply say that Christ is above these powers. He reaches for an emphatic compound, hyperanō: far above, high over. That is a claim about kind, not only rank. Christ is not the highest name on the chart, the senior officer at the top of a chain of command that also contains the others. He is not on the chart at all. He drew it.

All rule and authority and power and dominion. The ranks and titles Jews and Greeks used for orders of spiritual beings, including hostile ones (6:12), and also for human rulers. Paul recites the whole table of organisation, top to bottom, and puts the entire structure under one pair of feet. To the Ephesians this was not abstract; it was liberation. They had lived in dread of named powers that governed life and had to be appeased. Into that fear Paul announces: every power you feared is under the feet of the one who saved you. At the cross, which looked like defeat, he disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame (Colossians 2:15). They still operate and still oppose (6:12), but as defeated enemies, not sovereign lords. There is a vast difference between a roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8) and a reigning one.

And above every name that is named. In Ephesus this was an attack on an industry. In the magical world, power lived in names. To know a spirit’s name and pronounce it correctly was to gain leverage over it, and the city’s spells were famous across the empire. That is why Luke’s scene in the same city lands so hard: the seven sons of Sceva tried to use “the Jesus whom Paul proclaims” as one more name in the toolkit, and were beaten out of the house (Acts 19:13–16). The name of Jesus is not a lever to be operated. He is a Lord to be belonged to. And that is why the converts made a bonfire of their scrolls a few verses later. When you have the Person, you no longer need the formulas. You have your own names. You can usually find them by asking what you find yourself appeasing: the market, the algorithm, the scan result, the mortgage, the opinion of people whose approval you have never actually enjoyed. We do not burn incense to them; we organise our lives around them and lie awake for them. Every one of them is named in this verse, and every one is under his feet.

Can curses, horoscopes or evil spirits harm a Christian? They cannot own you, and they cannot undo what God has done. A believer belongs to Christ and is sealed with his Spirit (1:13), and he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4). No curse can reverse God’s blessing (Numbers 23:8). The devil can still tempt, accuse and oppose you (6:11–12), and he is to be resisted, not ignored (James 4:7). But a Christian should have nothing to do with horoscopes, tarot cards, Ouija boards, charms or spells (Deuteronomy 18:10–12), not because they are stronger than Christ, but because consulting them is looking to another lord for what only he gives. If you have dabbled, confess it and get rid of the things, as the Ephesians burned their scrolls (Acts 19:19). Then stop being afraid. You are seated with the one who is far above them all.

Not only in this age but also in the one to come. Jews divided history into two ages: this present age, marked by sin and death, and the age to come, when God would put everything right. Christ’s resurrection has brought the age to come into the present; the two now overlap until his return. Every power that has ever terrified anyone has had an expiry date printed on it. The empires that once looked permanent are now chapters that schoolchildren find boring. The thing pressing on you this week has a shelf life; he does not. His authority is not up for renewal at the end of history. The end of history is simply when everybody finds out.

What it does not mean. Not that evil powers have vanished. They are still active (6:12), but defeated and subject to Christ (Colossians 2:15).

In a sentence. Christ now sits far above every ruler, authority, power and lordship, above every name anyone can name, in this age and in the age to come.

On a Tuesday. Name the thing you are quietly appeasing this week. Then say it aloud: it is under his feet.

For worship. Every name that ever made a city tremble, Artemis, Caesar, the spirits of the air, has been outranked by the name of a carpenter’s son who died on a Roman cross. The Father has exalted him far above them all and given him the name above every name (Philippians 2:9). Their reigns are borrowed and their days are numbered; his is underived and without end. Bow before the Lord Jesus, who did not seize this throne but received it by obedience to death, and who will hold it when every lesser power is forgotten. There is no age, this or the next, in which he is not King.

verseByVerse.quote: And he put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the church,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the church,

He put all things under his feet. Paul is quoting Psalm 8:6, and every Jewish reader would catch it. That psalm is about humanity: the dignity God gave us at creation, crowned with glory and honour and set to rule his works. That was Adam’s commission, and it was lost. Hebrews quotes the same psalm and adds the ache: at present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. Then the turn: but we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honour (Hebrews 2:8–9). What Adam failed to hold, the last Adam has won. The feet once nailed to a cross are the feet under which every power is now placed. Their subjection is not yet fully visible, but it is already fully real: he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death (1 Corinthians 15:25–26).

And gave him as head over all things to the church. The sentence is easy to misread. It does not say only that Christ is head over the church and also over all things, though both are true. It says God gave the church a gift: Christ, who is head over all things. Stay with those last three words, because they are the strangest in the verse. Not to the angels, who never fell. Not to the nations, vast and impressive. To the church: a scattered collection of ordinary people, many of them slaves and tradesmen, meeting in borrowed rooms in a city that would not have noticed if they vanished. The universe has been placed under one head, and that head has been handed over as a gift to them. We picture two separate stories, the big one out there, empires, markets, wars, and the small one in here, our own life and church. This verse says there is one story, and it is being run with reference to the second.

If Christ rules all things for the church, why does the church suffer so much? Because he rules for her good, and her good is not the same as her comfort. The head over all things is the Lamb who was slain, and his body follows the way he went: through the cross to the crown. So persecution, decline and hardship are not signs that he has lost control; he rules even them. When persecution scattered the church in Jerusalem, the scattered went everywhere preaching the word (Acts 8:1–4). Nothing can separate his people from his love, and in all these things they are more than conquerors (Romans 8:35–37). The church will not always look as if she is winning, but the gates of hell will never overcome her (Matthew 16:18). Pray for the suffering church, and do not measure Christ’s reign by this week’s headlines.

Head. “Head” (kephalē) here clearly means authority, ruler, since it stands beside putting all things under his feet. In 4:15–16 it also carries the idea of the source of life and growth for the body. A head is the source from which the body is nourished and held together (Colossians 2:19). So Christ’s rule over everything is not only the guarantee that nothing can crush you; it is the arrangement by which you are fed. And a body goes where its head goes. If the head has been raised and seated above every power, the body cannot be left behind (2:6).

Where Christians differ: the head of the church. Roman Catholic teaching sees the pope as Christ’s visible vicar and head on earth. Verdict: Christ alone is head of the church (Westminster Confession 25.6), ruling by his word and Spirit through local elders. No human being shares that headship.

In a sentence. God put everything under Christ’s feet, and gave him, the head over everything, to the church.

For worship. When the world seems out of control, the question is never whether someone is in charge. Someone always is. The question is whose side he is on, and this verse answers before you can ask: he was given to you. Worship the Lord of all things, who rules them all for his people.

parallels.desc: you have put all things under his feet

verseByVerse.quote: which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.

Which is his body. The church is not a club or an organisation that admires Christ from a distance, but the body of Christ: united to him, living from him, the means by which he acts in the world. A body is simply how a person acts in the world. Your hands are how you are present to the things you pick up; your voice is how you are present to the people you speak to. Christ has chosen a body through which to act visibly, and it is not a building. It is the people who were in the room with you last Sunday, the ones you find difficult included. When they carry a meal to a widow, that is not only kindness organised by volunteers. It is Christ, present on a particular street.

The fullness of him who fills all in all. “Fullness” (plērōma). Why does Paul say Christ fills all things, and not only rules them? Because filling is richer than ruling. A king can hold authority over a land he has never visited. To fill something is to be present within it, leaving no part untouched. The language is soaked in the Old Testament. Do I not fill heaven and earth? declares the LORD (Jeremiah 23:24). When Solomon dedicated the temple, the cloud of God’s glory filled the house so that the priests could not stand to minister (1 Kings 8:10–11): not overseeing it from above, but filling it from within. Paul takes that whole tradition and applies it to the risen Jesus. The one whose glory filled the temple now fills all things, and his church is the new temple, made of living stones (2:21–22).

Where Christians differ: does the church fill Christ, or does Christ fill the church? There are two main readings. First, the church completes Christ, as a body completes a head. Calvin took this view and found it moving: Christ, who lacks nothing in himself, counts himself in some sense incomplete without his people. Second, the church is filled by Christ: the place he fills with his presence, life and gifts. Verdict: the second is more likely. Paul consistently speaks of Christ filling (4:10, he ascended that he might fill all things) and of believers being filled (3:19; 5:18), never of Christ being filled up by us; and Colossians 2:9–10 says the fullness of deity dwells in Christ and you have been filled in him. Christ lacks nothing. Yet Calvin’s point stands in its own way. Paul could have said king and kingdom, or master and servants, and kept himself entirely separate. He chose the one picture in which the greater looks unfinished without the lesser. A head without a body is not a lesser head; it is a horror. Christ does not need us as we need him, but he has bound himself to us so closely that he is not ashamed to be called our head. That is not a lack in Christ. It is a measure of how far love has committed itself.

Who fills all in all. Christ’s presence and rule extend through all creation (4:10). He fills the universe by his power; he fills the church by his saving presence. So there is nowhere you can go this week that lies outside him: the ward, the school run, the office where nobody prays, the flat you come home to when it is empty. You do not carry him into those places like a parcel. He is already filling them, and you go in as part of his body.

What it does not mean. Not that the church is perfect, or that Christ depends on it. It means the church is precious, with a dignity far above how it often looks.

In a sentence. The church is his body, filled by him who fills everything everywhere.

On a Tuesday. When church life seems small and ordinary, remember what it is: the body of the risen King, filled with his presence, and placed by him on your street.

For worship. The Christ who fills all things could have filled them alone, and needed nothing from us. Yet he has chosen to have a body, and to make poor, quarrelsome, forgiven people the place where his fullness dwells. The glory that once filled Solomon’s temple now lives among a congregation of sinners, and is not ashamed of them. Adore the Lord whose presence leaves no corner of creation untouched, and who has bound himself to his church as a head to its body, for ever. Heaven and earth are full of him, and so, by his grace, are we.

1.overview:
Ephesians opens with the longest sentence in the New Testament (vv. 3–14), a single breathless act of praise for every spiritual blessing God has given his people in Christ. The Father chose them before creation to be holy, predestined them in love for adoption, and freely gave them grace in his beloved Son. In Christ they have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, and they have been let into the secret of God’s plan: to unite all things in heaven and on earth under Christ. Jews who first hoped in Christ and Gentiles who later believed have both been sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, the down payment of their inheritance, all to the praise of God’s glory.

Then Paul prays (vv. 15–23). He does not ask for new blessings, but that they may see the ones they have: the hope of God’s calling, the riches of his inheritance in his people, and the immeasurable power at work in believers, the same power that raised Christ from the dead and seated him far above every power in this age and the next. God has made Christ head over everything for the sake of the church, which is his body. The chapter teaches that salvation begins in God’s eternal choice, rests on Christ’s blood, is sealed by the Spirit, and ends in praise.

2.title: Dead in Sin, Alive in Christ
2.text: <sup>1</sup>And you were dead in the trespasses and sins <sup>2</sup>in which you once walked, following the course of this world, following the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience — <sup>3</sup>among whom we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the flesh and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind. <sup>4</sup>But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, <sup>5</sup>even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ — by grace you have been saved — <sup>6</sup>and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, <sup>7</sup>so that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus. <sup>8</sup>For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, <sup>9</sup>not a result of works, so that no one may boast. <sup>10</sup>For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them. <sup>11</sup>Therefore remember that at one time you Gentiles in the flesh, called “the uncircumcision” by what is called the circumcision, which is made in the flesh by hands — <sup>12</sup>remember that you were at that time separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world. <sup>13</sup>But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. <sup>14</sup>For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility <sup>15</sup>by abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace, <sup>16</sup>and might reconcile us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility. <sup>17</sup>And he came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near. <sup>18</sup>For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father. <sup>19</sup>So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, <sup>20</sup>built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone, <sup>21</sup>in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord. <sup>22</sup>In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul reminds them that they were spiritually dead in their sins, living by the world’s ways and under the power of the spirit at work in the disobedient. All of us once lived for the flesh and were by nature deserving of wrath. But God, rich in mercy and great in love, made us alive with Christ even when we were dead: by grace we are saved. He raised us and seated us with Christ in the heavenly realms, to show for ever the riches of his kindness. Salvation is by grace through faith, God’s gift, not earned by works, so that no one can boast. We are God’s handiwork, created in Christ for the good works he prepared for us.
verseByVerse.theology:
Total Depravity, Sovereign Grace, and the New Creation

"Dead in trespasses and sins" is the Reformed doctrine of total depravity in its most direct biblical expression. Total depravity does not mean that fallen human beings are as evil as they could possibly be — common grace restrains the full expression of human sin. It means that every faculty of the human person — mind, will, affections, conscience — has been corrupted by the fall, so that no part of us naturally seeks God or is capable of saving itself. The will is not neutral, waiting to choose God if only given sufficient reason; it is enslaved, "following the prince of the power of the air" (v.2), "carrying out the desires of the flesh and the mind" (v.3).

Against this backdrop, the "but God" of v.4 is the hinge of history. God does not respond to a seeking sinner; he acts on a dead one. This is irresistible grace — not grace that overrides the will by force, but grace that transforms the will, making the dead alive, making the unwilling willing, making the seeking possible. If we seek the cause of our salvation, we find it not in ourselves but in God alone. The new birth is entirely God's work, and the faith through which we receive it is itself his gift (v.8).

The closing verse — "we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works" — is the Reformed answer to the charge that grace produces passivity. It does not. Grace produces the very thing that law could only demand. The person who knows they are entirely saved by grace, not by works, is freed from self-justifying performance and freed for genuine, joyful, Spirit-empowered good works — the works that God prepared beforehand for them to walk in.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The recipients of Paul's letter knew exactly what he meant by "dead in trespasses and sins" — it was their autobiography. Many had been worshippers of Artemis, practitioners of occult arts (Acts 19:19 tells us that converted Ephesians burned their magic books, worth fifty thousand pieces of silver). The darkness, the slavery to spiritual powers, the restless seeking for blessing through ritual and charm — they had lived it. The "but God" of v.4 was the turning point of their actual lives. The grace Paul describes was not theological theory to them; it was the story of what had happened to them, written in their own experience. This is why the passage carries such heat — Paul is describing something he and his readers have lived through, not merely thought about.

Now: "Dead in trespasses and sins" describes every human being outside of Christ, however educated, however moral, however spiritually sincere. The kind CEO, the generous philanthropist, the sincere seeker of truth — apart from Christ, all share the same condition: spiritual death, living under the dominion of the one who still holds sway over "the sons of disobedience" (v.2). This is not a comfortable diagnosis, but it is a necessary one — because a person who thinks they are merely ill will never seek the cure appropriate to death. The church must have the courage to declare both the diagnosis and the remedy with equal clarity: dead — but God.

verseByVerse.quote: You were dead in the trespasses and sins in which you once walked, following the course of this world, following the prince of the power of the air.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You were dead in the trespasses and sins in which you once walked, following the course of this world, following the prince of the power of the air.

Meaning first. Ephesians 2 shows what the power of God described in chapter 1 has done for us, in two movements. Verses 1–10 describe salvation as resurrection: we were spiritually dead, following the world, the devil and our own desires, and by nature under God’s wrath (vv. 1–3); but God, rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ, raised us and seated us with him, so that for ever his grace would be on display (vv. 4–7); salvation is entirely his gift, received through faith, not earned by works, yet it creates us for the good works he has prepared (vv. 8–10). Verses 11–22 describe salvation as reconciliation: Gentiles were once outsiders, without Christ, without God’s people, promises, hope or God (vv. 11–12); but in Christ they have been brought near by his blood; he is our peace, who tore down the wall between Jew and Gentile, ended the law as a dividing system, and created one new people reconciled to God through the cross (vv. 13–18). So Gentile believers are full citizens and family members, built with Jewish believers on the apostles’ and prophets’ foundation, with Christ as cornerstone, into a temple where God lives by his Spirit (vv. 19–22). Chapter 2 is the gospel in miniature: dead, but God; far off, but now.

The connection. Chapter 1 ended with God’s power raising Christ from the dead and seating him above every power (1:19–23). Chapter 2 shows the same power at work in us. To see how great it is, Paul first shows how dead we were. The sentence that begins in verse 1 does not reach its main verb until verse 5: God … made us alive. Verses 1–3 are the grave; verses 4–7 are the resurrection.

You were dead. The word lands like a stone: nekrous, dead. Not sick, not wounded, not weakened. Dead. Not physically, since the readers had been walking, working and worshipping idols, but cut off from the life of God (4:18). A corpse can be dressed beautifully and look presentable; it is still a corpse. Spiritual death means no power to perceive God (the natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit, 1 Corinthians 2:14), no desire for him (the mind set on the flesh does not submit to God’s law; indeed, it cannot, Romans 8:7), and no ability to change it. A weak man can try harder; a sick man can take medicine; a dead man can do neither. Lazarus did not help Jesus raise him. He heard a voice speak life into death, and came out (John 11:43–44). That is what salvation is. And this is what God warned of in Eden: in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die (Genesis 2:17). Adam did not drop dead that day, but he hid from God, and death began.

In the trespasses and sins. Two words for wrong. A trespass (paraptōma) is a false step, crossing a line God has drawn. A sin (hamartia) is missing the mark, falling short of what God made us for. Together they cover every way we fail: doing what God forbids, and not being what he commands. And notice: dead in them, not only because of them. Sin is not only the cause of the death but the sphere it is lived in. That is why the cure cannot be moral improvement. You do not improve a corpse. You raise it.

In which you once walked. “Walk” is the Bible’s word for a way of life (4:1, 17; 5:2, 8, 15). And here is the paradox: the dead were busy. Death, in Paul’s picture, walks. Careers, families, religion, pleasure, all lived as if God were not there.

Following the course of this world. Literally according to the age of this world. “The world” here is not the planet, which God made and loves, but human society organised without God: its values, fashions and pressures. It tells us what to want and whom to admire. It is a current, and the dead do not feel it, because nothing feels less like being swept along than swimming with the tide. You discover the current only when you turn and try to swim against it (1 John 2:15–17).

The prince of the power of the air. Satan, called elsewhere the ruler of this world (John 12:31) and the god of this world, who blinds the minds of unbelievers (2 Corinthians 4:4): a real person, not a figure of speech for society’s bad habits. In the ancient world the air, the space between earth and the heavens, was thought to be the home of spirits. Paul uses the language his readers knew: the powers they feared are real, and ruled by one evil prince. The air is near, everywhere, breathed without noticing. But he is not equal to God; he is a creature already defeated (1:21; Colossians 2:15).

The spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience. “At work” (energeō) is the same word Paul used of God’s power raising Christ (1:20). Two powers are at work in the world: the devil’s in the disobedient, God’s in those he raises. “Sons of disobedience” is a Hebrew way of saying people marked by disobedience.

Three enemies. Verses 1–3 name the three enemies the church has long called the world, the flesh and the devil: the world around us (v. 2), the devil above us (v. 2), and the flesh within us (v. 3). Culture makes sin normal, the devil makes it attractive, and our own nature wants it. And mark what the dead man is doing about them. He is not fighting them. He is following them. He is not a prisoner straining at the bars, but a body carried by the tide.

But I know kind unbelievers. Almost everybody feels this and few say it aloud: “dead”? I know unbelievers kinder, steadier and more generous than half the congregation. Think of cut flowers. A florist’s arrangement can be lovelier than anything still growing in the garden, brighter and more fragrant in the room. Nobody looking at it would say it is dead. Yet it has been cut from its root, and everything you admire about it is running on borrowed time. Paul is not claiming that unbelievers behave worse than believers, which would be plainly false and would insult people we love. He is speaking of connection, not comparison. The kindness is real. The beauty is real. The root is what is missing.

What it does not mean. Not that unbelievers are as bad as they could possibly be, or that they cannot do kind or good things in a human sense. Total depravity means that sin has reached every part of human nature, mind, will and desires, so that nothing in us is untouched, and nothing in us can turn us back to God. Nor does it mean that everyone outside Christ is consciously serving Satan. Most simply follow the crowd; that is the point. And it does not remove responsibility: the dead walked in sins; they did what they wanted.

Where Christians differ: how dead? Semi-Pelagian and Arminian traditions hold that the fall left people weakened but still able, with God’s general help (called prevenient grace), to accept or refuse the gospel; they read dead as separated from God rather than unable, and point to Jesus’ promise to draw all people to himself (John 12:32). Reformed theology holds total inability: the fallen will is free to choose what it wants, but it does not want God, and no one can come to Christ unless the Father draws him (John 6:44; Romans 8:7–8). Verdict: total depravity and inability (Westminster Confession 9.3). Paul’s image decides it: a corpse does not cooperate with its resurrection. And the diagnosis is not the sentence; it is the setup. The word dead exists to make verse 5 blaze. The depth of the death is the measure of the miracle (Ezekiel 37:1–14).

A test you can run. Corpses do not develop appetites. So if you find in yourself any hunger for God at all, if you would rather be near him than not, if his word sometimes lands with weight, if sin now grieves you where once it barely registered, then something has happened to you that you did not do. You are not looking at evidence of your strength. You are looking at evidence that a voice has spoken into a grave, and that you heard it.

In a sentence. You were spiritually dead in your wrongdoing and sins, the way of life you once followed, going along with the values of this world and obeying the ruler of the unseen evil powers, the spirit now at work in those who disobey God.

On a Tuesday. When you share the gospel, argue clearly, but pray first: you are speaking to people who need resurrection, not merely persuasion. And no one is too far gone, because God raises the dead.

For worship. Before Paul tells of the resurrection, he shows us the grave, and the grave is the measure of the God who opened it. He does not coax the willing or reward the seeking; he speaks into tombs, and the dead live. The prince of the power of the air held us, the world carried us, and we followed gladly, until the Lord of life took us from them both. Praise the God whose mercy is not a helping hand held out to the drowning but breath given back to the drowned, and the Christ whose voice is still raising the dead in every nation under heaven.
verseByVerse.note: “The prince of the power of the air” is Satan. The air was thought to be the realm of spiritual powers.

verseByVerse.quote: among whom we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the flesh and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
among whom we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the flesh and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind.

Among whom we all once lived. Verses 1–2 said “you”, the Gentile readers. Now Paul says “we”. A Jew might think that, with the law, the temple and circumcision, he stood in a different place from pagans. Paul, the strictest of Pharisees (Philippians 3:4–6), says no: Jew and Gentile alike were dead. This prepares for verses 11–22. If both were equally lost, both are saved the same way, and neither can look down on the other (Romans 3:9, 22–23).

The passions of our flesh. “Flesh” (sarx) here does not mean the body. God made the body good, the Son took one, and the resurrection is bodily. It means fallen human nature, the whole person turned in on itself, what Luther, following Augustine, called the heart curved in on itself. So its passions are not only sexual. Galatians 5 lists idolatry, jealousy, rivalry and fits of anger alongside immorality. The flesh produces boardroom sin as readily as bedroom sin.

The desires of the body and the mind. Literally the wills of the flesh and of the thoughts. Paul deliberately adds the mind, and closes the moralist’s last escape. Discipline your appetites and you may simply have moved the problem upstairs: to intellectual pride, the hunger for power, the craving to be admired. A man can be sober, chaste and hard-working and still live entirely in the desires of the mind. The respectable sins of clever and moral people are as much flesh as any other.

And were by nature children of wrath. The deepest statement of the problem. Not only did we do wrong; we were wrong. “By nature” (physei) is original sin in a phrase: by birth, by what we are as children of Adam, before and beneath any choice (Psalm 51:5). We are not sinners because we sin; we sin because we are sinners. “Children of wrath” is a Hebrew idiom: people on whom wrath rests (John 3:36). Nobody has ever had to teach a child to lie, or to grab, or to say “mine”. We teach the opposite, constantly, with great effort and mixed results. Every parent is an unwilling witness to this verse.

Wrath. Not a fit of temper, and not something unworthy of a loving God. God’s wrath is his settled, holy, just opposition to evil (Romans 1:18). A God who was not angry at child abuse, cruelty and betrayal would not be good. A judge who feels nothing when the guilty walk free is not merciful but corrupt. God’s wrath is always fair: no one receives more than he deserves. And this truth is not cruelty; it is the only ground on which real gratitude can be built. The one who is forgiven little, loves little (Luke 7:47). The shallowness of our worship usually matches the smallness of our sense of what we were saved from.

Like the rest of mankind. No exceptions. This is the universal human condition.

The tense is the comfort. Read the verb again: we were by nature children of wrath. Not are. Every dreadful word in these three verses stands in the past tense, dead, walked, followed, lived, were, and they are all held there, waiting, until two words in verse 4 break over them: But God. So if you are in Christ, this passage is not your diagnosis. It is your medical history. Read it the way a healthy man reads an old chart from the worst year of his life, and marvels that he is sitting up reading anything at all.

What it does not mean. Not that the body or physical desire is evil in itself. God made the body and called it good (Genesis 1:31); hunger and sexual desire are his gifts. Flesh means those desires, and the mind’s too, captured by the self and pursued outside God’s will. Nor does “children of wrath” mean God hates his creatures or takes pleasure in their ruin (Ezekiel 33:11). The very next words are But God, being rich in mercy.

Where Christians differ: original sin. Pelagius (fifth century) taught that each person is born innocent and sins only by following bad examples. Eastern Orthodoxy teaches that we inherit mortality and a tendency to sin from Adam, but not his guilt. Augustine and the Reformers taught that we inherit both a corrupt nature and the guilt of Adam’s first sin, because the whole race sinned in Adam, its head (Romans 5:12–19). “By nature children of wrath” fits only the last: wrath rests on us by nature, not only after we choose. Verdict: original sin as both inherited corruption and imputed guilt (Westminster Confession 6.3). And the same principle of representation is what saves us: as Adam’s sin was counted to us, so Christ’s righteousness is counted to those in him. You were not punished as an outsider for somebody else’s crime; you were born into a family and have signed its charter with your own hand every day since.

A common question: what about infants who die? If all are by nature children of wrath, what of babies and young children who die before they can believe? Scripture does not answer this directly, and believers should speak humbly. The Westminster Confession (10.3) says that elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when, where and how he pleases. Many in the Reformed tradition, among them Charles Spurgeon and B. B. Warfield, went further and held that all who die in infancy are among the elect, pointing to God’s judgement according to deeds done (Romans 2:6; 2 Corinthians 5:10), which infants have not done, and to David’s confidence that he would go to his dead child (2 Samuel 12:23). Jesus took the little children in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16). What is certain is that if any infant is saved, it is by grace in Christ, not by innocence; and that grieving parents may entrust their child to the Judge of all the earth, who will do what is just (Genesis 18:25).

In a sentence. All of us, Jews included, once lived like that, driven by the cravings of our sinful nature and doing whatever our bodies and minds wanted, and by our very nature we were under God’s wrath, just like everyone else.

On a Tuesday. The sins of your mind, the pride you feel when you compare yourself with others, are as much flesh as any sin of the body. Bring both to Christ.

For worship. Read this verse as a sinner looking at the wrath he deserved, and then look at who stood in its path. The Son of God, who alone was never a child of wrath, became the one on whom the wrath fell, so that children of wrath might become children of God (John 1:12). Every sin of the flesh and of the mind, the appetite and the pride, was laid on him. There is no worship deeper than this: that a holy God should be just in his anger against us, and then, in the person of his Son, bear it for us.

verseByVerse.quote: But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you have been saved—
verseByVerse.commentary:
But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you have been saved—

But God. After three verses of death, the subject of the sentence finally appears, and everything turns on it. You were dead, but God. A child of wrath, but God. Without hope, but God. Martyn Lloyd-Jones said these two words in a sense contain the whole gospel. If the story were “But we”, there would be no hope, because dead people cannot act. Every Christian testimony, however complicated, comes down to this hinge. And notice where the change begins: not in us, but in God.

Being rich in mercy. Mercy is God’s pity moving towards misery. Grace gives what we do not deserve; mercy withholds what we do deserve and relieves our distress. The Hebrew behind it is ḥesed, loyal covenant love; the Greek eleos is active compassion. Mercy sees the corpse and is not repelled; it does not wait for signs of improvement. It moves first. And God is rich in it (plousios, the language of wealth): not adequate mercy, not mercy that barely covers the debt, but mercy that does not run low or grow harder to obtain the more you have needed it. It had to be rich, because the debt was total.

Because of the great love with which he loved us. The reason God acted lies in him, not in us. Paul piles up the words: love, great love, love with which he loved. God did not act from duty. He looked at the spiritually dead, the children of wrath, and loved them, not what they would become, but what they actually were (Romans 5:8). We were not lovable; he loved us anyway, and his love made us lovely.

Even when we were dead in our trespasses. Hold on to the timing, because Paul is careful with it. Not once we had begun to stir. Not after a decent interval of moral effort had shown some promise. At the moment when there was least to work with and nothing whatever to reward, that is when he acted. And that quietly settles the question every anxious believer returns to sooner or later: might God yet think better of it and change his mind about me? You contributed nothing to your first resurrection. Your standing has never rested on your contribution, and it is not about to start now.

Made us alive together with Christ. The main verb of the whole sentence, and the thing God actually did. Not helped. Not improved. Not offered a second chance to make better use of the first. There is exactly one thing you can do for a dead man. You cannot offer him advice, or terms, or an opportunity. You can raise him. This is regeneration, the new birth (John 3:3–8; Titus 3:5): God giving spiritual life to the spiritually dead. And it is one Greek word, synezōopoiēsen, made alive with. That little prefix, syn-, comes twice more in the next verse: raised with him, seated with him. Our new life is not a separate miracle that happens to resemble Christ’s; it is a share in his. When Jesus came out of the tomb, you came out with him. Your resurrection is not pending approval somewhere. In him it already happened, outside Jerusalem, long before you were born. Read the sentence once more and let its shape speak. The subject is God. The verb is made alive. And the object, entirely passive from beginning to end, is you.

By grace you have been saved. Paul cannot wait until verse 8 to say it, so he breaks into his own sentence. “Have been saved” is a perfect tense in Greek: a completed act with lasting results. Saved, and still saved.

The order of salvation. Reformed theology reads this as showing that regeneration comes before faith in order (not necessarily in time). God first makes us alive; then we believe. We do not believe in order to be born again; we believe because we have been born again (John 1:12–13; 1 John 5:1). The first sign of the new life is that the dead begin to hear, believe and repent.

I cannot remember a moment when I was made alive. Does that mean it never happened? No. You do not remember being born either, and you are plainly alive. Many believers, especially those raised in Christian homes, cannot name a day; others can name the day but could not tell you what was happening. Scripture never asks for a date. It asks whether there is life now. The question is not, when did I first believe? but, am I trusting Christ today? The signs are the ones a newborn shows: a hunger for God’s word (1 Peter 2:2), a cry of Father to God (Romans 8:15), a new grief over sin, and love for his people (1 John 3:14). If those are there, however weak, the one who raised you knows the day. Like the man born blind, you may not be able to explain how, but you can say that once you were blind and now you see (John 9:25).

What it does not mean. Not that we are passive in the Christian life: once alive, we believe, repent, fight sin and walk in good works (v. 10). The point is that the first move, from death to life, is God’s alone. Nor does mercy mean that God overlooks sin. His mercy reaches us with Christ: through the death and resurrection of the one who bore the wrath of verse 3 in our place.

Where Christians differ: does God’s life-giving work depend on our consent? Arminians hold that God’s grace enables every person to believe, but that grace can be resisted, so the decisive factor in who is saved is the human response. Reformed theology holds that God’s regenerating grace is effectual: when God makes alive, the dead live (John 6:37; Acts 16:14, where the Lord opened Lydia’s heart). Verdict: effectual calling (Westminster Confession 10.1–2). God does not drag the unwilling; he makes them willing by giving them new hearts (Ezekiel 36:26).

In a sentence. But God, because his mercy is so rich and his love for us so great, made us alive together with Christ even while we were dead in our sins; it is by grace you have been saved.

For worship. You were dead, and he loved you, and he spoke, and you live. But God. There are no greater words.

verseByVerse.quote: And raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus.

Three “with” words. Paul coins compound words: made alive with (v. 5), raised with, seated with. Each matches a step in Christ’s story in 1:20, where the Father raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand. Not three events, but one reality seen from three angles. This is union with Christ: he is our representative head, and we are in him, so his history becomes ours (Romans 6:4–5; Colossians 3:1–3). The fate of the head determines the fate of the body.

Raised us up with him. Spiritually, now: we have passed from death to life (John 5:24). Physically, later: our bodies will be raised at his return (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). The first guarantees the second.

And seated us with him in the heavenly places. The most astonishing of the three, and it is stated not as a hope but as a fact, in the past tense. To be seated is to be at rest, finished, in a place of authority. The priests of the old covenant never sat down in the temple; their work was never done. Christ sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high because his one sacrifice was final (Hebrews 1:3; 10:12), and you are seated with him, sharing his rest, not by anything you earned, but because you are in him. The “heavenly places” (see 1:3) are the unseen realm where Christ reigns over every power (1:20–21). The very powers that once ruled the Ephesians (v. 2) are now beneath the one with whom they sit. They have changed sides of the throne.

In Christ Jesus. The reason for all of it. We are not seated there by our own spiritual height, but because we are in him. And so nothing here is graded. Paul does not say the mature are seated while the struggling stand at the back. The believer converted last Thursday, who still cannot find Habakkuk and is fighting something he has not told anybody about, is seated exactly where the apostle is seated, because neither is there on his own account. They are both there in Christ, and he is only seated once.

Already and not yet. Paul uses past tenses: he raised us, he seated us. This is our position, settled in God’s eyes. Our experience does not yet match it: we still struggle, suffer and die. Ephesians holds both together. We are seated (2:6), yet we must stand and fight (6:10–13). And the realm we are seated in is the very realm where the battle is (6:12). That saves this verse from becoming escapism. Paul is not offering a quiet room above the noise. He is telling you your position in the conflict. It is the difference between a soldier pinned down in a trench, who cannot see the field and does not know whether his side is winning, and a man standing beside the commander with the whole battle laid out before him. Both are in the war. Only one knows how it ends. The fight is real, but it is fought from victory, not for it.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians are already beyond struggle, sickness or sin, or that they can claim earthly power or success by their status. Paul writes this in chains. Nor is it an escape from earthly life: the seated church is sent to walk in good works on earth (v. 10).

In a sentence. And God raised us up with Christ and seated us with him in the heavenly realms, because we are united to Christ Jesus.

On a Tuesday. When the accuser says you are disqualified, do not produce your record; point to your seat. The boss, the diagnosis and the fear are real, but they are beneath your Lord’s feet, and you are seated with him.

For worship. The Lord Jesus is seated, and the seat is a sermon. It says that the sacrifice is finished, that the Father is satisfied, that every power has been put beneath him. And he has not taken that seat alone. Out of sheer kindness he has set beside himself the very people who once served his enemies, so that his rest is their rest and his victory their standing. Who but this King would share his throne with rebels? Worship him who sat down because there was nothing left to do, and who keeps his people where he is, because he will not be in glory without them (John 17:24).

verseByVerse.quote: So that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.

So that. Paul lifts his eyes from the miracle of salvation to its far horizon. God saved his people for their good, yes, but above all to display his own glory: the same goal as the refrain of chapter 1, to the praise of his glory (1:6, 12, 14). And God’s glory and our good are not rivals: he is glorified precisely by being kind to us.

In the coming ages. Not one coming age but ages, one after another without end. What we have tasted here, forgiveness, adoption, the Spirit, God’s presence in prayer, is the down payment. The coming ages are the feast. Think of the moment when grace was most real to you, when forgiveness felt most true and a promise landed so that you could barely breathe. That came through a fallen mind, a weak faith, a tired body, in a world still under the curse. What will it be when every barrier is gone? What you have tasted is real: one drop from an ocean with no shore. C. S. Lewis caught it at the end of The Last Battle: every room opens into a greater one, further up and further in, and the cry is, this is the land I have been looking for all my life.

He might show. The word means to demonstrate, to exhibit publicly (Romans 9:22–23). The audience includes the angels and powers: through the church God’s wisdom is made known to the rulers in the heavenly places (3:10). And notice what will be on display through the ages. Not galaxies or landscapes; God has those already, and they never cost him anything. What will be exhibited for ever is what he did with people. You are the exhibit.

The immeasurable riches of his grace. “Immeasurable” (hyperballon) means beyond all measuring, the word used of his power in 1:19. Grace is not merely sufficient; it overflows, and eternity will not exhaust it. And this turns something painful inside out. Most of us carry a chapter we would rather were left out: the wasted years, the thing we still cannot say aloud, the person we were. We assume heaven will involve a discreet silence about all that. But look at what is displayed: not your record, but the riches of his grace. And grace can only be measured against what it had to overcome. A restorer’s skill is never shown by a painting that was never damaged. The chapter you would erase is the part of you that will testify most loudly, for ever, to what he is like. In the coming ages nobody will be embarrassed by your past. They will be looking at it, and worshipping.

In kindness toward us. Grace is not cold or grudging, like a judge reluctantly signing a pardon. It comes in kindness (chrēstotēs): warm, personal, gentle goodness (Titus 3:4), the kindness of someone leaning towards you, not a benefactor signing a cheque at a distance. Eternity is not God finally getting round to a reward you were owed. It is God, for ever, delighting to be kind to people who had nothing coming.

In Christ Jesus. All of this kindness reaches us through one channel. Outside Christ, God’s kindness calls people to repentance (Romans 2:4); in Christ, it becomes an eternal inheritance.

What it does not mean. Not that God saves us as mere objects to make himself look good, like trophies on a shelf. The display is of kindness toward us: it is a display of love. Nor does grace run out after conversion; it will be shown, and grow brighter, for ever.

In a sentence. He did this so that, in all the ages to come, he could show the boundless riches of his grace in the kindness he has shown us in Christ Jesus.

For worship. Through all the ages to come, the angels will look at what God did with sinners like you, and they will learn what he is like. Begin the praise now.

verseByVerse.quote: For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.

For. Verses 8–9 explain verses 4–7. If God saved the dead, salvation cannot be our achievement.

By grace. The source. Grace (charis) is God’s free, undeserved favour: not a substance poured into us, but God’s attitude and action of kindness towards those who deserve wrath (v. 3). If it is deserved in any way, it is no longer grace (Romans 11:6).

You have been saved. Again the perfect tense, and in the passive. Something was done to you; it was finished; and its effect continues into the room you are sitting in now. That is why assurance is not arrogance. The one who says he is saved is no more boasting about his performance than a rescued swimmer boasts about the lifeboat. He is reporting a completed action carried out by somebody else. Saved from death (v. 1), from the world, the flesh and the devil (vv. 2–3), and from wrath (v. 3).

Through faith. The means: the empty hand that receives the gift. Faith is not a contribution, a small payment, or a virtue that earns God’s approval. It is trust, relying on Christ and what he has done instead of on ourselves, and its whole value lies in its object. Notice that Paul never praises the faith itself; he never calls it strong or sincere or sufficient. Weak faith in a sound bridge will carry you over the river; robust faith in a rotten one will drop you into it. The bridge does the saving. That is why Jesus spoke of faith like a grain of mustard seed, and why the father who cried, I believe; help my unbelief! went home with a healed son (Mark 9:24). So the question is never whether your faith is big enough. That question turns you back on yourself, and the honest answer will always be no. The question is what you are trusting. Put a trembling hand on Christ and you have all that he is; and the empty hand, which is all faith ever was, does not become any emptier for shaking. We are saved through faith, never because of faith.

And this is not your own doing. In Greek “this” (touto) is neuter, while “grace” and “faith” are both feminine. So “this” does not point to faith alone, nor to grace alone, but to the whole thing just described: salvation by grace through faith. Some take the grammar as a reason to say faith is not called a gift here. Grant the grammar entirely: it does not weaken the point; it strengthens it. If “this” sweeps back over everything Paul has said, then grace, salvation and the faith that receives it are all gathered into one word: gift. You do not make room for a human contribution by narrowing the pronoun. It is the gift of God.

Not a result of works. “Works” here means anything we do to put God in our debt: law-keeping, religious rituals, moral effort, good deeds. Paul had in view the works of the law, but the principle covers every human attempt to earn salvation (Romans 4:4–5; Titus 3:5).

So that no one may boast. The ancient world ran on honour; boasting was a social institution, and the only question was what you boasted in. Paul had a record to stand on: circumcised on the eighth day, a Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee, blameless under the law (Philippians 3:4–6), and he counted it as rubbish beside knowing Christ. If we contributed even one per cent, we could boast of that one per cent: I chose wisely when others did not; the difference, in the end, is me. God removes every ground of pride, so that the only boast left is in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:29–31). And boasting takes quiet forms: the sense that I believed because I was wiser or more open than others; the Calvinist grateful for election who privately feels more perceptive; the long-standing member eyeing the new convert with a touch of seniority. Both came to the cross with nothing; both left with the same righteousness of Christ. The properly told testimony does not cast the speaker as the hero who finally worked it out. The more undeserving the sinner, the brighter the grace: that saved a wretch like me. This gives a simple test of any version of the gospel: does it leave room for anyone to boast?

What it does not mean. Not that faith is unnecessary because God does everything: no one is saved without believing. Not that good works do not matter: verse 10 follows at once. And “not of works” does not mean that God saves people while they remain unchanged. He saves us from sin, not in it. Works are excluded as the ground of salvation, not as its fruit.

Where Christians differ: is faith itself a gift? Arminians hold that God offers salvation and gives everyone the ability to believe, but that faith itself is the human response. Reformed theology holds that faith, too, is God’s gift, granted to those he has made alive (Philippians 1:29; Acts 13:48; 2 Peter 1:1). Even if “this” in verse 8 refers to the whole package, faith is part of the package. Verdict: faith is God’s gift; we believe, but we believe because God has given us life (v. 5).

If faith is God’s gift, what should I do if I do not have it? Do what the gospel tells you to do: come to Christ, and ask. God does not give faith in some sealed room; he gives it through his word, because faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (Romans 10:17). So put yourself where that word is: read the Gospels, sit under faithful preaching, talk with a Christian you trust. And pray honestly, even if your prayer is only, Lord, I want to believe; help me. Jesus promised that the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13), and he has never turned away anyone who came to him (John 6:37). The very fact that you want faith may be the first stirring of the life this chapter describes. Do not wait until you feel ready. Turn to him now.

Where Christians differ: justification. Roman Catholic teaching (Council of Trent, 1547) holds that justification includes the inner renewal of the person, begins at baptism, can be increased by good works, and can be lost by mortal sin. The Reformers taught that justification is a legal declaration: God pronounces the sinner righteous, not because of any righteousness in him, but because Christ’s righteousness is counted to him, received by faith alone (Romans 3:24–28; 4:5). Renewal always follows, but it is not the ground of our standing with God. Verdict: by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone (Westminster Confession 11.1). Verses 8–10 together say it exactly: saved not by works, but for works.

In a sentence. For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith; and none of this comes from you, it is God’s gift, not a reward for anything you have done, so that no one can boast.

On a Tuesday. When you feel you have been a good Christian this week and God must be pleased with you, or a bad one and he must be finished with you, come back to this verse. Your standing rests on his gift, not on your week.

For worship. Grace is the most God-shaped word in the Bible, because it describes a giving only he could do. He gives to enemies, gives without price, gives even the hand that receives the gift, and leaves nothing behind for us to boast in but him. That is not a slight on us; it is the glory of the Giver. Every saved sinner in heaven will be living proof that salvation belongs to our God and to the Lamb (Revelation 7:10). Bless the Lord who will not share the credit for our rescue, because he will not let us lean on anything less sure than himself.
verseByVerse.note: “This” most naturally refers to the whole of salvation by grace through faith.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them.

For. Paul explains why salvation cannot come from our works (v. 9): because we ourselves are God’s work. A painting does not make the painter.

His workmanship. Greek poiēma, from which comes our word poem: something made, a work of craft or art, a masterpiece. The emphasis falls on his: his work we are, not our own. And poiēma appears only twice in the New Testament: here, and in Romans 1:20, where it means the created universe, the things that have been made, through which God’s power and divine nature are clearly seen. The word Paul reaches for to describe the galaxies is the word he reaches for to describe you. Of those two works, the second cost God far more. The first he spoke into being; the second required a death.

Created in Christ Jesus. Salvation is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17; Galatians 6:15). As God created the first world out of nothing by his word, so he creates new people in Christ. Not a renovation of the old self, but a new beginning.

For good works. The purpose of the new creation. Good works are actions that please God: done in faith, according to his commands, from love, for his glory. Paul gives no checklist, on purpose. They include the large and visible, mission, justice, generosity, and the small and hidden: honest work, a faithful marriage, patience with hard people, the very things he lists in 4:25–32. The plumber who works well and charges fairly, the employee who works as to the Lord (6:7), the parent who disciplines with warmth (6:4): these are good works in Paul’s sense. Listening well to someone lonely. Going back to apologise. Doing a hidden job thoroughly. We are God’s masterpiece, and masterpieces are made not to be stored, but displayed (Matthew 5:16).

Which God prepared beforehand. As God planned our salvation before the foundation of the world (1:4), he planned the good works that would follow. Not that you are a robot running a script, but that the Christian life is not something you must invent from scratch or keep going by willpower. God not only prepares us for good works; he prepares good works for us. So the question is not, what good works should I invent? but, what has God put in front of me today? The neighbour in need, the unexpected chance to serve, the gift waiting to be used.

What if I miss the good works God prepared for me? You will sometimes fail to do the good in front of you, and that is sin to confess, not a plan you have ruined. God prepared these works knowing exactly who you are, failures included, and his purpose for your life does not hang on your never putting a foot wrong (Romans 8:28). Nor are they hidden in a maze for you to find. Most of them are plain: the commands of Scripture, and the needs God puts in front of you, met as you have opportunity (Galatians 6:10). For the bigger decisions, a job, a move, whom to marry, choose wisely within what Scripture allows, take counsel, pray, and go forward without fear that you have picked the wrong door. The God who prepared the road also guides the walker.

That we should walk in them. A word Paul has already used in this chapter, and it slips past because it is so ordinary: walk. In verse 2 that is exactly what the dead were doing: in which you once walked, following the course of this world. Now, at the close of the same paragraph: that we should walk in them. The same verb, the opposite road. And he does not say we should admire good works, or intend them, or feel warmly towards them. Walk. A walk is made of steps, taken one at a time, usually with nobody watching. Conversion did not stop you walking. It changed the road. Chapters 4–6 will spell out what this walk looks like (4:1, 17; 5:2, 8, 15).

Not by works, but for works. Verses 8–10 together are the whole Reformation in miniature. Works are the fruit of salvation, never the root. A child does not obey to earn a place in the family; he obeys because he already belongs. The Reformers put it this way: we are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone. Faith that produces no works is not saving faith (James 2:17–18).

Not a masterpiece? Some readers meet the word masterpiece and think: not me. Notice that you are not the one asked to assess the work. You are standing inside it while it is still being made, the one place from which no work of art ever looked finished. A house halfway through renovation looks worse than before anyone touched it, walls opened, floors lifted, dust everywhere, and that is not evidence that the builder has failed. It is evidence that he has begun. The worth of a work is set by the artist, never by the material’s opinion of itself. He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6), and he does not abandon his canvases.

What it does not mean. Not that good works are optional extras for keen Christians: they are what we were created for. Nor that good works earn us anything: they are God’s gift too, since he prepared them and works in us to do them (Philippians 2:13). And “prepared beforehand” does not make us puppets. God’s plan works through our real choices, not around them.

In a sentence. For we are what God has made, created anew in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance for us to live out.

On a Tuesday. Ask God this morning to show you the good works he has prepared for you today, and expect to find them in ordinary places: your desk, your kitchen, your street.

For worship. The God who flung out the galaxies with a word has taken up the slower, costlier art of remaking sinners, and he works with the patience of a master craftsman. Not one of his works is an accident, and none is abandoned on the bench. He creates us in Christ, he prepares our good works before we exist, and then he works in us to walk in them (Philippians 2:13). From the first stroke to the last, the glory belongs to the Artist. When the finished work is at last unveiled, no one will admire the clay. They will praise the hands that shaped it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gentile believers should remember what they were: called uncircumcised, without Christ, excluded from Israel, strangers to God’s covenants, hopeless and godless. Now in Christ, those who were far away have been brought near by his blood. He is our peace: he has made Jew and Gentile one, demolishing the wall of hostility by setting aside the law’s commands and regulations, creating one new humanity and reconciling both to God through the cross. He came preaching peace to those far and near, and through him both have access to the Father by one Spirit. So Gentiles are no longer foreigners but fellow citizens with God’s people and members of his household, built on the apostles and prophets with Christ as cornerstone, growing into a holy temple, a dwelling for God by the Spirit.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Atonement and the New Community

This passage reveals the ecclesiological dimensions of the atonement — a dimension often underemphasised in evangelical theology. We tend to think of Christ's death in purely individual terms: He died for me, my sins are forgiven, I am reconciled to God. All of this is gloriously true. But Paul insists that the cross accomplished something more: it created a new community. Christ died not only to reconcile individuals to God (vertical reconciliation) but to reconcile estranged human beings to one another (horizontal reconciliation). He "reconciled us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility" (v.16).

This means that the unity of the church is not merely a practical or organisational goal; it is a theological reality purchased by Christ's blood. To live in division, to maintain the walls that Christ has torn down, to prefer the company of people like us over the diverse community Christ has created — this is a denial of the atonement. Every genuinely reconciled, cross-cultural Christian community is a proclamation of the gospel: not with words but with existence. Its very existence says: the cross is real, the wall is down, God has made one new man.

The metaphor of the temple (vv.19–22) carries the further implication that the church's holiness matters. The old temple was the place where God dwelt, and its holiness was fiercely guarded.
