The new temple — the church — is also the dwelling place of God by his Spirit. The community of believers is not merely a gathering of like-minded people; it is the sacred space where the Holy God has chosen to make his home on earth. This gives both dignity and responsibility to every local church: you are the temple of God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The stone wall of the Jerusalem temple — the soreg — was not a metaphor. Inscriptions warning Gentiles that entry beyond it meant death have been found by archaeologists. The barrier was physical, legal, and deadly. When Paul says Christ has broken down "the dividing wall of hostility," his Jewish and Gentile readers understood exactly what wall he meant. They may have stood on opposite sides of it. Now they sat side by side at the Lord's table, eating and drinking together, addressed as fellow citizens and members of the same household. The sociological miracle was visible and daily, and it pointed to a theological reality: the cross had accomplished what no social programme could.

Now: The church in our age still struggles with the walls that Christ has torn down. Racial segregation in churches persists in many places. Class divisions shape congregational culture in ways we rarely examine. Political tribalism has entered sanctuaries and split families of faith. Against all of this, Ephesians 2 speaks with prophetic force: the wall is down. Christ killed the hostility. The new humanity he created is more fundamental than any human division that preceded it. The church that reflects this — that is visibly, sacrificially, joyfully diverse across the lines that divide the surrounding world — is not merely being socially progressive. It is being theologically faithful. It is showing the world what the cross actually accomplished.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore remember that at one time you Gentiles in the flesh, called “the uncircumcision” by what is called the circumcision, which is made in the flesh by hands —
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore remember that at one time you Gentiles in the flesh, called “the uncircumcision” by what is called the circumcision, which is made in the flesh by hands —

Therefore. Because of verses 1–10. If God saved both Jew and Gentile by grace alone, with no works to boast of, then the wall between them has no ground left to stand on.

Remember. Paul does not suggest it; he commands it, because forgetting is what we do naturally, and Christians forget this particular thing faster than most. The believer of thirty years, or the one raised in a Christian home who cannot recall a time before, drifts towards feeling like the sort of person God would naturally have wanted, as though grace had found something in him worth finding. The cure is not a mood but an act of deliberate recollection. God trained Israel in exactly this. Again and again the law says, remember that you were a slave in Egypt, and it is nearly always attached to a command about somebody else: remember you were a slave, therefore release your servant generously (Deuteronomy 15:15); you know the heart of a stranger, therefore do not oppress him (Exodus 23:9). Memory of your own rescue was meant to drive your treatment of outsiders. Paul is about to tell a mixed and uneasy church to live as one body, and he begins by reminding the Gentile half how far outside they once stood.

You Gentiles in the flesh. “Gentiles” (ethnē, the nations) was the Jewish word for everyone else. “In the flesh” here means physically, by birth: they were not born into God’s covenant people.

Called “the uncircumcision” by what is called the circumcision. These were labels, and the first was an insult. Circumcision was the sign God gave Abraham of his covenant (Genesis 17:9–14), and it had become the badge of Jewish identity. Many Jews called Gentiles the uncircumcision with contempt, as David spoke of this uncircumcised Philistine (1 Samuel 17:26). Look at how the name works. It is not a description of anything they were; it defines a whole people by an absence, by the mark they did not carry. Every community has words like that, and they all reduce a human being to a lack. Paul quotes it on purpose, so that his readers hear once more the word that used to put them outside, and will never be comfortable using its like about anybody else. A man who genuinely remembers being on the outside cannot easily keep another person there. And Paul says “so-called” of both labels: both are names given by people, not God’s final verdict.

Which is made in the flesh by hands. A pointed phrase. In the Greek Old Testament “made with hands” is regularly used of idols (Leviticus 26:1; Isaiah 46:6). Paul hints that circumcision of the body, valued for itself, is merely human. God always wanted circumcision of the heart (Deuteronomy 10:16; 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4), and in Christ believers receive a circumcision made without hands (Colossians 2:11). The true Jew is one inwardly (Romans 2:28–29). He starts here because the wider the chasm looks, the more astonishing the bridge becomes.

What it does not mean. Not that circumcision was a mistake or that God’s covenant with Israel was worthless: it was his gift and pointed to Christ (Romans 3:1–2; 9:4–5). Paul objects to the outward sign being treated as the ground of standing with God, and used to despise others.

In a sentence. So remember that you were once Gentiles by birth, called the uncircumcised by those who call themselves the circumcised, though theirs is only a mark made on the body by human hands.

On a Tuesday. Think back to what you were before Christ. Then think of the people your church tends to look down on, and remember that you once stood where they stand.

For worship. The God of Israel never meant his covenant to stay a fenced field. He had promised Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed in him, and he kept that promise through every label and insult the nations bore. Christ, born under the law and circumcised on the eighth day (Luke 2:21), kept the covenant perfectly, and then gave the nations what no knife could give: a circumcision of the heart, made without hands (Colossians 2:11). Praise the faithful God who remembers outsiders, and who turns those once despised into his own treasured people.

verseByVerse.quote: remember that you were at that time separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
remember that you were at that time separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world.

At that time. Before they believed: the “once” of verses 2–3. Paul lines up five descriptions of life outside, each deeper than the last, the fullest portrait of lostness in the New Testament. Not to shame the reader, but so that the rescue in verse 13 lands with full weight. You cannot treasure the nearness without first feeling the distance.

1. Separated from Christ. “Christ” means Messiah, the anointed King God promised to Israel. The hope of the Messiah belonged to Israel (Romans 9:5). Gentiles had no share in it, no framework in which his coming could even be expected. This is the root loss from which the rest grow.

2. Alienated from the commonwealth of Israel. “Commonwealth” (politeia) means citizenship, membership of a nation with its rights. Israel was the people God had formed, ruled and lived among. Gentiles could watch the story from outside, but had no share in it.

3. Strangers to the covenants of promise. God made covenants with Abraham (Genesis 12; 15; 17), with Israel at Sinai, and with David (2 Samuel 7), and promised a new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31–34). All of them carried one great promise: I will be your God, and you shall be my people, and in Abraham’s offspring all nations will be blessed. Gentiles were outside these binding promises; a stranger (xenos) had no claim on what God had bound himself to give.

4. Having no hope. Not that they had no wishes or plans, but no sure hope beyond death. The ancient world was full of religion, with temples on every corner; what it lacked was any certain promise that death was not the end. A common epitaph on ancient tombs ran: I was not; I was; I am not; I do not care. Paul says the same elsewhere of those who grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

5. Without God in the world. Greek atheoi, from which comes our word atheist. And Ephesus was crowded with gods: Artemis, the emperor, a host of others. Paul does not mean they had no religion, but that they did not know the one true God who had revealed himself by name and kept his promises. Gods everywhere, and God nowhere.

What about people who have never heard of Christ? Paul does not soften it: outside Christ there is no hope, because there is no other name by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). But God’s judgement is perfectly fair. No one will be condemned for rejecting a Christ he never heard of. People are judged for their sins against the light they had, the witness of creation and conscience, which all of us have resisted (Romans 1:20; 2:12–16). No one is innocent, and no one will be able to say that God was unjust. That is exactly why the church sends missionaries: Paul asks how anyone can believe in one of whom he has never heard (Romans 10:14). God has people in every tribe and language, and he will gather them (Revelation 5:9). So leave the judgement to the Judge of all the earth, who will do right (Genesis 18:25), and give, pray and go.

The logic. The list moves from the specific to the total. Without the Messiah, no place in God’s people; without a place, no promises; without promises, no hope; without hope, no God. Everything hangs on the first: being separated from Christ is the root of every other loss.

The vocabulary of exclusion. Read the list with a particular reader in view, because Paul has assembled the exact language of not belonging: alienated, strangers, no hope, without God. If you have ever stood at the edge of a group and known, without anyone saying it, that you did not belong, the family you married into, the workplace where the others share a history you do not, even the church where everyone seems to have known each other for years, you already know the taste of every word here. Paul is naming one of the most painful experiences a human being can have, and telling you it was once your standing before God, in the only place where belonging finally counts. And what follows is aimed exactly where it hurts. The outsiders were not given advice, or a procedure, or a probation. They were brought near, in a single movement, by somebody else’s blood. And the five losses are not softened. They are reversed one by one: no longer separated from Christ but in him; no longer alienated but citizens; no longer strangers to the covenants but heirs; no longer without hope but holding an inheritance; no longer without God but his dwelling. The answer to the whole catalogue of exclusion is not a policy. It is a Person.

What it does not mean. Not that Gentiles were outside God’s rule or care: he gave them rain and harvests and did not leave himself without witness (Acts 14:17). Nor that every Jew was automatically saved: not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel (Romans 9:6). The point is Israel’s privileged position as the people of the promises, a position the Gentiles did not share.

In a sentence. Remember that at that time you were without the Messiah, shut out from citizenship in Israel, outsiders to the covenants that carried God’s promise, with no hope and without God in the world.

On a Tuesday. This describes many of your neighbours and colleagues. Pray for them with compassion, not contempt, and be ready to tell them about the hope that is in you.

For worship. Christ walked into a world crowded with temples and empty of hope, and he loved it. He did not wait for the nations to find their way into Israel’s promises; he came to the place where they stood, without hope and without God, and became their hope and brought them to God. Every privilege this verse lists was his by right as Israel’s Messiah, and every one of them he shares with those who had none. Worship the Christ who is himself the promise, the covenant, the hope and the presence of God, freely given to strangers.

verseByVerse.quote: But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.

But now. The second great turning point of the chapter, matching “But God” in verse 4. There the change was from death to life; here, from distance to nearness. The same Christ makes both possible. Five darknesses, and then a single light that makes all five vanish.

In Christ Jesus. The exact reversal of “separated from Christ” (v. 12). The first loss is undone, and with it all the others.

Far off … brought near. These were almost technical terms. Jewish writers used “far off” for the Gentile world, and “brought near” for a proselyte, a Gentile admitted into the covenant people. Isaiah had promised peace, peace, to the far and to the near (Isaiah 57:19), and Peter preached that the promise is for all who are far off (Acts 2:39). So Paul takes the standard word for Gentile distance and answers it with the standard word for admission, and then, in the verses that follow, blows the standard meaning apart. How near is near? Not near enough to watch from a respectful distance. Not admitted to an outer court and told to be grateful. Within nine verses these people are fellow citizens, then members of the household, and finally stones built into the temple where God lives. They began outside a barrier that threatened death to anyone who crossed it, and they end up being the building.

By the blood of Christ. “Blood” in Scripture means life given up in death, especially in sacrifice: the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement (Leviticus 17:11). The distance was never really geographical or cultural; it was moral. That is why the alternatives could never work. Dialogue does not remove guilt; time does not erase it; shared values do not answer for what has been done. And this was never only a Gentile problem. The Jew inside the barrier could not walk into God’s presence either. He watched a priest go in for him, once a year, and never without blood (Hebrews 9:7). The wall kept Gentiles out of the court; sin kept everybody out of the holiest place. So blood is not the outsider’s unfortunate entry fee, charged to latecomers. It always was the only door there has ever been. What changed at the cross is not that a second door was opened for a second class of people, but that the final sacrifice was offered once, and both walked through it together (1:7; Colossians 1:20).

Have been brought. Passive: someone else did it. We did not travel the distance; we were carried.

What it does not mean. Not that Gentiles now join Israel by becoming Jewish, nor that Jews remain near without Christ. Both come near to God in exactly the same way: through Christ, by the Spirit (v. 18). And the nearness was not produced by your feeling close to God, and it is not undone by your feeling far from him. It rests on an event outside you, at a cost you did not pay. A believer may feel a very long way off on a Tuesday afternoon and still be, in the only sense this verse means, near.

In a sentence. But now, in Christ Jesus, you who were once far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ.

For worship. You were far off, and you have been carried all the way into the presence of God, at the price of his Son’s blood. Nothing you feel today can move you back.

parallels.desc: peace, peace, to the far and to the near

verseByVerse.quote: For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility

For he himself. The Greek puts “he” first, with emphasis: autos. Peace is not a treaty, a programme or a feeling; it is a Person. Christ does not broker a settlement between two parties and step back. He is the peace, and it cannot be separated from him. Micah promised a ruler from Bethlehem of whom it would be said, he shall be their peace (Micah 5:5), and Isaiah named the Messiah the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6). Not as the world gives do I give to you (John 14:27): the world manages conflict; Christ gives himself.

Our peace. Peace here has two dimensions, which the passage takes in turn: peace between peoples (vv. 14–15), and peace with God (v. 16). The second is the foundation of the first.

Has made us both one. Jew and Gentile, the deepest religious division of the ancient world. Jews thanked God daily that they were not Gentiles; many Gentiles despised Jews as odd and antisocial. Not brought closer: made one. The way it works is union with Christ. Two people each joined to him are thereby joined to each other, whatever their cultures say, because the ground at the foot of the cross is perfectly level (Galatians 3:28).

The dividing wall of hostility. In the Jerusalem temple, a stone balustrade about one and a half metres high (the soreg) separated the outer Court of the Gentiles from the inner courts. Notices in Greek and Latin warned that any foreigner who went beyond it would be responsible for his own death. One of these inscriptions was found in 1871 and can be seen today in Istanbul. Paul himself was nearly lynched when he was accused of bringing a Gentile past it: Trophimus, an Ephesian (Acts 21:28–29). The Ephesians would know the story. That wall said, in stone and law: the presence of God is not for you; stay outside. Paul says Christ broke it down, not lowered it or made it easier to cross. When Paul wrote, it was still standing; it fell with the temple in AD 70. But in God’s eyes it had already fallen at the cross, the day the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51).

Of hostility. The wall of stone expressed a wall in hearts: mutual hatred, contempt and suspicion.

In his flesh. In his body, on a Roman cross, on a particular Friday. The wall was not dismantled by education, negotiation or goodwill, nor by a transaction at a safe distance. The one who hung there took both hostilities, between God and man and between Jew and Gentile, into himself, and did not pass them on (Colossians 1:20–22).

Was the Son undoing the Father’s work? If the separation between Jew and Gentile was in a real sense God’s own doing, the law, the covenant signs, the whole apparatus of holy distinction, how can Christ be praised for demolishing it? Because he is finishing it, not undoing it. The separation was like a cast on a broken limb. Its purpose was to preserve the people through whom the Messiah would come, and to teach the world, in terms nobody could mistake, that God is holy and access to him is no casual matter. The law was a guardian until Christ came (Galatians 3:23–25). When the bone has knitted, the cast comes off, not because it was a mistake, but because it has done its work.

It was expensive. This unity did not come naturally to anyone. For a Jewish believer it meant sitting at a Gentile’s table and eating what was on it, setting aside food laws his forebears had died rather than break. For a Gentile it meant accepting that salvation had come through a nation he had been raised to think peculiar. Much of Acts is the story of how hard it proved: a sheet let down from heaven three times before Peter would believe it (Acts 10), a council called because the argument would not settle (Acts 15), and Peter himself later withdrawing from Gentile tables until Paul opposed him to his face (Galatians 2:11–14). Paul announces an accomplished fact, and then spends the rest of the letter urging the church to go and live inside it.

What it does not mean. Not that ethnic, cultural or national differences disappear, as if all believers must become culturally the same. In Revelation people of every tribe and language worship together, still distinct (Revelation 7:9). What disappears is the hostility and the barrier: the idea that any group stands nearer to God, or is more worthy of his people, than another. Nor is peace among people possible without the cross. Christ is our peace; peace without him is a truce.

Is it wrong to have separate churches for different languages or cultures? Not in itself. Where people cannot understand one another, a congregation in their own language may be the loving thing, and the apostles took practical care that Greek-speaking widows were not overlooked by appointing men from among them (Acts 6:1–6). It becomes wrong when the arrangement becomes a wall: when a church is closed in practice to people unlike its members, or when Christians pick a church to avoid people of another colour, class or background. Test your own church with honest questions. Would a stranger from another culture be welcomed, befriended and given a full share, including in leadership? Do we treat Christians in other congregations as family? Do we ever pray or work with them? Christ has made us one. Our churches should look, as far as we can make them, like people who believe it.

In a sentence. For Christ himself is our peace: he has made Jews and Gentiles one, and in his own body he has broken down the wall of hostility that divided them,

On a Tuesday. The stone wall is rubble; the instinct that built it is not. Find your own wall with two questions: who do you sit near on a Sunday without ever having decided to? And whose home have you actually been inside? Racism, snobbery and cold welcomes deny what the cross has done. Christ died to destroy these walls; do not rebuild them.

For worship. The Prince of Peace did not bring peace from a distance; he became it. The wall that told the nations to keep out was answered not with a decree but with a body: his flesh, given up on the cross. In that one death he opened the way to God and the way to one another. Glory to the Christ in whom the bitterest enmities of the ancient world met and were ended, and who still stands among his people as their peace, so that former strangers kneel side by side before the same Father and call each other family.
verseByVerse.note: The temple courts had a stone barrier with inscriptions forbidding Gentiles, on pain of death, to go further.

parallels.desc: he shall be their peace

verseByVerse.quote: by abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace,
verseByVerse.commentary:
by abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace,

By abolishing. The word (katargeō) means to make ineffective, to put out of action. Christ did this in his death: the cross brought the old arrangement to its end.

The law of commandments expressed in ordinances. Paul piles up words for a legal system: law, commandments, ordinances. He means the Mosaic law as a whole covenant arrangement, especially the parts that marked Israel off from the nations: circumcision, food laws, sacrifices, the calendar of feasts and Sabbaths, purity rules (Colossians 2:14–17). These were God-given and good, a fence to keep Israel distinct until the Messiah came (Galatians 3:23–25), and a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:17). But they also made Jew and Gentile two peoples who could not eat together. When the reality arrived, the scaffolding came down so the building could be seen.

What it does not mean. Not that God’s moral will has been abolished. Paul quotes the fifth commandment in this very letter (6:2–3), and chapters 4–5 are full of moral commands. Reformed theology distinguishes the moral law, which reflects God’s character and binds all people at all times, from the ceremonial law (sacrifices, priesthood, purity), fulfilled in Christ, and the civil law of Israel as a nation, which expired with that nation (Westminster Confession 19.3–5). Jesus came not to abolish the law but to fulfil it (Matthew 5:17). What is abolished is the law as a covenant that divided and condemned, not God’s holy will. Nor does it mean that Christians become lawless: believers now keep God’s law from a new heart, by the Spirit (Romans 8:4).

How do I know which Old Testament commands I should still keep? Read each one through Christ, and ask what the New Testament does with it. The sacrifices, priesthood, food laws, feasts and purity rules pointed to him and are fulfilled in him: you keep them by trusting the sacrifice they foreshadowed, not by repeating them (Hebrews 10:1–14; Mark 7:19; Colossians 2:16–17). The civil laws of Israel as a nation are not a code for modern states, though they still teach principles of justice and mercy (Westminster 19.4). The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments and in loving God and neighbour, still shows how God’s children live, and the New Testament repeats it again and again (Romans 13:8–10). On the Sabbath command Reformed Christians differ: many keep it on the Lord’s Day, the first day of the week, as a day set apart for worship and rest (Westminster 21.7–8), while others see the Sabbath fulfilled in Christ’s rest (Colossians 2:16–17) and still gladly give the Lord’s Day to worship. The second is the view taken here: Christ is our Sabbath rest (Hebrews 4:9–10), and the Lord’s Day is a gift rather than the fourth commandment moved to Sunday, so no one should bind another’s conscience over it (Romans 14:5). You obey all this not to be saved, but because you have been.

That he might create in himself. Notice the verb: create (ktizō). Paul does not say Christ negotiated one new man, or organised one, or assembled one from the parts available. It is creation language, the word for what God did in Genesis, and the word Paul used five verses ago of you personally (v. 10). So the church is not at bottom an institution. Anyone can found an institution; committees do it every week. Nobody can make a creature. The unity of the church is not an achievement that gifted leaders could reproduce elsewhere with the right method. God made it, and the most any of us can do is refuse to damage it.

One new man in place of the two. “Man” here (anthrōpos) means a humanity, a new kind of people. Not Jews absorbing Gentiles, who need not be circumcised, nor Gentiles absorbing Jews, but a third thing: a new humanity in Christ, in which the old division no longer defines anyone (Galatians 3:28; Colossians 3:11). Early Christians were sometimes called a third race. And be clear what it does not mean. A Jew does not stop being a Jew, nor a Gentile a Gentile: remain as you were called (1 Corinthians 7:18–20). The last picture Scripture gives of the redeemed is not a uniform crowd but a great multitude from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages (Revelation 7:9). So this is neither a melting pot that boils the cultures away, nor a federation of groups keeping a polite distance. It is one new humanity in which the differences remain and simply stop deciding anything. Your background is still yours. It is no longer your standing.

So making peace. Peace here is not a mood that eventually settled over the situation, nor what happens when two parties grow tired of arguing. It was made, as anything is made, with materials, labour and cost. The material was his flesh; the labour was a crucifixion; the cost was everything he had. That is why peace in a church is never simply the absence of friction or good manners in the porch afterwards. It is the keeping of something expensive that somebody else paid for. Paul will put it exactly that way: eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (4:3). He does not tell them to create it. It has been created. He tells them not to lose it.

Where Christians differ: Israel and the church. Dispensationalists hold that Israel and the church are two distinct peoples with distinct promises: the church is a parenthesis, and God will resume his earthly plan for national Israel in a future millennium. Some have taught that the church has simply replaced Israel, and that the Jewish people have no further place in God’s purposes. Covenant theology holds that there is one people of God throughout history, the one olive tree of Romans 11, now including believing Jews and Gentiles together, and that the promises to Israel find their fulfilment in Christ and his church. Verdict: one people of God in Christ, as “one new man” and “one body” say. Gentiles are grafted into Israel’s olive tree, not planted beside it (Romans 11:17). But God has not finished with the Jewish people: Paul expects many Jews to come to faith in Christ (Romans 11:23–26), and they will come into the same one body, not a separate one.

In a sentence. by setting aside the law with its commandments and regulations, so that he might create in himself one new humanity out of the two, and so make peace,

On a Tuesday. Do not add extra rules, cultural habits or preferences as conditions for belonging to the church. Christ died to remove such walls.

For worship. Only the Creator can make a new humanity, and here he has done it, in his Son. Christ fulfilled every ordinance that marked Israel off from the nations: he kept every commandment and offered the sacrifice all the sacrifices foreshadowed, and so brought the shadows to their substance. Out of Jew and Gentile he has made one new man in himself, as truly as God once formed Adam from the dust. Praise the Lord whose cross is a workshop of creation, who did not merely end a quarrel but brought into being a people that had never existed before, bearing his own name.

verseByVerse.quote: And might reconcile us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And might reconcile us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility.

And might reconcile. To reconcile is to turn enemies into friends by removing the cause of the hostility. The word here (apokatallassō) is strengthened: a complete reconciliation, used only here and in Colossians 1:20–22. And it assumes something polite religion prefers to leave vague. You do not reconcile people who were merely unacquainted, or who drifted apart through busyness. Reconciliation is needed where there has been real enmity: while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Romans 5:10). The trouble was never that God was distant and we were confused. There was hostility, and that is why the remedy had to be a death and not an explanation.

Us both to God. Here is the logic of the whole passage. Jew and Gentile could not be at peace with each other while both were at war with God. The vertical problem lies beneath the horizontal one. Both were children of wrath (v. 3). When both are reconciled to God through the same cross, they find themselves standing side by side. That is why purely social attempts at unity cannot last: they try to mend the horizontal without the vertical.

Whose hostility? Our hostility to God is real (Romans 8:7; Colossians 1:21). But Scripture also speaks of God’s just opposition to us: we were children of wrath (v. 3). Reconciliation deals with both. At the cross, God’s wrath against sin was borne by Christ as our substitute (Romans 5:9–10; 2 Corinthians 5:21), and so the cause of the enmity is removed on God’s side; and through the gospel our hearts are won, so the enmity is removed on ours.

In one body. Probably a double meaning. First, Christ’s physical body on the cross, in which he reconciled us (Colossians 1:22). Second, the church, the one body of Christ (1:23; 4:4) into which both are brought. One body died, so that one body might live. And notice what that means. God did not reconcile us to himself and then, as a separate matter, suggest we try to get along with one another. The reconciling puts you somewhere. You are not saved privately and later invited to consider joining a church if convenient. The same act that brings you to God sets you down among people you did not choose, and who did not choose you. The arrangement is not open to renegotiation.

Through the cross. Not through Christ’s teaching or example alone, but through his death. Reconciliation is costly.

Thereby killing the hostility. Paul does not say the hostility was soothed, or managed, or talked through in a series of meetings. It was put to death, the way a living thing is put to death, because that is what hostility is: not a regrettable atmosphere, but something with a life of its own, which grows when fed and routinely outlives the people who started it. And see where it died. Human hostility usually kills people. They took Christ out and killed him, and in being killed, he killed the thing that was killing everybody. The cross is the one place where hostility did its absolute worst and was destroyed by the very thing it did. Christ did not kill his enemies; he died for them.

Must I be reconciled with a believer who wronged me and will not admit it? You must forgive, and you must be willing; but full reconciliation takes two. Forgiving means letting go of revenge and handing the account to God (Romans 12:19; Mark 11:25), and that you can do alone, today. Reconciliation means restored trust, and that needs repentance on the other side (Luke 17:3). So do what lies with you: pray for him, refuse to speak against him, and go to him privately; if he will not listen, follow the steps Jesus gave (Matthew 18:15–17). You are to live at peace as far as it depends on you (Romans 12:18), and not further. Where there has been abuse, forgiveness never means returning to danger. Get safe, tell the elders, and report any crime to the police. Trust, once broken, is rebuilt slowly, by evidence of real change.

What it does not mean. Not that the cross changed God from hating to loving: God’s love sent Christ (Romans 5:8). God himself provided the sacrifice that satisfied his own justice. Nor does it mean that everyone is automatically reconciled whether they believe or not: reconciliation is received through faith, which is why the next verse speaks of preaching (v. 17; 2 Corinthians 5:20).

In a sentence. and might reconcile both of them to God in one body through the cross, by which he put their hostility to death.

On a Tuesday. If you are at odds with a fellow believer, the order is not negotiable: vertical first. Go to the cross and look honestly at the size of what was forgiven you there. It is very hard to keep a grievance at full strength in that place, which is the whole point of the servant forgiven ten thousand talents who went out to collect a hundred denarii (Matthew 18:23–35).

For worship. Behold the wisdom of the cross. The hostility of man against God, and of man against man, poured itself out on one innocent body, and that body bore it all, together with the wrath our sin deserved, and rose from the grave with the enmity dead behind him. The Father did not wait for his enemies to make the first move; he gave his Son to make peace while they were still enemies (Romans 5:10). Worship the God who reconciles at his own expense, and the Son who went willingly to the place where every enmity was finally put to death. There is no true peace anywhere that does not flow from that hill.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near. For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near. For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.

He came and preached peace. Paul is quoting Isaiah: how beautiful are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace (Isaiah 52:7), and peace, peace, to the far and to the near (Isaiah 57:19). What the prophet announced has now been carried out in person. But when did Christ preach to those far off? During his earthly ministry Jesus went almost entirely to Jews; he never preached in Ephesus. Paul means chiefly the risen Christ, preaching through his messengers by his Spirit. How are they to hear without someone preaching? (Romans 10:14–15). The feet belong to the messenger; the voice belongs to Christ. That is not a pious flourish. It means that when the gospel is faithfully preached, from a pulpit, across a kitchen table, or by somebody nervous and doing it badly, Christ himself is doing the preaching. The Ephesians never saw him. They heard him. His first words to the disciples after rising were, Peace be with you (John 20:19–21).

Peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near. The repeated “peace” stresses that both needed it equally. The near ones, the covenant people, with the Scriptures, the temple and the promises, needed the identical message. Nearness was not the same thing as peace. There is a kind of person in every congregation who has never been far off in any social sense: raised in the church, fluent in its songs, never once an outsider. Paul says peace had to be preached to him too, on exactly the same terms.

For through him we both have access. “Access” (prosagōgē) was used of being brought into the presence of a king, ushered in by someone with the standing to bring you, a privilege few had. Under the old covenant, Gentiles could go no further than the outer court; Israelites could not enter the holy place; only the high priest entered the Most Holy Place, once a year, with blood (Hebrews 9:7). Now every believer, Jew or Gentile, can come straight to God, at any time, with confidence (3:12; Hebrews 10:19–22). The torn curtain (Mark 15:38) meant the same thing as the broken wall.

In one Spirit. Why “in one Spirit” and not only “through Christ”? Because the Spirit makes the access real now. Christ opened the way two thousand years ago outside Jerusalem. A believer enters it today not by travelling to Golgotha or by an act of memory, but by the Spirit who lives in him: God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!” (Galatians 4:6). The very cry of “Father” in your prayers is the Spirit at work. And it is one Spirit: not a Jewish route and a Gentile route, but the same welcome for both (1 Corinthians 12:13).

To the Father. The goal of access is not merely forgiveness but family: we come to God as Father (Romans 8:15).

The Trinity. Through the Son, in the Spirit, to the Father. This is the shape of all Christian prayer and worship. Whenever a believer prays, however haltingly, something Trinitarian is happening: the Father is approached, through the Son who opened the way, by the Spirit who carries the prayer from within (Romans 8:26–27). Prayer is never a lonely cry aimed at a distant deity. The Trinity is the architecture of welcome.

What it does not mean. Not that every religion or every sincere seeker has access to God. Access is through him, through Christ alone (John 14:6). Nor does it mean we need no mediator: we need exactly one, and we have him (1 Timothy 2:5). No priest, saint or ritual stands between the believer and the Father.

In a sentence. He came and announced the good news of peace to you who were far away and to those who were near; for through him both of us can come to the Father by the one Spirit.

For worship. The door into the throne room of heaven stands open, the Son holds it, and the Spirit within you cries, Father. Come in. You need no appointment.

verseByVerse.quote: So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone,
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone,

So then. Paul gathers up everything from verses 11–18, and reverses the losses of verse 12 one by one, in three pictures: a city, a family, a temple. The movement is from the edge to the centre, from outside to home.

No longer strangers and aliens. Two words for outsiders. A stranger (xenos) is a foreigner passing through, with no rights. An alien (paroikos) was a resident foreigner: allowed to live in the city, but second-class, without a citizen’s rights. The Gentiles had been both. Now neither.

Fellow citizens with the saints. We hear “citizen” as a mild civic word; in the Roman world it was anything but. Roman citizenship was the most prized status in the empire, with legal protection and the right of appeal to Caesar. Paul stopped a flogging while the straps were being tied simply by asking whether it was lawful to flog a Roman citizen uncondemned; the shaken officer admitted he had bought his citizenship for a large sum, and Paul replied, But I am a citizen by birth (Acts 22:25–29). Set that beside what he tells these Gentiles. They have been made citizens of a commonwealth beside which Rome is a temporary local arrangement, and they did not buy it. They were born into it. Our citizenship is in heaven (Philippians 3:20). “The saints” are God’s people (see 1:1), believing Israel of old and Jewish believers now. Gentiles are not second-class members or guests; they have full and equal citizenship.

Members of the household of God. A step warmer than citizenship (oikeioi). A citizen belongs to a state; a household member belongs to a family. Not a tolerated guest on probation, but family: a Father who provides, brothers and sisters in every nation, a home that cannot be taken away (1 Timothy 3:15).

Built on the foundation. Now the picture changes to a building, and it is temple language on purpose. A foundation is laid once, at the start, and everything rests on it.

Of the apostles and prophets. The apostles were those personally commissioned by the risen Christ as his authoritative witnesses (see 1:1). The prophets here are most likely New Testament prophets, not Old Testament ones: the order is apostles then prophets, and Paul says in 3:5 that the mystery has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets, and in 4:11 lists them together as gifts of the ascended Christ. They are the foundation in their teaching: the revelation of Christ they received and passed on, now preserved in the New Testament. Calvin said plainly that the foundation is the doctrine they preached; move away from it and the whole building falls. That is why sola Scriptura is not a preference but a structural necessity. A church that leaves apostolic teaching does not build higher; it builds on sand.

Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone. Know what that stone did. It was laid first, at the corner, cut and squared with great care, and every other stone in the building took its line and level from it (akrogōniaios). The mason did not measure each new stone against the one below; he measured against the corner. That is why an error there is never small. A wall built off a crooked corner is wrong all the way up, more obviously wrong the higher it rises, and cannot be put right by adjusting the top. That is how churches drift, almost never by one dramatic decision: they quietly begin to take their line from something other than Christ, a founder’s personality, a denomination’s habits, the culture’s instincts, the preferences of whoever gives most, and every stone laid after that looks fine on its own and is out of true. Isaiah promised a precious cornerstone laid in Zion (Isaiah 28:16); the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone (Psalm 118:22), and Jesus claimed it for himself (Matthew 21:42; 1 Peter 2:4–7). The builders said, this one does not fit. God said, this one holds everything together.

What it does not mean. Not that the apostles and prophets are more important than Christ: the foundation is their witness to him, and he is the stone that fixes it. Nor that new apostles and prophets with the same foundational authority continue today. A foundation is laid once; the building rises on it. This is one reason the canon of Scripture is closed: the foundation is complete, and the church is built on it, not added to it.

Where Christians differ: the continuation of prophecy. Continuationists hold that the gift of prophecy continues, often as a lesser, fallible gift distinct from the foundational prophets of this verse. Cessationists hold that apostles and prophets belonged to the foundation-laying period and ceased with it, and that God now speaks through the completed Scriptures. Verdict: cessationist, held charitably. If the apostles and prophets are the foundation, they cannot also be the walls. And whatever view one takes, no claimed word today may add to or stand alongside the apostolic foundation.

If prophecy has ceased, does God still speak to me personally? Yes: every time you open the Bible. Scripture is not God’s old voice, now silent; it is his living voice, and the Spirit uses it to comfort, warn and direct you personally (Hebrews 4:12; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). He also guides you by his providence and through the counsel of wise believers, and he may bring a verse or a person to mind at just the right moment. Such promptings can be his kindness, but they are not new revelation. Test every impression by Scripture, weigh it with others, and never say that God told you something as though it bound anyone else (Westminster 1.6). In his word you have everything you need for faith and life, so you need not hunt for hidden messages. Open the book: he is speaking.

In a sentence. So you are no longer foreigners and outsiders, but fellow citizens with God’s people and members of his household, built on the foundation laid by the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone.

On a Tuesday. Treat the new believer, the refugee and the stranger in your church as family, because they are. And test every teaching you hear by the apostolic foundation, the Scriptures.

For worship. The God who once filled the tabernacle and wrote his law on stone has taken outsiders into his own household and given them his name. He does not grant visas; he adopts. And the house he builds rests on the word of his apostles and prophets, which means it rests on Christ, the stone the builders rejected and the Father chose. Bless the Lord Jesus, precious and sure, laid in Zion so that whoever trusts in him will never be put to shame (1 Peter 2:6). Every outsider who comes to him finds the door already open and a place laid at the table.
verseByVerse.note: A cornerstone was the first, carefully placed stone that set the line of the whole building.

parallels.desc: a precious cornerstone

verseByVerse.quote: in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord.

In whom. In Christ, the cornerstone. The building has no unity or life apart from him.

The whole structure. Every part, Jew and Gentile, every congregation, every believer.

Being joined together. A builder’s word (synarmologoumenē), found only in Ephesians (again of the body in 4:16): stones cut, shaped and fitted precisely so that each bears on the next. Each believer is a living stone (1 Peter 2:5), and God shapes us to fit with others, often through the friction of living with very different people. And notice the tense: present, and passive. It is going on now, and it is done to the stones, not by them. No stone ever manoeuvred itself into place, and none chose its neighbours, which is worth remembering when the people beside you are not the people you would have picked. They did not pick you either. Neither of you is the mason.

Grows. Buildings do not grow; living things do (auxei, the word for the growth of a body or a plant). Paul mixes the pictures on purpose, because neither alone says what he means. The building gives the church its solidity: God is here. The body gives it life: still becoming what it is meant to be (4:15–16). And a church goes wrong in exactly two ways, each the loss of one picture. Lose the growing, and you have a building and nothing else: a congregation beautifully maintained in which nothing happens, kept open like a heritage site so visitors can admire the windows. Lose the building, and you get warmth without shape, a movement that glows for five years and then finds it has no foundation. Paul will have neither. Rooted and growing. Fixed and alive.

Into a holy temple. The word (naos) means the inner sanctuary, the place of God’s presence. In Ephesus the great temple of Artemis was one of the seven wonders of the world, four times the size of the Parthenon. Paul says the true temple is not marble but people. And in Jerusalem, the temple whose wall had kept Gentiles out (v. 14) is replaced: Gentiles are now not only allowed in, they are part of the building (1 Corinthians 3:16–17; 2 Corinthians 6:16).

In the Lord. The temple is holy because the Lord is in it, and it belongs to him.

Unfinished, and not ashamed of it. The building grows into a holy temple; it has not arrived. So when your church disappoints you, and it will, because a growing thing is always partly unformed, you are not looking at a ruin. You are standing on a building site. The dust and noise and half-built walls are not evidence that the project has failed. They are evidence that it is still going on, and that the Builder has not left.

What it does not mean. Not a church building of bricks: the temple is the people. Nor a single congregation alone: Paul speaks of the whole church across the world and through history, which each local church expresses.

In a sentence. In him the whole building is joined together and rises to become a holy temple in the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Ask two questions. Is anyone in your church bearing weight on you, someone for whom your absence would be a real problem, not just an empty seat? And whose weight are you carrying? If the honest answer to both is nobody, you are not yet built into the wall; you are a stone leaning against it. The difference is invisible from the road and total in a storm.

For worship. Paul’s readers walked past the great temple of Artemis every day, a wonder of the world that housed nothing but an image. God has built something greater out of forgiven people, and it houses God. The Lord whom the highest heaven cannot contain (1 Kings 8:27) has chosen to dwell by his Spirit among living stones, and he is still at work, joining them and raising them. Adore the Builder who never leaves the site, and the Christ in whom the whole structure holds together, until the temple stands complete and the glory of the Lord fills it for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit.

In him you also. The emphasis falls on “you also”: you who were far off, without God (v. 12), are now part of his dwelling. The outsiders have become the house.

Are being built together. Present tense, continuous and passive: happening now, and happening to you, not by you. The church is not finished. Each conversion adds a stone; each act of love and teaching builds up.

Into a dwelling place for God. Why would the God who fills all things (1:23) want a dwelling place? Because he has always longed to live among his people, and it is the thread that runs the length of Scripture. He walked with Adam in the garden (Genesis 3:8). When sin shattered that, he told Israel, let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst (Exodus 25:8), and his glory filled the tabernacle, and later Solomon’s temple, so fully that the priests could not stand to minister (Exodus 40:34–35; 1 Kings 8:10–11). He did not merely receive honour there; he moved in. Then came the catastrophe. Because of Israel’s idolatry, Ezekiel watched the glory leave the temple, slowly, reluctantly (Ezekiel 10–11), and the deepest wound was not the Babylonian army but the presence leaving before it came. Yet Ezekiel was promised that the glory would return (Ezekiel 43:1–5), and the city’s new name would be, The LORD is there (Ezekiel 48:35). And it returned in a form no one expected. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, literally pitched his tent among us, and we have seen his glory (John 1:14). The glory came back, not to a building of stone, but to a body. Then at Pentecost the Spirit came down not on a temple but on people, tongues as of fire resting on each one (Acts 2:3): God moving in again, now into his people. Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you? (1 Corinthians 3:16). And one day the whole new creation will be his home: behold, the dwelling place of God is with man (Revelation 21:3). The gathered church is the present chapter of that story.

By the Spirit. God lives in the church not symbolically but really, by the Holy Spirit. This completes the Trinitarian shape of the chapter: to the Father (v. 18), in Christ (vv. 13–21), by the Spirit (vv. 18, 22).

The address. Almost everyone who has wanted God has gone looking for his presence somewhere: a place, a view, a piece of music, a quality of silence early in the morning. That hunger is not silly. It is the oldest ache there is, and it began the afternoon two people heard God walking in the garden and hid. But notice the address Paul gives. Not a mountain, not a building, not an atmosphere: a people. God has moved into a congregation. The people near you on Sunday, the awkward ones, the one who talks too long afterwards, the family whose children never sit still, are not the setting in which you might meet God. Together, they are the place where he has chosen to live. And see how far the chapter has come to say it. It opened with corpses, walking in step with the world and the prince of the power of the air. It ends with those same people as the house God lives in. That is the distance grace covers, in twenty-two verses.

What it does not mean. Not that God is absent from individual believers: each believer’s body is a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19). But here the emphasis is corporate: God dwells among his people together. A Christian who stays away from the church is like a stone lying in a field instead of being built into the wall.

In a sentence. And in him you too are being built together with all the others into a home where God lives by his Spirit.

For worship. The glory that filled the tabernacle, left the temple, and came back in Jesus, now lives among his gathered people. When the church meets, God is at home. Come expecting him.

2.overview:
Chapter 2 tells the gospel twice. First as the story of every believer (vv. 1–10): we were dead in sin, ruled by the world, the devil and our own desires, and by nature under God’s wrath. “But God”, rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ, raised us and seated us with him, so that for ever he may display the riches of his grace. Salvation is entirely by grace through faith, God’s gift and not our achievement, and its fruit is a life of the good works God prepared for us.

Then as the story of two peoples (vv. 11–22). Gentiles were once outsiders, without Christ, without the covenants of promise, without hope and without God. Now, by Christ’s blood, they have been brought near. Christ himself is our peace: in his flesh he has torn down the wall of hostility between Jew and Gentile, ending the law’s regulations as a barrier, creating one new humanity and reconciling both to God in one body through the cross. Through him both have access to the Father by one Spirit. Gentile believers are no longer foreigners but fellow citizens and members of God’s household, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets with Christ as cornerstone, growing into a holy temple where God lives by his Spirit.

3.title: The Mystery of Christ and the Fullness of God
3.text: <sup>1</sup>For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles — <sup>2</sup>assuming that you have heard of the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you, <sup>3</sup>how the mystery was made known to me by revelation, as I have written briefly. <sup>4</sup>When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ, <sup>5</sup>which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit. <sup>6</sup>This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel. <sup>7</sup>Of this gospel I was made a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which was given me by the working of his power. <sup>8</sup>To me, though I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, <sup>9</sup>and to bring to light for everyone what is the plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God, who created all things, <sup>10</sup>so that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places. <sup>11</sup>This was according to the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord, <sup>12</sup>in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through our faith in him. <sup>13</sup>So I ask you not to lose heart over what I am suffering for you, which is your glory. <sup>14</sup>For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, <sup>15</sup>from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, <sup>16</sup>that according to the riches of his glory he may grant you to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in your inner being, <sup>17</sup>so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith — that you, being rooted and grounded in love, <sup>18</sup>may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, <sup>19</sup>and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God. <sup>20</sup>Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us, <sup>21</sup>to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul, a prisoner for the Gentiles, explains that God entrusted to him the administration of grace for them: the mystery revealed to him, which he has briefly described. In past generations it was not made known as it now has been by the Spirit to the apostles and prophets: through the gospel the Gentiles are co-heirs with Israel, members of one body and sharers in the promise in Christ. Paul became its servant by God’s gracious gift and power. Though the least of all God’s people, he was given grace to preach Christ’s boundless riches to the Gentiles and to make plain to all how this long-hidden mystery works out, so that through the church God’s manifold wisdom should now be shown to the heavenly rulers, according to his eternal purpose in Christ, in whom we approach God with freedom and confidence through faith. So they should not be discouraged by his sufferings for them, which are their glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Mystery Hidden and Revealed

The concept of "mystery" (mysterion) in Pauline theology is not something puzzling or obscure. It is a technical term for a secret previously hidden in God that has now been disclosed in the gospel. The mystery of Christ — the inclusion of the Gentiles as co-heirs — was not absent from the Old Testament, but it was not fully clear. It was there in the Abrahamic promise ("in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed," Genesis 12:3), in the prophets (Isaiah 49:6; 60:3), in the Psalms (Psalm 87; 96:3). But the full disclosure awaited the coming of Christ and the apostolic proclamation of the gospel.

This "already hidden, now revealed" pattern is the structure of all biblical revelation. The Old Testament is full of types, shadows, and partial disclosures that only become fully visible in the light of Christ. This is why the Reformers insisted on the unity of the two Testaments — they are one revelation progressively unfolding, not two contradictory religions. And it is why reading the Old Testament through the lens of Christ is not an imposition on the text but the fulfilment of its own internal logic. The mystery of the Gentiles was always there; the church is now living in the age of its full disclosure.

Paul's description of himself as "the very least of all the saints" (v.8) has been the theme of Reformed meditation on gospel humility. The man who had been the church's most zealous persecutor, who had dragged men and women to prison and consented to their deaths, now counts himself the least worthy recipient of the grace he proclaims. This is not false modesty; it is the grammar of genuine encounter with grace. The closer you are to Christ, the more clearly you see how far you fall short — and the more marvellous it becomes that grace extends even to you.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul describes his ministry as the proclamation of "the unsearchable riches of Christ" (v.8). The Greek word for "unsearchable" (anexichniastos) means literally "untraceable" — riches so vast that you cannot find their boundary, cannot trace their perimeter, cannot reach their end. To the Ephesian church, surrounded by the very traceable riches of Artemis and the mystery cults — gods who could be appeased, blessing that could be earned, secrets that could be unlocked for a price — Paul announces something of a different order entirely. The riches of Christ are boundless. They cannot be exhausted. The more you receive, the more remains to be given. No mystery religion could offer this.

Now: Paul is in prison when he writes this, and he explicitly tells the Ephesians not to lose heart because of his sufferings (v.13). The apostle who has been entrusted with the most glorious news in the universe is sitting in a Roman cell when he writes it. This is the pattern of the gospel: its glory travels in the most unlikely vessels. The imprisoned apostle, the persecuted church, the minority community that the world dismisses — these are the means through which the manifold wisdom of God is made known. When the church is most visibly weak, it is often doing its most significant cosmic work. The angels are watching — and what they see is the wisdom of God displayed in jars of clay.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles—
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles—

Meaning first. Ephesians 3 is a prayer interrupted by an explanation. Paul begins to pray (v. 1), but stops to explain why he, a prisoner, has the right to speak to Gentiles this way (vv. 2–13): God entrusted him with the stewardship of grace and revealed to him the mystery hidden for ages and now made known to Christ’s apostles and prophets by the Spirit, that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body and fellow sharers in the promise in Christ through the gospel (vv. 2–6). Paul, the least of all the saints, was made a servant of this gospel to preach Christ’s unsearchable riches and to bring the plan to light, so that through the church God’s many-sided wisdom is now displayed to the powers in the heavenly places, as he always purposed (vv. 7–12); so they must not lose heart over his sufferings (v. 13). Then he resumes the prayer (vv. 14–19): kneeling before the Father, he asks that they be strengthened by the Spirit within, that Christ may dwell in their hearts through faith, that rooted in love they may grasp with all the saints the immeasurable dimensions of Christ’s love, and be filled with all the fullness of God. He ends with a doxology to the God who can do far more than all we ask or think (vv. 20–21), closing the first, doctrinal half of the letter.

For this reason. Because of everything in chapter 2: Gentiles have been brought near and are being built into God’s temple (2:19–22). Paul is about to pray that they will experience this. But he breaks off after “Gentiles” and only picks up the prayer again in verse 14 with the same words. Verses 2–13 are a long digression, as if a man starting to pray suddenly thinks: they need to know why I can say this.

I, Paul. An emphatic, personal touch, used when Paul puts his own authority and story on the line (2 Corinthians 10:1; Galatians 5:2).

A prisoner of Christ Jesus. Humanly, Paul was a prisoner of Rome, under guard, chained to a soldier (Acts 28:16, 30). The chain is real, and so is the soldier on the other end of it. But he does not write a prisoner of Nero, or of Rome. He has quietly reassigned his own jailer. Rome believes it is holding him; Paul knows who actually put him there, and why (Philippians 1:12–14). The chain belongs to Christ.

On behalf of you Gentiles. This is far more literal than it looks. Paul was seized by a mob in the Jerusalem temple, shouting that he had brought Greeks past the barrier and defiled the holy place. Luke says exactly why they thought so: they had seen him in the city with Trophimus, and adds two words the readers of this letter cannot have missed: the Ephesian (Acts 21:27–29). Paul had not taken him through. But in a deeper sense the charge was true, because Paul had spent his life insisting that the wall was down. One chapter ago he told them that Christ had broken down the dividing wall (2:14). He wrote that sentence in prison, and he is in prison because he was accused of taking an Ephesian through it. The doctrine of chapter 2 is not theory to this man. It cost him his freedom, and he is explaining it to the very people it was about.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul is sorry for himself, or that his sufferings earn the Gentiles’ salvation. Only Christ’s sufferings save. Paul’s sufferings serve the spread of that salvation (Colossians 1:24).

In a sentence. That is why I, Paul, who am in chains as Christ Jesus’ prisoner for the sake of you Gentiles …

On a Tuesday. Listen to how you describe your situation. Most of us say some version of “I am stuck here because of”, and then name the employer, the diagnosis, the person. Paul had every right to that sentence and never used it. He does not call the chains good; he simply says whose they are. You are not the prisoner of your situation, but a servant of Christ placed where he wants you.

For worship. Look past the chain to the one who holds it. Christ Jesus is Lord even over a Roman cell, and he turns the imprisonment of his servant into a pulpit for the nations. He himself was bound and led away so that Gentiles might go free, and he does not waste the sufferings of those who follow him. Praise the sovereign Saviour who loved outsiders enough to send them an apostle, and who was willing that the apostle wear chains if that was how the gospel would reach them. Nothing that befalls his people lies outside his rule or beyond his love.
verseByVerse.note: Paul was imprisoned because of his mission to the Gentiles; he breaks off here and resumes in verse 14.

verseByVerse.quote: assuming that you have heard of the stewardship of God's grace that was given to me for you, how the mystery was made known to me by revelation,
verseByVerse.commentary:
assuming that you have heard of the stewardship of God's grace that was given to me for you, how the mystery was made known to me by revelation,

Assuming that you have heard. Or “surely you have heard”: a polite expression, not real doubt. Some readers of this circular letter (see 1:1) had not met Paul, but would have heard of his calling.

The stewardship of God’s grace. “Stewardship” is oikonomia, from oikos (house) and nomos (law, management): the running of a household, the same word as God’s own plan in 1:10. A steward was usually a trusted slave who ran the whole estate. He owned nothing and controlled almost everything: the keys, the accounts, the stores, the distribution of food to the household (Luke 12:42). So two things were true of him at once. Nothing in his hands was his. And everything in his hands was there to be given out. A steward who hoarded his master’s grain was not being careful; he was being unfaithful, because the grain existed to be distributed and he existed to distribute it. Paul is the steward of grace, not its owner (1 Corinthians 4:1–2).

That was given to me for you. The grace of his commission, his calling as apostle to the Gentiles (v. 8; Romans 15:15–16). It arrived addressed to somebody else: not for his honour, but for their benefit.

The mystery. In everyday English a mystery is a puzzle that cannot be solved. In Paul it means almost the opposite: a secret of God, hidden until God chose to reveal it, and now openly made known (Romans 16:25–26; Colossians 1:26). In the pagan mystery religions of the day, secrets were whispered only to initiates. Paul’s mystery is proclaimed to everyone.

Made known to me by revelation. Notice the passive. Paul did not work it out. He had the best training of his generation, sat at the feet of Gamaliel (Acts 22:3), and knew the Scriptures as well as anyone alive, and none of it produced this. It was disclosed to him on a road, by the one he was at that moment travelling to persecute (Galatians 1:11–12; Acts 26:16–18). That is a great mercy for the rest of us. If the mystery had to be deduced, only the clever would ever have it. It is revealed, and so it belongs to anyone willing to receive it.

What it does not mean. Not that the gospel is secret knowledge for a spiritual elite. That was the claim of later Gnostics. The Christian mystery is public, preached, and open to all.

In a sentence. surely you have heard how God entrusted me with the task of giving out his grace to you, and how he showed me his secret plan by direct revelation,

On a Tuesday. Take an honest inventory: money, skills, a spare room, a marriage that is going well, years of experience, the gospel itself. Put the steward’s question to each item. Not, am I using this wisely? A careful man can answer that comfortably without ever opening the storehouse. Ask instead: who was this given to me for?

For worship. God is not a hoarder. The secret he kept in himself through all the ages he has now opened and given away, and he chose a former persecutor to hand it out. The grace Paul stewards is God’s own wealth, meant for distribution, and its supply never runs low. Bless the Lord who reveals what no scholar could have deduced, who met Saul on the road and showed him the risen Christ, and who still delights to give his treasure to those who have nothing to pay. The mystery is out, because the Father wanted his children to know.
verseByVerse.note: A stewardship is a trust given to a household manager.

verseByVerse.quote: as I have written briefly. When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
as I have written briefly. When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ,

As I have written briefly. Paul refers back to this very letter, especially 1:9–10 (God’s plan to unite all things in Christ) and 2:11–22 (Jew and Gentile one in Christ), not to an earlier, lost letter.

When you read this. Letters in the early church were read aloud in the congregation (Colossians 4:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:27). Paul expects his words to be read publicly and repeatedly.

You can perceive my insight. “Insight” (synesis) means understanding, the ability to put things together. Paul is not boasting. The authority of his message can be tested by reading it: it hangs together, and it unlocks the Old Testament promises.

The mystery of Christ. Paul borrows a word from the mystery cults and empties it. Their mystērion was a secret rite, sworn from outsiders. His is not kept secret but proclaimed, not for a few but for all nations, not hidden in ritual but written down and read aloud. Whenever Paul says mystery, hear: something God was keeping until the right moment, now brought into the open. And its content is Christ, what God has done in him, including the joining of Jew and Gentile in one body (v. 6).

What it does not mean. Not that we need special visions or secret experiences to understand God’s purposes. What Paul received by revelation, we receive by reading. The written word is how apostolic insight reaches us.

In a sentence. as I have already briefly written; when you read it you will be able to see that I understand the secret of Christ,

On a Tuesday. If you want to understand God’s plan, read the letters he gave. Read Ephesians through in one sitting this week.

For worship. The mystery of Christ is not a riddle about Christ; it is Christ himself, and what the Father has done in him. Every page Paul wrote is a window onto the Son: his cross that reconciles, his body that gathers the nations, his reign over every power. The Lord who opened the Scriptures to two travellers on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:27) still opens them to anyone who reads in faith. Glory to the God who did not leave us guessing at his heart, but made it plain, had it written down and put it into ordinary hands, so that his Son might be known and loved.

verseByVerse.quote: The mystery of Christ, which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mystery of Christ, which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit.

Not made known to the sons of men in other generations. “Sons of men” simply means human beings. Before Christ, people did not grasp this mystery.

As it has now been revealed. The word “as” matters. Paul does not say the mystery was completely unknown, but not known as it is now. The Old Testament did promise blessing to the nations: in Abraham all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3), and the Servant would be a light for the nations (Isaiah 49:6; see also Isaiah 2:2–4; Amos 9:11–12). What was not clear was how: that Gentiles would come in not by becoming Jews, through circumcision and the law, but directly in Christ, as full and equal members of one new body. That was the surprise.

Stand with the men who did not get to see it. Peter says the prophets searched and inquired carefully, inquiring what person or time the Spirit of Christ in them was indicating when he predicted the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories (1 Peter 1:10–11). Picture it. Isaiah writes of a man pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, and then goes back over his own page trying to work out whose face he has just described. Daniel is told to shut up the words and seal the book (Daniel 12:4). They were handling material they were not allowed to open. And Peter adds the line that ought to stop us: it was revealed to them that they were serving not themselves but you (1 Peter 1:12). We tend to assume the great age of faith was back then, and that we are latecomers reading the record. Jesus said the opposite: many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see, and did not see it (Matthew 13:16–17). Angels, Peter says, long to look into these things. So on an ordinary morning, with a cup of tea and an open Bible, you know the thing Isaiah went back over his page trying to see. You know whose face it was. That is no reason for pride, since none of it was earned. It is a reason to stop handling your Bible as a duty and start handling it as what it is: the answer to somebody else’s lifelong question, put into your hands.

To his holy apostles and prophets. “Holy” means set apart by God for this task, not personally sinless. The apostles and prophets are the foundation of the church (2:20); this is why. They received the revelation of the mystery and passed it on. The prophets here are New Testament prophets, listed after the apostles (2:20; 4:11), not the Old Testament prophets, to whom this was not made known as it is now.

By the Spirit. The Holy Spirit is the revealer (1 Corinthians 2:10–13; John 16:13). The New Testament is the Spirit’s work through these men.

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament is irrelevant or contradicted. The New Testament reveals what the Old Testament promised in shadow. Christ is the key that opens the Old Testament (Luke 24:27, 44–47). Nor does it mean revelation of this kind continues today; it was given to the founding generation and written down for us.

When someone says “God told me”, is that the same thing? No, not in the sense of this verse. What the apostles and prophets received was revelation binding on the whole church, and it was written down once for all as Scripture (Hebrews 1:1–2; Jude 3). God still guides his people today: by his word, by the Spirit opening our eyes to it, by the counsel of others and by his providence. A verse may come home to you with great force, and that is the Spirit at work. But an impression in your heart, however strong, is not a new word from God, and it never carries Scripture’s authority (Westminster 1.6). So test every “God told me”, your own included, by the Bible. If it adds to Scripture or contradicts it, set it aside. If it agrees, the authority lies in Scripture, not in the impression.

Where Christians differ: was the church entirely hidden? Classic dispensationalists teach that the church was completely unknown in the Old Testament, a parenthesis inserted into God’s programme for Israel, which will resume after the church is removed. Covenant theology holds that the church fulfils God’s promises to Abraham and the prophets, now revealed far more clearly. Paul’s word “as” (not known as it is now) implies that something was known before, and elsewhere he shows that the Gentiles’ inclusion fulfils the promise to Abraham (Galatians 3:8, 29) and the prophets (Romans 15:8–12). Verdict: the church is the fulfilment of God’s one plan, partly foreseen and now fully revealed.

In a sentence. a secret that was not made known to people in earlier generations in the way that the Spirit has now revealed it to Christ’s holy apostles and prophets.

On a Tuesday. Read the Old Testament as a Christian: look for the promises to the nations, and see how they come true in your own church.

For worship. For centuries the Spirit of Christ spoke through prophets who could not yet see the face they were describing, and the Lord was content to wait. He is the God of the long promise and the perfect moment. When the fullness of time came, he did not merely explain the mystery; he sent his Son, and the shadows took flesh (Galatians 4:4). Worship the Lord of history, who kept his secret through every generation without once forgetting it, and who has now given his church what kings and prophets longed to see. The same Spirit moved them and has opened our eyes, and both bear witness to one Christ.
