verseByVerse.quote: This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel.

This mystery is. Literally “that the Gentiles are”. Paul now defines what he has been talking about.

Three “fellow” words. Paul uses three Greek compounds beginning with syn (with, together), and feel what he is doing to the language. The middle one appears nowhere in Greek before this letter. He seems simply to have made it up. Here is a man reaching for a word that does not exist, because the thing he is describing had never existed either.

1. Fellow heirs. Synklēronoma: co-heirs. Gentiles inherit everything God promised Abraham and his descendants (1:11, 14, 18; Galatians 3:29). An heir received the whole estate of the father. Gentile believers are not tenants or guests on Israel’s estate; they inherit it equally.

2. Members of the same body. Syssōma: co-bodied, the coined word. Not two bodies, one Jewish and one Gentile, side by side, but one body with one head, Christ (2:16; 4:4). The Gentile is not attached to the body, or admitted alongside it. He is body with you.

3. Partakers of the promise. Symmetocha: co-sharers. The promise is God’s great promise to Abraham and his offspring, summed up in the gift of the Holy Spirit (1:13; Galatians 3:14) and in God’s pledge to be their God.

In Christ Jesus. Everything they share is in union with him. He is the true offspring of Abraham (Galatians 3:16), and all who are in him share his inheritance.

Through the gospel. The means of inclusion is the good news believed, not ancestry, circumcision or law-keeping. This is why Paul fought so hard against those who wanted Gentiles circumcised (Galatians 2:3–5; 5:2–6).

Second-class, without anyone saying so. Nobody writes second-class membership into a church constitution. It simply grows, quietly, in who gets treated as family and who as a guest. The convert with a visible past whom people are glad to see and slow to trust. The newcomer who has not learned the vocabulary. The one who cannot give, or host, or arrives with noisy children. None of them is ever told they are lesser; they are simply never quite folded in. But fellow heir means they will inherit exactly what you inherit: not less, not later, not on conditions. Paul had to invent a word to say this. The least we can do is not quietly unsay it.

What it does not mean. Not that Gentiles replace Jews, or that Jewish believers lose anything. It is fellow heirs: sharing, not taking over. Nor that ethnic identity is erased (see 2:14). The point is equal standing before God and equal belonging in his family.

Does God still have a purpose for the Jewish people? Yes. Paul says plainly that God has not rejected the people he foreknew (Romans 11:1–2), and that his gifts and calling are irrevocable (Romans 11:29). But that purpose is not a separate road to salvation running beside the church. There is one olive tree, one body and one way in: faith in Jesus the Messiah (Romans 11:17–24; John 14:6). Jewish people need Christ exactly as Gentiles do, and many Reformed Christians, reading Romans 11:25–26, expect a great turning of Israel to Christ before the end, natural branches grafted back into their own tree. So love your Jewish friends and neighbours, pray for them, and share the gospel with them gladly. It came to them first (Romans 1:16), and the promises you now share were spoken first to their fathers.

In a sentence. The secret is this: through the gospel, the Gentiles share the inheritance together with Israel, belong to the same body, and share together in the promise in Christ Jesus.

On a Tuesday. On Sunday, find the person you would least naturally have chosen. Then ask whether you really believe that in the age to come the two of you will stand on identical ground, with the identical inheritance from the identical Father. If that is true then, it is true now, and the way you treat them this week is either a rehearsal for it or a contradiction of it.

For worship. You were born outside the promise, and God has made you co-heir with Abraham, co-body with Christ. Give thanks for an inheritance you were never born into.

verseByVerse.quote: Of this gospel I was made a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which was given me by the working of his power. To me, though I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of this gospel I was made a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which was given me by the working of his power. To me, though I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ.

Of this gospel I was made a minister. “Minister” is diakonos, servant, the word from which deacon comes. It was used of a waiter at table. Paul’s highest title is servant. And “I was made”: God appointed him; he did not apply.

According to the gift of God’s grace. His ministry is a gift, not a reward.

By the working of his power. The same language as 1:19–20: the power that raised Christ from the dead. It took resurrection power to turn Saul the persecutor into Paul the apostle (Acts 9:1–22), and it takes the same power to sustain his ministry (Colossians 1:29).

Though I am the very least of all the saints. Paul invents a word again: he takes the Greek for “least” and adds a comparative ending, “leaster”, less than the least. It is not false modesty, and he means something specific. Luke says what he was: Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison (Acts 8:3). House after house. A door opening at the wrong hour, a man in the room, a mother taken out in front of her children. At Stephen’s stoning the witnesses laid their coats at his feet (Acts 7:58). Notice too the tense. Decades on, an apostle with churches across the empire, he does not say “I was” but “I am”. The memory never left him. And it never disqualified him either. And watch how his self-description moves through his letters: least of the apostles (1 Corinthians 15:9, about AD 55), least of all the saints (here, about AD 61), foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15, about AD 63). The older he grew in grace, the lower he saw himself.

This grace was given. Paul cannot speak of his ministry without speaking of grace (1 Corinthians 15:10). Both halves stand in one sentence: to me, the very least, this grace was given. He does not resolve the tension. He lives inside it.

To preach to the Gentiles. To announce, as a herald announces good news.

The unsearchable riches of Christ. “Riches” is one of Paul’s favourite words in this letter: the riches of grace (1:7; 2:7), of glory (1:18), and now of Christ himself, because no word is large enough. “Unsearchable” (anexichniaston) means untraceable, without footprints: like a path through a forest whose tracks simply stop, a land so vast no explorer could trace it to the end (Romans 11:33). And these riches are not an asset Christ hands out at arm’s length; they are him. Forgiveness, adoption, wisdom, the Spirit, hope, an inheritance, and deepest of all, the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord (Philippians 3:8; Colossians 2:3). They do not run down as more people draw on them. No theology exhausts them, no lifetime of preaching empties them, no eternity reaches their bottom. And they were handed, for preaching, to a man who had dragged women out of their houses for believing in him.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul’s sense of unworthiness made him timid. The man who called himself the least of the saints also wrote with full apostolic authority. Humility is not hesitancy; it is knowing that everything is grace.

In a sentence. I became a servant of this gospel by the gift of God’s grace, given me through his mighty working; to me, the very least of all God’s people, he gave the privilege of announcing to the Gentiles the endless riches of Christ,

On a Tuesday. Is there something in your past that you assume has ruled you out of usefulness? When someone says God uses ordinary people, do you add silently, but not people who have done what I did? Put it beside what Paul did, and ask honestly whether it is worse. Paul is not the exception that proves your case; he is the pattern. Your past does not disqualify you from serving him; only pride does.

For worship. The riches of Christ are unsearchable, and the grace that handed them to Saul of Tarsus is just as deep. Here is a Saviour whose wealth does not shrink when it is shared, whose mercy can make a persecutor its herald, and whose power turns the least of the saints into a servant of the nations. Every forgiveness, every adoption, every hope ever preached is drawn from him and leaves him no poorer. Worship the Christ whose treasure is himself, and who gives himself away to the unworthy without ever coming to the end of what he is.

verseByVerse.quote: and to bring to light for everyone what is the plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God, who created all things,
verseByVerse.commentary:
and to bring to light for everyone what is the plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God, who created all things,

To bring to light. To illuminate. Light does not make what it shows. Switch a lamp on in a dark room and nothing is created: the furniture was there all along, and you had been barking your shins on it. The plan of God did not begin when it was announced; it stood complete before the world was made. What changed at Christ’s coming is that the light went on. A Christian is not someone who has thought up a better explanation of things. He is someone who has been shown the room he was already standing in.

For everyone. Not only Gentiles, but all people. God’s plan is public.

The plan of the mystery. “Plan” is oikonomia again (see v. 2; 1:10): the ordered running of a household by a purposeful manager. Nothing random, nothing wasted, everything moving towards an intended end. The church, the one new humanity, is not a contingency or a revision, but exactly what God was managing towards from the beginning.

Hidden for ages in God. The plan was not absent; it was in God, kept in his own counsel from eternity (1:4, 9–11), out of reach of every creature until he chose to disclose it. No angel knew it; no searching could have found it, because it was hidden not in the world but in the one who stands behind the world. None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:7–8). It was revealed not by discovery but by disclosure.

Who created all things. Why mention creation here? Because the God who saves is the God who made everything. Redemption is not a repair job on a project that went wrong, but the Creator carrying through his original purpose: to unite all things in Christ (1:10). Creation and redemption have the same Author and the same horizon. The new creation (2:10, 15) is the goal of the first.

Nothing wasted? That is an easy sentence to write and a hard one to believe on a Thursday afternoon. Most of us can point to stretches that look like waste: the years in a job that led nowhere, the decade lost to illness or a broken marriage, the door that closed and never opened. Paul does not deny the experience. He names who is doing the managing. And here is a test you can run on paper tonight. Trace how you came to hear the gospel at all. Who actually told you? How did you come to be in that room, that school, that ward, that friendship? Follow it back four or five links, and you will find a chain of things that looked entirely accidental, most of them arranged by people who had no idea what they were doing. Someone moved house. Someone fell ill. Someone invited the wrong person by mistake. That is the household being run. If he managed all that without once consulting you, the years you have written off are far more likely to be rooms in the same house than evidence against it.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “fellowship” (koinōnia) instead of “plan” (oikonomia), and add “by Jesus Christ” after “created all things”. Verdict: “plan” is original, supported by the earliest manuscripts, and “by Jesus Christ” is a later expansion. The truth it adds is biblical (Colossians 1:16), but it is not part of this verse.

In a sentence. and of making plain to everyone how God is carrying out the plan he kept hidden through all the ages in himself, the Creator of all things,

On a Tuesday. History is not random. The God who made the world is working out his plan in it, and your small part in his church belongs to that plan.

For worship. The God who saves is the God who made the stars, and he has never once lost hold of his world. Before he spoke light into being he had already purposed the church, and nothing since, not the fall, not the flood, not the cross itself, has knocked his plan off course. Every century has been a room in his house, managed towards the day when all things are gathered up in his Son (1:10). Praise the Creator who is also the Redeemer, whose wisdom kept its secret through the ages and then let in the light, so that we might see him and marvel.

verseByVerse.quote: so that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
so that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places.

So that. The purpose of Paul’s preaching (vv. 8–9), and of the mystery itself. This is one of the most breathtaking purpose statements in the New Testament.

Through the church. Not through the stars, or the great events of world history, but through the church: ordinary people gathered in Christ. The Greek ekklēsia means assembly, the gathered people of God. The church is not only the beneficiary of the mystery; it is God’s showcase, his display to the universe.

The manifold wisdom of God. “Manifold” (polypoikilos), found only here, means many-coloured, richly varied, the word used of embroidered cloth or a meadow of flowers. God’s wisdom is not one colour but a whole spectrum, and it is seen in the variety of people he gathers: Jew and Gentile, slave and free, rich and poor, every culture, joined in one body without losing their variety. No diplomacy ever dissolved the division between Jew and Gentile; the only explanation is what God did in Christ. The wisdom shows in the method too. He chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise (1 Corinthians 1:27–28): a crucified Messiah as cornerstone, a persecutor as chief missionary, forgiven sinners as the display of his glory. A church of people who are all alike shows less of this wisdom.

The back of the cloth. Anyone who has watched embroidery being made knows it has two sides. From the back it is a mess: knots, loose ends, threads running off at angles, colours stopping dead in the middle of nowhere. Turn it over, and every thread turns out to have been going somewhere. That is the honest position of anyone in an actual congregation. From where you sit, the church does not look like the display of the wisdom of God. It looks like a rota that keeps failing, two families not speaking, a treasurer worried about the roof, a sermon that went on too long, and a man in the third row you privately gave up on. You are looking at the back of the cloth. Paul does not say the knots are imaginary. He says you are not the one standing in front of it.

Might now be made known. Now, in this age, before the end. The display is already happening.

To the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places. Spiritual beings, angelic and demonic (1:21; 6:12; Colossians 2:15), unusually prominent in this letter perhaps because Ephesus was gripped by fear of named powers (Acts 19:19). Good angels watch with wonder: things into which angels long to look (1 Peter 1:12). Evil powers watch their defeat. Christ disarmed them and put them to open shame (Colossians 2:15), and the church is the ongoing public announcement of that victory. Every time former strangers call the same God Father, God is saying to every power in the universe: look what my wisdom has done. You could not predict it, could not prevent it, and cannot undo it. And notice which moments are on display: not the ones anyone photographs. Two members quietly reconciling after eighteen months of coldness. A widow driven to the hospital by someone who does not much like her. Six people at a prayer meeting on a wet Tuesday. A former enemy passing the bread to a former enemy. That is the embroidery. The powers are studying it, and it tells them that the crucified one has won.

What it does not mean. Not that the church preaches to angels, or that we should try to address or command spiritual powers. The church makes God’s wisdom known simply by being what it is: a reconciled people. Nor does “wisdom” mean cleverness. God’s wisdom is his skill in achieving his good purposes, above all through the cross, which looks like foolishness to the world (1 Corinthians 1:18–25).

Do angels not already know everything about God? No. Angels are wise and holy, but they are creatures, and they learn as creatures do. Jesus said that even the angels in heaven do not know the day of his return (Matthew 24:36), and Peter says they long to look into the things of the gospel (1 Peter 1:12). They saw God make the world and shouted for joy (Job 38:7), but they had never seen anything like a crucified Lord gathering former enemies into one family. They learn the depths of God’s wisdom by watching what he does, and here they watch it in the church. That should change how you think of an ordinary Sunday. Heaven is not bored by your congregation. It is studying it.

In a sentence. so that now, through the church, the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms would see the rich variety of God’s wisdom.

On a Tuesday. If angels are examining your church for evidence of God’s wisdom, they are not assessing the building or the music. They are watching what happens between people who would never otherwise have been in the same room. The next time you decide some relationship in the church is not worth the effort, remember: it is not a distraction from the display. It is the display.

For worship. Angels watched God lay the foundations of the earth, and still they learn something new by watching a church. The wisdom on display is many-coloured: the wisdom of turning a defeat into a coronation, and a scattered humanity into one family without erasing a single nation. Only the God who planned redemption before the ages could have woven it. Glory to the Father whose wisdom shames the clever and silences the powers, and to the Son whose cross is the thread on which the whole pattern hangs. The universe is watching, and what it sees, in the end, is him.

verseByVerse.quote: This was according to the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord, in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through our faith in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This was according to the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord, in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through our faith in him.

The eternal purpose. Literally the purpose of the ages. The church is not an afterthought or plan B. God planned it before time (1:4, 11).

That he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord. “Realized” means carried out, in Christ’s life, death, resurrection and ascension. The plan is not only foreseen; it has been done.

In whom we have boldness. Paul said this in 2:18, and now he says it again, stronger, because it needed saying twice. His readers had come out of a world of spiritual dread: gods who were unpredictable and unapproachable, managed by ritual; and even the true God so holy that access ran through a priest, a sacrifice and long purification. “Boldness” (parrēsia) was the free citizen’s right to speak openly in the assembly, plainly, in his own words, without first getting permission. Listen to the praying of someone who does not believe he has that right. It is hedged. There is much throat-clearing before anything real is said. “If it be your will” comes early, not as submission but as insurance, so that nothing has quite been asked and nothing can be refused. The requests stay small, because small requests are safer. The voice changes into a tone used at no other hour of the day. And after a bad week the praying stops, on the grounds that it would be decent to stay away until things improve. Every one of those instincts belongs to a servant on probation, and Paul says that is not what you are. The grief may come out as grief, the confusion as confusion, the anger where there is anger, not because God needs informing, but because a son does not brief his father the way a petitioner briefs an official.

And access. Prosagōgē: the right of entry into the king’s presence, granted by one with the standing to bring you in (2:18). Your introducer is Christ himself, whose welcome at the throne is permanent. Being in him, you share it, and it does not rise and fall with how your week has gone.

With confidence. Assurance that we will be welcomed, not turned away. Those who were far off and without God (2:12–13) can now come boldly to the throne of grace (Hebrews 4:16; 10:19–22). And check the tense: we have. Present possession, held at this moment by a man in chains, and shared with everyone reading over his shoulder.

Through our faith in him. The way to this confidence is faith: trusting Christ, not our performance. Our confidence is not self-confidence but Christ-confidence.

Textual and translation note. The phrase can be translated “through his faithfulness” (Christ’s own faithfulness), and some scholars argue for that. Verdict: the usual translation, faith in him, best fits Paul’s usage in Ephesians, where faith is the believer’s trust in Christ (1:15; 2:8). Either way, our confidence rests on Christ.

What it does not mean. Not casualness or presumption before God. Free speech before a King is not familiarity with an equal. We draw near with confidence, and what we draw near to is a throne (Hebrews 4:16; 12:28). We come with reverence and awe, but without fear of rejection, as children come to a father.

In a sentence. This was God’s eternal purpose, which he has carried out in Christ Jesus our Lord, in whom, through faith in him, we may now come to God freely and with confidence.

For worship. The King of heaven has given you the freedom of his throne room, and his Son walks you in. Come today, not because you have had a good week, but because Christ is your access.

verseByVerse.quote: So I ask you not to lose heart over what I am suffering for you, which is your glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I ask you not to lose heart over what I am suffering for you, which is your glory.

So I ask you. The digression of verses 2–13 ends where it began: with Paul’s chains (v. 1). And notice which way the comfort is travelling. The man in the cell is worried about the morale of the people who are free. He does not open with a request for sympathy; he opens with this: do not lose heart.

Not to lose heart. To grow weary, to lose your nerve, to give up (enkakein). The readers might reason: if the apostle of this gospel is in prison, perhaps the gospel is failing. That danger is real, and it still empties pews. What makes people give up is very often not their own suffering but somebody else’s. A respected pastor is diagnosed at fifty-two. A couple who prayed for years for a child end up burying one. A missionary family comes home broken. Nobody announces a change of belief; it happens quietly, in the gap between what was preached and what was watched, and people conclude that the thing does not seem to work. Paul knows the Ephesians are doing that arithmetic about him, and he interrupts it.

Over what I am suffering for you. Paul is in prison because he took the gospel to the Gentiles (see v. 1). His suffering was the price of their hearing.

Which is your glory. His sufferings show how much their salvation is worth: if an apostle thinks it worth chains to bring Gentiles the gospel, they must be precious in God’s sight. And his suffering serves their glory: it advances the gospel through which they will share Christ’s glory (2 Timothy 2:10; Philippians 1:12–14). Paul does not say “despite my sufferings” you have the gospel, but that through them you have your glory. It is the same logic as the cross, where the death that looked like the end was the turning point. And notice his restraint. He does not explain why God allowed the arrest, or when release might come. He gives them one sentence about what the suffering is for, and leaves everything else alone. Most of our attempts to comfort one another go wrong by trying to supply reasons we do not have.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul’s sufferings add anything to Christ’s atoning work. Christ’s suffering alone saves. Paul suffers to bring that salvation to others.

In a sentence. So I ask you not to be discouraged by what I am suffering for you; it is for your glory.

On a Tuesday. When someone faithful is suffering, what is your first instinct? For many of us it is to look for the flaw, the hidden sin, the wrong decision, the weak faith, because a flaw would make the arithmetic work again. Paul offers no flaw to find. He offers a purpose. Meet the next hard providence, yours or someone else’s, with that as your first question, not your last.

For worship. The pattern of Paul’s chains is the pattern of the cross, and both point to a God who brings glory out of suffering. Christ did not save us by avoiding pain but by entering it, and the Father exalted him because he humbled himself (Philippians 2:8–9). That is the way of our God: he wins by losing, gives life through death, and makes the hardships of his servants serve the joy of his people. Praise the Lord who is never defeated by what defeats us, and whose purposes run straight through the prison and the grave and come out the other side in glory.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul kneels before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named. He asks that, out of his glorious riches, God will strengthen them with power in their inner being through his Spirit, so that Christ may make his home in their hearts through faith. Rooted and established in love, may they have power with all God’s people to grasp how wide, long, high and deep Christ’s love is, and to know this love that surpasses knowledge, so that they may be filled with all the fullness of God. To him who can do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine, by the power at work in us, be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus through all generations for ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Indwelling Christ and the Fullness of God

The prayer of Ephesians 3:14–21 reveals the goal of the Christian life with startling clarity: not moral improvement, not doctrinal accuracy, not even evangelistic fruitfulness — but the fullness of God. "Filled with all the fullness of God" (v.19) is a goal so vast it cannot be reached in a lifetime, which is precisely the point. The Christian life is not a project with a completion date; it is a journey into an infinity that perpetually exceeds the traveller. Paul set no limit to his desires for the Ephesians — he asked for the infinite, because the infinite is what God offers.

The means of this fullness is the indwelling of Christ. "That Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith" (v.17) — the verb "dwell" (katoikein) means to settle, to take up permanent residence, as opposed to merely passing through. This is not the occasional visitation of religious experience; it is the abiding presence of the living Christ in the interior life of the believer. The Reformers consistently emphasized that union with Christ — not merely forgiveness, not merely a changed record before God, but genuine, living union with the risen Lord — is the foundation of the entire Christian life. It is from this union that everything else flows: assurance, holiness, prayer, service, suffering, joy.

The doxology of vv.20–21 is also a theology of prayer. It teaches us that God is not limited by the smallness of our asking. The greatness of our petitions cannot exhaust his capacity to answer; the boldness of our faith cannot outrun his willingness to give. The God to whom we pray is the God who can do more than we can imagine asking — and the power by which he does it is "at work within us." It is the same resurrection power of Ephesians 1:19–20. Our prayers are small; his answers are not required to match them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The mystery religions of Ephesus promised spiritual fullness — union with the divine, access to hidden power — through initiation, through ritual, through the gradual ascent of the initiated. The costs were significant: financial, social, sometimes physical. And the fullness promised was always partial, always provisional, always requiring the next level of initiation. Paul prays for his readers to receive a fullness that no mystery religion could offer and no initiation could achieve: the fullness of God himself, freely given, received through faith, sustained by the Spirit. The contrast with what Ephesus was selling could not have been more pointed.

Now: "Far more abundantly than all that we ask or think" — this phrase has stood as one of the great encouragements of Christian prayer across the centuries. When we pray small, God answers large. When we cannot find words, the Spirit intercedes. When the situation seems beyond recovery, we serve the God who raises the dead. The doxology of Ephesians 3 is not merely a liturgical flourish; it is a declaration of the character of the God to whom we pray. He exceeds our prayers not because he is indifferent to them but because he is inexhaustibly generous. Every time this doxology is spoken in corporate worship, the church is reminding itself — and the watching powers — of who their God is.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named.

For this reason. The same words as verse 1, picking up the thought again: Gentiles are now part of God’s family and temple (2:19–22), and Paul prays that they will know it.

I bow my knees. Jews normally stood to pray (Mark 11:25; Luke 18:11, 13). Kneeling was kept for the moments that mattered too much for the usual form: Solomon at the dedication of the temple (1 Kings 8:54), Daniel three times a day at his open window (Daniel 6:10), the Lord himself in Gethsemane (Luke 22:41). And this man is in custody. A prisoner going down on his knees on a stone floor, probably watched, to pray at length for churches hundreds of miles away that he may never see again, is not performing devotion for anyone. There is nobody in that room to impress.

Before the Father. Prayer is addressed to the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit (2:18). Paul prays as a child to his Father, which is exactly the access he has just described (v. 12).

From whom every family in heaven and on earth is named. A wordplay English loses: Father is patēr, family is patria, a family group descended from one father. Every family derives its existence from God, the original Father. To name something, in the Bible, is to give it its identity and to have authority over it (Genesis 2:19–20). And the direction matters. God is not called Father because human fathers exist, as if we took the idea and projected it upward. He is Father first, eternally, in his own being, and human fathers are faint copies. Every good father you have known is a dim echo of this one. And for anyone whose father was absent, harsh or cruel: your experience is not the standard by which God is measured. He is the standard, and what you knew was a distortion of an original that is undistorted and unfailing (Luke 15:20–24; Psalm 68:5).

In heaven and on earth. Including the ordered communities of angels as well as human families. Since Jew and Gentile are now one family (2:19), Paul prays to the Father of them all.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add “of our Lord Jesus Christ” after “the Father”. Verdict: not original. The shorter reading is found in the earliest manuscripts and makes the wordplay with “family” clearer.

What it does not mean. Not that every human being is a child of God in the saving sense. All are God’s creatures and owe him their being (Acts 17:28), but the fatherhood that saves is adoption through Christ (1:5; John 1:12; Romans 8:15). And kneeling is not required for prayer: posture is a help, not a law.

In a sentence. That is why I kneel before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth gets its name,

On a Tuesday. Next time you pray, notice what face you are imagining. Nearly everyone imagines one: disappointed but too polite to say so, or distracted, or already looking for the fault. That face usually belonged to somebody, and it has been on loan to God ever since. You will not change it by trying to feel differently. Change it by looking at Jesus, the exact imprint of God’s nature (Hebrews 1:3): whoever has seen me has seen the Father (John 14:9). Watch him touch the leper (Mark 1:41), talk with the woman at the well (John 4), promise paradise to a dying thief (Luke 23:43). That is not Jesus being kinder than the Father. That is the Father, showing you his face.

For worship. Before there was ever a family on earth, there was the Father, loving his Son in the communion of the Spirit from all eternity. Every household, every lineage, every ordered company of angels takes its name from him, and in Christ he has become our Father too, by adoption and by grace. Bow with Paul before the One whose fatherhood is the source of every other, and whose love has never once failed his children. He is the Father of the Lord Jesus, and through Jesus he has gathered Jew and Gentile into one family that will never be broken up.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “family” renders patria, a word closely related to “father” (pater) in verse 14.

verseByVerse.quote: That according to the riches of his glory he may grant you to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in your inner being.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That according to the riches of his glory he may grant you to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in your inner being.

The shape of the prayer. Verses 16–19 are one sentence, a chain of requests, each leading to the next like steps on a staircase: strengthened by the Spirit (v. 16), so that Christ dwells in your hearts (v. 17), so that you may grasp the dimensions of his love (v. 18), so that you know that love (v. 19), so that you may be filled with all the fullness of God (v. 19).

According to the riches of his glory. “According to” matters. Not out of his riches, which could mean a small gift from a large fortune, but in proportion to them. A millionaire who gives a coin gives out of his riches; one who gives in proportion to his wealth gives lavishly. God gives in proportion to his glory: without limit.

He may grant you. Paul asks for a gift. Inner strength is not achieved by self-effort; it is given.

To be strengthened with power. Two words for strength, piled up: made strong with might. And notice what Paul does not ask for. Not power over circumstances, not health or protection from trouble, good as those are to pray for. Power in the inner being.

Through his Spirit. The strengthening is done by a Person, not achieved by a technique (Romans 8:11; Galatians 5:22–23). That is why the right response to finding yourself weak is not a programme of self-improvement. It is to ask. The whole sentence is a prayer; Paul is not only describing the strength, he is showing you how to get it.

In your inner being. Literally the inner man: the self no one else sees, your will, your faith, your capacity to trust God when nothing visible supports it. Picture two people facing the same illness or grief. From outside they look alike, but one is quietly falling apart while the other is held somewhere the storm cannot reach. The difference is not temperament but the condition of the inner person. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16): Paul wrote that years earlier, and it is true now in this prison, the outer man in chains, the inner man being renewed. This strength holds you when prayer feels like talking to the ceiling; gives endurance when suffering is long (Colossians 1:11); produces love when natural love has run out; and gives a peace that does not depend on circumstances (Philippians 4:7). God’s first work is not rearranging the furniture of your circumstances, but building something in you that they cannot shake.

What it does not mean. Not a prayer for spectacular experiences: the strength in view is the strength to know and love Christ, as the next verses show.

How do I actually pray this prayer? Use Paul’s words as your outline; that is partly why they were written down. Take verses 16–19 slowly and turn each clause into a request, for yourself and then for others by name: Father, strengthen her inside by your Spirit; make Christ at home in his heart; root them in your love; help me grasp how wide and long and high and deep it is; fill us with all your fullness. It is right to pray it for yourself, since Paul prays it for whole churches and you are in yours. Do not wait to feel something first, and do not judge the answer by tomorrow morning’s mood. This is a prayer God delights to answer, because it asks for what he has already promised to give (1 John 5:14–15). Then close as Paul does, with the doxology of verses 20–21, thanking him in advance.

In a sentence. and I pray that out of his glorious riches he will strengthen you with power in your inner self through his Spirit,

On a Tuesday. Put your own prayer list beside Paul’s. Most of ours are almost entirely external: a diagnosis, a job, an exam, safe travel, a difficult colleague. Nothing wrong with any of it. But Paul’s request, that a person be strengthened inside by the Spirit, appears on few prayer lists in an average month. We pray almost only about the outside of people’s lives, and then wonder why they are not stronger on the inside. Pray this for a friend in trouble today.

For worship. The riches of God’s glory are the measure of what he gives, and they have no bottom. He does not strengthen his people from a reserve that might run out, or by lending them a little more of their own resolve. He gives his Spirit, God himself, to dwell in the hidden self and hold it fast. Adore the triune God: the Father who gives from boundless glory, the Son whose risen life is the strength conveyed, and the Spirit who comes to live where no one else can see. Our weakness is no embarrassment to him. It is the place he chooses to display his might.

verseByVerse.quote: So that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, that you, being rooted and grounded in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, that you, being rooted and grounded in love.

So that Christ may dwell. The word is katoikeō: not to visit or lodge (paroikeō), but to settle down and make one’s permanent home, to move in and unpack. Christ already lives in every believer (Romans 8:9–10). Paul prays that he would be more fully at home: not visiting in a crisis and then going quiet, but present in the ordinary Monday, at work, in the argument with your spouse, in the moment of temptation. The Puritans used the picture of a house: Christ enters at conversion, but we must open every room to him. It is possible to be a real Christian and give him the guest room instead of the master bedroom.

In your hearts. In the Bible the heart is the centre of the person: thought, will, desire and feeling together (see 1:18). Christ’s dwelling there means he rules and shapes everything we are.

Through faith. Christ dwells in us as we trust him: not a single decision, but the daily turning of the heart to him. Abide in me, and I in you (John 15:4–5).

That you, being rooted and grounded in love. Two pictures. “Rooted” is from the garden: a tree is only as strong as its hidden roots, and everything above ground, its height, its fruit, its standing in a storm, depends on what is underground (Colossians 2:7; Psalm 1:3). “Grounded” is from building: a house is only as safe as its unseen foundation (Matthew 7:24–25). Love here is above all Christ’s love for us (vv. 18–19), which then produces our love for him and others. The deeply rooted believer bends in the storm but does not fall, because he knows what the wind cannot change: I am loved, and that is not in question. And notice something English hides. Both words are passive and perfect: you have been rooted; you have been founded. Trees do not plant themselves, and no building ever laid its own foundation. Someone put you in the soil and set you on rock. Sending your roots deeper is real work, but it answers a planting that already happened and was never your idea. You are not asked to manufacture a foundation; you are asked to build on one.

The test. You will never discover what you are rooted in on a good day. A storm has to come, and the most revealing storm is not illness or loss. It is your own sin. So ask honestly: after you have failed badly, what happens to your sense of being loved by God? If it collapses, and stays collapsed until you have made up the ground with a stretch of better behaviour, then whatever you believe about grace, you are rooted in your own performance. That explains the whole pattern: the shame, the distance, the not praying, waiting until you feel presentable before coming back. But if, under the real grief over the sin, there remains something that does not move, a floor you have not fallen through, the stubborn knowledge that you are loved by a God who knew about this before you did it and set his love on you anyway, then you have found the foundation. It was there before the storm. It was laid by somebody else. And it is the one thing your worst week cannot get underneath.

What it does not mean. Not that Christ enters and leaves believers depending on their mood or behaviour. His indwelling is permanent (John 14:23). Paul prays for a deeper experience of it, not its beginning. Nor is “love” here a vague feeling: it is the self-giving love shown at the cross (5:2, 25).

What does opening a room to Christ actually look like? Begin by naming the room. It is usually the part of life where you would rather not have his opinion: how you spend money, what you watch when alone, the grudge you are keeping, the plans you have already made. Bring it to him in plain words: Lord, this is yours too; show me what you want here. Open your Bible on that subject, not only on comfortable ones, and let it speak. Tell one trusted believer about it, because rooms kept secret tend to stay locked. Then do the first obedient thing you can see, however small: give the gift, cancel the subscription, make the call, say sorry. Christ does not batter the door down. He makes his home with those who love him and keep his word (John 14:23).

In a sentence. so that Christ will make his home in your hearts through faith; and I pray that you, with roots going down deep into love and resting on love as your foundation,

On a Tuesday. Is there a room in your life where Christ is not welcome: your money, your screen, your grudges, your ambitions? Open the door.

For worship. The eternal Son, by whom all things were made (John 1:3), is willing to make his home in a human heart, and not as a guest who keeps his coat on. That is condescension beyond telling. He who had nowhere to lay his head on earth (Matthew 8:20) now makes his dwelling among sinners, and roots them in a love they did not plant and cannot uproot. Praise the Christ who came to stay, who settles in by faith and never leaves, and who makes the ground beneath his people as firm as his own love for them.

verseByVerse.quote: may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth,

May have strength to comprehend. Notice the odd word at the front: strength. Understanding normally calls for intelligence or time, not strength; nobody says he lacked the strength to follow an argument. And here the prayer knits together, because this answers a question left open two verses earlier. Paul asked that they be strengthened with power in the inner being (v. 16). What is the power for? Not for miracles, or surviving persecution, or great achievements. It is so that you can take in how much you are loved. That sounds strange until you have watched someone try. It takes little strength to accept a compliment. It takes a great deal to accept a gift you can never repay, from someone who knows exactly what you are, with no way of ever levelling the account. Everything in us resists being loved on those terms. We would rather be admired for something, or at least be useful. To stand still and be loved, with nothing to contribute, undoes a person, and it takes the power of God in the inner man not to flinch and start earning again.

With all the saints. We grasp the love of Christ together, not alone. No single Christian sees all of it. The old saint who has suffered, the new believer full of joy, the church in another culture: each sees aspects of Christ’s love the others need. Private spirituality alone, reading one tradition and knowing one kind of believer, will always grasp less.

What is the breadth and length and height and depth. Paul does not say of what, but verse 19 makes clear he means the love of Christ. Many preachers map the four onto the cross; it preaches well, but Paul does not make that link. Four directions were the ancient way of describing the whole of space. Go as far as you can in any direction, and the love is still there: no edge, no ceiling, no floor. Held lightly, the four still help.

Breadth. Wide enough to embrace Jew and Gentile and every nation (chapter 2): wide enough to include you, your history, your failures, your doubts, and the person beside you whose life looks nothing like yours. It has never met a person and thought, this one is too far out.

Length. From before the foundation of the world (1:4) to the ages to come (2:7). It did not begin when you became lovable, and it never ends: neither death nor life will be able to separate us (Romans 8:38–39).

Height. High enough to seat you with Christ in the heavenly places (2:6) and bring you before the Father with boldness (3:12).

Depth. Deep enough to reach you where you actually are, not where you pretend to be: the shame, the addiction, the grief, the thing you have never told anyone. It went down into death itself at the cross. Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (Romans 5:20).

Background. Job asks whether anyone can find out the deep things of God, higher than heaven, deeper than Sheol, longer than the earth and broader than the sea (Job 11:7–9). As high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is his steadfast love (Psalm 103:11). Paul says that in Christ this immeasurable love is now known.

What it does not mean. Not that Christ’s love is something we can finally measure and map; the point is the opposite. Nor is this only an exercise of the mind: “comprehend” includes the heart. It is possible to describe the love of Christ accurately and not be moved by it at all.

In a sentence. may have the strength, together with all God’s people, to grasp how wide and long and high and deep it is,

On a Tuesday. If you have ever read a passage like this, felt something begin to rise, and then found yourself changing the subject or suddenly remembering a job that needed doing, that is not a lapse in concentration. It is the very thing Paul is praying about. Stay a little longer. Then talk with another believer this week about how Christ’s love has met you; you will grasp it better together than alone.

For worship. No compass point leads out of the love of Christ. Go as wide as the nations, as far back as eternity, as high as the throne, as deep as the grave, and he is already there, having gone further first. This is the love that held him to the cross when he could have called for angels (Matthew 26:53), and that holds his people now. Worship the Saviour whose love is not a feeling about us but a deed done for us, measured in nail wounds and an empty tomb. The saints of every age have explored it together, and none has ever come back reporting that it ran out.

parallels.desc: higher than heaven, deeper than Sheol

verseByVerse.quote: and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.

To know the love of Christ. “Know” (gnōnai) in the Bible is personal, experiential knowledge, as one knows a friend (John 17:3). Paul prays not that they would learn facts about Christ’s love, which they already knew, but that they would experience it more deeply.

That surpasses knowledge. A deliberate paradox: to know what is beyond knowing. You can know facts about the ocean without ever standing on the shore and feeling its size. Paul wants you on the beach, feeling the spray, knowing in your bones that this ocean has no far shore. We can know Christ’s love truly but never fully. A child can truly know the sea by wading in it, though it will never cross the ocean. Perhaps Paul also has in view the claims of false teachers who prized knowledge (gnōsis): love surpasses that kind of knowing (1 Corinthians 8:1).

That you may be filled. The goal of the whole prayer, and the largest thing Paul could ask.

With all the fullness of God. Literally filled up to all the fullness of God. “Fullness” (plērōma) is a key word in Ephesians and Colossians: in Christ the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily (Colossians 2:9), and the church is his fullness (1:23). Paul prays that believers would be filled with everything God is and gives: his life, love, holiness, joy and peace, as fully as creatures can be filled. Picture a jug held under a waterfall. The waterfall is beyond all comparison larger, yet the jug can be completely full, every inch, with nothing in it but what pours from the fall. In practice it means a life increasingly marked by what God is: loving more deeply because he is love, a patience not native to your temperament, a joy that does not evaporate when things are hard.

Be filled. Passive (plērōthēte), not “fill yourselves”. The fullness of God is not the reward for a disciplined enough life; it is a gift. The jug does not fill itself; it holds itself under the water. Our part is to stay open to it: returning to the source through prayer, the word, worship, confession, the company of the saints (5:18).

What if I believe Christ loves me but cannot feel it? Then you are in good company, and you are not outside this prayer. Feelings rise and fall with health, sleep, grief and temperament; Christ’s love does not, and it is measured at the cross, not by what you feel this week (Romans 5:8). Paul prays that we may know it, which means God is willing to make it more real to us, and he usually does so over time. So keep to the ordinary ways he does it. Look long at Christ in the Gospels, especially at how he treats sinners. Pray this very prayer for yourself. Sing truths you cannot yet feel. Take the Lord’s Supper as his pledge to you. Stay close to believers who have known his love in dark times. This knowing often arrives slowly, like dawn, and it is no less real for being quiet.

The hollow. You do not pray for someone to be filled unless there is a space in them. Everyone knows the feeling, though we do not always name it: the restlessness that survives getting what you wanted. The promotion is pleasant for a fortnight. The house is bought, the qualification finished, the relationship secured, and within a season the same low hum returns, the sense that something has still not arrived. We usually assume we picked the wrong thing, and choose another. But Paul is describing a capacity that no created thing was ever the right size for. The hollow is not a design fault. It is the shape of a container built for the fullness of God, and nothing smaller will ever sit in it.

Every “you” is plural. Paul is not asking that a series of individuals be privately topped up. He asks that a congregation, this mixed, awkward Jew-and-Gentile assembly, would together be filled with the fullness of God, as he said in 1:23 that the church is his fullness. So some of this filling only ever arrives through the people you have been joined to, including the ones you would never have chosen. Hold yourself apart from them, and there are dimensions of it you will never be filled with.

What it does not mean. Not that believers become God or lose their creaturely nature. The Creator–creature distinction is never erased. A cup filled from the ocean is full of the ocean, but it is still a cup. Some traditions speak of deification (theōsis); Reformed theology speaks rather of union with Christ and being conformed to his image (Romans 8:29). Nor is this a once-for-all experience. It is a growing filling, answered more and more as we grow in Christ, and completely when we see him face to face and are made like him (1 John 3:2).

In a sentence. and to know this love of Christ, though it is beyond all knowing, so that you may be filled to the measure of all the fullness of God.

For worship. The love of Christ has no far shore, and the fullness of God is pouring. Hold out whatever in you is still empty.

verseByVerse.quote: Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us,

Now to him who is able. Paul does not end the prayer with a quiet amen but with a burst of praise. He has asked for enormous things: inner strength, the indwelling Christ, the fullness of God. Now he steps back: the God I have been praying to can do immeasurably more than all of it.

To do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think. Paul stacks the words (hyperekperissou): beyond, out of, overflowing, all together, because no single word goes far enough. The thought climbs in steps: God is able to do what we ask; more than we ask; more than we can imagine; far more abundantly than all we can imagine. Our requests are limited by our words, our imagination by our minds; God is limited by neither.

But my prayer was answered no. Handle this honestly, because this promise can wound. Someone reads it with a particular prayer in mind that met a plain no: the healing that did not come, the marriage that ended anyway, years of asking that returned only silence. To them the verse can sound like mockery: I asked, and received less, not more. The answer is in two small words easily skipped: or think. God does more than we ask, and more than we know to ask. Our prayers are often not only too small but wrong in content, asking for the lesser thing because we cannot yet see the greater. A loving father does not give a child everything the child names, and the withholding is not the failure of his love but its exercise. Paul himself asked three times for his thorn to be removed. The answer was no, and the “more” turned out to be grace sufficient and power made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:8–9): not what he asked, but more. And where no better thing is yet visible, the more is not cancelled but kept, for the coming ages (2:7), for the day God wipes away every tear (Revelation 21:4). The God who cannot be out-asked has not closed the account, and it does not close at the grave.

According to the power at work within us. Not distant, not dormant, not waiting to be switched on by enough faith: working now (energoumenēn). And Paul has named it already: the power that raised Christ from the dead (1:19–20) and raised us with him (2:5–6). Why does it so often not feel like it, the same old sin, the same weakness? Because it works whether felt or not, as a seed breaks through concrete without anyone seeing it move; because it is aimed first at the inner person, not the outer circumstances, so you may be waiting for it to change your situation while God is using your situation to change you; and because it is most visible in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). The one who has run out of his own strength is exactly where God’s power takes over: not his power plus God’s, but God’s power where his used to be.

The hinge of the letter. This doxology is not a decorative flourish. Everything from 1:3 to here has been about what God has done: chosen, redeemed, sealed, raised, seated, reconciled, built, revealed. Apart from one call to remember (2:11), not one command has been given in three chapters. Then, the moment the praise ends, the tone changes: I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling (4:1), and the rest of the letter is almost all instruction. And look at what Paul has put between the doctrine and the duty. Not a summary. Praise: a man on his knees running out of words. That order is deliberate and it does not reverse. Anyone who takes up chapters 4–6 without first being undone by chapters 1–3 will find the commands crushing, trying to produce by effort a life that was only ever meant to overflow from astonishment. The obedience of this letter runs downhill from a doxology. If it is running uphill in your life, you may have started in the wrong chapter.

What it does not mean. Not a promise that God will give us whatever we imagine, or that big prayers guarantee health, wealth or success. Paul is still in prison. The context is verses 16–19: being strengthened, knowing Christ’s love, being filled with God. God’s “more” is more of these things, and more of his good purposes for us than we could ever plan (Romans 8:28–32).

In a sentence. Now to him who can do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine, by his power that is at work in us,

On a Tuesday. Pray bigger prayers for your spiritual life, your church and your unbelieving friends. And trust God when he answers differently from what you asked.

For worship. Paul’s doxology does not end with him; the church takes it up in every generation. The God who can do more than all we ask is the God who has already done more than anyone thought to ask: he gave his Son. No one in Israel prayed for a crucified Messiah, and no Gentile imagined adoption into the family of God. That is the measure of his ability, and the same power is at work in us still. To him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus through every generation, for ever (3:21). We will spend eternity discovering how far beyond our imagining he has gone.

verseByVerse.quote: to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.

To him be glory. Behind the word stands the Hebrew kābôd, weight (see 1:17): the overwhelming reality of who God is. To give him glory is not to add anything to him, as though he grew more glorious by our saying so; the sun does not brighten because someone looks at it. It is to recognise and declare what is already true, and to live in line with it. That takes three ordinary forms. Honest praise: kneeling by your bed on a Tuesday night, no audience, saying, you are good and I am not; you saved me when I had nothing, and I am grateful (Psalm 50:23). A life that points to him: when you are patient with a difficult colleague and they wonder what you have that they do not, God is glorified without a religious word spoken (1 Corinthians 10:31; Matthew 5:16). And trusting him when it is hard: I do not understand this, but I trust you. Though he slay me, I will hope in him (Job 13:15). That may be the deepest of all, because it tells every watching soul that this God is worth trusting when it costs. This is the goal of everything in chapters 1–3 (1:6, 12, 14).

In the church and in Christ Jesus. Let the strangeness of the pairing register. These two stand side by side, in one breath, as the places of God’s eternal glory. One is the risen Son, seated above every power. The other is a congregation, with its rota problems, its awkward silences, and its roof that needs money nobody has. Paul neither apologises for the pairing nor explains it away, because he has already told us why it holds: the church is his body, and the glory of the head shines in the body he fills (1:22–23). The church is not glorious in itself, but as the place where Christ’s glory shines. Which means you are not a spectator of something happening elsewhere. You are one of the places where God’s glory is meant to be seen.

Throughout all generations, forever and ever. Literally to all the generations of the age of the ages. Empires rise and fall; the church goes on, and its praise of God will never end. Your Tuesday-night prayer is not a small thing that vanishes by morning. It joins the unbroken chorus of every generation of believers, and it will still be sounding when time itself has finished.

Amen. A Hebrew word meaning firm, true, so be it. It was the people’s response in worship, saying yes to what was said (1 Corinthians 14:16; Nehemiah 8:6). It is not a pious full stop. Paul has written the sentence; the Amen is where the reader signs it. And saying it commits you: to asking to be one of the places where that glory becomes visible, in the particular congregation you will sit in this Sunday, for as long as you are given. Paul has finished his half of the letter. The word at the end of it is where you finish yours.

The turning point. This doxology ends the first half of the letter. Chapters 1–3 describe what God has done; chapters 4–6 describe how we should live. Between them stands praise. Right doctrine leads to worship, and worship leads to right living.

What it does not mean. Not that the church adds to God’s glory, as if he needed it. God’s glory is complete in himself. The church displays it, as a mirror displays the sun.

In a sentence. to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus through every generation, for ever and ever. Amen.

For worship. Glory to the Father, who planned it; to the Son, who did it; to the Spirit, who makes it ours; in the church and in Christ Jesus, for ever. Say the Amen aloud, and mean it.

3.overview:
Paul begins to pray (v. 1), then breaks off to explain his own role in God’s plan (vv. 2–13). God gave him, a prisoner for the Gentiles’ sake, a stewardship of grace: the revelation of the mystery of Christ, hidden in earlier generations and now revealed by the Spirit to the apostles and prophets. The mystery is that Gentiles are fellow heirs with Israel, members of the same body and sharers in the promise through the gospel. Paul, the least of all the saints, was given the task of preaching Christ’s unsearchable riches to the nations, so that through the church God’s many-sided wisdom might be displayed to the powers in the heavenly places. His sufferings are for their glory, so they must not lose heart.

Then he resumes his prayer (vv. 14–21), kneeling before the Father from whom every family takes its name. He asks that they be strengthened by the Spirit in the inner person, that Christ may dwell in their hearts by faith, and that, rooted in love, they may grasp the immeasurable dimensions of Christ’s love that surpasses knowledge, and be filled with all the fullness of God. The chapter ends in a doxology to the God who can do far more than we ask or imagine, to whom be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus for ever.

4.title: Unity, Gifts, and the New Self
4.text: <sup>1</sup>I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called, <sup>2</sup>with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, <sup>3</sup>eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. <sup>4</sup>There is one body and one Spirit — just as you were called to the one hope that belongs to your call — <sup>5</sup>one Lord, one faith, one baptism, <sup>6</sup>one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all. <sup>7</sup>But grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift. <sup>8</sup>Therefore it says, “When he ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men.” <sup>9</sup>(In saying, “He ascended,” what does it mean but that he had also descended into the lower regions, the earth? <sup>10</sup>He who descended is the one who also ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things.) <sup>11</sup>And he gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers, <sup>12</sup>to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ, <sup>13</sup>until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, <sup>14</sup>so that we may no longer be children, tossed to and fro by the waves and carried about by every wind of doctrine, by human cunning, by craftiness in deceitful schemes. <sup>15</sup>Rather, speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ, <sup>16</sup>from whom the whole body, joined and held together by every joint with which it is equipped, when each part is working properly, makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love. <sup>17</sup>Now this I say and testify in the Lord, that you must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their minds. <sup>18</sup>They are darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, due to their hardness of heart. <sup>19</sup>They have become callous and have given themselves up to sensuality, greedy to practice every kind of impurity. <sup>20</sup>But that is not the way you learned Christ! — <sup>21</sup>assuming that you have <sup>23</sup>and to be renewed in the spirit of your minds, <sup>24</sup>and to put on the new self, created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness. <sup>25</sup>Therefore, verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Walk Worthy: The Unity of the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As a prisoner for the Lord, Paul urges them to live worthy of their calling: completely humble and gentle, patient, bearing with one another in love, and working hard to keep the unity the Spirit gives through the bond of peace. There is one body and one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God and Father of all, over all, through all and in all.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Unity of the Church as Theological Reality

The passage reveals that the unity of the church is not an aspiration or a programme — it is an ontological reality that precedes and grounds every effort to express it. The Spirit has already created one body. The question is not whether unity exists but whether our behaviour honours the unity that does. This distinction between the given reality and the required response is characteristic of Paul's ethical method throughout the letter: indicative first, imperative second. Be what you are. Express what is already true.

The four virtues through which unity is maintained — humility, gentleness, patience, forbearance — are a portrait of Christlike character applied to community life. They are not soft virtues; they are demanding ones. Humility means thinking of others' interests above your own (Philippians 2:3). Gentleness (prautēs) belongs to the word Jesus used of himself (“I am gentle and lowly in heart,” Matthew 11:29) — strength in service of love. Patience is the willingness to absorb rather than retaliate. Forbearance is the daily choice to keep choosing the person in front of you rather than withdrawing when they disappoint. Together these virtues create the environment in which the given unity of the Spirit can be made visible.

The Reformers consistently emphasised that doctrinal unity and relational unity are inseparable. The sevenfold “one” of vv.4–6 grounds the relational unity of vv.2–3 in doctrinal reality. We are not called to unity by ignoring our differences or pretending that doctrine doesn't matter. We are called to unity because there is genuinely one Lord, one faith, one baptism — and the body that confesses these things is, by that very confession, one. Preserving this unity is not sentimentality; it is theological faithfulness.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church was the most socially diverse community in the city. Former Artemis worshippers, Jewish converts, Greek philosophers, slaves and freedmen, wealthy merchants and harbour workers — all brought together by the preaching of the gospel. The centrifugal forces were enormous. Every human instinct would have been to fracture along existing social fault lines. Paul's “therefore” connects the unity he calls for directly to the cosmic reality of chapter 2: the wall has already come down. The body is already one. Now: walk like it. Bear with one another. Choose the humility that makes room for people unlike you. This was not a small ask in first-century Ephesus.

Now: The church in our age is under intense pressure to fragment — along political lines, cultural lines, worship-style lines, theological nuance lines. The market logic of contemporary Christianity encourages us to shop for churches that suit our preferences, reinforcing the very homogeneity that Paul's vision challenges. Against this, Ephesians 4:1–6 calls the church to a costly unity rooted not in shared preference but in shared confession: one Lord, one faith, one baptism. The local church that perseveres through its internal differences — that chooses patient, humble, forbearing love over the easier path of fragmentation — is doing something more theologically significant than it knows. It is bearing witness to the one God who is over all and through all and in all.

verseByVerse.quote: I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called.

Meaning first. Ephesians 4 is the hinge of the letter: having shown what God has done (chapters 1–3), Paul now shows how to live because of it (chapters 4–6). He urges believers to walk worthy of their calling, with humility, gentleness and patient love, guarding the unity the Spirit has already created, which rests on one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism and one God and Father (vv. 1–6). Within that unity, the ascended Christ, like a victorious king sharing the spoils, has given gifts to each believer, and has given the church apostles, prophets, evangelists and pastor-teachers to equip all the saints for ministry, so that the church grows to maturity in Christ, stable against false teaching, speaking the truth in love, each part doing its work (vv. 7–16). Then he calls them to stop living as the unbelieving world does, with darkened minds and hardened hearts, because that is not how they learned Christ; they have put off the old self, are being renewed in mind, and have put on the new self created to be like God (vv. 17–24). He spells this out in practice: truth instead of lies, anger dealt with before sunset, work and generosity instead of theft, words that build up instead of rotten talk, no grieving of the Spirit, and kindness and forgiveness instead of bitterness, as God in Christ forgave us (vv. 25–32).

Therefore. Feel the turn, because it is the sharpest in the letter. For three chapters Paul has given almost no commands, only one call to remember (2:11). He has been describing: chosen, redeemed, sealed, made alive, raised, seated, reconciled, built, indwelt. Then a doxology. Chapters 4–6 hold about forty commands. And the order matters. Paul does not say, live like this, and God will accept you. He says, God has accepted you; therefore live like this. Christian ethics flows out of grace, never the other way round. Theologians call this the move from indicative (what is true) to imperative (what to do).

I … a prisoner for the Lord. Literally in the Lord. Paul repeats 3:1, not to win sympathy, but to show that he asks nothing he has not paid for himself. And notice who is asking you to walk: a man whose own walking has been reduced to the length of a cell. He asks others to do freely the very thing that has been taken from him.

Urge. Parakaleō: to call alongside, to appeal, to encourage. Not a cold order, but a pastor’s earnest plea. The same word is used for comfort.

To walk. After the size of chapters 1–3 you might expect something towering. What arrives is: walk. It is the plainest verb available, and it is chosen on purpose. It organises everything that follows: walk worthy (4:1), not as the Gentiles walk (4:17), walk in love (5:2), walk as children of light (5:8), walk wisely (5:15). Walking is what a person does all day without thinking about it. Nobody schedules it, nobody photographs it, and it cannot be done in bursts. That tells you where the Christian life is actually lived: not in the peaks, but in the ordinary going-along of an ordinary week.

In a manner worthy. “Worthy” (axiōs) first meant of equal weight, a merchant’s word: two pans of a balance, the goods in one answered by the weights in the other. And notice which pan you are asked to attend to. You cannot add anything to the calling side; it was filled by God before the world was made. You are asked to bring your side up to match it. A son who bears the family name worthily is not earning the name; he already has it, and nothing today will win or lose it. He is asked to live like a man who has it.

Of the calling to which you have been called. In Paul, God’s calling is not a general invitation but his effective summons, by which he brings a person to Christ (1:18; Romans 8:30; 2 Timothy 1:9). We were called to be holy and blameless (1:4), to be his children (1:5), to be one body (4:4). Not first a job or a career, though those matter, but the call to belong to Christ.

What it does not mean. Not that our conduct makes us worthy of being called, or that God calls those who are worthy. He calls the dead (2:1–5). Nor is it a life of grim effort under a heavy load: the same God who called also equips (4:7, 11–12) and works in us (3:20).

In a sentence. So I, a prisoner because I belong to the Lord, urge you to live in a way that matches the calling God has called you to,

On a Tuesday. Before the day starts, remember who God has called you to be. Then ask, at each decision: does this fit the name I bear?

For worship. Before Paul asks anything of us, God has already filled the calling side of the scales, and filled it before the world was made. Bless the God whose summons does not invite the worthy but raises the dead and gives them his own name. And adore the Lord Jesus, who walked the whole road worthy of his calling, from the manger to the cross, never once falling short of his Father’s will, so that people who could never balance the scales are clothed in his perfect walk. The prisoner in chains is only a faint echo of the Lord who was bound for us and is now free for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 1–3 set out what God has done; chapters 4–6 show the life that follows.

verseByVerse.quote: With all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love.

Why these come first. Paul is about to speak of the unity of the church (v. 3). What most often destroys unity is not doctrine but pride. These four qualities are the specific graces by which unity is kept; Paul’s sentence runs unbroken from “walk worthy” to “maintain the unity”. They are the ligaments of peace.

With all humility. Tapeinophrosynē: lowliness of mind. In the Greek world it was not a virtue but a fault, the cringing posture of a slave. Christ made it a virtue. He washed his disciples’ feet (John 13:1–17), and humbled himself, taking the form of a servant, to the point of death (Philippians 2:3–8). Humility is not thinking badly of yourself; it is thinking of yourself less, and seeing yourself truly before God, a sinner saved by grace (3:8).

And gentleness. Prautēs, often translated meekness, was used of a horse broken to the bridle. The animal has lost none of its strength; that was never the aim. The strength now answers to a hand other than its own. So gentleness is not being mild-mannered. A naturally timid man is not gentle in this sense; he simply has nothing that needs restraining. Gentleness is what strength looks like once it has been brought under command. Jesus called himself gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29), and he drove the traders out of the temple.

With patience. Makrothymia: long temper, the opposite of short-tempered. It is the patience God shows us (Romans 2:4), especially patience with people, the slow, the difficult, the wrong, more than with circumstances.

Bearing with one another in love. The word means to put up with, to carry the weight of. And Paul does not say bear with the difficulties, or the world outside. He says one another: the weight in question is other Christians. Make it concrete. The man who tells you the same story every time you meet. The woman who is late to everything and always has a reason. The one whose theology is slightly off and who would like to discuss it after the service, at length. The person who takes twenty minutes to say what needed three. Nobody in that list is sinning. They are simply heavy, in the way people are, and the instruction is to pick up the weight and keep walking. Love is what makes the others last. Without it, humility becomes self-contempt, gentleness becomes passivity, and patience becomes resentment.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should tolerate sin or false teaching without a word: Paul will command speaking the truth in love (v. 15) and exposing wrong (5:11). Bearing with one another is about personal faults and differences, not excusing evil. Nor is humility a pretended low opinion of oneself, or a refusal to use one’s gifts (v. 7). False modesty is still focused on self.

In a sentence. always humble and gentle, patient, putting up with one another in love,

On a Tuesday. Everyone reading this casts himself as the one doing the bearing. Turn it round: who in your church is bearing with you?
