Someone finds your manner difficult, your opinions tiring, your blind spot wearing, and has decided, quietly, to put up with it and go on loving you. You are somebody’s Wednesday morning. When that lands, humility stops being a doctrine and becomes possible.

For worship. Every grace in this verse was first a portrait of Christ. The Lord of glory, who could have come with thunder, came gentle and lowly in heart, strength under perfect command, washing the feet of friends who would desert him that night. His patience is longer than any temper. He has borne with us, not for an afternoon but through every year of our wandering, and he carried the full weight of our sins on the cross. Praise the Saviour whose meekness held back twelve legions of angels (Matthew 26:53) so that he might bear with sinners until they were brought home.

verseByVerse.quote: Eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

Eager. Spoudazontes: making every effort, hurrying to it, making it your business. Unity is a gift; keeping it is work. Nothing is maintained by enthusiasm. A house is maintained by somebody clearing the gutters in November; a marriage by two people apologising more often than they would like.

To maintain. Everything turns on this word. You are not asked to build unity; you could not, because it is not the kind of thing that can be manufactured. You are asked to keep, guard and preserve it, because it already exists. It is the difference between founding a family and not wrecking one. Nobody creates his own family. He finds himself in it, and what remains to be settled is how he treats people he did not choose.

The unity of the Spirit. The unity the Spirit creates. Every believer has the same Spirit (2:18, 22; 1 Corinthians 12:13), and Christ has already made Jew and Gentile one (2:14–16). This unity is a fact, not a goal; God’s work, not a human agreement. We can display it or obscure it, guard it or damage it.

In the bond of peace. A bond is something that ties together, like a cord or a ligament. Christ is our peace (2:14), and the peace he made at the cross must be lived out between people. And be concrete about what damages it, because we imagine the threat is doctrinal and it very seldom is. Churches do not usually divide over the person of Christ. They divide over a message never returned, a decision taken without consulting someone who expected to be consulted, a remark repeated to the wrong person, a slight at the door that was probably not even intended. The breach is almost never theological at the start. Theology gets recruited afterwards, to give the wound a respectable name.

What it does not mean. Not unity at any price, or unity that ignores truth. Paul grounds it in one faith (v. 5) and describes a unity of the faith and knowledge of Christ (v. 13). The unity of the Spirit cannot include those who deny the gospel itself: Paul curses another gospel (Galatians 1:8–9), and John forbids welcoming those who deny Christ’s teaching (2 John 10). But among those who share the gospel, Christians should not divide over secondary matters such as church government, the details of the last things or the style of worship. They may worship in different churches, but they should treat one another as brothers. Nor does unity require one worldwide church organisation, or uniformity in every practice.

Is it ever right to leave my church? Yes, but more rarely than we think, and never lightly. It is right to leave when a church abandons the gospel, will not teach the Bible faithfully, refuses to deal with serious sin or abuse, or binds your conscience where Scripture does not. It may also be right when you move house, or are genuinely needed elsewhere. It is not usually right to leave because the music changed, a friendship cooled or someone offended you; those are exactly the places where verse 3 is meant to be obeyed. If you do go, speak to your elders first, leave without running anyone down, and join another faithful church soon. Leaving a church is sometimes necessary. Drifting away from church altogether never is (Hebrews 10:24–25).

In a sentence. doing everything you can to keep the unity the Spirit gives, held together by peace.

On a Tuesday. The bond of peace never breaks in the abstract; it breaks between two particular people. Is there anyone in your church you are not at peace with: someone you avoid at coffee, or whose name produces a small tightening? That is where this verse is addressed, and no amount of general goodwill towards the church covers it. Go and repair one specific ligament.

For worship. The unity we are told to keep was bought, not negotiated. Christ made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20), breaking down the dividing wall in his own flesh, and the Spirit then bound us together with a cord no quarrel can finally cut. Glorify the God who did not wait for his people to agree before making them one. What we so easily fray, he wove; and the Father who gave his Son to make strangers into a family will not let the work of his Son be undone.

verseByVerse.quote: There is one body and one Spirit — just as you were called to the one hope that belongs to your call — one Lord, one faith, one baptism,
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is one body and one Spirit — just as you were called to the one hope that belongs to your call — one Lord, one faith, one baptism,

The shape. Count them: one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father. Seven times in three verses Paul strikes the same note. He is not writing elegantly here; he is hammering. And the list is arranged around the Trinity: one Spirit, with the body and the hope he creates (v. 4); one Lord, with the faith and baptism that focus on him (v. 5); one God and Father, over all (v. 6). The unity of the church is not organisational or emotional, but rooted in the unity of God himself. We are one because Father, Son and Spirit are one, and we are caught up into that life.

One body. The church, the body of Christ (1:23; 2:16). There are many congregations, but one church, with one head. A Christian in Ephesus and a Christian in China today belong to the same body.

One Spirit. The Holy Spirit, who indwells every believer and makes them members of the body (1 Corinthians 12:13). There is no believer without the Spirit (Romans 8:9).

The one hope that belongs to your call. When God called us, he called us to a single future: the inheritance in Christ, his return, the resurrection, the new creation (1:18). And take it personally, because it has an edge. The same finish line means the same finishing group. The people you find hardest in your church are not a temporary arrangement you will be relieved of at the end. They are the people you will be with, in unshadowed friendship, for ever. Learning to love them now is an early start on what you will be doing for eternity anyway.

One Lord. Jesus Christ, to whom every believer has bowed. In the Roman world “Lord” was Caesar’s title; for Christians, there is one Lord (1 Corinthians 8:6). This is the confession that makes someone a Christian: Jesus is Lord (Romans 10:9).

One faith. Both the act of faith, all believers trusting the same Christ in the same way, and the content of faith, the gospel believed (Jude 3). Christian unity is not shared feeling but shared truth.

One baptism. Baptism is the sign of entry into Christ and his body, given once (Romans 6:3–4; Galatians 3:27). Every believer is baptised into the same name, of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19). Some take it to mean Spirit baptism, but water baptism as the sign of union with Christ best fits the list. Its oneness also means it is never repeated.

What it does not mean. Not that all who call themselves Christians are thereby one, whatever they believe. The one faith sets a boundary: unity is among those who confess the one Lord and the one gospel. Nor does one baptism mean that baptism saves by itself: it is the sign of union with Christ by faith, not its cause.

Where Christians differ: one baptism, but whose? Christians disagree about who should be baptised and how. Paedobaptists (Presbyterian, Anglican and others) baptise the infants of believers as the new covenant sign, parallel to circumcision (Colossians 2:11–12). Credobaptists (Baptists and others) baptise those who profess faith, holding that baptism signifies a union with Christ by faith that infants cannot yet profess (Acts 2:41; 8:12). Sadly, many churches do not recognise each other’s baptisms. Verdict: credobaptist, held charitably. Believers’ baptism best fits the New Testament pattern, but paedobaptist Christians who trust Christ are brothers and sisters in the one faith and the one body. The disagreement is real, but it must not break the unity of verse 3.

I was baptised as a baby. Should I be baptised now? If you now trust Christ, the view taken here is yes, held gently. If baptism is the sign a believer receives on professing faith, then being baptised as a believer is not a second baptism but your first, and the oneness of baptism is not broken. Paedobaptist friends will see it differently, and they are not your opponents; treat the question with patience, and do not despise what your parents meant, for they were asking God to bless you. Talk it through with a pastor and read the passages for yourself (Acts 2:38–41; 8:36–38; Romans 6:3–4). Do not let it become a matter of pride or quarrelling. Baptism does not save you; Christ does. But obeying his command is a joy, not a burden.

In a sentence. There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called to one shared hope; one Lord, one faith, one baptism,

On a Tuesday. Bring to mind the last serious disagreement you saw in a church, the one that cooled a friendship or emptied a few seats. Run it against Paul’s seven. Was it about the one body, the one Spirit, the one hope, the one Lord, the one faith, the one baptism, the one Father? For most church disagreements, the honest answer is that the subject is nowhere on the list: the music, the timing, the building, how a decision was announced. Count how much you share before you count what divides you.

For worship. Seven times Paul strikes the note of one, and every stroke rings back to the God who is one. Adore the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, whose eternal fellowship knows no rivalry and no breach, and who has stooped to draw scattered sinners into that very life. There is one Lord, and he is not Caesar: he is the crucified and risen Jesus, before whom every believer from Ephesus to the ends of the earth has bowed. One hope awaits us because one Saviour has gone ahead, and the whole church will stand together before him, lost in one song.

verseByVerse.quote: one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.

One God. The great confession of Israel: Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one (Deuteronomy 6:4). Paul, a Jew, has not abandoned it. The one God is now known as Father, Son and Spirit (vv. 4–6), without becoming three gods. The God who is one makes his people one, which is why a church that splinters over secondary things acts against its own deepest nature.

And Father of all. In context, Father of all believers, his family of Jews and Gentiles (2:18–19; 3:14–15). Paul is not surveying humanity in general; he is in the middle of a passage about the church, and the “all” is the all of the preceding chapters: Jew and Gentile together, the two made one, the wall down. That is the astonishing thing he celebrates, and it is emptied, not enlarged, by being stretched to mean everyone without distinction. There are no stepchildren in God’s family.

Who is over all and through all and in all. Three small prepositions that between them cover everything. Over all: his transcendence. Nothing outranks him; there is no committee above this Father. Through all: his providence. He is no distant owner but is at work in and through every circumstance, including the ones you would never have chosen. In all: his presence. He dwells in his people by his Spirit (2:22). Over you, at work through your week, living within you. That leaves no position from which anything could reach you without passing him first.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add “you” (in you all) or “us”. Verdict: the shorter text, “in all”, is original. The addition gives the right sense, though: the “all” in view is God’s people.

What it does not mean. Not pantheism, the idea that God is everything or everything is God. God is over all, distinct from his creation. Nor universalism, that everyone is God’s child and will be saved. God is Father of all as Creator, in that he made and sustains every human being (Acts 17:28), but the language of sonship in the saving sense belongs to those who receive Christ: to all who did receive him, he gave the right to become children of God (John 1:12). Paul has just called people by nature children of wrath (2:3) and alienated from the life of God (4:18).

In a sentence. one God and Father of all, who rules over all, works through all and lives in all.

For worship. Over you, working through every hour of your week, living within you: one God and Father. Worship him with the whole church, across the world and through history, which worships him with you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Each believer has received grace as Christ apportioned it. As the psalm says, the conqueror ascended with captives and gave gifts to people; the one who ascended first descended, and he ascended above the heavens to fill everything. He gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, and pastors and teachers, to equip his people for service and build up his body, until all reach unity in faith and knowledge of the Son, maturity and the full stature of Christ. Then we will no longer be like children tossed by every wind of teaching and human trickery, but, speaking the truth in love, will grow in every way into Christ, the head, from whom the whole body, joined and held together, builds itself up in love as each part does its work.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ascended Christ and the Equipping Ministry

The passage grounds all ministry in the ascension of Christ — a movement of Pauline theology that is often underemphasised. It is the ascended Christ who gives gifts to his church. The one who has “ascended far above all the heavens” (v.10) is also the one who “fills all things” — present everywhere, sovereign over all, distributing gifts according to his wisdom and his grace. Ministry is not primarily a human enterprise; it is a dimension of the ongoing, active reign of the risen and ascended King.

The list of gifted persons — apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers — has generated significant debate about which offices are permanent and which ceased with the apostolic age. The Reformed tradition has consistently held that the foundational offices (apostles and prophets, Ephesians 2:20) were unique to the founding of the church, while the equipping offices (evangelists, pastor-teachers) continue throughout the church's history. What remains constant in every age is the purpose: equipping the saints for ministry until the whole body reaches the fullness of Christ.

The metaphor of the body in vv.15–16 is Paul's most developed statement of mutual ministry. The body grows “when each part is working properly” — not when a few parts are exceptionally active while the rest remain passive, but when every member is fulfilling their function. This is the vision of a church in which every person is a minister — not because every person preaches, but because every person contributes the grace-gift they have received to the building up of the whole. The body that achieves this grows toward Christ in every way. The body that fails at this — where a few do everything and the many receive — stunts its own growth.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church had known extraordinary leadership — Paul himself had spent three years there, and the elders he had appointed knew the weight of shepherding a flock in a hostile city (Acts 20:28–31). Now Paul is gone, and his letter is itself an act of equipping: preparing the church to continue faithfully without his physical presence. The gifted leaders he describes in vv.11–12 are, in the first instance, the elders and teachers of the Ephesian church — men charged with the immense responsibility of preparing every member for a ministry that would build the body in Paul's absence. This was not a programme; it was a pastoral theology applied to a real community facing real challenges.

Now: The consumer church — where the congregation pays for spiritual services delivered by professional clergy — is the precise opposite of Paul's vision. It produces spiritual infants who cannot feed themselves, who are vulnerable to every wind of doctrine, who have no sense of their own giftedness or their own call to ministry. The equipping church — where gifted leaders deliberately, systematically invest in the ministry capacity of every member — produces a body that is robust, maturing, and growing in love. The question for every church leader is not “How well am I performing?” but “How well am I equipping?” And the question for every member is not “Am I being fed?” but “Am I contributing?”

verseByVerse.quote: But grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift.

But. A turn from “all” (vv. 4–6) to “each”. The church is one, but not a uniform mass. Unity and diversity belong together, like the parts of a body (1 Corinthians 12:12–27).

Grace was given. Here “grace” means not saving grace, which all share equally, but grace for service: the gift and ability to serve in a particular way. Paul spoke of his own calling as grace given to him (3:2, 7–8). God’s grace does not stop at the doorstep of salvation; it floods every room of the Christian life, including the room of service. And the giving is the work of the whole Trinity: here Christ gives (vv. 7, 11), elsewhere the Spirit distributes and the Father works the same gifts (1 Corinthians 12:4–6, 11). One divine generosity, from three Persons.

To each one of us. No exceptions. There are no giftless Christians, no passengers in the church (1 Corinthians 12:7; 1 Peter 4:10). The gifts may be public, like teaching, or quiet, like helping, giving, showing mercy or administration (Romans 12:6–8). The question is not, do I have a gift? but, am I using what Christ has given me?

According to the measure of Christ’s gift. Christ decides what each receives and how much, and that removes both pride and envy at a stroke. If your measure is smaller than someone else’s, you have not been short-changed: it was measured out by the one who knows exactly what he intends to do with you, and envy is finally a complaint about his arithmetic. If your measure is larger, there is nothing to be proud of: a bigger allocation of something you did not earn is not an achievement. It is simply a larger delivery (1 Corinthians 12:11).

How do I find mine? The New Testament never suggests you identify your gift first and serve afterwards. It works the other way round, which is a relief. Begin with what is in front of you. What needs doing in your church that nobody is doing? What need are you uncomfortable walking past? What do people keep thanking you for, especially when you thought you had done nothing much? What do others keep asking you to do? Answered honestly across a year of ordinary service, those four questions will tell you more than any questionnaire. Gifts are found in use, the way a muscle is found by lifting something.

What it does not mean. Not that the gift is for the person’s own benefit or status. Gifts are given for the building up of the body (v. 12). Nor does every believer have the same gift, or need a spectacular one to be useful.

In a sentence. But each one of us has been given grace, in the measure Christ chose to give it.

On a Tuesday. Whose gift in your church do you quietly envy? And whose do you quietly think does not matter much? Both answers point to the same mistake, treating gifts as possessions to be ranked instead of assignments to be used. Nobody in a body admires the hand and looks down on the liver.

For worship. Every gift in the church is a piece of Christ’s own generosity, measured out by a hand that never miscalculates. He who had all the riches of heaven first gave himself, and from the fullness of his victory he goes on giving, not grudgingly by the spoonful but in a measure fitted to each of his people. Praise the Lord whose kindness reaches the quiet helper as surely as the gifted preacher. Father, Son and Spirit pour out one generosity, and no member of the body has been forgotten by the one who holds the measure.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore it says, 'When he ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore it says, ‘When he ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men.’

Therefore it says. Paul introduces Scripture. “It says” means God says it in the Scripture.

Psalm 68. A victory psalm. It celebrates God marching from Sinai and going up to his sanctuary on Mount Zion as a conquering king, with captives in procession behind him and the spoils of battle shared out. Picture the scene Paul is borrowing, because every subject of Rome knew it. A Roman triumph was the most spectacular public event of the ancient world: the victorious general in a chariot with laurel on his head, the army behind him, the treasure of the defeated carried through the streets on carts, and walking in chains, in full view of the crowd, the conquered kings themselves. At the end, the spoil was handed out.

When he ascended on high. Paul applies the psalm to Christ. God’s ascent to Zion is fulfilled in Christ’s ascension to heaven after his resurrection (Acts 1:9–11), where he is seated far above every power (1:20–21). The cross was the decisive battle; the ascension is the triumphal procession; the gifts to the church are the spoils of war.

He led a host of captives. Literally he took captivity captive. Christ’s defeated enemies, paraded in his triumph: sin, whose penalty he bore; death, which he walked into and came out of the other side, stripped of its sting (1 Corinthians 15:54–57); the devil and his powers, whom he disarmed and put to open shame (Colossians 2:15); and the law’s power to condemn, which he bore in our place (Galatians 3:13). Some read it of the people he freed from captivity, now following him; the military picture favours the first. Either way, Christ won.

And he gave gifts to men. Here is the puzzle. The Hebrew of Psalm 68:18 says the king received gifts among men; Paul says he gave gifts to men. Paul is not misquoting carelessly. In an ancient triumph, receiving tribute and sharing it with one’s soldiers were two halves of one event, and Paul presses the giving half because that is his point. The Aramaic paraphrase of the Psalms used in synagogues (the Targum) also read “gave”, and the psalm itself goes on to describe God giving to his people (68:10, 19, 35). The King who received the spoils now distributes them, the Spirit first of all (Acts 2:33). Christ ascended to give.

Which part of the procession were you in? The captives being led are the powers that once held you. But by the account of chapter 2, you were on their side of the parade: dead in trespasses, following the prince of the power of the air. You were not a spectator who happened to back the winning general. You were in the camp that lost, and the campaign that broke it was fought for you, not by you. That is why nobody in the New Testament boasts about a spiritual gift, and why boasting about one is so absurd. Loot is not an achievement. A soldier who spent the battle being carried off the field does not, on receiving his share of the spoil, make a speech about his contribution. Everything in your church that actually works, the teaching, the hospitality, the administration nobody notices, the person who is unaccountably good with the dying, is plunder from a battle in which we were the ones rescued.

The gifts. They are named in verse 11: not abilities in the abstract, but people. Christ gives the church gifted servants.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul changed Scripture to suit his argument. He interprets it, as Jewish teachers did, in the light of its fulfilment in Christ. Inspired by the Spirit, Paul shows what the psalm was pointing to all along.

In a sentence. That is why Scripture says: When he went up on high he led captives in his train and gave gifts to his people.

For worship. Every gift you have received in the church came off a battlefield, bought at a price you did not pay, and put into your hands by a King who went down into the grave to win it. Take the gift seriously and yourself lightly, and thank him.
verseByVerse.note: The psalm pictures God ascending Mount Zion in victory, receiving tribute; Paul applies it to Christ, who in triumph gives gifts. A Jewish Aramaic paraphrase of the psalm also reads “gave gifts.”

parallels.desc: you ascended on high, leading a host of captives

verseByVerse.quote: (In saying, 'He ascended,' what does it mean but that he had also descended into the lower regions, the earth? He who descended is the one who also ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
(In saying, ‘He ascended,’ what does it mean but that he had also descended into the lower regions, the earth? He who descended is the one who also ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things.)

The logic. To ascend implies a descent before it. If the psalm about God ascending is fulfilled in Christ, then Christ must first have come down from heaven. This identifies Christ with God: he came from heaven before he returned there (John 3:13; 6:62). The one who went up is the one who first went down.

The lower regions, the earth. The Greek is literally “the lower parts of the earth”. There are three main views of what Paul means.

1. The incarnation. The lower parts, that is, the earth: Christ came down from heaven to earth. Grammatically, “the earth” explains what the lower regions are, and this fits the contrast with “far above all the heavens”.

2. A descent into Hades. The parts lower than the earth: Christ went to the realm of the dead between his death and resurrection, perhaps to proclaim his victory. This idea leans chiefly on one difficult and much-debated verse (1 Peter 3:19), and it lies behind the line in the Apostles’ Creed, “he descended into hell”.

3. Pentecost. Christ ascended, then came down again in the Spirit to give gifts. This is less likely, because the descent comes before the ascent in Paul’s words.

Verdict: the incarnation: Christ’s coming down from heaven to earth, including the whole of his humiliation down to death and the grave (Philippians 2:6–8). Do not read a tour of the underworld out of this text; Paul is not mapping the afterlife, but tracing the sweep from the lowest place to the highest. Calvin and the Westminster Larger Catechism (Q. 50) understand the Creed’s phrase in a similar sense: that Christ endured the depths of humiliation, in Calvin’s account the very anguish of hell on the cross in our place, and in the Catechism’s that he remained in the state of the dead until the third day. A Christian can say the Creed’s words with full meaning and import no legend.

The descent, step by step. Count it out instead of summarising it, because “he descended” covers a very long way down. From the throne, where he was worshipped without ceasing, to a womb. From the womb to a manger (Luke 2:7). To a village with a poor reputation (John 1:46), and long years as a carpenter (Mark 6:3). To a wandering life with nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58). To being thought out of his mind by his own family (Mark 3:21). To a friend’s kiss in a garden at night, and all the rest running away (Mark 14:45, 50). To a courtyard where the man who had sworn to die with him denied knowing him (Mark 14:66–72). To a rigged trial, a whipping, a crown of thorns made as a joke (Mark 15:15–17). To an execution kept for slaves and rebels, stripped, between two criminals (Mark 15:24–27). To a cry of forsakenness (Mark 15:34). To a corpse. To a grave with a stone rolled across it. Every stair of it goes down. Misunderstood by those who should have known him best; let down by friends at the moment it mattered; praying in anguish and met by silence; shamed publicly and unjustly; broken in body; dead. He has stood in every one of those places, and he did not visit any of them as an observer.

Far above all the heavens. Not merely into the sky, but beyond every created realm, to the throne of God (Hebrews 4:14; 7:26). The one who went lowest has been raised highest.

That he might fill all things. Christ ascended not to leave the world, but to fill it with his presence, power and rule. The word runs through this letter like a river: the church, the fullness of him who fills all in all (1:23); filled with all the fullness of God (3:19); the fullness of Christ (4:13); be filled with the Spirit (5:18). He fills the universe as Lord, the church as Head, each believer by his Spirit, from the throne pouring out his Spirit and gifts (Acts 2:33). And the one who filled the far country of death now fills the far country of your suffering.

Textual note. Later manuscripts add “first” (he also descended first), as in the King James Version. Verdict: an early explanatory addition, not original, though it correctly states the order.

What it does not mean. Not that Christ’s ascension was a departure that left the church alone. He is more present to the whole church now, by his Spirit, than he was to the disciples in Galilee (John 16:7).

In a sentence. What does he went up mean, except that he had first come down to the lower regions, the earth? The one who came down is the same one who went up far above all the heavens, so that he might fill the whole universe.

On a Tuesday. Name the one place you suspect he cannot reach: the thing about your situation that feels beyond anyone’s sympathy, his included. Then hold it against that list. There is no cellar in your life with a floor lower than the one he has already stood on, and he has come up from it.

For worship. Behold the Son who went down every stair, from the throne to the manger to the grave, and was not diminished but glorified in the going. No angel was asked to take that road; the Lord of glory took it himself. And now the one who went lowest has been lifted highest, far above every power and every name, and he fills all things, not as a distant ruler but as the same Jesus who knew the cold of the tomb. Worship him, for there is no depth he did not reach and no height he does not now command.
verseByVerse.note: “The lower regions, the earth” may mean his coming down to earth in the incarnation.

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers.

And he gave. The emphasis is on “he”: Christ himself gave. These servants are not the church’s invention or employees, but Christ’s gifts to it. To despise faithful leaders is to despise his gifts. And notice exactly what he gave: not programmes, structures or a curriculum, but people. The ascended Lord’s provision for his church arrived with a name, a family, a limited constitution, and a phone that rings at inconvenient hours. That is far better than any resource, because a book cannot sit with you in a hospital corridor at two in the morning, and a recording does not notice that you have stopped coming. It also means the gift will disappoint you as a resource never would. Your pastor has a temperament, and some of it will grate. He will preach a thin sermon in the very month you needed a good one. Churches sometimes conclude that the wrong man was given, when what has happened is that a man was given, which was the arrangement from the beginning.

The apostles. Those personally commissioned by the risen Christ as his authoritative witnesses: the Twelve and Paul, with a few others in a wider sense (Acts 1:21–26; 1 Corinthians 9:1; 15:7–9). They laid the church’s foundation (2:20), and their teaching is preserved in the New Testament.

The prophets. New Testament prophets, who received and spoke revelation from God for the church in the foundation-laying period (2:20; 3:5; Acts 11:27–28; 13:1).

The evangelists. Those gifted to proclaim the gospel, especially where it has not been heard, and to plant churches. Philip is called an evangelist (Acts 21:8), and Timothy was told to do the work of one (2 Timothy 4:5). Something like missionaries and church planters, and the church needs them in every generation.

The shepherds and teachers. The Greek links these two with one article: probably one group, pastors who teach. “Shepherd” (poimēn) is the word translated pastor (Latin pastor means shepherd). A shepherd feeds, leads, protects and seeks his flock, and in the church he does it chiefly by teaching God’s word (Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 5:2; John 21:15–17). In the New Testament these are the elders, also called overseers (Titus 1:5–7). Christ is the chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:4); they are under-shepherds.

The common thread. Every gift listed is a ministry of the word. Christ builds his church by his word, spoken by the people he gives.

What it does not mean. Not a complete list of gifts (compare Romans 12:6–8; 1 Corinthians 12:8–10, 28). Nor does it mean that only these people serve: the next verse says they equip everyone else to serve.

Where Christians differ: apostles and prophets today. Some churches, especially in newer charismatic and apostolic movements, recognise living apostles and prophets with authority to direct the church, and speak of a fivefold ministry that must continue until we all attain to the unity of the faith (v. 13). Others use “apostle” today in a weaker sense, of missionaries or church planters. Cessationists hold that the foundational offices of apostle and prophet ended with the apostolic age, because a foundation is laid once (2:20), and that Scripture is now complete. Verdict: cessationist, held charitably. No one today holds the apostles’ authority, and the prophetic foundation is complete in Scripture. Evangelists, pastors and teachers continue, and the church needs them as much as ever.

In a sentence. And it was Christ who gave some to be apostles, some to be prophets, some to be evangelists, and some to be pastors who teach,

On a Tuesday. When did you last pray for your pastor by name, about the specific things you know he carries? And when did you last tell him something particular that helped? Most ministers live on general encouragement and precise criticism: the criticism comes with details and dates, the encouragement as “nice sermon” at the door. Reverse those two for a year, and you would hardly recognise the man at the end of it.

For worship. The ascended King, seated far above all the heavens, did not forget the small congregations he left behind. From the throne he sent people: apostles to lay the foundation, evangelists to carry the news, shepherds to feed his flock. Each is a gift from his own hand, and each points beyond himself to the chief Shepherd, who laid down his life for the sheep and still seeks, feeds and guards them by his word (John 10:11). Praise the Lord who rules the universe and still knows every one of his sheep by name.
verseByVerse.note: “Shepherds” is the word often translated “pastors.”

verseByVerse.quote: to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ,

To equip. Katartismos, a rich word. It was used of setting broken bones, of mending torn fishing nets (Mark 1:19), of fitting out a ship for a voyage, and of training someone for a task. Pastors and teachers mend, restore, train and fit out believers for service. Their chief tool is Scripture, which makes the person of God complete, equipped for every good work (2 Timothy 3:16–17).

The saints. All believers (see 1:1), not a special class.

For the work of ministry. “Ministry” is diakonia, service. The whole weight of this verse rests on where the commas fall. The King James Version reads: for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ: three parallel tasks, all belonging to the leaders. Modern versions drop the second comma: he gave leaders to equip the saints for the work of ministry. Now the ministry is what the saints do, with the leaders preparing them to do it. It has been called the most consequential comma in the history of the church. The modern reading has the better case, and the reason survives translation: Paul changes his preposition. The first phrase uses pros (with a view to); the next two use eis (resulting in). Three truly parallel items would naturally take the same word three times. The change marks a chain: leaders equip the saints, which results in the work of ministry, which results in the body built up. The saints are not the objects of ministry. They are the ones doing it.

What the ministry includes. Not only pulpit or platform. Care for the sick, the widow, the stranger (Matthew 25:35–36; James 1:27); encouragement that strengthens faith (Hebrews 3:13); teaching and discipling, older and younger, one to one (2 Timothy 2:2; Titus 2:3–5); witness to neighbours and colleagues (1 Peter 3:15); prayer (6:18); and generous giving (2 Corinthians 9:6–8). The woman who visits the lonely widow, the man who opens his home, the teenager who shares the gospel with a classmate: all are doing the work of ministry.

For building up the body of Christ. Two pictures merge: a building (2:20–22) and a body. The goal of all ministry is the growth of the church: in number as the lost are welcomed, in depth as members grow towards the fullness of Christ (v. 13), and in unity as the parts work together in love (v. 16).

What it does not mean. Not that pastors and teachers are unnecessary, or that everyone can do everything. The gift of pastor-teacher is distinct, and it matters. But the leaders’ task is not to be the only ones who serve; it is to make others able to serve. A church where only the pastor ministers is like a team where only the coach plays.

In a sentence. to train and equip God’s people for works of service, so that the body of Christ may be built up,

On a Tuesday. We usually measure a church by its minister: was the sermon good, does he visit enough? This verse measures something else: are the members working? If your pastor were taken away for six months, how much of your church’s actual ministry would simply stop? If the answer is nearly all of it, that is not a compliment to him. Ask your elders where you can serve, and start.

For worship. Christ is the true mender of nets and setter of broken bones. He took a people torn by sin and broken by the fall, and through his word he is fitting them out for service in his kingdom. Marvel that the King of kings should want ordinary saints as his fellow workers, and should take such patient care in preparing them. The whole building rises because he is building it (Matthew 16:18), and every act of service in his church is, in the end, the work of his own hands.

verseByVerse.quote: until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, so that we may no longer be children, tossed to and fro by the waves and carried about by every wind of doctrine, by human cunning, by craftiness in deceitful schemes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, so that we may no longer be children, tossed to and fro by the waves and carried about by every wind of doctrine, by human cunning, by craftiness in deceitful schemes.

Until. Ministry continues until the goal is reached. Fully, that will be at Christ’s return; but the church moves towards it now. Maturity is a direction of travel, not a destination reached in this life.

We all. Not a few spiritual heroes, but the whole church.

The unity of the faith. In verse 3 the church must guard the unity it has; here it grows into a fuller one: shared conviction about the whole truth of the gospel, received and confessed together (Jude 3). Not the unity of indifference to truth, or agreement on the lowest common denominator.

And of the knowledge of the Son of God. “Knowledge” is epignōsis, full, personal knowledge (1:17): not only a set of truths, but knowing a Person. The aim of all ministry is not a better informed congregation, but one more deeply captivated by Jesus himself. This is the only time Paul calls Jesus “the Son of God” in Ephesians.

To mature manhood. Literally to a complete man, a full-grown adult, in contrast with “children” in verse 14. It refers to the whole church as one new man (2:15) growing up, not only to individual men; women and men alike are included. Maturity here is not the absence of struggle but the presence of stability: a faith not easily capsized.

To the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ. The standard is staggering: not the best Christian you know, but Christ himself in his fullness (Romans 8:29; Colossians 1:28). The destination is a people who, together, look like him.

So that we may no longer be children. Children in the bad sense: unstable, gullible, easily impressed. Not the childlike trust Jesus praised (Matthew 18:3), but childishness (1 Corinthians 14:20; Hebrews 5:13–14).

Tossed to and fro by the waves and carried about by every wind of doctrine. A picture from the sea, familiar to a port city: a small boat with no keel, ballast or anchor. Tossed by the waves: the movement from underneath, the swell of feeling and circumstance. Carried about by every wind: the push from outside, whatever is blowing this season. A boat like that is not steered anywhere; it goes wherever the water and the air last decided. In practice it is the Christian whose convictions can be dated by whatever he last read or listened to; who is enthusiastic about a new teacher roughly every eighteen months, each time the one who has finally made sense of everything; who is persuaded by whoever spoke most confidently. Paul’s word is not an insult; it describes a stage, and the only tragedy is staying there.

By human cunning. The word (kybeia) means dice-playing, and so trickery: the sleight of hand of a cheat at dice.

By craftiness in deceitful schemes. “Craftiness” (panourgia) is the word Paul uses for the serpent deceiving Eve (2 Corinthians 11:3), and the serpent opened not with a denial but with a question (Genesis 3:1). “Schemes” (methodeia) is the word used of the devil’s schemes in 6:11. Error never announces itself. It comes warmly, from likeable and sincere people, wrapped around a great deal of truth. If it presented itself as error, nobody would take it. What makes it dangerous is that nine-tenths of it is right, and the remaining tenth is load-bearing.

What it does not mean. Not that mature Christians never change their minds or learn anything new. Maturity is teachable, but stable: it grows deeper roots instead of being uprooted by each new idea. And the cure is not to become suspicious of everything, which produces a hard, frightened Christian, not a mature one. It is to know the Son of God so well that counterfeits show themselves by contrast, the way someone who handles genuine banknotes all day needs no course in forgery.

In a sentence. until all of us reach unity in the faith and in knowing the Son of God, and become mature, grown up to the full measure of Christ; then we will no longer be like children, thrown about by the waves and blown here and there by every wind of teaching, by the trickery of people and their clever, deceitful schemes.

On a Tuesday. Over the last five years, has your view of something important shifted more than once? Trace why: was it a passage of Scripture you finally understood, or a person you found compelling? Both can move you; only one anchors you. Read the whole Bible, sit under faithful preaching, and learn the historic confessions of faith.

For worship. The goal of all the church’s labour is Christ himself: his fullness, his stature, his likeness reflected in a whole people. How great he must be, if the measure of maturity is nothing less than him. Every wind of doctrine blows and dies away, but the Son of God remains the same, the true coin by which every counterfeit is exposed. Praise him that he does not leave his people adrift. He is anchor, keel and harbour, and he will bring his whole church, not a few heroes only, to stand complete in him.

verseByVerse.quote: Rather, speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and held together by every joint with which it is equipped, when each part is working properly, makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rather, speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and held together by every joint with which it is equipped, when each part is working properly, makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love.

Rather, speaking the truth in love. One Greek word (alētheuontes): truthing, living and speaking the truth. Against the deceivers of verse 14, the church holds to the gospel truth, and speaks it, in preaching, in correction, in the daily witness of a consistent life (Colossians 3:16). But “in love”. Truth without love becomes harsh and proud; it wins arguments and loses people. Love without truth becomes sentimental and empty; it comforts people on their way to ruin. And “in love” means more than a pleasant tone. It is love with a goal: the good of the other, speaking the truth for someone instead of at them. Love is what separates the surgeon’s scalpel from the bully’s fist; both may cause pain, but only one is aimed at healing. Faithful are the wounds of a friend (Proverbs 27:6).

Two ways to abuse this phrase. It is probably the most quoted and most misused phrase in the chapter. First, a man decides something must be said, says it plainly, and afterwards feels the particular satisfaction of having been faithful, and everyone who heard it knows the satisfaction was the point. The sentence was composed in advance and delivered with relish. It cost him nothing and left the other person with no way forward. That is not truth in love; it is bluntness with a Bible verse pinned to the front. Second, and far more respectable: someone is drifting, a marriage is quietly failing, a man’s temper is frightening his children, and nobody says a word. We call the silence love. It almost never is. It is the avoidance of an unpleasant conversation, with love recruited to cover for it. If you have belonged to a church for years and never once said a hard thing to anyone in it, that needs a better explanation than gentleness. Three questions usually tell which you are doing. Have you prayed for this person more than you have rehearsed the sentence? Will it cost you something, or only them? And would you be willing for someone to do the same to you next month, about your own blind spot?

We are to grow up in every way into him. Growth in every area, no partial growth: not knowledge while love withers, not zeal while wisdom lags, but doctrine, character, relationships, worship, witness and suffering, all moving one way, into Christ. He is not only the model of maturity; he is its substance (2 Corinthians 3:18).

Who is the head, into Christ. In the ancient world, the head was seen as the source of direction and of life for the body. Christ rules the church and supplies its life (1:22; Colossians 1:18).

From whom the whole body. Growth comes from Christ. The church grows not by human techniques, but by drawing life from its head.

Joined and held together. The same builder’s word as in 2:21: fitted together, every part in its place.

By every joint with which it is equipped. Joints or ligaments are the points of contact through which supplies pass. Christ’s life flows to the members through their connections with each other. No Christian receives all he needs from Christ in isolation; much of it comes through other believers. And notice how growth actually happens: not through the heroics of a few, but through the faithful, ordinary contribution of every part. The encourager who seeks out the one who is struggling. The small group that holds one another under pressure. The older woman discipling a younger. The deacon who visits the sick, the giver who funds the missionary, the one who prays before it is light. The ligament is never seen and the joint never applauded, but remove them and the body collapses.

When each part is working properly. Every member has a function (v. 7). When some parts stop working, the body is weakened. A church in which only a few serve grows unhealthy.

Makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love. The body builds itself up, but only as Christ supplies it, and only in love. Maturity without growing love is only sophistication. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up (1 Corinthians 8:1). And a body overflowing with such love becomes itself the church’s best evangelism: by this all people will know that you are my disciples (John 13:35).

What it does not mean. Not that “speaking the truth in love” is only about confronting people with their faults. Above all, it means holding to and speaking the truth of the gospel, against error, in a loving way. Nor does church growth mean only numerical growth; Paul’s concern is maturity.

In a sentence. Instead, holding to the truth in love, we will grow up in every way into Christ, who is the head; from him the whole body, joined and held together by every supporting ligament, grows and builds itself up in love as each part does its work.

For worship. The risen Christ is feeding his whole body through ordinary people, one joint at a time, and you are one of them. Thank him for those who have helped you grow, and ask him to make you a joint through which his life reaches someone else.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — Put Off the Old, Put On the New
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul insists they must stop living like unbelieving Gentiles, whose thinking is futile, whose understanding is darkened, and who are cut off from God’s life by ignorance and hardened hearts; having lost all sensitivity, they give themselves to sensuality and every kind of impurity. That is not how they came to know Christ, if they truly heard and were taught the truth that is in Jesus: to put off the old self, corrupted by deceitful desires, to be renewed in their minds, and to put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Renewal of the Mind and the New Humanity

The “old self” and “new self” of this passage are not psychological categories — they are eschatological ones. The old self is the Adamic humanity: the self that has inherited Adam's corruption, lives under the dominion of sin, and is “corrupt through deceitful desires” (v.22). The new self is the new humanity created in Christ — what Paul elsewhere calls “the last Adam” (1 Corinthians 15:45). To be “in Christ” is to have been transferred from the old humanity to the new, from the domain of the first Adam to the domain of the Second.

The renewing of the mind (v.23) is the cognitive dimension of this transfer. Romans 12:2 makes the same point: “be transformed by the renewal of your mind.” The mind that has been shaped by the world — its values, its assumptions, its desires — must be reshaped by the word and Spirit of God. This is not achieved in a moment; it is the work of a lifetime. Every act of sustained Bible meditation, every time truth displaces a lie, every time a Spirit-given desire overcomes a flesh-driven one, the mind is being renewed. This is the slow and glorious work of sanctification.

The goal of the renewal is “the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness” (v.24). This is the restoration of the image of God that was defaced at the fall. God made humanity in his image; sin corrupted that image; Christ has come to restore it. The new self is not merely morally better than the old — it is ontologically different, created anew after the very likeness of God. This is why the Christian life is not ultimately about rule-keeping but about becoming who you already are in Christ: the image-bearer of God, restored and renewed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ephesus was a city of extraordinary sensual abundance. The temple complex of Artemis, the bath-houses, the theatre, the commercial district — pleasure was available in every form and at every price. To be a Christian in Ephesus was to swim against a powerful and relentless current. Paul does not tell the Ephesian Christians to try harder or to exercise greater willpower. He gives them something more powerful: a new identity. You are not the old self anymore. The garment of the old life is to be put off — not held on to, not worn occasionally for old time's sake, but removed and discarded. And in its place: the new self, created after God's own likeness.

Now: The pornified, entertainment-saturated, hyper-stimulated culture of the 21st century is Ephesus with better technology. The mechanisms of desire-manipulation are more sophisticated; the availability of darkness is more immediate; the cultural current against a holy life runs faster. Paul's answer is unchanged and still the most powerful available: not more discipline applied to the old self, but the daily renewal of the mind in the truth of the gospel — who you are in Christ, what you have been given, who you are becoming. The Christian who meditates daily on Scripture, who submits their thinking to the word of God, who asks the Spirit to renew their mind — this person is not swimming against the current on their own. They are being transformed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now this I say and testify in the Lord, that you must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their minds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now this I say and testify in the Lord, that you must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their minds.

Now this I say and testify in the Lord. “Testify” (martyromai) is heavier than it looks: from martys, witness, the root of our word martyr. It belongs to the solemn, legal register: to affirm as under oath. “In the Lord” means with Christ’s authority. This is not Paul’s opinion; it is Christ’s command. And that he must say it at all tells us something: conversion does not automatically make us live as God wills. The old patterns do not vanish overnight.

You must no longer walk. “Walk” again (see v. 1). A change of way of life is required. “No longer”: they once did walk this way (2:1–3).

As the Gentiles do. The readers were Gentiles by birth, but Paul now uses “Gentiles” for unbelieving pagans. Their identity has changed so completely that they are no longer counted as Gentiles in that sense. They belong to God’s people; they must stop living like outsiders.

In the futility of their minds. “Futility” (mataiotēs) means emptiness: the word the Greek Old Testament uses for idols, vain things that cannot see, save or satisfy (Jeremiah 2:5), and for the refrain of Ecclesiastes, vanity of vanities. The Preacher tried pleasure, work, wealth and wisdom and called it all hevel, a vapour you cannot hold. “Mind” (nous) is the whole faculty by which a person weighs what is real and decides how to live. So the diagnosis is exact: not muddled thinking, but a mind whose every judgement is bent because the thing at its centre is empty. Ephesus was built around the temple of Artemis: a life of praying to stone, buying charms, consulting magicians, busy and even religious, aimed at gods who were not there. Only the idols have changed clothes: the bigger house, the endless scroll, the next achievement that was finally going to satisfy. Plenty of motion; no destination.

The hunger underneath. God made the heart for himself. As Augustine prayed, our heart is restless until it rests in you. We try to fill that ache with good things, family, work, a hard-earned holiday, gifts of God every one, but never built to carry that weight. And none of this stops at conversion. You are redeemed, and you still catch yourself reaching for the old empty wells. How do you fight it? Not mainly by gritting your teeth to want less; a hungry heart is not talked out of eating. Thomas Chalmers named the real cure: the expulsive power of a new affection. You do not drive out a lesser love by willpower but by a greater one. So when the itch comes, if I just had that, I would be content, name it: that is the hunger again, and that thing cannot fill it. Feed the real hunger at its only source, the word, prayer, the Lord’s table, God’s people. And receive the good gifts, your spouse, your work, your rest, not as gods that must satisfy, but as gifts from a Father who already has.

What it does not mean. Not that unbelievers are stupid, or that everything they think is false. By God’s common grace, unbelievers discover much truth in science, art and wisdom. The futility is at the root: without God, the deepest questions (who am I, why am I here, how should I live, what happens at death) are left without true answers. And the cure is exact: the same nous that is futile here is the very thing grace renews: be transformed by the renewal of your mind (Romans 12:2).

In a sentence. So I tell you this, and insist on it in the Lord: you must no longer live as the pagans do, with their empty thinking.

On a Tuesday. God is not calling you out of a good life into a grey one of chores. He is calling you out of the empty life into the full one. Notice how many of your daily assumptions about success, pleasure and money come from the culture instead of from Christ, and hold each one up to the light.

For worship. Every idol of Ephesus was empty, and every idol of our own age is empty too; but the living God is the one fullness that never runs dry. He alone made the heart, and he alone can satisfy it. Adore him for not leaving us to the vapour. The Son came into a world subjected to futility, bore its curse in his own body, and rose to give it hope (Romans 8:20–21). In him the restless heart at last finds rest, and a mind emptied by idols is filled with the knowledge of a glorious God.

verseByVerse.quote: They are darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, due to their hardness of heart. They have become callous and have given themselves up to sensuality, greedy to practice every kind of impurity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They are darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, due to their hardness of heart. They have become callous and have given themselves up to sensuality, greedy to practice every kind of impurity.

The order. Read the chain from the inside out: (1) hardness of heart, which causes (2) ignorance, which leads to (3) alienation from the life of God and (4) darkened understanding; and then (5) callousness, (6) giving themselves up to sensuality, and (7) greed for impurity. The root is not in the head but in the heart. People do not reject God because they lack information; they lack understanding because their hearts are hard towards him. This is the predictable anatomy of a life moving away from God.

Darkened in their understanding. The form is passive: not only that they darkened themselves, but that they have been darkened. This is not stupidity; these people may be brilliant. It is the faculty by which a person decides what is worth living for, so that the needle still swings confidently but points the wrong way. Back then it looked respectable: a man pouring his years into status and the favour of Artemis, every neighbour nodding at how wisely he lived. It looks just as respectable now: a decent, hard-working man pouring his one life into the career, the retirement fund, the renovated house, the evenings handed to a screen, nothing scandalous, all reasonable, aimed at a horizon that ends at the grave. And Paul has already prayed the cure for this very darkness, in this letter: having the eyes of your hearts enlightened (1:18). The god of this world blinds (2 Corinthians 4:4); the God who said, Let light shine out of darkness, shines in the heart (2 Corinthians 4:6).

Alienated from the life of God. There are two kinds of life: the life you can measure, breath and heartbeat, and God’s own life flowing into a soul. Picture a flower cut for the table. On Monday it looks perfect, but cut from its root it is already dying; it simply has not shown it yet. This is the spiritual death of 2:1, and the very thing Christ came to reverse: I came that they may have life and have it abundantly (John 10:10).

Because of the ignorance that is in them. Not innocent ignorance, as of someone who has never heard, but wilful ignorance: the not-knowing of a man who keeps shutting his eyes against the sun and then complains that it is night (Romans 1:21).

Due to their hardness of heart. “Hardness” (pōrōsis) was a medical word for calcification, hard tissue forming where there should be living flexibility; it was also used of marble. It is not one dramatic rebellion, but small refusals piling up, each making the next easier. Pharaoh is the case study: again and again he hardened his own heart, and again and again the LORD hardened it (Exodus 8:15; 9:12). He hardened himself until God confirmed him in the hardness he had chosen. That is the most frightening sentence a soul can receive: not lightning, but a handing over, God ceasing to interrupt. Which is why Scripture pleads, Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts (Hebrews 3:7–13).

They have become callous. Literally past feeling. The conscience that once protested has gone numb, like skin burned so often it no longer feels pain. What once caused shame no longer does.

And have given themselves up to sensuality. “Sensuality” (aselgeia) is appetite with the brakes removed: open, unrestrained self-gratification that no longer bothers to hide. In Romans 1:24 Paul says God gave them up; here they give themselves up. Both are true: God’s judgement is to hand people over to what they have chosen.

Greedy to practise every kind of impurity. “Greedy” is pleonexia, wanting more, the word translated covetousness in 5:3. Indulgence does not satisfy; it inflames. The one who thought freedom lay in removing every limit finds himself a slave to cravings that cannot be fed. And that very hunger is the backhanded proof of what the soul was made for: a thirst this deep was never meant for the far country, but for the one who says, whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again (John 4:14).

The sweetest reversal. A heart can harden itself, but it cannot soften itself; calcified tissue does not choose to become supple again. So God promises to do the one thing the sinner cannot: I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26). Not a hard heart lectured into softness, but a new heart given. And because the hardened heart was the engine of the whole descent, when grace turns the root, the rest turns with it.

How do I know whether my own heart is hardening, and could it be too late? The warning signs are quiet: sins that once troubled you no longer do; you hear Scripture and feel nothing, and do not mind feeling nothing; you avoid people who might challenge you; you explain away every conviction. If you see some of that in yourself, do not despair, but act today, while it is called today (Hebrews 3:13). Confess it plainly, get back under the word and among God’s people, and ask for the heart of flesh God promises (Ezekiel 36:26). And if you are afraid it is already too late, that fear is itself evidence that it is not. A heart past feeling does not lie awake worrying that it is past feeling. Christ still promises that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37).

What it does not mean. Not that every unbeliever is equally sensual or depraved. Paul describes where the road leads. Many unbelievers are restrained by conscience, upbringing, law and God’s common grace. Nor does it mean Christians cannot be affected: Paul warns believers precisely because they can drift back. They read this with recognition, not superiority: this was the road we were on, and grace interrupted it.

In a sentence. Their understanding is darkened and they are cut off from the life of God, because of the ignorance that comes from their hardened hearts; having lost all sense of shame, they have given themselves over to sensuality, eager to indulge every kind of impurity, always wanting more.

On a Tuesday. None of this begins with a dramatic fall: a little hardness, a little less sensitivity, a little more drift. Do not trust the fact that something no longer feels wrong. Test your conscience by Scripture, not Scripture by your habits.

For worship. Glory to the God who softens stone. No hardened heart ever reasoned its way back to life, yet he speaks, and calcified hearts become flesh. Behold his mercy in the light he shines into darkened minds, the same light that first shone at creation. Christ was handed over so that we need not be handed over to our cravings; he drank the cup of wrath so that the thirsty might drink living water. Every believer who reads this passage was once on that road, and every one has been turned back by sovereign grace.

verseByVerse.quote: But that is not the way you learned Christ!
verseByVerse.commentary:
But that is not the way you learned Christ!

But that is not the way. The Greek is emphatic: but you, not so. After the bleak description of verses 18–19, Paul turns on a coin. That world is not what you were brought into.

You learned Christ. An unusual phrase, found nowhere else in Greek literature. Not “you learned about Christ”, or “you learned Christ’s teaching”, but you learned Christ: a Person, not a curriculum. In the ancient world you learned a philosopher’s ideas; the philosopher was only the delivery man. Here the Teacher is himself the lesson. Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29). A disciple (mathētēs, a learner) was never someone who mastered a syllabus, but an apprentice to a Person, until his life reshapes yours, and at the far end a man can say, it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me (Galatians 2:20).

How you learn a person. Nobody learns a person the way he learns a subject. It takes time, attention, presence, and much watching him under pressure. So use the ordinary means that way. Read the Gospels not mainly for information but in order to watch him: how he handles interruption, what makes him angry, whom he stops for, how he speaks to people who have failed badly. Pray as conversation, not recitation. And obey, the part we usually leave out. Jesus said that whoever keeps his commandments is the one to whom he will show himself (John 14:21). Obedience is not the fee for knowing him; it is one of the ways the knowing happens, because you find out what a person is like chiefly by doing things alongside him.

The logic. If you have truly learned Christ, you cannot be at ease with the life of verses 17–19. You cannot learn the pure, self-giving Christ and conclude that sensual, self-serving living is fine. A man handed a rule-book keeps rules badly and resents them by Thursday. A man who has come to love a Person finds his behaviour changing from somewhere deeper than his will. Paul lays this down before two chapters of instruction, because everything that follows would be impossible on any other footing.

What it does not mean. Not that learning Christ is a purely intellectual exercise. It includes knowledge, but it is the knowledge of a disciple following a master.

In a sentence. But that is not how you came to know Christ,

On a Tuesday. Try to say in one sentence what Jesus is like: not what he did, taught or achieved, but what he is like to deal with. Most of us can say a great deal under the first three and find the fourth surprisingly hard. That gap is the difference between learning about him and learning him. And when you are tempted, ask: would the one I have learned recognise himself in what I am about to do?

For worship. What a Saviour, that he is himself the lesson. No philosopher ever offered his own person as the curriculum, but Christ does, because there is nothing truer, lovelier or more worth knowing than he is. To learn him is to learn the heart of God, gentle and lowly, holy and patient, and the knowing never comes to an end. Praise him that he does not merely send down rules from a distance, but draws near as Teacher and Friend, and over a lifetime makes his learners like himself.

verseByVerse.quote: assuming that you have heard about him and were taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
assuming that you have heard about him and were taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus,

Assuming that you have heard about him. Or “surely you heard him”. The Greek can mean heard him: when the gospel was preached to them, Christ himself was speaking through his messengers (2:17). That is a high view of preaching (Romans 10:14, 17). Paul is not doubting their conversion; he is reminding them what they received.

And were taught in him. Notice the little word: in him, not by him. Had Paul meant only that Christ taught them, he could have said through him. He writes “in him”, the language of union that fills this letter. The teaching did not arrive from outside, a parcel of facts handed over at arm’s length; it happened within their union with Christ. That is why the futile mind of verses 17–19 could never arrive here, and why what follows is not a rule-book posted from a distance, but instruction able to produce a new self (v. 24).

As the truth is in Jesus. The only place in Ephesians where Paul uses the human name Jesus alone, without Christ or Lord. The emphasis falls on the historical person, the man from Nazareth who touched lepers, was crucified under Pilate and rose. Truth is not an abstract idea or an inner feeling; it has taken flesh in a real life. You could hand a man the dictionary meaning of courage, accurate and bloodless, or point him to the soldier who threw himself on a grenade for his friends: courage with a face. A piano teacher can explain the theory of a sonata, or sit down and play it: there, that is how it is meant to sound. In Jesus, the truth about God and about what a human life was made to be stopped being a concept and became a life you can watch. And hold this axis of the passage: the truth is in Jesus (v. 21); the old self is corrupted by deceitful desires (v. 22). Truth against deceit is the real contest. False teachers detached “Christ” from the real Jesus; Paul ties them together (1 John 4:2–3).

What it does not mean. Not that truth is relative or personal (“my truth”). There is truth, and it is found in Jesus (John 14:6), who is the same yesterday and today and forever (Hebrews 13:8). Nor is every teaching that uses Jesus’ name true: the test is whether it matches the Jesus of the apostolic witness.

In a sentence. if indeed you heard him and were taught in him, as the truth is found in Jesus:

On a Tuesday. Test what you hear about Jesus, online or anywhere, by the Jesus of the Gospels. If it does not match him, it is not the truth as it is in Jesus.

For worship. The truth of God has a name, a face and a home town. Adore the eternal Son who took flesh in Nazareth, so that truth could be seen touching lepers, weeping at a grave and dying under Pilate. All the promises of God find their Yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20). And marvel that this Jesus still speaks: when his gospel is faithfully preached, his own voice reaches his sheep. We were not taught at arm’s length, but drawn into union with the one who is himself the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: to put off your old self, which belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires,
verseByVerse.commentary:
to put off your old self, which belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires,

The grammar. Verses 22–24 give the content of what they were taught (vv. 20–21): to put off the old self, to be renewed, and to put on the new self. Scholars debate whether these are commands (put off!) or a description of what happened at conversion (you have put off). Colossians 3:9–10 speaks of it as having happened. Verdict: both. At conversion, the old self was decisively put off in union with Christ (Romans 6:6); now believers must keep living out that change, day by day (vv. 25–32 give the commands).

To put off. A picture of clothing: to take off and throw away old garments. Clothing in Scripture often pictures character (Isaiah 61:10; Zechariah 3:3–5). But this is not adjusting your wardrobe; it is stripping off an entire identity. Early converts may have taken off old clothes before baptism and put on new white ones, picturing this change.

Your old self. Literally the old man (as in Romans 6:6; Colossians 3:9): not the body or the personality, and not just bad habits, but the whole person you were in Adam, before union with Christ, ruled by sin (2:1–3). It is not a part of you; it is the old you.

Which belongs to your former manner of life. The old self and the old life are bound together; you cannot keep one and lose the other. The old way of living is the old self’s natural home. It is out of date, like clothes from a former life, and it does not fit who we now are.

And is corrupt. Present tense: is being corrupted, decaying, rotting, like a corpse or spoiled food. You do not renovate what is rotting; you put it off.

Through deceitful desires. Literally desires of deceit. They are called deceitful because they make promises they cannot keep, and it is worth writing the promises down, because there are remarkably few and they hardly ever vary. Just this once, and then never again. You have earned this; look at the week you have had. Nobody will ever know. You will feel better afterwards. You can stop whenever you decide to. Everybody does this. That is nearly the whole script, and it does not need to be clever, because it is delivered at the one moment when you are least inclined to examine it. Then notice what is actually delivered. Ten minutes afterwards there is no real satisfaction. There is a slight flatness, and the beginning of a wish that it had not happened. The thing that was going to make you feel better has made you feel worse, and left you a little further in than before. That is what Paul means by corrupting. The trouble with the desire is not that it is naughty. It is that it lies, and the lie costs you something every time you believe it (Hebrews 3:13; James 1:14–15). The serpent’s lie in Eden still works the same way (Genesis 3:4–6).

How do you put off something so deep? Not by willpower wrestling a living master to the ground, but by faith reckoning on a death already died. We know that our old self was crucified with him (Romans 6:6). To put off is not to kill what is thriving, but to stop dressing a dead man each morning, to leave off the grave-clothes of a corpse. And you were raised with Christ too (Colossians 3:1–3), which is why the next word is not another command to grit your teeth, but a promise: be renewed.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians have two equal natures fighting inside them, or are still the old self with a new layer on top. The old self has been put off; believers are new people (2 Corinthians 5:17). But remaining sin still lives in us and must be fought (Romans 7:21–25; Galatians 5:17). The fight is real, but the identity is settled. Nor does putting off happen by willpower alone: it flows from union with Christ, by the Spirit (Romans 8:13).

In a sentence. you were taught to take off your old self, which belongs to your former way of life and is being ruined by its deceitful desires,

On a Tuesday. Bring to mind the thing that most reliably pulls at you. Put one question to it: not whether it was pleasant, but what its record is. Has it ever once delivered what it promised: the satisfaction, the relief, the sense that things would now be all right? A desire with a perfect record of lying to you has no claim on your trust. You are not being asked to give up something that works.

For worship. The old self was not merely reformed; it was crucified with Christ (Romans 6:6). Praise the Saviour who went into death bearing the man we were, and left him in the grave. Every lie that desire whispers is answered by a truer word: the Son of God loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20). He has never deceived us, and never failed to deliver what he promised. Where deceitful desires corrupt and decay, his grace clothes and renews, and the one who took off our grave-clothes will finish dressing us in glory.
verseByVerse.note: The “old self” (literally “old man”) is the person we were in Adam, before union with Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: and to be renewed in the spirit of your minds,
verseByVerse.commentary:
and to be renewed in the spirit of your minds,

And to be renewed. Between “put off” (v. 22) and “put on” (v. 24) stands the hinge. The verb is present and passive. Present: continuous, a daily process, not a single event. Passive: something done to us, by God, through his Spirit and his word. We do not renew ourselves; we are renewed. That rules out both passivity and mere willpower: work out your own salvation … for it is God who works in you (Philippians 2:12–13). We cannot manufacture renewal, but we can put ourselves in its way: Scripture that retrains the mind, prayer, honest friendship, the preached word (Romans 12:2). To neglect these is not to be passive; it is to starve the very faculty God is renewing.

In the spirit of your minds. Not the Holy Spirit here, but our own inner spirit: the deep attitude or mindset from which our thinking flows. Not changing a few opinions, but changing the whole outlook opinions come from. The futile mind of verse 17 is replaced by a mind being made new.

Why the mind? Because the problem began with darkened understanding (v. 18). Behaviour follows belief. What we think about God, ourselves and the world shapes what we desire and do. Lasting change in behaviour comes through changed thinking, and that comes through the truth as it is in Jesus (v. 21).

Reflexes, not only information. A renewed mind is not chiefly a mind with more in it; it is a mind whose reflexes have changed. Notice where your mind goes on its own.
