Someone criticises you in front of others: what happens in the first half-second, before you arrange your face? A colleague you consider less able is promoted over you: what is the first movement of the heart, before the congratulations? Money is tight and you are awake at two in the morning: what does the mind reach for? In every case there is a default, installed long before you were converted. You can agree to almost any doctrine at little cost. So measure renewal not by your convictions, but by the unguarded reaction. And be encouraged, not crushed, by what you find, because this is exactly the faculty God has undertaken to renew, slowly and from underneath. The first sign is rarely that the wrong reflex has gone. It is that you notice it. A year ago the resentment simply was the truth about the situation; now it arrives, and something in you recognises it as an intruder and declines to agree with it. That is the renewal showing its first light.

What it does not mean. Not that Christianity is merely intellectual, or that knowing the right things automatically produces holiness. The mind here includes the heart’s attitudes. Nor is renewal instant or complete in this life. It is a promise before it is a command: he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6), from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18). Think of John Newton, once the hard-hearted captain of a slave ship, renewed by God degree by degree over a lifetime until that same mind gave the church Amazing Grace. Near the end, his memory almost gone, he said: I remember two things, that I am a great sinner, and that Christ is a great Saviour. That is a renewed mind, and the God who did it for Newton is doing it for you.

In a sentence. to be made new in the attitude of your minds,

On a Tuesday. What you fill your mind with shapes who you become. Count the hours you give to screens and the minutes you give to Scripture, and adjust.

For worship. Renewal is God’s work before it is ours, and that is cause for praise. The Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation now broods over minds bent by years of sin, and patiently, from underneath, he makes them new. He is never hurried and never defeated. Bless the Father who has undertaken it, the Son whose truth is its material, and the Spirit who applies it day by day. The God who turned a slave-ship captain into a singer of grace will not abandon what he has begun in any of his children.

verseByVerse.quote: and to put on the new self, created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and to put on the new self, created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness.

To put on. The clothing picture again (see v. 22). It is not enough to strip off the old; one must be clothed with the new. You do not get dressed by accident. Elsewhere Paul says to put on the Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 13:14; Galatians 3:27). The new self is likeness to Christ.

The new self. Literally the new man: the person we are in union with Christ. “New” (kainos) means new in kind, fresh, not merely more recent. It is the personal side of the “one new man” of 2:15.

Created. God’s act, like the first creation (2:10). Becoming a Christian is not self-improvement but new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17).

After the likeness of God. Literally according to God, reaching back to Genesis 1:26–27. Humanity was made in God’s image; the fall defaced it, though it did not destroy it. In Christ, the perfect image of God (Colossians 1:15), the image is being restored: renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator (Colossians 3:10). Salvation does not make us less human, but truly human again. And it is more than Eden restored. Adam was innocent but untested, able to fall. The pattern of the new self is not the first Adam but the last (1 Corinthians 15:45): Christ, tried in every way, obedient to death, risen and beyond all falling. The destination is a likeness to him that can never again be lost (Romans 8:29).

In true righteousness and holiness. Literally in righteousness and holiness of the truth, in contrast with “desires of deceit” (v. 22). The old self was driven by lies; the new self is shaped by truth. Righteousness leans towards what we owe our neighbour: honesty, justice, love. Holiness leans towards God: reverence, devotion, purity. Together they describe a life that reflects God’s own character, the real thing and not a mask.

How do you actually do it? Paul’s brevity is a clue: it is not complicated. To put on the new self is to act from who you now are in Christ, not who you used to be. Picture a child taken off the street and adopted into a noble house. His birth has not changed, but his belonging has, entirely. The old instincts linger: he hoards food, flinches at kindness, waits to be thrown out. Learning to put on his new self is nothing more than learning to live as what he truly is: a son at his father’s table. He does not earn the sonship by behaving like a son; he behaves like a son because he already is one (1:5). So in any moment, a conversation, a temptation, ask what the person you are in Christ would do, and do it by faith before the feeling follows. Measure it by direction, not perfection. The adopted son still flinches, and is a son all the same.

What it does not mean. Not that believers produce their new self by their own effort, or that putting on is an outward act, like a costume. The new self is God’s creation, and putting it on means living according to what God has made us. Nor are believers already perfect: the new self is real, but it grows to maturity over a lifetime.

In a sentence. and to put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness.

For worship. God is remaking you in his own likeness, the likeness of his Son, and when he has finished, you will never be able to lose it. Praise the God who makes all things new, beginning with you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So they must stop lying and speak truthfully to one another, for they are members of one body. In anger they must not sin, nor let anger outlast the day and give the devil a foothold. Thieves must stop stealing and work honestly, so as to have something to share with those in need. No unwholesome talk should come from their mouths, only what builds others up and gives grace to those who hear. They must not grieve the Holy Spirit, with whom they were sealed for the day of redemption. They must get rid of bitterness, rage, anger, brawling, slander and malice, and be kind and compassionate, forgiving one another as God forgave them in Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Grieving of the Spirit and the Ethics of Grace

Verse 30 — “do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” — is one of the most searching statements in the New Testament about the nature of the Spirit. He can be grieved. The Holy Spirit is not an impersonal force that responds mechanically to human sin; he is a Person with genuine emotional sensibility who is affected by the moral life of the community he inhabits. The sins Paul has listed — falsehood, uncontrolled anger, stealing, corrupting speech, bitterness, wrath, malice — do not merely harm the community; they wound the indwelling Guest.

The phrase “by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” provides the context for the warning. The Spirit who can be grieved is the same Spirit who has sealed us for the final day — who is our guarantee of the inheritance (1:14), the deposit of our future glory. To grieve him is therefore not a trivial matter; it is to harm the very relationship that is the ground of our assurance and the means of our transformation. This is not a threat to the believer's salvation; Paul does not say “by whom you were sealed unless you grieve him.” The sealing is certain. But the quality of the Spirit's presence and work in the community is affected by how the community lives.

The climactic command — “forgive one another, as God in Christ forgave you” (v.32) — sets the standard for Christian forgiveness at the level of the cross: freely given, fully extended, without conditions. The Reformers consistently emphasised that forgiveness is not a feeling but a decision — the decision to release the debt, to no longer hold the offence against the offender, to treat them as God treats us in Christ: with kindness and grace. This is impossible from human resources. It is possible only for those who have received it from God and draw on the same source to extend it to others.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church was extraordinarily diverse. With diversity comes friction. The command against falsehood (v.25) — “speak truth with your neighbour, for we are members of one another” — addresses the social lubricant of deception that holds many human communities together. In the body of Christ, truth-telling is not optional; it is structurally necessary. A body in which the members lie to one another cannot function. The command against corrupting speech (v.29) — only what builds up — addresses the tongue that tears down, the word that diminishes, the comment that cuts. In a diverse community under pressure, these are the sins most likely to do lasting damage.

Now: “Do not let the sun go down on your anger” is one of the most practically demanding commands in Scripture, and one of the most consistently violated in married life, family life, and church life. We carry grievances. We nurse wounds. We let distance harden into walls. The apostle's word cuts through all of it: move toward resolution before night falls.

This does not mean every conflict is resolved in an evening — some wounds take weeks of patient, humble work to heal. But the direction must always be toward each other, not away. The community that actually practices this — that refuses to let resentment calcify, that keeps short accounts, that forgives as God in Christ forgave — will be noticed. It will be extraordinary. It will be a sign of the Kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, having put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, having put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbour.

The pattern. Verses 25–32 follow a simple pattern: stop doing this; start doing that; here is the reason. Each command has a negative (put off), a positive (put on), and a gospel motive. Christian morality is never only “don’t”.

Therefore. Because you have put off the old self and put on the new (vv. 22–24).

Having put away falsehood. The form describes something already done as the basis for the command: you put away falsehood in principle when you put off the old self, and now you must live consistently with it. “Falsehood” (pseudos) is more than outright lying: it covers half-truths designed to mislead, flattery that says what people want to hear, silence when honesty is needed, and the careful management of how others see you. It connects to the desires of deceit (v. 22) and stands against the truth as it is in Jesus (v. 21). Lying is the mark of the old self, and of the devil, the father of lies (John 8:44).

Let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbour. Paul quotes Zechariah 8:16, where God tells his restored people to speak truth to one another. “Neighbour” reaches to anyone you deal with, but the next phrase narrows the focus to fellow believers.

For we are members one of another. The reason. In a body, each part depends on the others telling it the truth. If the eye lied to the hand about where the fire was, the hand would be burned. Press the picture, because it describes an actual disease. In leprosy, the damage that destroys hands and feet is not done directly by the illness; it is done because the nerves have stopped reporting. The sufferer does not feel the stone in his shoe, so he walks on it all day. Nothing hurts, and that is the catastrophe, because an injury that cannot be felt cannot be treated. A church in which people do not tell one another the truth is a body in exactly that condition. The marriage quietly failing, the man drifting towards a decision that will wreck him, the coldness between two families: every one is a pain signal that never arrives. And the falsehood that does this is almost never a lie. It is one word, said thousands of times on a Sunday: fine. Trust is the nervous system of the church.

What lying includes. Not only outright falsehoods, but exaggeration, flattery, half-truths that leave a false impression, false excuses, broken promises, and pretending to be what we are not.

The hard case. Is it ever right to deceive? Not the self-serving lie Paul condemns, but the lie that shields a life: a family hiding refugees behind a false wall with soldiers at the door; a man asked by a violent husband where his wife has gone. Scripture itself puts the case. The Hebrew midwives disobeyed Pharaoh’s order to kill the boys and gave him an answer that was plainly not the truth, and God dealt well with them (Exodus 1:15–21). Rahab hid the spies and sent the king’s men the wrong way, and she is commended twice in the New Testament (Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25). The most careful answer in the Reformed tradition runs like this. The commandment forbids bearing false witness against your neighbour, speech that wrongs someone who has a right to what you know. A murderer at the door has forfeited that right; he is not a neighbour asking a question but an attacker demanding a weapon, and words are the weapon. And notice that in both cases the deception served someone else’s life, not the speaker’s comfort. Two guards keep this from becoming a licence. It is an extremely narrow door: an aggressor with no right to the answer, and a life at stake. It does not stretch to the awkward conversation, the padded figure, or the reputation being managed. If you reach for Rahab to excuse something that merely spares you embarrassment, you have already left the category. And some in the tradition say such a person does no wrong; others, more cautiously, that she chooses the lesser evil in a fallen world and needs the same grace as the rest of us. Both agree on what she should do. Corrie ten Boom’s family hid Jews behind a false wall in Haarlem and disagreed about what could rightly be said at the door. Not one of them doubted what they owed each other inside the house, and that is Paul’s subject here.

What it does not mean. Not that we must say everything we think, or be tactless. Speaking the truth is done in love (v. 15). Silence is not always lying, and some things are rightly kept private.

In a sentence. So put away lying, and each of you must speak the truth to your neighbour, because we all belong to one another.

On a Tuesday. Over the last month, did you tell anyone the truth about how you actually were? Is there one person in your church who knows the real state of things with you, not just the summary? If not, you are a nerve that has stopped reporting, and the body cannot feel where it hurts. Watch for small lies today too: the exaggerated story, the flattering comment, the excuse for being late.

For worship. God cannot lie (Titus 1:2), and every word he has spoken to his people is true. Christ is the faithful and true witness (Revelation 3:14), who never flattered, never managed appearances, and never hid the real state of things to spare himself; yet his truth was always full of grace (John 1:14). Praise the God who has made us members of one another in the body of his truthful Son, and who, knowing the whole truth about each of us, has not turned away but has loved us to the end.

parallels.desc: speak the truth to one another

verseByVerse.quote: Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger,

Be angry and do not sin. Paul quotes Psalm 4:4 from the Greek Old Testament. The form is not a command to get angry, but a concession and a warning: when you are angry, do not sin. There is such a thing as righteous anger. God himself is angry at evil (2:3); Jesus looked on hard-hearted people with anger (Mark 3:5) and cleared the temple (John 2:13–17). Not to be angry at child abuse, cruelty or injustice would be a moral failure; never to be angry at anything is not holiness but indifference. The sin is not the anger, but what you do with it. A colleague takes credit for your work: the anger is legitimate. But if you then tell everyone in the office, or start quietly undermining him, or lie awake rehearsing it and adding to it, the anger has crossed into sin.

How to tell the difference. Two questions do most of the sorting, in under a minute. First, what exactly was injured? Righteous anger is provoked by damage to someone else, or to God’s honour: the child mistreated, the truth twisted, the vulnerable used. Sinful anger is almost always provoked by damage to me: my standing, my convenience, being overlooked, corrected or made to look foolish. It is remarkable how much of what feels like moral indignation turns out, under that question, to be wounded pride in a better coat. Second, what does the anger want? Righteous anger wants the wrong put right, and is satisfied when it is; it can even want the good of the one who did it. Sinful anger wants the person made smaller, and repair does not satisfy it. You can tell, because when the offender apologises there is a faint disappointment, and the grievance is reluctant to be given up. Anger that does not want to be resolved has already told you what it is.

Do not let the sun go down on your anger. The word here (parorgismos) means irritation, provocation, being stirred up. Deal with it quickly. In Israel, wages had to be paid before sunset (Deuteronomy 24:15); the debt of anger should be settled the same day. Anger nursed through the night hardens: a fair grievance in the evening becomes resentment by morning, and something darker by next week. Before the day ends, do something: go to the person if you can, or at least hand the anger over to God in prayer instead of carrying it into tomorrow (Matthew 5:23–24).

The anger that goes underground. The command cuts the other way too. Some conscientious Christians have decided that anger is unspiritual and permit themselves none. Ask whether they are angry and they will say, sincerely, no. And the anger has gone nowhere; it has only stopped announcing itself. It comes out as sarcasm that can always be defended as humour. As a coolness that never quite amounts to rudeness. As the sudden discovery of urgent work whenever one particular person needs something. As an unreturned message, a withdrawal of warmth, a decision taken without consulting somebody: all deniable, none accidental. Buried anger is not put to death; it is put to work, and it does more damage underground, because nobody can address a grievance that has never been stated.

Is it a sin to be angry with God? Anger at God always rests on a mistake about God, because he has never done anything that deserves it; so it is not something to defend. But the Psalms show what to do with it: bring it to him, not away from him. The psalmists ask him how long, and why, and why he seems to have forgotten them (Psalm 13:1; 22:1; 42:9), and they ask it in prayer, as children, not as accusers walking out of the room. Job complained bitterly and was answered, not destroyed. So tell him honestly what you feel, then keep listening, and let him point you to the cross, where he showed what he is really like. Anger spoken to God in prayer tends to soften into trust. Anger nursed against him in silence hardens into unbelief.

What it does not mean. Not a command to be angry, nor permission for rage, outbursts or sulking. Nor a rigid rule that every conflict must be resolved before bed; sometimes it takes longer, and a late-night argument may be better postponed. The principle is: do not nurse anger, and do not let it settle in.

In a sentence. In your anger do not sin; do not let the sun go down while you are still angry,

On a Tuesday. Is there anger you have carried for more than a day? Ask the two questions honestly: what was injured, and what does it want? Then deal with it today.

For worship. Here is the only anger that never sinned. Jesus was grieved and angry at hardness of heart, and his anger always sought the good of others and the honour of his Father. More wonderful still, the righteous anger of God against our sin was not left unresolved. It was poured out on the Son at the cross, and before that day’s sun went down the account was settled in full (John 19:30). Adore the God whose wrath is holy and whose mercy paid the debt himself, so that for his people nothing remains outstanding.

parallels.desc: be angry, and do not sin

verseByVerse.quote: and give no opportunity to the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and give no opportunity to the devil.

And give no opportunity. The “and” means as a result: this is what happens if the sun goes down on your anger. “Opportunity” is topos, literally a place: a foothold, a beachhead, an opening inside your lines from which an enemy can operate, like a squatter moving into an empty room.

To the devil. Diabolos, the slanderer, the accuser, the one who divides. His aim in a church is division (2:14–16; 4:3), and unresolved anger is his best material. He is a real, personal enemy (6:11–12). And he does not need to tempt you into great sin if he can get you to leave a small wound unattended (2 Corinthians 2:10–11).

How the foothold grows. Picture two elders who disagree sharply over a decision. Words are exchanged; neither goes to the other to clear the air, because it feels awkward and the matter was technically settled. A week later they are polite on Sunday, but something has cooled. Months later the church feels a tension in its leadership without quite naming it; people sense which elder they are more comfortable with; within a year there are two quiet camps. No one planned it. A small, unresolved anger was simply given time to harden, and the devil, who is in no hurry, used it.

The sentences that open the door. A foothold is almost always granted by something we say to ourselves, not by anything that feels like a decision. Listen for these. It would be awkward. It is not a big deal; I would look petty raising it. He probably did not mean it that way. I will leave it and see if it happens again. I have forgiven it, so there is nothing to discuss. Each can be perfectly true, and each can be the polite name for avoidance. The enemy is content either way, because the outcome is the same: the thing stays unsaid and gets a night’s growth.

What it does not mean. Not that every angry Christian is demon-possessed, or that the devil is to blame instead of us. We give the opportunity; he takes it. Nor should we be afraid: the devil is defeated (1:20–21), and if we resist him, he will flee from us (James 4:7).

In a sentence. and do not give the devil a foothold.

On a Tuesday. Is there a conversation you have been not having, with the person you now sit a little further from, or reply to a little more briefly? That is the ground in question. The remedy is embarrassingly ordinary: a message tonight, not tomorrow; a sentence at the door: can I check something with you, did I take that the wrong way? Most footholds are closed by one short, awkward exchange that turns out far less terrible than the fortnight of imagining it.

For worship. The devil looks for a foothold, but Christ has already taken the ground. Praise the risen Lord who disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them at the cross (Colossians 2:15), and who is now seated far above every power (1:21). The accuser has no case left against those who are in Christ, for Christ himself intercedes for them (Romans 8:33–34). The enemy is patient, but our Lord is stronger and more patient still, and he guards his flock with a watchfulness that never sleeps (Psalm 121:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Let the thief no longer steal, but rather let him labour, doing honest work with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let the thief no longer steal, but rather let him labour, doing honest work with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need.

Let the thief no longer steal. Were there really thieves in the church? Evidently; Paul is not writing in theory. These congregations were full of day labourers, dockworkers and household slaves living hand to mouth, and petty theft was part of survival: pilfering from a master’s stores (Titus 2:10), skimming at the harbour, forgetting to return what was borrowed. The culture barely blinked. Paul does: in the body of Christ the common thing is no longer the acceptable thing.

But rather let him labour. “Labour” means hard, tiring work. And notice with his own hands. In Paul’s world that was not a neutral phrase. Manual work was widely despised; a gentleman did not work with his hands, and the philosophers said so. Paul, trained at the highest level (Acts 22:3), made tents for a living and was not embarrassed by it (Acts 18:3; 20:34; 1 Thessalonians 2:9). So he is not only prescribing an alternative to stealing; he is honouring a kind of work his culture looked down on, in a letter that has spent three chapters in the heavenly places. The one laying bricks, cleaning floors, driving a van or stacking a warehouse is doing something the New Testament counts honourable.

Doing honest work. Literally working the good: work that is good in itself, done honestly.

So that he may have something to share with anyone in need. The great surprise, in three steps: stop stealing; work honestly; so that you can give. The gospel never merely empties a life; it refills it, aimed the other way. The hand that once took becomes the hand that gives. Zacchaeus got there in an afternoon: the tax collector who took became, the day salvation came to his house, a man who gave half his goods away (Luke 19:8–9). Paul does not say “so that he may support himself”, true and necessary as that is (1 Timothy 5:8; 2 Thessalonians 3:10–12). He says, so that he may have something to share. It is more blessed to give than to receive (Acts 20:35).

What theft includes. Not only shoplifting or burglary. Also padding expense claims, wasting paid time, the cash job kept off the books, borrowed tools that never come home, pirated software, cheating on taxes, failing to pay a fair wage (Leviticus 19:13; James 5:4).

I stole in the past. Do I have to pay it back? Where you can, yes. God’s forgiveness is full and free the moment you turn to Christ, and repaying does not buy it. But real repentance wants to put right what it can. The law required a thief to restore what he took and add to it (Exodus 22:1–4; Numbers 5:6–7), and Zacchaeus, without being told, offered to repay four times over (Luke 19:8). So return the item, repay the employer, settle the debt, correct the tax return, even when it costs you. If the person cannot be found, give the amount to those in need, which is exactly where this verse points. Where the sum is beyond you, take wise counsel and do what you honestly can. It may also mean owning up. That is humbling, and it is freedom.

What it does not mean. Not that earning well, owning property or saving is suspect. The command against stealing assumes that property is real and rightful. Paul assumes that work will produce more than you need; the question is what you do with the surplus. Wise saving, providing for one’s family and planning for the future are good; covetousness is wanting more for its own sake, or trusting wealth instead of God (Luke 12:15–21; 1 Timothy 6:17–19). And this verse is not weighing the worth of anyone who is ill, out of work or past working. It describes the direction a redeemed life travels whenever it has the means: from taking, through honest getting, to giving. Some who cannot work give more than the employed, though not in money.

In a sentence. Anyone who has been stealing must steal no longer, but must work, doing something useful with their own hands, so that they have something to share with those in need.

On a Tuesday. Look at your bank statement. Is there anything in it that exists on purpose for giving, planned first, before the rest is allocated? Or does giving come out of whatever survives the month? Most of us find our generosity is funded by the remainder, and the remainder is a notoriously unreliable donor.

For worship. Behold the generosity of Christ, who though he was rich became poor for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9). The carpenter of Nazareth honoured the work of hands with his own, and the hands that shaped wood were at last nailed to it so that thieves might be forgiven. The first man to hear the promise of paradise from his lips was a dying thief (Luke 23:43). Praise the Saviour who does not only stop the taking hand but opens it, and makes the grasping heart a channel of his own overflowing kindness.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear.

Let no corrupting talk. “Corrupting” (sapros) means rotten, putrid: used of rotten fruit or bad fish (Matthew 7:17–18; 13:48). Speech that tears down, gossips or belittles is as out of place in the body of Christ as rotting meat at a feast. It includes gossip, slander, crude jokes, cutting sarcasm, grumbling and flattery. Does it include swearing and coarse jokes? Yes: Paul says so plainly a few verses later (5:4; Colossians 3:8), and Jesus said we will give account for every careless word (Matthew 12:36).

Come out of your mouths. Words come from the heart (Matthew 12:34). Rotten talk reveals rot within; changing the speech requires a changed heart.

But only such as is good for building up. The same word as in verses 12 and 16: speech is one of the main ways the body builds itself up. And notice the loophole this closes. Most of us screen our speech with one question: is it true? That is only half a filter. Gossip is very often true; that is exactly what makes it feel permissible. Paul does not ask whether it is accurate. He asks whether it builds.

As fits the occasion. Literally according to the need: the right word for the moment and the person. Comfort for the grieving, encouragement for the discouraged, warning for the wandering, truth for the confused. A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver (Proverbs 25:11).

That it may give grace to those who hear. The word is charis, the same grace this letter uses for God’s undeserved gift. Your words can carry it: an honest encouragement to someone doubting, a gentle truth to someone drifting, a simple acknowledgement to someone who feels invisible. Grace delivered through a human mouth. And the reverse is true: a careless word can undo in a moment what months of encouragement built. Hear it in one case. Two members learn that a third, James, has lost his job. “Did you hear about James? I always thought he wasn’t cut out for that role.” Possibly true, no grace, and James is now worse off than before those words. Or: “James has just lost his job and he’s shaken. Could we pray for him now, and someone ring him this week?” Same information; grace given; the body moves towards him instead of past him. When Jesus taught, people marvelled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth (Luke 4:22), literally words of grace. Grace-giving speech is not a knack but an imitation.

The filter. Before it leaves your mouth: is it true? And also: is it constructive, building instead of flattening? Is it timely, does this moment call for it, or am I unloading? And is it for them, will the hearer be better off, or am I the one who gets the relief? Run an ordinary day’s speech through those, and it is a sobering audit. Much of what we say passes the first gate and fails the other three.

Is it gossip to talk to a friend about someone who has hurt me, or to ask for advice? Not necessarily; it depends on what the conversation is for. Asking a wise believer how to respond, seeking a pastor’s help, or reporting wrongdoing to someone responsible for dealing with it is not gossip. It becomes gossip when the aim is to be agreed with, to lower the other person in the hearer’s eyes, or simply to enjoy the telling. Three checks help. Tell as few people as you need to. Say no more than they need to know. And where it is safe to do so, speak to the person himself before you speak about him to others (Matthew 18:15). A good counsellor will usually send you back to that person, not keep you company in the grievance.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians may only speak about spiritual things, or never joke. Humour that builds up and gives joy is good. Nor that we must always be soft and never confront: sometimes building up needs a hard word, spoken in love.

In a sentence. Do not let any unwholesome talk come out of your mouths, but only what helps build others up according to their needs, so that it brings grace to those who listen.

On a Tuesday. Measure your words by the empty chair. Gossip does its work in the hearer, about someone who is not in the room to answer. What did the absent person just lose, and would you have said it with him sitting there?

For worship. When Jesus opened his mouth, grace came out (Luke 4:22). Not one word he spoke was rotten, careless or cruel, yet he never flattered and never trimmed the truth. Adore the eternal Word made flesh, whose speech raised the dead, stilled the storm and told sinners that their debts were forgiven. And worship the Father, who has spoken his final word to us in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), a word that builds a people up rather than tearing them down. Every gracious word in the church is a small echo of his voice.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.

And do not grieve. This verse arrives like a sudden change of key, and it is meant to. Paul has been speaking of words and community, and then he pulls back the curtain and shows who is in the room: the Holy Spirit himself, hearing every word, affected by every choice. To grieve is to cause sorrow, the pain of close relationships. And notice the word Paul chose. He does not say, do not anger the Spirit, or provoke him, or defy him. He says, do not grieve him. Grief is not the reaction of an official whose rules have been broken; it is the reaction of someone who loves you. You cannot grieve a stranger. A traffic warden is not grieved when you park badly. Before it is a warning, the verse is a staggering statement of how the Spirit regards you. Your sin does not chiefly irritate him; it wounds him, because he loves you.

Which sins? The command sits among commands about speech and relationships (vv. 25–32): falsehood, though he is the Spirit of truth (John 16:13); unresolved anger, though he is the Spirit of the unity kept by peace (4:3); corrupting talk, though he builds up the body; bitterness and slander (v. 31), the opposite of his fruit (Galatians 5:22–23). The Spirit who makes believers one is grieved by what divides them. He is not grieved by weakness, failure or honest struggle; those he meets with intercession (Romans 8:26). He is grieved by willing, unrepentant persistence in what Christ died to remove.

The Holy Spirit of God. A full, solemn title. He is holy, so sin grieves him; and he is God’s Spirit, so to grieve him is to grieve God.

Only a person can be grieved. You cannot grieve a force or an influence. The Holy Spirit is a person, who knows, wills and loves (1 Corinthians 2:10–11; 12:11; Romans 15:30). Isaiah says Israel rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit in the wilderness (Isaiah 63:10). Paul echoes it: the church must not repeat Israel’s sin.

A third kind of sin. Most of us privately file our sins as either rule-breaking or self-harm: I broke a commandment, or I hurt myself. Both are true and both are strangely bearable. This is a third category, and it reaches people the first two never touch. Sin grieves a Person who is present: done in front of someone living inside you, nearer than the friend in the next chair, who feels it. There is a kind of man who will break a rule without a flicker, and be undone the moment he realises he has hurt his mother. Paul is speaking to that man, which is to say all of us.

By whom you were sealed. The Spirit is God’s seal on believers (see 1:13–14): the mark of ownership and the guarantee of security, like a stamp on goods being shipped, protecting them until delivery.

For the day of redemption. The day when redemption is complete: Christ’s return, the resurrection of the body, full freedom from sin (1:14; Romans 8:23). Believers are redeemed now (1:7), but not yet fully.

What it does not mean. Not a threat that sin will make the Spirit leave, or that believers can lose their salvation. The very verse says they are sealed until the day of redemption: the seal holds. The Spirit grieves precisely because he stays. His grief is the grief of a love that will not let go. The appeal is not fear but love: a child does not obey a loving father merely to avoid being disowned, but because he does not want to hurt the one who loves him. Nor does it mean God is fragile or controlled by our actions: his grief is the grief of holy love, not weakness.

I know I have grieved him. What do I do now? Go straight back, today, without waiting until you feel worthy. Name the sin to God plainly, without excuses, and trust his promise that if we confess our sins he is faithful and just to forgive us (1 John 1:9). Christ’s blood covers this sin too, and he is pleading for you with the Father at this moment (1 John 2:1). Where you have wronged someone, put it right with them as well. Then do not keep your distance as a self-imposed punishment; that is the instinct of the servant on probation (see 3:12). The Spirit’s grief is not cold anger waiting to be paid off. It is love wanting you back, and the way to stop grieving him is not to hide, but to come home and walk with him again.

In a sentence. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, with whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.

On a Tuesday. Next time you are on the edge of the thing you keep going back to, the second look, the cutting reply already loaded, the story about someone’s failure you are about to pass on, do not reach first for “this is forbidden”, true as it is. Reach for this: someone who loves me is here, and this will hurt him. You can grow hard to a rule and its penalties. It is very hard to keep wounding, to his face, a Person who has decided never to leave.

For worship. Stand in awe of the Holy Spirit of God, a divine Person who loves with such tenderness that he can be grieved, and with such faithfulness that he never leaves. He has sealed us, and his seal does not crack. Praise the Father who sent him, the Son who poured him out from the throne, and the Spirit himself, who has bound his own heart to sinners until the day of redemption. That the eternal God should open himself to grief over people like us is a mercy almost too high to think about.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership and security until delivery.

parallels.desc: they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamour and slander be put away from you, along with all malice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamour and slander be put away from you, along with all malice.

Let all … be put away from you. “All”: not some, or most, but every trace. “Put away” means removed, carried off, thrown out. Six words, laid down like weapons to be surrendered.

Bitterness. Pikria: the settled sourness of a soul that has been wounded and chosen to nurse the wound instead of releasing it. It is the one that does not feel like sin at all. The other five are easy to recognise; wrath makes a scene you regret, and slander you know is unkind even as you say it. But bitterness feels like justice. It grows in genuinely wronged soil: you really were treated badly, and the resentment feels less like a sin to repent of than a fact to be honoured. That is why it is the most dangerous, and why Paul lists it first. And it does not punish the person who wronged you. It punishes you, daily, on his behalf. He may be asleep, untroubled, having forgotten the whole thing, while you lie awake rehearsing it, giving him free lodging in a mind he does not know he occupies. Resentment is drinking poison and waiting for the other person to die. Hebrews adds what we never see coming: a root of bitterness springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled (Hebrews 12:15). Many, not just you. It leaks into your tone, your assumptions, the warnings you pass on, the slight coldness a whole room can feel.

Wrath and anger. Two words. Wrath (thymos) is the sudden hot flare, the outburst that leaves wreckage (James 1:19–20). Anger (orgē) is its cold twin: settled, brooding resentment that builds a case and waits.

Clamour. Kraugē: shouting, brawling, loud quarrelling. Anger that has found its voice, and a private grievance turned into a public scene.

Slander. Blasphēmia: speech that damages another person’s name, whether false or maliciously true. Gossip, character assassination, telling stories behind backs. The same word is used for blasphemy against God, and in the church it attacks the members of Christ’s body, and so in a real sense Christ himself (Acts 9:4).

Along with all malice. Kakia: ill will, wishing others harm, taking pleasure in their misfortune. It comes last because it is the root, the soil the others grow in. To put away malice is to have the heart itself changed, not merely the behaviour managed.

The progression. Read in order, the list shows how resentment grows when it is not dealt with: from a bitter spirit within, to outbursts of temper, to settled anger, to shouting, to slander behind the back, to a settled wish for the other’s harm. It begins in the heart and ends by poisoning a whole church. It is the same anatomy as verse 18: the road runs from the heart outward, and the cure must begin where the road begins.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians must pretend they have never been hurt, or never feel the pain of injustice. Grief over wrong is not bitterness; bitterness is refusing to let the wrong go, and nursing it. Paul does not say the wrong did not happen, or that you were oversensitive to mind. He says set down the thing you are carrying. Nor does this forbid naming wrong or seeking justice through proper channels; it forbids the inner poison and the destructive speech.

In a sentence. Get rid of all bitterness, rage and anger, shouting and slander, and every kind of malice.

On a Tuesday. Is there a name that produces a small tightening when you hear it, a person whose good news you cannot quite be glad about? That is the place. You will not talk yourself into feeling differently. Do what the next verse says: release the debt at the foot of the cross, where a far larger one was released for you.

For worship. Christ had more cause for bitterness than anyone who has ever lived. He was slandered, shouted down, struck and mocked, and when he was reviled he did not revile in return (1 Peter 2:23). On the cross he prayed for the men who drove the nails (Luke 23:34). Worship the Lamb in whom no root of bitterness ever grew, whose heart under the worst injustice the world has seen remained pure love. And praise him that the malice poured out on him became the very means of our healing (Isaiah 53:5).

verseByVerse.quote: Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.

Be kind to one another. “Kind” (chrēstos) means useful, good, generous: kindness in action, not only feeling. The word was used of old wine, mellowed and no longer sharp (Luke 5:39), and Jesus uses it of his own easy yoke (Matthew 11:30). God himself is kind, even to the ungrateful and evil (Luke 6:35), and he showed his kindness to us in Christ (2:7). Kindness looks for ways to be good to the people around you, especially the difficult ones.

Tenderhearted. Eusplanchnos: literally with good bowels. The ancients located deep emotion in the gut, as we say heart. It means a heart genuinely moved by another’s pain, not sympathy at a safe distance: the compassion of Christ himself for the harassed crowds (Matthew 9:36), and the exact opposite of the hardened heart of verse 18.

Forgiving one another. The Greek word (charizomenoi) shares its root with charis, grace: gracing one another. To forgive is to give someone what they do not deserve and cannot earn, releasing them from the debt they owe you. Why is it so hard? Because it feels like injustice, like letting them off.

As God in Christ forgave you. The measure and the motive. At the cross the debt was not cancelled by pretending it did not exist; it was absorbed by the one who was wronged. God did not overlook sin; he paid for it himself. Christian forgiveness follows the same pattern: you absorb the cost instead of passing it on. That is not weakness; it is the most Christlike act a person can do. Having been forgiven so much, we cannot refuse to forgive others so little (Matthew 18:21–35). And God is the standard for all three words: kind (the riches of his kindness, Romans 2:4), tender (as a father shows compassion to his children, Psalm 103:13), and forgiving at infinite cost. We are only passing on what we have already received.

How it hides. Sarah fell out with Mark over a decision six months ago. He was dismissive, spoke sharply in front of others, and never apologised. She serves beside him on Sundays but keeps her distance, answers his messages with bare courtesy, has told two friends what happened, and tells herself she has forgiven him because she no longer thinks about it every day. Paul’s three words show where she really is: the kindness gone, the tender heart closed, the forgiveness incomplete. She has let go of the sharp pain but kept the verdict. The way forward is not a feeling but a decision made in prayer at the cross: Lord, I release this. Mark owes me nothing. I received forgiveness I did not deserve; I give the same. Then behaviour follows: a genuine word to him, an end to the quiet commentary. It will not feel natural at first, and may need to be made again tomorrow.

Where Christians differ: must the offender repent first? Jesus said, if he repents, forgive him (Luke 17:3), so some Christians hold that forgiveness, like God’s, is complete only when the offender repents. Verdict: both are true when forgiveness is seen in its two parts. In the heart, before God, the wronged person lets go of bitterness and the wish for revenge, whether or not the other repents (v. 31; Mark 11:25). The restored relationship, the forgiveness spoken and received, waits for repentance, as God’s reconciliation with us does. So a believer must not nurse a grudge, but neither must he pretend that nothing happened.

What it does not mean. This verse is one step from a cruelty if it is misused, and it has been said, in a kind voice, to people it then badly hurt. Forgiveness does not mean the wrong was small, or calling evil good. It does not mean you must feel warmly. It does not always mean restoring trust at once: trust is rebuilt over time, and wisdom may require boundaries, especially where there has been abuse. It never means returning to a place where you are still being harmed, or dropping a safeguard. It does not remove just consequences: a forgiven thief may still need to repay, and crimes should be reported to the authorities God has appointed (Romans 13:1–4). And it is not the same as reconciliation, which needs both sides. What forgiveness does mean is releasing the debt, refusing revenge, refusing to keep bringing the wrong up, and wishing the other person good. Where the wound is deep, it is often done again on Tuesday, having been done on Monday, without that meaning it was insincere the first time.

If I have forgiven, why do I still remember it and feel it? Because forgiving is not forgetting, and feelings heal more slowly than decisions are made. When God says he will remember our sins no more (Jeremiah 31:34), he has not lost the memory; he means he will never hold them against us. That is what you are promising too: not that the memory will vanish, but that you will not use it as a weapon, in your words, in how you treat the person, or in private rehearsals. When the memory returns, and the old heat with it, that is not proof that you never forgave. It is the moment to forgive again: Lord, I released this, and I release it again. Over time the memory usually loses its sting, until it reminds you more of God’s grace than of the wound.

In a sentence. Be kind and compassionate to one another, forgiving each other, just as God forgave you in Christ.

On a Tuesday. Who do you need to forgive today? Begin by remembering, in detail, what God has forgiven you. And if you cannot get there yet, the honest place to stand is not pretence. It is the prayer of someone who wants to want it: Lord, I am not able to release this; make me willing. That prayer is not a failure of the command; it is the beginning of obeying it.

For worship. Every truthful word, every anger surrendered before sundown, every hand that gives instead of takes, every debt released: this is the bride being made ready. Christ is not merely tidying our behaviour; he is dressing his bride for the day she sees his face, without spot or wrinkle (5:27; Revelation 19:7–8). Thank him for all he has forgiven you, at the cost of his blood.

4.theology:
Ephesians 4 stakes out the great Reformed doctrine of the inseparability of justification and sanctification. The same grace that declares the sinner righteous also begins to make them righteous. Not simultaneously, not automatically — but inevitably. Where the root is real, the fruit will come. Paul’s commands in this chapter are not the conditions of acceptance; they are the evidence of it. The indicative always precedes and grounds the imperative.

The chapter also gives the church its most searching doctrine of common life. The body of Christ is not a collection of private spiritual journeys happening in the same building. It is an organism, with every member genuinely joined to every other — responsible for each other’s growth, dependent on each other’s gifts, harmed by each other’s sin. Falsehood in the body is not a private failure; it is a systemic wound. Unresolved anger is not a personal problem; it is a strategic opening for the enemy. This is the doctrine of the church made viscerally practical.

And at the centre stands the renewal of the mind — the hinge on which all change turns. Not willpower, not behaviour management, but transformation at the level where thinking happens. This is the Spirit’s sovereign work, received through the ordinary means of grace: the word, prayer, honest community, and obedience to what is already known. The Christian does not renew themselves. But they can position themselves daily in the hands of the One who does. cf. Rom. 12:1–2; 2 Cor. 3:18; Phil. 2:12–13.
4.examples:
Then: The Ephesian believers had come out of a culture saturated with the very patterns Paul describes in vv. 17–19 — a world of mystery religions, sexual licence, and moral relativism where the only sin was public embarrassment. To be told to “put off” this was not a minor adjustment; it was a complete reorientation of identity. And the alternative Paul offered — speaking truth, controlling anger, working honestly, forgiving freely — would have looked countercultural to the point of strangeness. The church in Ephesus was being asked to be a visible sign that a different humanity was possible.

Now: The culture has changed; the pressure has not. The same patterns Paul named are alive and well: the mind drifting, the conscience growing quieter, the appetite demanding more. The same temptations assault the same pressure points: to manage rather than truth-tell, to nurse grievance rather than forgive, to speak what entertains rather than what builds. And the same command stands: no longer walk as those who do not know God. Not because you must earn your standing — that is secured in Christ — but because you have been made new, and new creatures do not live in the old way.

You, reading this chapter on a Monday morning, can take one thing to work: the person sitting across from you is either a fellow member of the body or a neighbour made in God’s image. Either way, what you say matters, what you do with your anger matters, how you handle the truth matters. The renewal of the mind is not a mystical event. It is what happens when the Christian opens the Bible instead of the phone, prays instead of broods, speaks the honest word instead of the comfortable one — and does it again tomorrow. This is how the body builds itself up in love.
4.overview:
With chapter 4 Ephesians turns from what God has done (chapters 1–3) to how his people must live (chapters 4–6). The first call is to walk worthy of their calling, in humility, gentleness and patient love, keeping the unity the Spirit has created, for there is one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism and one God and Father of all. Within that unity, the ascended Christ has given gifts to each believer, and has given the church apostles, prophets, evangelists and shepherd-teachers to equip all God’s people for ministry, until the whole body reaches maturity, no longer tossed about by false teaching, but speaking the truth in love and growing up into Christ the head.

Then Paul describes the new life. Believers must no longer live like the Gentiles, darkened in understanding and hardened in heart, given over to impurity. That is not how they learned Christ. They have been taught to put off the old self, be renewed in mind, and put on the new self, created to be like God in righteousness and holiness. The chapter ends with practical examples: truthfulness, anger without sin, honest work that enables giving, speech that builds up, and the kindness and forgiveness that mirror God’s forgiveness in Christ, so as not to grieve the Holy Spirit.

5.title: Walking in Love and the Mystery of Marriage
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children. <sup>2</sup>And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God. <sup>3</sup>But sexual immorality and all impurity or covetousness must not even be named among you, as is proper among saints. <sup>4</sup>Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving. <sup>5</sup>For you may be sure of this, that everyone who is sexually immoral or impure, or who is covetous (that is, an idolater), has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God. <sup>6</sup>Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience. <sup>7</sup>Therefore do not become partners with them; <sup>8</sup>for at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light <sup>9</sup>(for the fruit of light is found in all that is good and right and true), <sup>10</sup>and try to discern what is pleasing to the Lord. <sup>11</sup>Take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them. <sup>12</sup>For it is shameful even to speak of the things that they do in secret. <sup>13</sup>But when anything is exposed by the light, it becomes visible, <sup>14</sup>for anything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says, “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.” <sup>15</sup>Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, <sup>16</sup>making the best use of the time, because the days are evil. <sup>17</sup>Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is. <sup>18</sup>And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit, <sup>19</sup>addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart, <sup>20</sup>giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, <sup>21</sup>submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ. <sup>22</sup>Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord. <sup>23</sup>For the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church, his body, and is himself its Savior. <sup>24</sup>Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands. <sup>25</sup>Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, <sup>26</sup>that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, <sup>27</sup>so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish. <sup>28</sup>In the same way husbands should love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. <sup>29</sup>For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church, <sup>30</sup>because we are members of his body. <sup>31</sup>“Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.” <sup>32</sup>This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church. <sup>33</sup>However, let each one of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As God’s dearly loved children, they must imitate him and live a life of love, following Christ, who loved us and gave himself as a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God. Among God’s holy people there must be not even a hint of sexual immorality, impurity or greed, nor obscenity, foolish talk or coarse joking, which are out of place; instead there should be thanksgiving. No immoral, impure or greedy person, which is idolatry, has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. They must not be deceived by empty words, for these things bring God’s wrath on the disobedient, so they must not share in them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Cruciform Love as the Pattern of the Christian Life

“A fragrant offering and sacrifice to God” (v.2) — Paul's description of Christ's self-giving at the cross is drawn directly from the Old Testament sacrificial language. The burnt offering was described as “a pleasing aroma to the LORD” (Leviticus 1:9; 8:21) — a sacrifice that God receives with satisfaction, that expresses the proper worship of creature before Creator. Paul applies this language to the cross: the death of Christ was the ultimate sacrifice, the perfect offering, the worship that satisfied the holiness of God and secured the salvation of his people.

The implication for ethics is profound: to walk in love in imitation of Christ is to participate in a form of worship. Every act of genuine, self-giving love — every moment of costly service, every forgiveness extended at personal cost, every preference of another's need over one's own comfort — is offered to God as a fragrant offering. The Christian life is not divided into sacred acts (prayer, church attendance) and secular acts (daily life, work, relationships). All of it is worship. The love that looks like Calvary, lived out in the ordinary texture of daily life, is received by God as the aroma of Christ himself.

Covetousness is identified in v.5 as idolatry — a striking identification that requires reflection. Covetousness is not merely wanting what others have; it is the orientation of the heart toward things rather than toward God, treating the creature as the source of satisfaction rather than the Creator. In this sense it is the root of sexual immorality as well: the sexualised culture is a culture of covetousness, of insatiable appetite, of treating persons as objects to be consumed. The gospel addresses this at the root by offering the only love that actually satisfies — the love of God in Christ, which surpasses knowledge and fills us with all the fullness of God (3:19).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: “Be imitators of God” — in the Greco-Roman world, this language had a specific resonance. The philosophical schools spoke of likeness to God as the goal of the spiritual life. But the path they offered was typically ascetic withdrawal, esoteric knowledge, ritual elevation. Paul offers a radically different path: imitate the God who descended, who gave himself up, who went to the cross for his enemies. The divine pattern to be imitated is not the god on the Olympian heights, remote and powerful, but the God who came down in love and poured himself out in death. The imitation called for is not upward escape but downward love.

Now: Sexual immorality has been rebranded in our age as liberation, as authentic self-expression, as the natural pursuit of desire. Covetousness is marketed as aspiration, ambition, the engine of economic progress. Paul's gospel cuts through all of it — not with a longer list of prohibitions, but with a higher vision. You are a beloved child of the God who gave his Son for you. You have been loved with a love that went to the cross. Now walk in that love: freely, lavishly, cruciformly, without counting the cost. This is not the moralism of a killjoy god; it is the invitation of a Father who wants his children to look like him and to know the joy of doing so.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children.

Meaning first. Ephesians 5 continues the call to live as God’s new people, using Paul’s word walk. Believers are to imitate God as his loved children and walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself as a sacrifice (vv. 1–2); so sexual immorality, impurity, greed and crude talk have no place among saints, for those whose lives are ruled by them have no inheritance in God’s kingdom, and his wrath comes on the disobedient (vv. 3–7). Once darkness, they are now light in the Lord, and must walk as children of light, producing goodness, righteousness and truth, exposing the deeds of darkness rather than sharing them, because light transforms what it reveals (vv. 8–14). They must walk wisely, making the most of the time, understanding the Lord’s will, and instead of being controlled by wine, be continually filled with the Spirit, which shows itself in singing to one another, thanking God for everything, and submitting to one another in reverence for Christ (vv. 15–21). That submission then takes shape in marriage (vv. 22–33): wives are to submit to their own husbands as the church submits to Christ, and husbands are to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, to make her holy; for marriage, from the beginning, was designed to picture the profound mystery of Christ and his church.

Therefore. The verse continues 4:32: forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you. The chapter division hides the link. What God has done, forgiven us, becomes the pattern for what we do.

Imitators of God. Greek mimētai, from which we get mimic. The only place in the New Testament where we are told to imitate God directly (compare Matthew 5:48). How can creatures imitate God? Not in his power or knowledge, but in his character as he has shown it: his kindness, mercy, forgiveness and holiness. And Paul’s first readers heard this against a background we do not share. “Likeness to God” was a standing phrase in the philosophical schools for the goal of the spiritual life, but the route was always upward: withdrawal, discipline, secret knowledge, shedding the body, until the soul rose near the divine. Every path led away from ordinary life, and the higher you climbed, the fewer people you were any use to. Paul takes the same idea and reverses its direction. The God we imitate is the God who came down, who gave himself up for his enemies and died in public between two criminals, which is why the next verse defines the likeness as walking in love. The imitation commanded here is not an ascent out of the world but a descent into it.

As beloved children. Watch how children actually do this. No father sits a three-year-old down and explains how to be like him. The boy simply appears one Saturday with a plastic hammer, having noticed what his father does. He picks up a phrase and uses it slightly wrongly at the table. He stands with his hands in his pockets the way his father stands. It is not effort and not even obedience; it is what nearness does. Children imitate whoever they spend time with, without being asked and mostly without knowing. That explains something earnest effort never manages. The fastest way to become like the Father is not to try harder at it, but to be with him more. When the council looked at Peter and John, what they recognised was not their training but that they had been with Jesus (Acts 4:13). And the principle cuts both ways: you are being formed now by whatever you spend your hours with.

The love comes first. Not as servants hoping to be noticed, not as applicants under review: as beloved children. We do not imitate God in order to become his children or win his love. We imitate him because we already are his children, adopted and loved (1:5). Love received becomes love reproduced. Paul goes on to describe this family likeness with one picture, walk: walk in love (v. 2), walk as children of light (v. 8), walk wisely (v. 15).

What it does not mean. Not that we can become divine, or earn our place by copying well. It is the family likeness of those already in the family.

In a sentence. So, as God’s dearly loved children, copy him.

On a Tuesday. When you fail badly this week, notice what you instinctively want to do. If the reflex is to keep away from God until you feel more presentable, you are working as a hired man, not living as a son. A child who has broken something runs to his father, because nothing he broke put his sonship in question. And if you want to know how far you have come in becoming like God, do not ask how high you have climbed. Ask what it has cost you lately to love somebody.

For worship. The Father whose likeness we bear did not climb away from the world; he came down into it. Adore the God who adopted rebels and calls them beloved, and who has shown his heart most fully not in the heights of heaven but in the Son who knelt, served and died in public for his enemies. Every family likeness in his children traces back to kindness he first lavished on them. Praise the Father who wants his children near him, so that, being with him, they become like him.

verseByVerse.quote: And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God.

Walk in love. “Walk” is the spine of the whole letter, and it is the least glamorous picture available. Paul does not say soar in love, or burn with love, or feel love. He says walk: what you do on an ordinary Tuesday, in one direction, at an unremarkable pace, one foot after the other so many times you stop counting. And it is a present command: keep walking. That is the first mercy in the verse. Love here is not a temperature to be checked but a direction to be kept. You do not have to feel it in order to walk it, and if you wait until you feel it you will not move. A man walking north is walking north whether or not he is enjoying the weather.

As Christ loved us. Not love as the world defines it, warm feelings, or giving people what they want, but love as Christ showed it. The word is agapē: love that chooses the other’s good at cost to itself. It asks not, what do I get? but, what does this person need, and what will it cost me to give it? And notice whom Christ was loving: not admirers. God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8). This love was never a response to loveliness in its object, which is exactly why it can be commanded of you towards people who have not earned it.

Gave himself up for us. Christ did not only give things or time; he gave himself, to death, in our place (Galatians 2:20), freely: no one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18). Freely given and enormously costly, and the two never separated. That is the shape of Christian love.

A fragrant offering and sacrifice. Old Testament language, and worth standing where it was first spoken. Noah steps off the ark onto a planet that is a graveyard. Everything he ever knew is under the mud. The first thing he does is build an altar, and the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma and said in his heart that he would never again curse the ground (Genesis 8:21). It is not that God likes the smell of burning meat. Something went up from the earth, and God received it, and bound himself to the world in peace. That is a fragrant offering: something given that God accepts with delight. Every sacrifice in Israel pointed to this one. Repeated sacrifices could never finally deal with sin (Hebrews 10:1–4), but by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14). The Father was fully pleased; our sin was truly dealt with.

Your love, the same fragrance. Paul uses that exact phrase, a fragrant offering, once more, and not about the cross. The Philippians had sent a parcel to a man in prison: money, supplies, whatever Epaphroditus could carry. Paul writes back and calls their gift a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God (Philippians 4:18). Someone packed a bag for a friend in trouble, and the apostle reaches for the language of the altar. The meal cooked for the family whose week has collapsed; the bill quietly paid; the afternoon given to someone whose company you do not much enjoy: Paul says these go up. And that answers an ache many carry without naming it: the weariness of loving someone who does not notice. The parent of a teenager who registers nothing. The daughter who drives every Saturday to sit with a mother who no longer knows her name. The person who has held a marriage together alone for eleven years and never once been thanked. Read the last two words: to God. The direction of the smoke is up, not across. Whether the person noticed, deserved it, returned it or remembers it is a different question from whether it arrived. It arrived. Nothing you have ever spent in love has gone nowhere.

Before it is a pattern, it is a gift. “As Christ loved us” is not a standard anyone survives being measured by. If you read that and felt the floor go, you read it accurately, but in the wrong order. Before the cross is a pattern in this verse, it is a gift: he loved us and gave himself up for us. And the fragrance is where your acceptance lives: we are the aroma of Christ to God (2 Corinthians 2:15). When God is pleased with you, what pleases him is not the quality of your loving this week, but the fragrance of an offering someone else made, which you are covered in. You will never smell sweeter to God than you do at this moment, and no bad week can sour it.

What it does not mean. Not that love has no limits or must tolerate sin. Christ’s love aims at our holiness (v. 27). And “gave himself up” has been quoted at people to keep them where they are being harmed, as if likeness to Christ meant absorbing whatever is done to you and calling it love. But Christ’s self-giving was chosen, purposeful, and aimed at rescue. Someone who extracts sacrifice from you by force, fear or manipulation is not making you like Christ. If that is your home, tell someone who can act. The command to walk in love has never contained a command to stand still and be destroyed.

In a sentence. Live a life of love, just as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us as an offering and sacrifice that pleased God like a fragrant aroma.

On a Tuesday. Look back over the last seven days and find one time when loving someone actually cost you something you wanted: an evening, money, a preference, the last word in an argument you could have won. If nothing comes to mind, what you have been calling love has so far been free.

For worship. The smoke from Calvary has never stopped rising, and the Father has never stopped being pleased with it. You are covered in its fragrance. Thank Christ, who gave himself up for you.
verseByVerse.note: A “fragrant offering” recalls the Old Testament sacrifices that pleased God.

verseByVerse.quote: But sexual immorality and all impurity or covetousness must not even be named among you, as is proper among saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But sexual immorality and all impurity or covetousness must not even be named among you, as is proper among saints.

But. The contrast with v. 2. Love gives itself for another; these sins take from others for oneself. They are love’s counterfeits.

The setting. In first-century Ephesus sexual licence was woven into ordinary life and into its religion. Pagan worship came with festivals, temple banquets and drunken revels (the cult of Dionysus was strong in the city), at which licence was expected, not hidden. Outside the temples, prostitution was legal and taxed, and a husband’s use of slaves or prostitutes was not counted as adultery. As one Athenian orator put it, mistresses we keep for pleasure, concubines for daily care, wives to bear us legitimate children. (The popular claim that the temple of Artemis kept sacred prostitutes is not well supported; she was a virgin goddess.) In Ephesus, sexual sin and idolatry were often the same act, which is why Paul ties them together (v. 5). The church was to be the one community in the city where these things were not normal.

Sexual immorality. Greek porneia: every sexual act outside marriage between a man and a woman, including adultery, sex before marriage, prostitution, homosexual acts and pornography (the words share a root). Not because the body is evil; it belongs to God (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). But sexual union is a covenant act that pictures the union of Christ and his church (vv. 31–32).

All impurity. Greek akatharsia, uncleanness. A wider word: the moral filth of which sexual sin is one part. It covers impure thoughts, words, images and desires as well as acts (Matthew 5:28). “All” closes the loopholes: what never reaches the bed still defiles the heart.

Covetousness. Greek pleonexia, literally wanting more: the restless craving to have more than God has given, often at someone else’s expense. Plato and Aristotle had already called grasping after more than one’s share the root of injustice. What was new was setting it beside sexual sin and calling it idolatry. In Ephesus that was not even a metaphor: the temple of Artemis was also the great bank of the province, where kings and cities deposited their wealth in the goddess’s keeping. The god and the money were kept in the same building, and when the gospel threatened the trade in silver shrines, Demetrius raised a riot with profit and piety in one speech (Acts 19:25–27). Why put greed beside lust? Because they are one appetite: the conviction that what God has given is not enough, and what belongs to another should be mine (1 Thessalonians 4:6). And greed is the sin respectable people commit and rarely confess, which is why Paul names it so bluntly.

Must not even be named among you. Paul has just named all three, so he plainly does not mean silence. He is not forbidding the sermon that warns, the confession that admits, the friend who tells the truth about his struggle, the parent who explains to a teenager what pornography does to a soul; that kind of naming is exactly what the light does (vv. 11–13). He forbids the naming that makes a thing ordinary: the story told with a laugh, the affair discussed as entertainment over coffee, the casual remark that assumes everyone thinks it no great matter. Nothing becomes acceptable by being argued for. Things become acceptable by being mentioned often enough in a relaxed tone.

As is proper among saints. “Saints” means holy ones, people set apart for God. Every believer is one already (1:1). Paul does not say “become holy to be saints”; he says “you are saints, so live in the way that fits.”

What it does not mean. Not that owning, earning or saving is wrong. Working hard, planning ahead, providing for your family and managing money well are good stewardship (Proverbs 6:6–8; 1 Timothy 5:8), and enjoying God’s good gifts is gratitude, for he richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17). Honest ambition is not sin either. Paul was ambitious and said so: I make it my ambition to preach the gospel where Christ has not been named (Romans 15:20). The difference from greed is not the size of the goal but its direction. Greed measures itself against a neighbour and wants a larger share; godly ambition measures itself against the task and wants it done well, for others and for God. Seek great things for yourself? Seek them not (Jeremiah 45:5): the fault was never the “great”. The line runs through the heart. What is driving it, love and responsibility, or an appetite that upgrades and at once eyes the next upgrade? Is it held open-handed as a trust, or clutched as security? Does it produce generosity or hoarding? Likewise, desire for marriage, and sex within it, is good (1 Corinthians 7:2–5); impurity is desire outside God’s bounds.

What it does not mean: temptation is not the same as sin. Paul condemns sexual sin, not the experience of being tempted. The difference matters greatly, both to keep us from excusing sin and to keep tender consciences from despair.

Jesus was tempted. He in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). Being tempted, even strongly and repeatedly, cannot in itself be sin, or Christ would have sinned.

How temptation becomes sin. James traces the steps: each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin (James 1:14–15). A thought or image arrives, an attraction is felt: that is temptation. Sin is conceived when the heart says yes: when we welcome it, dwell on it, feed it, replay it, fantasise about it, or act on it. Jesus’ words about lust describe exactly this: looking at someone with lustful intent (Matthew 5:28), the look that keeps looking in order to desire. Luther, borrowing an old saying, put it plainly: you cannot stop the birds flying over your head, but you can stop them building a nest in your hair. The unwanted thought that flashes in and is hated is a call to fight, not a verdict of guilt, and the distress it causes is itself a sign that the heart has not consented.
