Where Christians differ: are the desires themselves sinful? Roman Catholic teaching holds that the inclination to sin left in us (concupiscence) is not itself sin until we consent. Reformed theology holds that the corruption remaining in believers, and its first stirrings, are truly sinful and need Christ’s forgiveness, though they are not deliberate acts (Westminster Confession 6.5; Romans 7:17–23). Verdict: the Reformed view is more faithful to Romans 7: our fallen desires are not neutral, and we never treat them as harmless. But three things must be kept distinct. First, temptation from outside, which Jesus himself faced, is no sin at all. Second, fallen desires that rise in us unbidden are the remnant of sin we fight, grieve over and bring to Christ, and for those in him there is no condemnation (Romans 8:1). Third, consenting to them, entertaining them or acting on them is sin committed, which needs repentance.

What this means in practice. A believer who feels sexual attraction to someone not his spouse, or who struggles with unwanted desires of any kind, including same-sex attraction, is not by that fact one of the “impure” Paul describes in v. 5. He is a soldier in a fight. The question is not, did a tempting thought come? but, what did I do with it? Turn away at once (flee youthful passions, 2 Timothy 2:22), turn the mind to something good (Philippians 4:8), pray, tell a trusted believer, and remove what feeds the desire (Romans 13:14). With every temptation God will also provide the way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13). And if you fall, do not hide: confess quickly and receive his forgiveness (1 John 1:9). If such thoughts are persistent and tormenting, tell a wise pastor or friend; they lose much of their power in the light (v. 13).

The other danger. Some excuse sin by calling it “just temptation” while they keep feeding it. Others drown in guilt for temptations they did not choose. The first needs repentance; the second needs the comfort of Christ, who was tempted as we are and helps those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18).

In a sentence. But among you there must not even be a hint of sexual immorality, of any kind of impurity, or of greed, because these are not fitting for God’s holy people.

On a Tuesday. Listen to how these subjects come up in your conversation this week. Not whether they come up, but how: as things to be grieved, resisted and honestly confessed, or as material? If a Christian tells a story about sexual sin and the room laughs, the room has learned something no sermon will easily undo. Saints are people among whom certain things simply cannot be made funny.

For worship. God is not grudging. Lust and greed both whisper that he has given too little, but the Father who did not spare his own Son will graciously give us all things with him (Romans 8:32). Praise the Holy One who made the body for himself and pictured in marriage the pure love of Christ for his church. And worship the Saviour who was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin, who never once grasped at more than his Father gave, and who now helps the tempted with the sympathy of one who has stood where they stand (Hebrews 2:18).

verseByVerse.quote: Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving.

From deeds to words. Paul moves from what we do (v. 3) to what we say. Speech shows the heart (Luke 6:45) and also shapes it: what we joke about, we begin to take lightly.

Filthiness. Shameful, obscene talk.

Foolish talk. Greek mōrologia, literally moron-talk: empty, senseless speech, especially the kind that drifts into the indecent.

Crude joking. Greek eutrapelia: the quick verbal turn, the ready wit. In the Greek world it was a compliment; Aristotle listed it as a virtue. Paul, remarkably, names it a vice. Not because it is clever, but because of what that particular cleverness is usually used for: making degrading things funny, through double meanings and innuendo, and turning people into material.

Out of place. It does not fit who you are, like muddy boots at a wedding.

But instead let there be thanksgiving. The surprising cure. The obvious answer to a mouth problem is restraint: catch it before it leaves. Paul does not say that. He says thanksgiving, which replaces the habit instead of merely suppressing it, as the thief is told not only to stop stealing but to work and give (4:28). Crude joking treats people and God’s gifts, especially sex, as material for a moment’s laugh. Thanksgiving treats them as gifts and names the Giver. The two cannot easily live in the same mouth. A man who begins genuinely thanking God for his wife will find the jokes about her drying up without ever having made a rule. The same Greek word (eucharistia) gives us Eucharist, the meal of thanksgiving at the heart of Christian worship: the table where we remember what Christ gave is meant to shape everything we say away from it.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians must be humourless, speaking only in careful, devotional tones; anyone who has met a church that took it that way knows the result is not holiness but strain. God invented laughter, and there is wit in Scripture, a good deal of it on the lips of Jesus: a camel through the eye of a needle (Mark 10:25) and the log in your own eye (Matthew 7:3–5) are meant to be funny. The target is humour that degrades.

What about the comedy and drama I watch? The same test applies to the screen as to the office, because laughing along on the sofa is still laughing along. Christians are free to enjoy good comedy, and to watch serious drama that shows sin honestly; Scripture itself tells of David’s adultery without making it funny or enticing. The question is what the programme is doing with the sin it shows: grieving it, exposing it, or selling it as entertainment. A show whose humour runs on innuendo and contempt is training your sense of what is normal every evening you give it, whether or not you notice. So ask plainly: does this leave me more thankful or more jaded? Do I switch it off when the children come in because I know what it is? If you already know the answer, the remote is in your hand.

In a sentence. Nor should there be obscenity, silly talk or coarse joking, which are out of place; instead, let there be thanksgiving.

On a Tuesday. The test is not whether the room laughed, but what the laughter was aimed at. Could the subject of the joke stand in the doorway without the tone changing? And what has the joke taught the youngest Christian in the room about how seriously we take this? When office banter turns crude, you do not need to preach; you need not to join in. Be the grateful one.

For worship. Thanksgiving is the right language for this mouth, because there is so much to thank him for. Every good gift comes down from the Father of lights (James 1:17), and the greatest of them is set before us at his table: the body and blood of Christ, given for us. Adore the God who invented laughter and joy, whose Son spoke with wit and warmth and never once degraded anyone he spoke about. The one who gave everything is worthy of the gratitude of every tongue he has redeemed.

verseByVerse.quote: For you may be sure of this, that everyone who is sexually immoral or impure, or who is covetous (that is, an idolater), has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you may be sure of this, that everyone who is sexually immoral or impure, or who is covetous (that is, an idolater), has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God.

For you may be sure of this. Literally knowing, know this: emphatic. This is settled truth, not opinion.

That everyone who is sexually immoral or impure, or who is covetous. The same three sins as v. 3. Paul uses nouns that describe a person by his way of life: the sexually immoral person (pornos), the impure person, the covetous person (pleonektēs). He is describing people whose lives are marked and ruled by these things, not people who have ever fallen into them.

(That is, an idolater). Not that greed is like idolatry, or leads to it. It is it. Most of us can see how a man worships a carved image, and cannot see how a man worships a bank balance. So ask what an idol does for its worshipper. It tells him who he is: his worth is settled by what he has or achieves. It tells him he is safe: the figure in the account stands between him and disaster. It receives his best hours and sharpest thinking. It sets the terms of his joy, so that a good day is a day the idol prospers. And it decides what he will sacrifice: time, integrity, his marriage, his children’s memory of him. Run those five through a man who has never bowed to a statue but cannot stop wanting more, and every one fits. In a city full of idol temples, Paul says the most common idol is not in a temple but in a wallet (Matthew 6:24; Colossians 3:5). And it is the hardest idol to see, because greed looks like diligence, prudence and providing for the family, all real virtues, which is its disguise. It is admired at work and congratulated at church. Nobody has ever taken a man aside to ask gently whether he might be worshipping his career.

Has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God. “Inheritance” (klēronomian): what children receive from their father. God’s children inherit his kingdom (1:14, 18). Those who live as slaves to these things show that they are not his children, and so they receive nothing. “The kingdom of Christ and God”: one kingdom, shared by the Son and the Father, a quiet witness that Christ is God.

A question that troubles many believers. A Christian who struggles with lust, pornography or greed may read this verse and fear that he is lost. Three things help. First, Paul is describing a settled pattern of life that a person accepts and does not fight, not the believer who falls, hates it, confesses it and keeps fighting (Romans 7:18–25; 1 John 1:8–9). The difference is not whether you sin, but whether you are at peace with it or at war with it. The one who has no inheritance does not fight his sin; he makes peace with it. The one who cries, wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me? (Romans 7:24) is not the voice of the excluded, but of one who belongs to Christ and knows he is not yet what he will be. The mark of the believer is not that he never falls, but that he cannot stay down. Second, Paul includes the covetous, which should humble every reader: no one can read this list and think it is only about other people. Third, Paul writes this to people already saved by grace (2:8–9) and sealed by the Spirit (1:13–14). In 1 Corinthians 6:9–11 he gives a similar list and then says, and such were some of you. But you were washed. So if this verse troubles you, that trouble is itself a sign of life. The person Paul warns is not troubled at all. The cure for a troubled conscience is not to soften the warning, but to run to Christ.

Where Christians differ: can a true believer lose the inheritance? Those who hold that true Christians can finally fall away read this verse as a warning that a believer who returns to these sins will lose the kingdom. Verdict: the warning is real and must be taken seriously, but it does not describe a true believer losing what God has sealed (1:13–14; 4:30). Those who are truly God’s children will not settle into a life ruled by these sins; if someone does so and never repents, it shows he never truly belonged to Christ, whatever he professed (1 John 2:19; 3:9). God uses warnings like this to keep his people persevering.

What it does not mean. Not that any believer who has ever sinned this way is lost, or that a Christian who stumbles has lost salvation. It means that a settled, unrepentant life given over to these sins marks a person as outside the kingdom, whatever he professes.

In a sentence. For you can be certain of this: no one who lives a sexually immoral, impure or greedy life (for a greedy person is really an idol-worshipper) has any share in the kingdom of Christ and of God.

On a Tuesday. An idol only holds power while it goes by another name. So ask two questions. What loss would feel like the end of you, not just painful, but the end? And what did you last spend a sleepless night over? Whatever answers those is functioning as your god. Name it, and you can stop asking it for what it was never able to give.

For worship. The kingdom of Christ and God is one kingdom, because the Son shares the Father’s throne; here is a quiet glory to adore, that Jesus is Lord and God. Every idol promises safety and identity and never delivers, but the living God is our true security and our sure inheritance. Praise the Father who makes sinners his heirs, the Son who washes those who once were idolaters, and the Spirit who seals them for the day of redemption. Such were some of us, but we were washed (1 Corinthians 6:11): glory to the God who does such things.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience.

Let no one deceive you. Some in and around the church taught that the body did not matter, or that grace made sin harmless. Every age has its voices saying, God does not care what you do with your body or your money.

Empty words. Words with nothing true inside them. And each contains a half-truth, which is the whole of its power; a plainly false lie persuades nobody. God is gracious; this does not really matter. The first half is the ground everything stands on. But grace is not God’s indifference to sin; it is what it cost him to deal with it. Measure sin’s seriousness by the cross: this is what it took. To say grace makes sin unimportant is to say Calvary was an overreaction. Everyone struggles with this. True, and a good reason to be gentle with others; not a reason to stop fighting. That everyone is ill does not make the illness harmless. And notice the sleight of hand: the word struggle is usually used by someone who has stopped struggling and would like to keep the word. A loving God would never judge. We do not believe this about anything we care about. A father who watched his child being destroyed and felt nothing would not be loving; he would be dead. Wrath is not the opposite of love; indifference is.

Where empty words come from. Not usually from the enemies of the faith, who rarely bother to talk us out of anything. They come from within: from a friend who wants us comfortable, from a teacher who has learned that the pleasant half of the message fills a room, and most often from ourselves, at eleven at night, building a case in our own favour.

The wrath of God. Not a temper tantrum, but God’s settled, holy opposition to evil, not arbitrary punishment but his opposition to all that destroys those made in his image. A God who loves people cannot be indifferent to what destroys them. It is shown now (Romans 1:18) and will come in full at the judgement (Colossians 3:6).

Comes upon. Present tense: it is already falling, and will fall finally.

Sons of disobedience. A Hebrew way of saying people whose character is disobedience, as Paul described all of us before Christ (2:2–3).

What it does not mean. Not that believers should fear God’s wrath as their sentence. Christ has borne it for those who trust him (Romans 5:9), and there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). The warning is aimed at the conscience that wants permission, not at the believer who fights, grieves and returns. But believers must not take lightly what God judges.

In a sentence. Do not let anyone deceive you with empty arguments, because it is for these very things that God’s anger comes on those who disobey him.

On a Tuesday. When a line of reasoning arrives that happens to permit exactly what you already wanted, treat its convenience as evidence against it. Truth is often unwelcome; an argument that lands where your appetite was already standing has some explaining to do.

For worship. God is not indifferent, and that is part of his glory. His holy wrath is the fierce opposition of perfect love to everything that destroys those who bear his image. And here is the wonder: the wrath that comes on the sons of disobedience fell first and fully on the obedient Son, so that all who trust him are saved from it (Romans 5:9). Grace was never cheap. Adore the God whose holiness took our sin seriously enough to judge it, and whose love took it seriously enough to bear it himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not become partners with them;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore do not become partners with them;

Setting and background. Paul has just warned that sexual immorality, impurity and covetousness bring the wrath of God on the sons of disobedience (v. 6). Converts in Ephesus lived among friends, family and trade guild members who still practised these things as normal parts of city life, in temple feasts, guild gatherings and private homes.

Therefore. Because these things bring God’s wrath (v. 6), believers must not take part in them.

Do not become partners with them. “Partners” (symmetochoi, co-sharers) is the very word Paul used in 3:6 for Gentiles who are now fellow partakers of the promise in Christ, and it appears nowhere else in the New Testament. He is asking which partnership you are really in. You cannot be a co-sharer in Christ and a co-sharer in the works of darkness at once; the two are competing for the same word. And “become” is present tense: do not drift into becoming partners. Compromise is rarely a decision. It is usually a silence: the laugh you gave so as not to seem difficult, the objection you did not raise.

What it does not mean. It does not mean withdrawal from unbelievers. Paul had to correct exactly that misunderstanding in Corinth: he did not mean the immoral of this world, since then you would need to go out of the world, but anyone who bears the name of brother and lives that way (1 Corinthians 5:9–11). Jesus was called a friend of tax collectors and sinners (Matthew 11:19), and ate with people the religious would not sit near. The line runs not between people but between practices: not whether you go to the party, but whether you take part in what happens there; not whether you keep the friendship, but whether your presence signals approval of what you both know is wrong. It is the difference between being among and being with.

In a sentence. So do not join in with people who live like that, or share in what they do.

On a Tuesday. You can sit with colleagues at lunch without sharing their gossip, their dishonesty or their jokes. In a situation you would rather not have to describe, ask not, am I doing anything wrong? but, if the people I love and the Lord I serve were both watching, what would my being here be saying? And then the plainest question of all: could I stand before the Lord in this situation, as I am, and not want to hide?

For worship. Before Paul forbids one partnership, he has already announced a better one: Gentiles made fellow partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus (3:6). Praise the Saviour who was called the friend of sinners and sat at their tables, yet never once shared in their sin. He came among us without becoming like us in our darkness, so that we might share in his light. What a fellowship he has opened to outsiders: a share in the inheritance of the Son of God himself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Once they were darkness, but now they are light in the Lord, so they must live as children of light, whose fruit is all goodness, righteousness and truth, and find out what pleases the Lord. They must have nothing to do with the fruitless deeds of darkness, but expose them; it is shameful even to mention what the disobedient do in secret. Everything exposed by the light becomes visible, and so the call goes out: sleeper, wake up, rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.
verseByVerse.theology:
Light, Darkness, and the Prophetic Witness of Holiness

The ontological language of this passage — “you were darkness,” “you are light” — reflects the radical nature of regeneration. The new birth is not a moral improvement programme; it is a change of nature. What was dark has become light. What was oriented toward self and sin has been reoriented toward God and holiness. This is the consistent teaching of the Reformed tradition: regeneration is sovereign, total, and irreversible — a work of God in the interior of the person that creates a new appetite, a new orientation, a new capacity for the things of God.

The call to “take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them” (v.11) raises the question of the church's relationship to culture. The Reformed tradition has generally resisted both the temptation to total withdrawal (a pietism that disengages from the world) and the temptation to total accommodation (a liberalism that conforms to it). The middle path — engagement without assimilation, presence without compromise — is what it means to be light in the world. The church that is genuinely, visibly holy is not only doing something good for its own members; it is doing something necessary for the world, exposing by contrast what the world cannot see about itself.

The awakening hymn of v.14 — “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you” — is widely thought to be an early Christian baptismal hymn. It captures the eschatological urgency of the whole passage: the world is asleep, the darkness is presenting itself as normal and comfortable, and the church is called to be the community of the awakened, the risen, the enlightened. Not by shouting but by shining.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The darkness Paul describes in v.12 — “the things they do in secret” — was not merely a moral category. Ephesus had a fully developed underground of occult practice, of ritual darkness, of things done in the night that could not bear the daylight. The mystery religions operated precisely in the realm of secrets, of hidden things, of initiation into darkness. The church's commitment to transparency — to lives that could be lived fully in the open before God — was itself a form of witness against the culture of secrecy. You have nothing to hide because you have nothing to fear. You live in the light because Christ has shone on you.

Now: “Awake, O sleeper” has the ring of an alarm clock going off in a dark room. The world is sleeping — comfortable in its darkness, unaware of its danger, presenting its way of life as simply the normal and natural way to live. The church is called to wake up and to be awake — to see the world as it really is in the light of God's word, to live accordingly, and thereby to be the kind of community whose quality of life is itself an invitation: come and see what happens when Christ shines on you. In a culture that is drowsy with distraction and numbed by comfort, the church's wakefulness is among its most urgent callings.

verseByVerse.quote: for at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light
verseByVerse.commentary:
for at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light

At one time you were darkness. Paul is not being vague about that past; he has written its biography earlier in this letter. Dead in trespasses, following the course of this world, children of wrath (2:1–3); having no hope and without God in the world (2:12); darkened in understanding, callous (4:18–19). Darkness here is not a mood; it is a life with a history. And notice: not “in the dark” but darkness itself. Before Christ it was not only around us; it was our nature. That means more than doing dark things from time to time. It means the source itself was dark: our desires, our thinking and our will were turned away from God, so that even our good deeds were done without love for him (Romans 8:7–8). We did not stumble into the dark by accident; left to ourselves we preferred it, as Jesus said, loving darkness rather than light (John 3:19). And we could no more change that by trying harder than a dark room can light itself.

But now you are light. Not “you are in the light” or “you have some light”. You are light: a change of nature, not only of location. It means the centre has changed. The Spirit of Christ now lives in you, so you begin to love God and what he loves, you want the truth about yourself to be seen rather than hidden, and you shine on the people around you as a lamp lights a room (Matthew 5:14–16). It is not light you generate; you are light in the Lord, bright the way the moon is bright, with all of it received from him who is the light of the world (John 8:12). Nor does it mean you no longer sin. It means that when you do, you no longer love it: you hate it, confess it and fight it, because your nature has changed sides. And notice what Paul does not say happened. Not that God found a spark in you and fanned it, or saw potential worth developing. There was nothing to work with; darkness has no raw material in it. What happened was creation: God, who said, Let light shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts (2 Corinthians 4:6). That is Genesis 1:3 spoken over a human being. The first light in the universe was not coaxed out of the dark; it was spoken into a formless dark that contributed nothing. So was yours. Hold on to that if you have ever suspected that God got less than he bargained for with you. Nobody was a promising case. If God needed a spark to work with, the world would still be dark.

In the Lord. Not in ourselves. Think of the moon. It is truly light; sailors have crossed oceans by it, and on the right night you can read by it. It is also true that every particle of that light is borrowed, and that turned away from the sun it is a cold rock. Neither fact cancels the other. That is your position (John 8:12; Matthew 5:14). So the honest reader who thinks about what went through his mind on the drive home and concludes that “light” cannot describe him is looking in the wrong place. He is searching himself for a glow of his own, and the verse never said he had one. The question is not whether you can find light inside yourself, but whether you are turned towards him. Do not go rummaging through your interior for evidence. Turn round.

Walk as children of light. In Hebrew idiom a son of something derives his nature from it and is marked by it; Jesus spoke of the sons of this world over against the sons of light (Luke 16:8; John 12:36). And it is the same word as in 5:1: there beloved children told to imitate, here children of light told to walk. Both times the family you belong to is the reason for the behaviour, never the price of admission. The order is everything. “You are light” comes first, as a fact; “walk as children of light” second, as a command. Most of us are trying to walk well enough to earn the identity. Paul hands you the identity and then asks for the walk. And that he asks at all shows the gap is real: you can be light and walk badly. That is not a contradiction; it is every Christian’s ordinary experience, and it is why the letter has three chapters of instructions.

What it does not mean. Not that believers are sinless. The command to walk as light shows that we still need to grow into what God has made us.

In a sentence. For you were once darkness itself, but now you are light in the Lord; so live as children of light

On a Tuesday. Think of the last time you sinned badly enough to be ashamed. Not what you did, but what you concluded afterwards. Did some part of you say, that is not who I am? Sin in a child of light is a self-contradiction, and it feels like one: it sits wrong, will not settle, wants confessing. A stain shows on white cloth and disappears on black, and the fact that yours showed is telling you what colour the cloth is.

For worship. Glory to the God who speaks light into the dark. He did not find a glimmer in us to fan into flame; he said, Let there be light, over people who were darkness itself. Christ is the light of the world (John 8:12), and every believer shines as the moon shines, with borrowed glory, turned towards him. Adore the Lord who did not wait for promising material, but who gives life to the dead and calls into being things that were not (Romans 4:17).

verseByVerse.quote: (for the fruit of light is found in all that is good and right and true), and try to discern what is pleasing to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
(for the fruit of light is found in all that is good and right and true), and try to discern what is pleasing to the Lord.

The fruit of light. Fruit grows; it is not manufactured. A life in Christ’s light naturally bears these things. Not rules to perform, but fruit to bear.

Textual note. Later manuscripts read “fruit of the Spirit” (as in the King James Version), from Galatians 5:22. Verdict: “fruit of light” is original.

Good, right, true. Three sides of the light’s fruit. Goodness: generous kindness towards others. Righteousness: doing what is right before God and people. Truth: honesty and integrity, in contrast to the empty words of v. 6.

Try to discern. Greek dokimazō: to test and approve, as a metalworker tests gold. Paul normally gives direct commands, but here he does not say, obey this list. He says, discern. The Christian life cannot be reduced to a rule-book. Rules cover the cases the lawmaker foresaw; life keeps producing cases no rule-book addressed. What Paul asks for is deeper than compliance: the developed ability to read a situation in the light of knowing Christ (Romans 12:2; Philippians 1:9–10).

What is pleasing to the Lord. And notice the object. Not, discern what is permitted, but what is pleasing. Most of us instinctively ask a boundary question: is this allowed? Where exactly is the line? That question can always be answered, and it is asked by someone who wants to know how close he may go. Paul’s question cannot be answered that way. A husband who asks what he can do and still be technically faithful has already told you the state of his marriage; a husband who asks what would please his wife is in a different marriage entirely. Watch the two questions on an ordinary case. You are offered a promotion: more money, more standing, and sixty hours a week for three years, with two children at home. The boundary question returns nothing useful: ambition is not a sin, and no commandment is broken. Now ask Paul’s question, and the relevant things arrive from every side: the years with those children you cannot get back; whether this is stewardship or the greed of verse 5 in respectable clothes; what your real motive is; what your wife would say if she thought you truly wanted the answer. None of that can be looked up. It is what a person sees who knows the Lord well enough to know what pleases him.

What it does not mean. Not that each of us invents our own morality. Discernment works within Scripture and is trained by it. It is a skill, and skills come by practice: the mature have their powers of discernment trained by constant practice to distinguish good from evil (Hebrews 5:14). That is why a Christian of thirty years often sees at once what a younger believer must agonise over. Not because he is cleverer, but because he has asked the question ten thousand times and his palate has changed.

In a sentence. (for the light produces everything that is good and right and true), and try to find out what pleases the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Take one decision this week, a small one will do, and put the second question to it instead of the first. Not, am I allowed? but, what would please him? You will not always get it right. But the one who asks it a thousand times will find one day that he can see the answer.

For worship. All goodness, righteousness and truth have their fountain in God. He is good and does good (Psalm 119:68); his righteousness stands like the mighty mountains (Psalm 36:6); his word is truth (John 17:17). In Christ these three walked among us as one life, never once at odds. Praise the Lord who is himself the pleasure we are learning to discern, and whose Son could say without exaggeration that he always does what pleases the Father (John 8:29). To know such a God well enough to please him is the highest delight a creature can have.

verseByVerse.quote: Take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them. For it is shameful even to speak of the things that they do in secret.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them. For it is shameful even to speak of the things that they do in secret.

Unfruitful works of darkness. Light bears fruit (v. 9); darkness produces only barren works, nothing that survives. Sin promises much and gives nothing that lasts (Galatians 6:8).

Take no part. The same word root as “partners” in v. 7: do not be co-sharers.

Expose them. Greek elenchō: to bring into the open, convict, show something for what it is. What does that mean on a Thursday? Not becoming an investigator, hunting for what people hide; a Christian with an appetite for uncovering others’ sin has misread the passage. Not exposing persons; Paul says expose the works. And not loudly denouncing a world that is behaving exactly as one would expect; judging outsiders is not our business (1 Corinthians 5:12–13). It has three ordinary forms. First, living so that the contrast shows: a man who simply does not join in has made something visible without a word (Matthew 5:16). Second, refusing to let a thing pass as normal: not a sermon, but the quiet sentence that declines to laugh, or says, I don’t think that’s right, and lets the silence sit. Third, and hardest, going privately to a brother about something you can see and he cannot (Matthew 18:15; Galatians 6:1).

The smell of smoke. Ephesus was the magic capital of the ancient world. Its written spells were famous enough to have a name, the Ephesian Letters, and its mystery cults were built on secrecy: rites at night, knowledge only for initiates. Secrecy was not incidental to that religion; it was the product being sold. When the gospel took hold there, those who had practised magic brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all, worth fifty thousand pieces of silver (Acts 19:19). Burned publicly, at ruinous cost, by people who had every reason to sell them on. Some of those holding this letter had stood in that crowd. Paul is not introducing a new idea; he is reminding them of the smell of smoke.

Shameful even to speak of. Some things done in secret are so degrading that dwelling on the details is itself corrupting. Verse 12 does not withdraw the command; it governs its manner. You can bring a thing into the open without describing it in detail. The difference is whether the telling serves repentance or curiosity. An account so vivid that hearers are entertained instead of sobered has stopped exposing darkness and started selling it.

Between two ditches. One ditch is withdrawal: treating darkness as contamination and retreating, until a church knows nobody outside itself and shines only into a mirror. The other is accommodation: staying in the world and becoming indistinguishable from it, until there is nothing left to expose because the contrast has gone. Paul asks for neither, but for presence without participation. That is harder than either ditch, because each offers a relief and this offers none, and it is the only one of the three that leaves anyone with something to see.

What it does not mean. Not a licence to police unbelievers, spread gossip or shame people publicly. The aim of exposing is repentance and healing, not humiliation (v. 13).

What if the thing I know about is a crime, or someone is being harmed? Then exposing it means telling those who can stop it, and quickly. The private approach of Matthew 18:15 is for a brother’s sin against you; it was never meant for the abuse of a child, violence in a home or serious fraud, where going quietly to the offender can warn him and leave the victim in danger. God has given the civil authorities the sword to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4), and reporting a crime to them is obedience, not betrayal. Tell the police or the proper safeguarding body, and tell your church’s elders, but do not let anyone, a church leader included, persuade you to keep it inside the church instead. Speaking up for those who cannot speak for themselves honours Christ far more than protecting the reputation of his people (Proverbs 31:8–9).

In a sentence. Have nothing to do with the barren deeds of darkness, but rather expose them; for it is shameful even to mention what such people do in secret.

On a Tuesday. Before you speak about someone’s sin, ask what you are hoping for. If it is that they would be restored and the thing would end, you are exposing. If part of you hopes to be proved right, or seen as the one who noticed, that is not light; it is the pleasure of holding a torch.

For worship. The works of darkness are barren, but the light of God is fruitful, and nothing hidden can stand before it. Praise the Lord whose holiness is not afraid of the dark, who brought the secret books of Ephesus into the open and burned away their power. Adore the God who sees what is done in secret and defends those who cannot speak for themselves. And bless the Saviour who was himself stripped and exposed to public shame on the cross, so that our hidden shame might be covered and healed.

verseByVerse.quote: But when anything is exposed by the light, it becomes visible, for anything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says, 'Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when anything is exposed by the light, it becomes visible, for anything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says, ‘Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.’

Exposed by the light, it becomes visible. When sin is brought into God’s light, it is seen for what it is.

Anything that becomes visible is light. A difficult phrase. Its likely meaning: what is exposed and confessed does not stay darkness; it is changed into light. When a person’s sin is brought into the light and he repents, he himself becomes light (1 John 1:7–9). Think of a believer who has carried a hidden sin for years, never told anyone, the weight growing. The moment it is finally brought into the light, confessed to God and to a trusted friend or pastor, its grip weakens. Not because confession is magic, but because secrecy is the one condition sin truly needs. Shame’s whole power is one sentence: if they knew what you are, they would be finished with you. As long as nobody knows, that sentence is never tested, and so it is believed. Confession puts it to the test. You say the thing aloud to a Christian friend, and he does not recoil; he prays with you, and the next week he asks how you are getting on. The lie you have lived under for fifteen years is disproved in front of you by someone who now knows the worst and is still sitting there. That is why James says, confess your sins to one another … that you may be healed (James 5:16). The healing comes through the one another.

Therefore it says. Not an Old Testament quotation, but probably an early Christian hymn, perhaps sung at baptism, echoing Isaiah 26:19 (your dead shall live … awake and sing) and 60:1 (arise, shine, for your light has come).

Awake, O sleeper. Sleep pictures a life unaware of God and of danger. It is first a call to the unconverted. But Paul is writing to saints, and the words are wide enough to reach the man who woke years ago and has since dozed off in a comfortable pew. Scripture keeps addressing him: the hour has come for you to wake from sleep (Romans 13:11); wake up, and strengthen what remains (Revelation 3:2). The sleeping Christian has not renounced anything. He is at church most Sundays and would answer every doctrinal question correctly. But nothing costs him anything; no sin has been fought in years; prayer has become words without an address; and he cannot remember when he last expected God to do anything. He is not in rebellion. He is asleep, a state in which everything looks normal and nothing is happening. And the sleeper does not know he is asleep, which is why the summons has to come from outside: a hymn, a sermon, a friend, a verse that will not leave him alone.

Arise from the dead. More than sleep: spiritual death (2:1). Only God can raise the dead, which is why the call carries power.

Christ will shine on you. Like the sun rising on someone waking. The command is not the point of the sentence; the promise is. Not, wake up and sort out your discipline and God may take an interest. The light is already shining, and the only thing between the sleeper and the sunrise is a pair of closed eyes. The light that exposes is the same light that warms and gives life.

In a sentence. But everything exposed by the light becomes visible, and whatever is made visible becomes light; that is why it is said: Wake up, sleeper, rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.

For worship. Christ is already shining, on the sleeper, on the ashamed, on you. Open your eyes to the light that has been on your face for some time, and pray that he will shine on someone you love who is still asleep.
verseByVerse.note: These lines are not found in the Old Testament; they may come from an early Christian hymn, echoing Isaiah.

parallels.desc: awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust
arise, shine, for your light has come

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They must be very careful how they live, not as unwise but as wise, making the most of every opportunity, because the days are evil. They must not be foolish but understand the Lord’s will. Instead of getting drunk on wine, which leads to ruin, they must be filled with the Spirit: speaking to one another with psalms, hymns and songs from the Spirit, singing and making music from the heart to the Lord, always giving thanks to God the Father for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Fullness of the Spirit and the Worshipping Community

“Be filled with the Spirit” (v.18) is a present passive imperative — go on being filled, continuously, repeatedly. The fullness of the Spirit is not a one-time crisis experience; it is the ongoing reality of a life open to and dependent on God's Spirit. The passive voice is significant: we do not fill ourselves; we are filled. We create the conditions — prayer, the word, corporate worship, obedience — and God does the filling. The Spirit is given to those who ask (Luke 11:13), and the asking is to be persistent, humble, and expectant.

The triad of “psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (v.19) has been the subject of considerable historical discussion about the nature of Christian worship. What matters more than the categorisation is the character: the worship is corporate, directed toward God, spirit-animated, joyful, and overflowing into the rest of life. Worship is not an event on Sunday that is unrelated to life on Monday; it is the expression of a fullness that shapes everything the Spirit-filled person does.

The closing imperative — “submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ” (v.21) — is the theological hinge on which everything that follows turns. Paul will apply mutual submission to wives and husbands, children and fathers, servants and masters. But the foundation is the mutual submission of the Spirit-filled community: a posture of other-centredness, of preferring one another, of deferring in love to the needs and preferences of those around us. This is the overflow of a life that has been filled with the Spirit of the One who “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself” (Philippians 2:6–7).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Several of the cults of Ephesus, above all that of Dionysus, were soaked in wine, in ecstatic states, in the pursuit of transcendence through altered consciousness. The Dionysian festivals were characterized by drunkenness and sexual abandon as means of communing with the divine. Against this entire religious culture, Paul offers the Spirit-filled community as the true alternative: not the dissipation of Dionysus but the fullness of the Holy Spirit, not the frantic ecstasy of the cult but the joyful, ordered, outward-facing overflow of a community that has been possessed not by wine but by God. The church was, in Ephesus, a genuinely countercultural gathering — a community whose worship looked and sounded like nothing else in the city.

Now: We live in an age of spiritual hunger and an age of extraordinary means for filling the void — entertainment, substance, distraction, the endless dopamine of the digital feed. None of it satisfies. The hunger returns, more insistent than before. Paul's word to a hungry generation is unchanged: be filled with the Spirit. The fullness he gives is not the temporary satiation of appetite but the genuine, overflowing, outward-directed joy of a life in which God himself has taken up residence. The church that is genuinely, visibly, joyfully full of the Spirit — that sings with gratitude, that submits in love, that gives thanks for everything — is offering the watching world a glimpse of what it was made for.

verseByVerse.quote: Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time, because the days are evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time, because the days are evil.

Look carefully then how you walk. Literally see accurately how you walk, like someone picking his way along a narrow path. A surgeon does not walk into an operating theatre the way she walks into a supermarket. She is aware of what each moment requires: not anxious, but trained and focused. Paul asks for that kind of attention to the whole of life: not anxiety, but wakefulness; not frantic busyness, but a refusal to drift.

Unwise and wise. In Scripture wisdom is not cleverness but skill in living God’s way, rooted in the fear of the Lord (Proverbs 9:10). The unwise are not necessarily ignorant; they simply drift with whatever the culture does. Nobody makes a dramatic decision to waste his life. The unwise simply never decide not to.

Making the best use of the time. Literally buying up the time (exagorazomenoi), a merchant’s word, from the same root as redemption, used of buying a slave’s freedom. Every purchase costs something. Time cannot be saved, only spent, and you cannot make more of it. So you are buying continuously, whether or not you are choosing, and the currency is the only thing you own that does not renew. The man who says he has no time for prayer has not run out of time; he has bought something else with it. And the word for time is kairos: opportunity, the right moment. Opportunities have expiry dates. A conversation with an ageing parent while he can still follow it. A neighbour who will move next year. A friend in crisis, soft and asking questions now, who in eighteen months will have rebuilt his defences and not raise the subject again. A child at the age when he still wants your company. None of these announces its closing time. That is why Paul says, buy it up (Colossians 4:5; Psalm 90:12).

Because the days are evil. The present age is under the influence of evil (2:2; 6:12). The current runs against you. A boat on a river does not stay still by doing nothing; it drifts downstream. Drift is the default; wisdom requires intention.

What it does not mean. Not frantic busyness or guilt about rest. Redeeming the time is not maximising output. The Lord of these Christians was never in a hurry. He had three years and the weight of the world on him, and still stopped for a blind man on the road (Mark 10:46–52) and slept in a boat during a storm (Mark 4:38). A frantic life and a wasted life can be equally unredeemed. The question is not how much you got through today, but what you bought.

In a sentence. So be very careful how you live, not as foolish people but as wise ones, making the most of every opportunity, because the days are evil.

On a Tuesday. Name one person God has placed within reach whose window is closing: the parent, the neighbour, the friend, the child, the colleague who has started asking questions. Then name what has actually been buying up your evenings this month. Set the two side by side, and the price becomes visible.

For worship. The Lord of time walked through his days unhurried and unwasted. He knew his hour, and when it came he went to meet it, buying with his own life the redemption of a people who had squandered theirs. Praise the Christ who stopped for a blind beggar on the road and still finished the work his Father gave him to do (John 17:4). Every moment we are given is the gift of the eternal God, who stands outside time and yet entered it, sending his Son when the fullness of time had come (Galatians 4:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.

Foolish. Greek aphrōn: senseless, without understanding. Not low intelligence, but living without thinking about God.

Understand. Grasp it, put it together. Christian obedience uses the mind. This is the great steering question of the wise life: not what is convenient, or what everyone else does, but what does the Lord want here?

The will of the Lord. Christians agonise over this phrase more than almost any other, and most of the anguish comes from confusing two senses. There is God’s hidden will: his sovereign purpose, what he has decreed will actually happen. It governs everything, and it is not published. The secret things belong to the LORD our God (Deuteronomy 29:29). And there is God’s revealed will: what he has told us plainly he wants, which fills the Bible and is not mysterious at all. Now notice which one we spend our energy on. Almost everything people mean by “finding God’s will” concerns the hidden one: which house, which career, which person, and above all the fear of missing the single correct path. But that will was never given to you to read. Meanwhile the revealed will sits open on the desk: this is the will of God, your sanctification (1 Thessalonians 4:3); give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you (1 Thessalonians 5:18). God’s will is not a hidden dot you must locate and are ruined for missing. It is a direction he has already described in detail, and a person he is making you into. The one pursuing holiness, giving thanks, telling the truth, loving his wife and doing good work is in the will of God, whichever of two reasonable job offers he accepts.

What it does not mean. Not that God has hidden secret instructions you must decode. Within his revealed will, you have freedom to make wise choices, and the discernment for the genuinely open questions grows out of obeying what is already clear (v. 10).

In a sentence. So do not be thoughtless, but understand what the Lord wants.

On a Tuesday. If you are stuck, change the question. Not, what is the one thing God wants me to do? but, what has God already made clear, and am I doing it? Most people who cannot hear God on the large decision have a small one outstanding that they can hear perfectly well.

For worship. God has not hidden himself behind a riddle. Praise the Father who has made known to us the mystery of his will (1:9) and laid open his heart in Scripture, so that the humblest believer can know what pleases him. His secret purposes he keeps, and they rest in wise and loving hands; his revealed will he gives freely, and it is good, acceptable and perfect (Romans 12:2). Adore the Son, who came down from heaven not to do his own will but the will of the one who sent him (John 6:38), and did it all the way to the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit,

The setting. Drinking was central to Greek social life, and at the festivals of Dionysus, god of wine, drunkenness was thought to bring people close to the divine: the self surrendered to an outside power. Paul refuses the counterfeit. The true way to be filled with God is not wine but the Spirit.

And do not get drunk with wine. Scripture consistently warns against drunkenness (Proverbs 23:29–35; Galatians 5:21).

For that is debauchery. “Debauchery” (asōtia): a life out of control, wasting itself, the word for the prodigal son’s reckless living (Luke 15:13).

But be filled with the Spirit. “Be filled” (plērousthe). Why compare wine and the Spirit? Both can fill a person and influence how he speaks and acts. Wine takes away self-control and leads to waste. The Spirit gives self-control (Galatians 5:23) and leads to praise, thanks and humble service (vv. 19–21). The comparison is in the influence, not in the experience: the Spirit does not make people behave as if drunk. To be filled is to be governed and driven by him, the way a sail is filled with wind.

A command that is passive. The verb is a present, passive command: keep on being filled. How can someone be commanded to have something done to him? The picture of the sail answers it. A sail cannot make wind; nothing a sailor does will produce a breath of it. But a sail can be raised or left furled, and that is the sailor’s business. Everything that opens a life to the Spirit is canvas going up; it does not make the wind, but it means you will not miss it when it comes. And grieving or quenching the Spirit is furling the sail, after which a man may sincerely complain that he feels becalmed. Every believer already has the Spirit (1:13); being filled means being more and more governed, shaped and moved by him. It is a continuing life, not a single event, less like a tank topped up once than like breathing.

How is a believer filled? The best guide is Colossians 3:16–17, Paul’s parallel passage. Set them side by side. Here: be filled with the Spirit, addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing, giving thanks always, submitting to one another (5:18–21). There: let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing, giving thanks, and then wives, husbands and children (Colossians 3:16–18). The results are the same, in the same order, almost in the same words. Only the cause is put differently. So these are not two separate attainments, one ordinary and one rare. They are two descriptions of one reality, because the Spirit wrote the word and works through it. In practice: take in God’s word, ask (how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him! Luke 11:13), obey what you already know, keep short accounts with God so as not to grieve him (4:30; 1 John 1:9), do not quench his promptings (1 Thessalonians 5:19), stop numbing your inner life with substitutes, and join God’s people in worship.

How would I know? Paul does not send you inward to check your feelings. He gives the test himself in the next three verses, and it is all outward: Is there song in you? Is there thanksgiving, always and for everything? Are you submitting to others, which is the least likely product of any counterfeit filling in the world? That is why the comparison with drunkenness fits. Nobody has to be told when a man is drunk: it shows in how he speaks and how he treats people. The other influence should be just as visible. The Spirit does not fill people to make them more impressive or dominant, but more like servants. If you want to know which is filling you, ask the people who live with you.

Should I expect to feel something when I am filled with the Spirit? Sometimes, but feelings are not the test. At times God gives a strong sense of his nearness: joy in worship, a sudden settled assurance, sweetness in prayer or in reading Scripture, a peace in a crisis that you know you did not produce (Romans 5:5; 1 Peter 1:8). Receive those with thanks. But the filled life is just as real on the grey days, when you obey without any glow and keep loving a difficult person out of plain faithfulness. When the believers in Acts 4:31 were filled, what followed was not a sensation but boldness to speak the word. So do not chase experiences, and do not doubt the Spirit’s work because you feel flat. Feelings follow sleep, health and temperament; the fruit Paul names follows the Spirit.

Where Christians differ: is the filling a second blessing? Some Pentecostal and charismatic teaching links being filled with a second experience after conversion, often called the baptism in the Spirit and marked by speaking in tongues. Verdict: every believer is indwelt and sealed by the Spirit from conversion (1:13; Romans 8:9; 1 Corinthians 12:13). Being filled is the ongoing life of a Spirit-governed believer, nourished by the word and shown in the fruits that follow (vv. 19–21). Believers may be filled afresh many times, as the apostles were (Acts 2:4; 4:31), and God may grant times of special strength; but no Christian is a second-class believer without the Spirit.

What it does not mean. Not a ban on wine, which Scripture treats as God’s gift: wine to gladden the heart of man (Psalm 104:15). Jesus made wine at Cana (John 2:1–11), and Paul told Timothy to take a little for his health (1 Timothy 5:23). The sin is being controlled by it. But freedom has limits: a Christian should not drink in a way that harms himself or causes a brother to stumble (Romans 14:21), and some, for their own weakness, their family or their witness, wisely choose not to drink at all. Nor does it mean that a Spirit-filled person is emotional, loud or ecstatic; the marks Paul gives are worship, gratitude and humility. The Spirit-filled life is not marked by extraordinary experiences, but by an ordinary life made extraordinary from within.

Where is the line between drinking and being drunk? It is crossed well before you are falling over. Drunkenness begins when drink starts to take the controls: when your judgement, your speech or your restraint is no longer fully your own. An honest test is whether you would say, do and drive exactly as you would sober. If you drink in order to feel the loosening, to unwind by switching yourself partly off, you are already asking wine to do what Paul says the Spirit does. Watch, too, for dependence: needing a drink to get through an evening, hiding how much you have had, being irritable without it. Those are signs to stop altogether and to tell someone. And the same principle reaches beyond alcohol to anything taken to alter the mind for pleasure, recreational drugs included: your mind is meant to be governed by the Spirit, not handed over to a substance.

In a sentence. Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to wild, wasted living; instead, keep on being filled with the Spirit,

For worship. The Holy Spirit is no force to be poured from a jar. He is the Lord and Giver of life, God himself, who has come to live in ordinary believers and fill them with his own presence. Wine promised the Ephesians a counterfeit nearness to their god; the true God gives himself. Praise the risen Christ who, exalted at the right hand of the Father, poured out the Spirit on his church (Acts 2:33), and praise the Spirit, who blows where he wills and never fails to fill those he has sealed.

verseByVerse.quote: addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart, giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart, giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,

The first sign of the Spirit’s filling. Not spectacular experiences, but singing, thanksgiving and submission (vv. 19–21). In Greek these are all participles flowing from “be filled”: they are what being filled with the Spirit looks like.

Addressing one another. Singing is not only to God but to each other: teaching and admonishing one another (Colossians 3:16). Sunday singing is not a room of individuals each having a private moment with God. Which is why the congregation matters so much to the man in the third row who could not have told you one true thing about God that morning. His marriage is coming apart, or he buried someone on Tuesday, and the words will not come out of him. He does not have to produce them. They are being sung over him by people who can manage it this week, and he is carried on a sound he had no strength to make. And think of your worst week, and what came to you at three in the morning. For most people it is not a paragraph from a sermon, but a line they have sung a hundred times without paying much attention, arriving with the tune attached and carrying truth into a mind too tired to reason. What you sing is what you will believe when you cannot think.

Psalms, hymns and spiritual songs. Probably the psalms of the Old Testament, hymns of praise to God and Christ, and other songs prompted by the Spirit. Paul does not define the terms or legislate the repertoire; what interests him is the direction the singing travels: to one another, and to the Lord.

Where Christians differ: psalms only, and instruments? Some Reformed churches sing only the biblical Psalms (exclusive psalmody), reading all three words as kinds of psalm, and it is a serious position: all three words appear in the Greek Old Testament’s own psalm headings. Some also sing without instruments, holding that the New Testament gives no warrant for them in worship. Verdict: the Psalms deserve a far larger place in our worship, but Scripture-filled hymns are also fitting: the New Testament itself contains Christian songs about Christ (5:14; Philippians 2:6–11; Revelation 5:9–10). And instruments are a help to singing, not a substitute for it; the Psalms call God’s people to praise him with lute and harp (Psalm 150:3), and nothing in the New Testament withdraws that.

Singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart. The word for making melody (psallō) first meant to pluck a string, and the instrument Paul names is not in your hands. It is you. If you have a poor voice, or were once told you cannot sing and have believed it ever since, the Lord is listening to the instrument, and yours is in tune. Nobody is disqualified by his larynx. But “with your heart” is not permission to stand in silence and call it inward worship; the other half of the verse needs someone to hear you.

Always and for everything. The hardest words in the sentence. Not only in all circumstances, as Paul puts it elsewhere (1 Thessalonians 5:18), but for all things, and anyone who has buried a child or sat with a scan result may stop and ask whether it can mean what it says. It does not mean calling evil good. Scripture never asks you to call a tumour a blessing or a betrayal a gift; God calls evil evil, and he is against it. Nor does it mean grief is a failure of faith. The same Bible contains a Psalter in which about a third of the songs are complaints, and God put how long, O LORD? into the church’s hymnbook permanently. Thanksgiving does not suppress lament; they live in the same Bible, often in the same chapter.

To God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Here is what makes it possible. Thanks is given to a Father, not to fate or a process, and this letter has told you what kind: one who chose you before the world began (1:4) and adopted you at the cost of his Son (1:5). You are not asked to believe that everything that happens is good, but that nothing reaches you except through that Father’s hands, and that he can take what was meant to destroy you and make it serve you. We know that for those who love God all things work together for good (Romans 8:28): not that we feel it, or see it, but know it, which is something you can still say with a wet face. And “in the name of” Jesus is not a password that unlocks God’s attention. A name stands for the whole person. We give thanks through Christ as our mediator, on his authority as children admitted by his invitation, and in line with his character and purposes (John 16:24; Hebrews 13:15). By the Spirit, through the Son, to the Father.

What it does not mean. Job, having lost his property and ten children in one day, fell on the ground and worshipped: the LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD (Job 1:21). Read it closely. He does not bless the loss, then or ever, though the book gives him forty more chapters to do so. He blesses the Name. Not gratitude for the wreckage, but gratitude, in the wreckage, to a Father who has not moved. And this verse describes what a Spirit-filled life overflows into; it was never meant to be handed to a grieving person as an instruction across a hospital bed. If you cannot do it today, you have not failed the verse. Fruit is not produced by being demanded.

In a sentence. speaking to one another with psalms, hymns and songs from the Spirit, singing and making music from your heart to the Lord, and always giving thanks to God the Father for everything, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,

On a Tuesday. If “thank you for this” is beyond you, take a smaller step: thank you that you are still my Father in this. That is not a lesser thanksgiving; it is the same one offered from further back, and it is where most of us have to start. Christians who have walked far with God are often grateful, twenty years on, for things they could only weep over at the time.

For worship. The Father to whom we give thanks has never once left his throne or withdrawn his love, whatever the night has brought. Adore the God who gave his people a hymnbook that holds both praise and lament, and who listens to every heart he has tuned. Sing to the Lord Jesus, who sang a hymn with his friends on the night he was betrayed (Mark 14:26), and who now leads the praise of his brothers in the midst of the congregation (Hebrews 2:12). Through him our halting songs rise to the Father, accepted and beloved.

verseByVerse.quote: submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.

The hinge. Verse 21 completes the description of being filled with the Spirit and introduces the household sections (5:22–6:9): wives and husbands, children and parents, slaves and masters. “Submitting” is the last of a chain of participles hanging from the one command of v. 18: be filled, speaking, singing, giving thanks, submitting. Two of them are what we would expect, song and thanksgiving. The other two are about how you treat the person beside you. And in Greek v. 22 has no verb of its own; it borrows “submit” from v. 21. So the marriage passage is not a separate block that can be lifted out and applied on its own. It is welded to the filling of the Spirit, and the moment it is detached from that it is being misused. Nobody here is told to be filled with the Spirit so that he may govern his household. They are told that a household ordered like this is what the filling looks like when it reaches the kitchen.

Submitting. “Submitting” (hypotassomenoi) was originally a military word: to arrange under, to take one’s ordered place, to put another’s good and rightful leadership before one’s own way. Two things must be said about it, and neither may be dropped. First, it says nothing about worth. The Son submits to the Father, and will hand over the kingdom to him at the end (1 Corinthians 15:28), and no Christian has ever concluded that the Son is a lesser God. Equal in being, ordered in relation: the pattern is drawn from the life of God himself. Second, it is voluntary, in the middle voice: chosen, not forced. Submission is something a person gives; nobody can submit someone else. No one in this passage is told to make others submit. A man who sets out to make another submit has already made it impossible, and shown that what he wants is not submission but control.

To one another. “One another” (allēlois). This is where the debate lies.

Where Christians differ: mutual submission? Egalitarians (for example Gordon Fee) read “submitting to one another” as fully mutual: every believer submits to every other in the same way, so that husbands submit to wives as wives submit to husbands, and there are no distinct roles of leading and following in marriage. Complementarians (for example John Stott in his own nuanced way, and Wayne Grudem more strongly) point out that the verses that follow specify who submits to whom: wives to husbands, children to parents, slaves to masters, never the reverse, and husbands are told not to submit but to love. They note that the verb, wherever it is used in the New Testament, describes submitting to someone in a position of authority (Luke 2:51; Romans 13:1; 1 Peter 2:13), and that “one another” can mean some to others, as when Revelation 6:4 says people slay one another (not everyone killing everyone). Verdict: the complementarian reading, with its truth fully honoured. Verse 21 sets the spirit in which all Christians relate: humble, other-centred, putting others first (Philippians 2:3–4). Husbands, parents and masters are not exempt from that spirit. But within that humility, the following verses show that God has given a particular order in marriage and family, where some lead and others follow, and both serve. Mutual humility does not erase distinct roles, any more than Christ’s humility erased his headship.

What every first reader would have felt. The household codes of the ancient moralists addressed the head of the house about managing his wife, children and slaves. Paul speaks to the wife, the child and the slave first, directly, as responsible people who answer to Christ themselves. And when he turns to the one holding the power, he asks more of him, not less: the husband gets three times as many lines as the wife, and what he is commanded is to love as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her. Whatever else is true of the structure, the weight of cost in it runs downhill towards the strong.

Out of reverence for Christ. Literally in the fear of Christ. It is both the engine and the limit. The engine: you do not yield because the other person has earned it or will appreciate it, but before the face of the Lord who yielded everything. The limit: because the reverence is for Christ, it can never require what Christ forbids. A submission that would demand you sin has cut the very cord it hangs on. Every relationship in the household is lived before Christ.

What it does not mean. Not that anyone must submit to sin, cruelty or abuse; submission to people is always limited by obedience to God (Acts 5:29). Nor that leaders are above others in worth. Every believer is equally a child of God and equally loved.

In a sentence. and putting yourselves under one another out of reverence for Christ.

On a Tuesday. The test of whether this is real in you is not what you do when submission is deserved, but what you do when it is not.

For worship. The order in this verse is drawn from the life of God himself. Adore the eternal Son, equal with the Father in glory, who delights to do his Father’s will and will one day hand the kingdom to him, not as a lesser God but as the perfect Son. And worship the Lord who, holding all authority, took a towel and knelt. The strong one in this story has always carried the heaviest cost. Every humble yielding in his church is a small reflection of the Christ who emptied himself and became obedient to the point of death (Philippians 2:7–8).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wives should submit to their own husbands as to the Lord, for the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is head of the church, his body, of which he is the Saviour; as the church submits to Christ, so wives should to their husbands in everything. Husbands must love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself for her, to make her holy, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word, and to present her to himself radiant, without stain or wrinkle, holy and blameless. Husbands should love their wives as their own bodies; whoever loves his wife loves himself, for no one hates his own body but feeds and cares for it, as Christ does the church, for we are members of his body. That is why a man leaves his parents and is united to his wife, and the two become one flesh. This is a profound mystery about Christ and the church. But each husband must love his wife as himself, and the wife must respect her husband.
verseByVerse.theology:
Marriage, Headship, and the Gospel Mystery

Ephesians 5:22–33 is the most theologically freighted passage on marriage in all of Scripture. Its central claim — that marriage is a living image of the relationship between Christ and the church — elevates the institution beyond any merely human social arrangement. Marriage is a sign. Its structure (the husband's headship, the wife's willing embrace of it) is not arbitrary or culturally conditioned; it images something real and eternal: the self-giving authority of Christ over his church, and the church's joyful, trusting response to her Lord.

The husband's headship is defined entirely by the cross: “as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (v.25). Any interpretation of headship that does not immediately move to sacrifice and self-giving has misread the passage. The head of the church is the one who died for it, who washed it, who nourishes and cherishes it (v.29). The husband who exercises headship in this mode is not dominating but descending — following the pattern of the One who “came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:28).

The wife's calling — to “submit to your own husband, as to the Lord” (v.22) — is the free, willing, graced response of a woman who is secure in Christ. It is not coerced compliance; it is the image of the church's joyful response to her loving Lord. This mutual imaging of the gospel — husband as Christ, wife as church — requires both partners to draw from wells deeper than themselves. No man can love his wife as Christ loved the church from his own resources; no woman can embody the church's response to Christ on her own. Both require the same Spirit who filled the community in v.18. Marriage is a Spirit-dependent vocation for both.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In the Greco-Roman world, the husband's authority over his wife was nearly absolute and assumed to be primarily for his benefit. The paterfamilias was the household's lord in every sense. Paul's command for husbands to love their wives sacrificially — to give themselves up for them, to nourish and cherish them as their own bodies — was not a reinforcement of existing cultural norms. It was their radical subversion. The Roman husband used his authority to be served. The Christian husband was to use his authority to serve. This was not a minor adjustment to the household code; it was a revolution grounded in the cross.

Now: Christian marriage swims against two powerful currents simultaneously. The first is the culture's dismissal of permanent covenant — the reduction of marriage to an expressive partnership that may be dissolved when it no longer meets individual needs. The second is the sometimes shallow version of complementarianism that invokes headship without the cross, demanding submission without offering service. Against both, Ephesians 5 offers the third way: covenant love, shaped by the cross, sustained by the Spirit, oriented toward the other's flourishing, and pointing always beyond itself to the love that holds the universe together. A marriage like this is a miracle — and miracles point to a Miracle Worker.

verseByVerse.quote: Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord.

The setting. Ancient household codes, from Aristotle onward, told wives, children and slaves to obey the head of the household, but addressed only him. Paul speaks first to wives directly, as responsible persons who choose freely before God. That alone was startling.

Wives, submit. The verb is not in the Greek here; it is carried over from v. 21: wives are called to the same posture Paul has just urged on every believer, now applied to their own husbands. To submit is to arrange yourself under, to support and follow his leadership. It is the wife’s own choice, offered to Christ. It is not the husband’s right to demand; Paul never tells husbands to make their wives submit. It speaks of role, never of worth: in Christ there is no male and female as to standing before God (Galatians 3:28), just as the Son submits to the Father without being any less God (1 Corinthians 11:3).

To your own husbands. “Your own” (tois idiois). Not women to men in general, at work, in the street or in the church foyer, but a wife to her husband: one man, the man she made promises to. The instruction is covenantal and has a boundary around it, and the verse has often been stretched far past it.

As to the Lord. Both the motive and the limit. The motive: her submission is ultimately service to Christ, and she offers it because she trusts him. The limit: it never extends to sin, since no husband can ask what the Lord forbids (Acts 5:29).

What submission looks like. In practice it is mostly the texture of ordinary life: not undermining his leadership in front of the children, speaking well of him, and choosing to trust after her voice has been fully heard. She is no silent, opinionless presence; she brings her full wisdom, gifts and voice, and a good husband depends on it (Proverbs 31:10–31 describes a wife with business, property and authority over a household). Take a real decision. A husband is offered a significant post in another city; the wife is deeply reluctant, because her friendships, her work and her ageing parents are all here. They talk it through honestly, and he still believes they should go. Submission here is not being overruled without a voice. It is choosing to trust his judgement after her concerns have been truly weighed, and not letting the decision harden into a permanent grievance, while he for his part carries its weight and owes her every sacrifice to make it work. Godly submission is not weakness; it is strength placed in service.

And if he is not leading? The relocation example assumes a husband who listens and carries the cost. Many women are not in that marriage. They are married to a man who is not abusive, but spiritually passive or self-absorbed: who will not pray with her, leaves every hard decision to drift, and is present in the house but absent from the marriage.
