Scripture does not pretend she does not exist. Peter writes to exactly this woman: even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives (1 Peter 3:1–2). He does not tell her that her position is hopeless or that her only options are nagging and despair. He tells her that her steady life has power in it, and that God can use it to reach a man sermons have not reached. That is not a consolation prize; it is a real calling, and a harder one than that given to the wives of good men. And the church should come alongside her and call the husband to his responsibilities.

Common questions. What if her husband is not a believer? Peter tells such wives to submit, so that their husbands may be won by their conduct (1 Peter 3:1–2), but never by joining in sin. What if there is abuse or danger? Then the limit of “as to the Lord” applies: no one is required to submit to violence. A husband who abuses his wife is not exercising headship but violating it catastrophically. A wife in danger should seek safety, report crimes to the authorities, and receive the church’s protection. Using this verse to keep a woman in danger is a terrible misuse of Scripture.

Does abuse mean only physical violence? No. Abuse is a pattern of control through fear, and it can be carried on without a blow: threats and intimidation, constant belittling, cutting a wife off from friends and family, controlling all the money so that she cannot act, sexual coercion, checking her every move. These are not the hard edges of headship but its opposite, because Christ never rules his bride by fear. A wife who recognises this pattern should tell someone outside the home: a trusted friend, a pastor, and where there is danger, the police or a domestic abuse helpline. Separating for safety is right, and no one should tell her that leaving to protect herself or her children breaks her vows; he has broken them. Whether such a marriage may finally be ended is a question for the elders to weigh with her, carefully, in the light of Scripture’s teaching on desertion (Westminster 24.6).

Where Christians differ: is this cultural? Egalitarians see the instruction as a first-century cultural arrangement, like slavery, which the gospel eventually set aside. Verdict: the complementarian view. Paul does not ground the wife’s submission in culture but in two things that do not change: creation (v. 31, Genesis 2:24; compare 1 Corinthians 11:8–9; 1 Timothy 2:13) and Christ’s relationship with the church (vv. 23–24). Slavery is regulated in Scripture but never grounded in creation or in Christ. So the pattern holds today; it is to be lived with gladness and humility, and never used as a weapon.

What it does not mean. Not inferiority: husband and wife are equal in worth, equally made in God’s image and equal heirs of the grace of life (Genesis 1:27; 1 Peter 3:7). Not silence, passivity or giving up her judgement or conscience. Not submission of all women to all men. And not a burden uniquely hers. It comes right after the call to all believers to submit to one another (v. 21), and is followed by the far heavier charge to the husband (v. 25). If the wife is called to submit, the husband is called to die.

In a sentence. Wives, put yourselves under your own husbands, as you do to the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Submission is easy to counterfeit, and the counterfeit is compliance with the heart withheld: doing what was decided while making sure he knows what it cost you, or going along with it and then being conspicuously unhelpful about the consequences. The question is not whether you did what was agreed, but whether you did it in a way that left him freer or heavier. And it can be done even when he has not earned it, because you are trusting the Lord who ordered this, who sees exactly what it is costing you, and who has never once asked a wife to submit to a man without himself standing behind her.

For worship. Behind every wife in this verse stands the Lord to whom she offers her trust, and he is worthy of it. Christ is the true Husband of his people: he never demands what he has not first given, never rules by fear, and never asks anything of his bride that he has not paid for with his own blood. Adore him as the one who sees every hidden cost, who defends the oppressed and breaks the arm of the wicked (Psalm 10:15), and whose love for his bride is safe in every season. No human husband is her final security; he is.

verseByVerse.quote: For the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church, his body, and is himself its Savior. Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church, his body, and is himself its Savior. Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands.

For the husband is the head of the wife. “Head” (kephalē). What does Paul mean by head?

Where Christians differ: does head mean authority or source? Some egalitarian scholars (for example Catherine Kroeger and Gordon Fee) argue that in Greek kephalē often meant source, like the head of a river, so that the husband is the source of the wife (as Eve came from Adam), not her authority. Others (for example Joseph Fitzmyer and Wayne Grudem) studied the ancient uses and found that when kephalē is used of a person in relation to others, it regularly means one in authority or prominence. Verdict: authority, exercised as Christ exercises it. In this very letter Paul uses head of Christ in a way that clearly means authority: God put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things (1:22). And here the wife’s response to the head is to submit (v. 24), which fits authority, not source. Yet Paul also uses head for the one who nourishes and gives growth to the body (4:15–16; v. 29). Christ’s headship includes both: he rules his church and he gives it life. The husband’s headship is meant to mirror both. And Paul does not leave the word to be defined from a dictionary. He defines it himself, in the next two verses, with a cross.

Even as Christ is the head of the church, his body. The husband’s headship is defined by Christ’s, not by the world’s idea of power. And the analogy both grants authority and radically reshapes it. It means taking ultimate responsibility. The head carries the weight of the household, and when things go wrong he does not look for someone to blame but asks what he failed to do. Adam’s sin was that he stood by, silent and passive, when he should have led (Genesis 3:6), and God came looking for him first (Genesis 3:9). It means starting love instead of waiting for it, as Christ loved while we were still enemies (Romans 5:8), and leading the spiritual life of the home in prayer and the word, instead of handing it to his wife as her department. And it means that decisions are shaped by service: not, I lead, therefore I decide, but, I lead, therefore I bear the cost of this for her sake.

And is himself its Saviour. “Saviour” (sōtēr). Here Paul marks the limit of his own picture. The husband is head as Christ is head. He is not Saviour, and the picture stretches no further. He cannot atone for anything, forgive sin, or be the ground of her standing before God. Christ alone fills that place. And that diagnoses two common ways marriages go wrong, mirror images of each other. There is the wife who has made her husband her saviour, who needs him to be the one who finally makes her feel secure, valuable and at peace, and so finds him failing at a job he was never given. No man can carry the weight of another soul’s ultimate hope; he will either collapse under it or resent the one holding him to it. And there is the husband who has taken that role on, who thinks he must fix her and be her sufficiency, and ends up exhausted or controlling. This clause frees them both. He is to love her as Christ loved the church. He is not to be Christ to her, and she must not ask it of him.

Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit. The church submits to Christ willingly, trustingly and gladly, because his leadership is good. And notice the order. The church does not submit to Christ in order to secure his love, nor to a Lord whose intentions are unproven. She submits to one who has already given himself for her entirely. The response comes after the demonstration and rests on it. So a husband who wants the response while withholding its ground has turned the very picture he is quoting upside down. A man who has to remind his wife that he is the head is like a man who has to remind people that he is funny. Christ never once told the church to submit to him; he washed feet (John 13:5) and went to a cross, and the church has been following him ever since. Headship like that does not need to be asserted, because it is visible.

In everything. In every area of married life, so that she does not treat some parts of life as outside the marriage. Still limited by “as to the Lord” (v. 22): never in sin, since no husband has authority to command what Christ forbids. The church submits to Christ, not to anyone who contradicts him.

What it does not mean. Not that the husband rules his wife as a master rules a servant, or that she has no voice. Godly headship listens, consults, serves and takes responsibility. It is not spiritual superiority: she may be the more mature and the more discerning. A husband who hears her honest disagreement as a threat is protecting his ego, not exercising headship; Christ is not threatened by the church’s questions but invites them. And it is not a place of comfort but of cost. If he is resting while she is exhausted, pursuing his own interests while hers go unmet, he is not leading; he is being served. A husband who uses this verse to dominate has missed the word Saviour.

What should I do if my wife will not follow my lead? Not try to make her. Nothing in this passage tells a husband to secure his wife’s submission; that is her obedience to Christ, not your project. Your command is to love her as Christ loved the church, and it has no condition attached (v. 25). So begin with yourself. Ask her honestly, and listen without defending yourself: has my leading been safe to follow? Have I listened, carried the cost, kept my word, prayed with you? A wife’s resistance has often been taught by years of decisions made carelessly or selfishly. Where you have failed, own it specifically. Then keep leading gently in ordinary things: in prayer, in kindness, in taking responsibility. If the deadlock continues, ask your pastor or a wise older couple to help you both. Leadership that is truly Christlike is rarely refused for long.

In a sentence. For the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is the head of the church, his body, of which he is the Saviour; so as the church submits to Christ, wives should also submit to their husbands in everything.

On a Tuesday. Picture a husband, decent and hard-working, who provides well and is rarely harsh, but is largely absent from the spiritual life of the home. He does not pray with his wife or lead the children, and when she speaks of her loneliness he listens for a few minutes and moves on. He holds the position without bearing its cost. Headship as Paul means it would look different: he starts the hard conversation before she has to; he owns his absence as his failure; he begins, awkwardly at first, to pray with her. None of it needs a new personality, only the decision to lead as Christ leads, turning towards her instead of away. It is not a crown to be claimed, but a cross to be carried.

For worship. Christ alone is Saviour, and that one word lifts every marriage off foundations it was never meant to bear. Praise the Head of the church, who did not first demand his bride’s allegiance but laid down his life for her while she was still far from him. His rule gives life: he nourishes and grows his body, and his authority has never once been used for his own comfort. Adore the Lord whose headship is seen in the marks of the nails, and whose people follow him gladly because he went first, all the way to the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her,

Husbands, love. Familiarity has flattened how strange this was. Ancient household codes told husbands how to rule their wives, children and slaves. None told a husband to love his wife as a Saviour gave himself up for her. Marriage was for property, heirs and an orderly household; a wife’s affection was a pleasant extra. The men in the room in Ephesus were braced for the usual instruction about managing their households, and received instead a command none of them had ever heard. And Paul does not say first, lead your wives. He says, love your wives. The leadership is shaped entirely by the love; the authority exists to serve her flourishing, not to assert itself.

Love. Agapaō: self-giving covenant love that seeks the other’s good, not a feeling that comes and goes.

As Christ loved the church. The standard is not other husbands, or what she deserves, but Christ. And ask what the church was like when he gave himself up for her. Paul has already said, and not gently: dead in trespasses and sins, following the prince of the power of the air, by nature children of wrath (2:1–3). That is the bride. He did not find her radiant and decide she was worth it; he gave himself up for her in that condition, and the radiance came afterwards, which is exactly what the next two verses say he is doing. So the order is fixed, and it closes the escape hatch every husband reaches for. The love does not respond to loveliness; it produces it. “When she is easier to live with”, “when she stops doing that”, “when she deserves it”: in this passage these are all arguments for withholding the very thing that would change the situation. Christ did not wait for a bride worth dying for. He died, and so gained one.

Gave himself up for her. The measure is the cross. Headship means going first in sacrifice: his comfort, preferences, time and if necessary his life for her good. And this standard is meant for an ordinary week. It looks like a husband who notices what she carries and moves to relieve it without being asked: she has had a hard week with the children, and he takes over the evening without comment, because Christ did not wait for the church to state her need before he acted. It looks like giving up his preferences cheerfully, without the pointed silence that makes her feel guilty for asking. It looks like taking her walk with God seriously: praying for her, asking how she is doing with God. It looks like choosing her above career and comfort when they truly conflict. And it looks like asking forgiveness specifically and promptly: I was unkind this morning, and I am sorry; will you forgive me? with no “but you also”. Repeated over years, that small act builds a marriage in which she knows she is safe with him.

For whom did Christ die? Paul says he gave himself for the church, his bride: a pointer to the particular, effective love of the atonement (Acts 20:28; John 10:11).

Where the power comes from. A husband who has read this far honestly is in a hard place. If you have been measuring yourself against Calvary, the reasonable conclusion is despair, and it is half right: you cannot love like this, and the standard is not lowered. But this command does not stand on its own feet. The whole household code grows out of one command seven verses earlier: be filled with the Spirit (v. 18). This is the same filled life reaching the home. It is fruit, not an entrance requirement. So the question for a husband who keeps failing is not chiefly, how do I try harder? He has tried, in bursts, for years, and the bursts are the problem. The question is whether the man who comes through the door at six is being filled, because a marriage is lived largely on the overflow, and nothing pours out of a life it was never poured into. A husband whose praying has dried up and whose Bible has been shut for months will find that the tenderness he truly intends is simply not available at seven on a Thursday evening when he is tired and she says the wrong thing. And there is comfort here. If this love were a matter of temperament, naturally warm men would have an advantage no one else could make up. It is not temperament; it is fruit, and fruit grows on a branch because the branch is attached (John 15:4–5). The husband who grew up in a house where nobody said anything kind, and has no model for this, is not disqualified. He is asked to stay attached, which he can do.

What it does not mean. Not that a husband gives his wife whatever she wants. Christ’s love aims at his bride’s holiness and good (v. 26).

What if I no longer feel any love for my wife? Then you are in exactly the place this command was written for. Paul does not tell you to feel love; he tells you to love, and the verb is about what you do: give yourself up for her good. Feelings very often follow actions rather than lead them. So begin doing what love does: the kindness you stopped bothering with, the attention, the apology, the evening given to her. Pray for her daily by name, and ask God to restore what has cooled. Look honestly at what may be draining your affection: resentment never dealt with, exhaustion, or attention given elsewhere, a screen included. Many couples who once felt nothing have found warmth return after a season of patient, deliberate love. And if you cannot find a way forward, ask for help early, from your pastor or a wise counsellor, not after the walls have gone up.

In a sentence. Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her,

On a Tuesday. The standard is not “provide” but “gave himself up”. Providing can be done without giving up anything a man wanted, and long hours can be an escape dressed as devotion. So name one thing, an ambition, a friendship, a hobby, a Saturday, a picture of the life you assumed you would have, that you gave up in the last year for her flourishing instead of your own. If nothing comes to mind, the verb in this verse is not yet working in your marriage, however well the household runs.

For worship. Here is the love that every human love only shadows. Christ did not find his bride lovely and then die for her; he loved her when she was dead in sin, gave himself up for her, and so made her lovely. Adore the Bridegroom who went first in sacrifice, who counted no cost too great and kept no score, and who laid down his life for the particular people his Father had given him (John 17:6). Whatever any marriage on earth is, or fails to be, the church has a Husband whose love has never once faltered.

verseByVerse.quote: that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish.

That he might sanctify her. “Sanctify” (hagiasē): make holy, set apart for him. Christ’s love does not leave us as we are; it aims at our holiness, now in part and perfectly at the end.

Having cleansed her. Washed from sin’s guilt and stain.

By the washing of water with the word. “Washing” (loutrō, bath). There are two backgrounds. A Jewish bride took a ritual bath before her wedding, and in Ezekiel 16:8–14 God washes his bride Israel and adorns her. And early Christians thought of baptism, the washing with water that marks entry into Christ. “With the word” (en rhēmati): with a spoken word, probably the gospel promise preached and believed, or the word spoken at baptism.

Where Christians differ: does baptism itself cleanse? Roman Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran traditions understand verses like this to teach that baptism itself, as God’s act, washes away sin and gives new birth (baptismal regeneration). Verdict: Christ is the one who cleanses, and he does it by his word, the gospel received by faith. Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you (John 15:3); God cleansed the Gentiles’ hearts by faith (Acts 15:9); we have been born again through the living and abiding word of God (1 Peter 1:23). That is why Simon Magus could be baptised and still be in the gall of bitterness (Acts 8:13, 23), while the thief on the cross, never baptised, went that day to paradise (Luke 23:43). Baptism is the visible sign and seal of the cleansing, not its cause (1 Peter 3:21: not the removal of dirt, but the appeal of a good conscience). To collapse the two is to trust the picture instead of the gospel it pictures.

So that he might present the church to himself in splendour. “Present” (parastēsē). In an ancient wedding, the bride was prepared by others and then presented to the groom, who received what they had made ready. Here the groom does both. He prepares her himself, and he receives her himself: not presented to the Father, nor to the watching world, but to himself. That tells you what all this labour is for. He is not repairing a damaged asset out of duty. He is getting her ready because he wants her. It was for the joy that was set before him that he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2). You are looking at the joy.

Without spot or wrinkle or any such thing. Not the same defect twice. A spot is a stain: something that landed on her from outside, the mark of what has soiled her. A wrinkle is not contamination at all; it is what comes with time, the mark of wear and years. He removes both. The promise is larger than cleaning. Everything that has stained her, and everything that has merely aged and tired her, is dealt with together: the guilt and the exhaustion (Revelation 19:7–8; 21:2, 5). That is worth hearing if what you feel about yourself is less like dirtiness and more like fatigue. He is not only washing his bride; he is making her new.

That she might be holy and without blemish. The same goal as 1:4: what God chose us for, Christ brings to completion.

For husbands. A husband cannot sanctify his wife; only Christ does. But his love aims the same way: at her growth in Christ. Think of a wife who grew up under a critical father, who dismisses her own gifts and struggles to believe she is truly loved by God. A husband loving as Christ loves makes it his slow work to speak truth into exactly those places: when she waves off a gift, he names specifically what he sees; when she doubts God’s love after a hard season, he opens Scripture with her, not to win an argument but to wash her with the word; he prays for her by name, against the particular lies she has told him she believes. He is not her therapist or her pastor. He is her husband.

What it does not mean. Not that the husband is his wife’s spiritual improver, who notices her faults, corrects her theology and holds up the standard until she rises to it. This passage has been misused that way, and it will not carry it. Look at how Christ does it: he gave himself up for her. The sanctifying is the purpose; the cross is the method. He does not cleanse his bride by listing her blemishes, but at his own expense. Nor is the church already spotless; she is being cleansed. And a husband is not responsible for his wife’s sins; each answers to God. But he is responsible for loving her towards holiness.

In a sentence. to make her holy, cleansing her by washing her with water through the word, so that he could present her to himself as a radiant church, without stain or wrinkle or any other flaw, but holy and blameless.

On a Tuesday. Husbands: when you think of your wife’s growth, which list comes more readily, the things that need to change in her, or the things it will cost you to help her flourish? Every husband has the first list. This passage is about the second. A wife is rarely made radiant by being told what is wrong with her. She is often made radiant by being loved at cost by a man who has stopped keeping score.

For worship. Behold the Bridegroom who prepares his bride with his own hands and receives her to himself with joy. He washes away every stain of guilt and smooths every wrinkle of weariness, and he does it not reluctantly but because he wants her. Praise Christ, for the day is coming when the church, long soiled and tired, will stand before him radiant, holy and without blemish, and the marriage supper of the Lamb will begin (Revelation 19:9). What he chose us for before the foundation of the world (1:4), he will finish.
verseByVerse.note: Before a wedding the bride was washed and adorned.

parallels.desc: I bathed you with water

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way husbands should love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the same way husbands should love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself.

In the same way. As Christ loves the church, his body.

As their own bodies. Not as possessions, but as part of himself: husband and wife are one flesh (v. 31). A man does not ignore a pain in his shoulder because he is busy, or tell his own body it is being too sensitive when it signals distress. He attends to it, because it is his. Do the same for your wife. James has been so absorbed in a demanding season at work that he has not noticed Sarah pulling back for three weeks: quieter at dinner, slower to reach for him, carrying something he has not asked about. He tells himself she is fine and he will check in when the pressure eases. He would never apply that reasoning to a pain in his own chest. Her withdrawal is his signal; her heaviness is his concern.

He who loves his wife loves himself. In a sense, they share one life. To harm her is to harm himself; to care for her is to care for himself. And notice how shrewd Paul is. He nowhere commands a man to love himself; he assumes it and builds on it. Self-love is the one kind of love that needs no instruction, no reminders and no accountability. Nobody has ever had to be urged to notice his own hunger. So the force of the command is not, rise to a standard beyond you. It is: you already have exactly the competence required, and you use it a hundred times a day in one direction. Turn it round.

Two measures, one instruction. Why does Paul give two standards? In verse 25 it is Christ’s love for the church, impossibly high. Here it is a man’s care for his own body, embarrassingly close to hand. But they are one measure. The church is Christ’s body (1:23; 4:12; 5:30), so when Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, he was loving his own body. The towering standard and the homely one are the same instruction seen from two ends.

What it does not mean. Not that self-love is the goal or should be cultivated. Paul assumes we already care for ourselves (v. 29) and turns that natural instinct outward to the wife. And for the man who does not love himself at all, who neglects his body and speaks of himself with contempt, this does not mean his wife should expect the same neglect. Paul has already given the deeper measure, which does not depend on self-regard: love her as Christ loved the church. The cross is the measure when the shortcut fails.

In a sentence. In the same way husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies; the man who loves his wife loves himself.

On a Tuesday. Do not ask whether you love your wife; every husband says yes. Ask this: if her needs received the same automatic, unprompted, unresented attention that your own hunger, tiredness and pain receive, would she be better cared for than she is now? Most of us know the answer within a second, and the second is uncomfortable.

For worship. Christ never neglects his own body. Every ache in his church, every hidden heaviness and unspoken sorrow, he feels as his own; when Saul persecuted the church, the risen Lord asked why Saul was persecuting him (Acts 9:4). Adore the Head who cares for his members without being prompted and without resentment, who notices the quiet ones drawing back and draws near to them. The towering love of the cross and the tender care of a body are one love in him, and it is set on his people for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church, because we are members of his body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church, because we are members of his body.

No one ever hated his own flesh. In ordinary life, people feed, protect and care for their bodies without thinking. And notice what Paul does not say. He does not say, do not hate her. He is not writing to men trying to destroy their wives. He is writing to men who are simply not feeding them, and that is how most marriages actually fail: not in an atrocity, but in a slow drop in temperature neither could put a date on. Asked what is wrong, she cannot name one thing. He has never raised his hand or his voice, never been unfaithful; he works hard and the bills are paid. She would sound ridiculous complaining about him. And she has been cold for four years. Nothing was done to her; something was never done for her.

Nourishes and cherishes. Two verbs, and neither is heroic. To nourish (ektrephō) is to feed something up to full growth, the word Paul uses for fathers bringing up their children (6:4): twenty years of meals, no single one of which looks like love. To cherish (thalpō) is literally to keep warm: the Greek Old Testament uses it of a mother bird settled on her nest (Deuteronomy 22:6), and Paul of himself among the Thessalonians, like a nursing mother taking care of her own children (1 Thessalonians 2:7). Stripped of decoration, the charge to a husband is this: feed her, and keep her warm.

Just as Christ does the church. And check the tense. Not that Christ nourished and cherished the church, but does: present and continuous. The giving up of himself is finished and will never be repeated (v. 25); the feeding and warming have not stopped for a single day since. He is not a husband who did something magnificent once and has been coasting on it ever since. While you read this sentence, he is doing it, through his word and at his table, and with his love. And that answers the ache verse 27 may have opened. There the church was presented in splendour, without spot or wrinkle. Then you look at the church you actually belong to, and at yourself, and it is spots and creases everywhere. Has he changed his mind? No. Verse 27 is the presentation, and it is future. Verse 29 is what he is doing in the meantime, and it is present. He is not standing at the far end of the aisle with his arms folded, waiting for you to make yourself presentable. He is at the near end, feeding you.

Members of his body. The word (melē) is the ordinary word for limbs and organs: not subjects of Christ, or admirers, or only servants, but parts of him. Saul of Tarsus never touched Jesus of Nazareth, and was knocked flat on the road by a voice asking, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4). He had been arresting Christians, and the Christ of heaven called it an attack on himself. That is not sentiment; it is anatomy. Touch the hand, and the head says, me. And turned over, it is the safest thing in the letter. A body does not amputate a part for being weak; a broken arm gets more of the body’s attention than a sound one (1 Corinthians 12:22–26). For Christ to neglect you, he would have to neglect himself, and this verse has just told you no one has ever done that.

Textual note. Later manuscripts add “of his flesh and of his bones” (as in the King James Version), from Genesis 2:23. Verdict: probably not original.

In a sentence. After all, no one ever hated their own body, but they feed and care for it, just as Christ does the church, for we are parts of his body.

On a Tuesday. Two verbs, two tests. Is she growing, not coping, but growing: more alive, more herself, more at home with God than the year you married? Name your part in it. And the faster test that cannot be cheated: what happens to her face in the two seconds after you come through the door, before she has decided what to say? Warmth is measured at the door. And to the wife reading this as a list of what she does not have: warmth is not an extra. God commanded it, so the wanting of it is not weakness; say so plainly to someone, and if there is more than coldness in your home, tell someone who can act. But you have not gone unfed. Christ has been feeding you all along, in ways you may have filed under other names.

For worship. Our Lord is not a Bridegroom who did one great thing and then grew distant. Today, and every day since he rose, he feeds his people with his word, warms them with his love and spreads his table for them. Adore the Christ whose care is in the present tense, who treats every member of his church as part of himself and gives the weakest the most attention. He has never once grown cold towards his bride, and he never will, for he would sooner forget his own body than forget the least of his people.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.

Therefore. Paul has just said we are members of Christ’s body (v. 30), and to prove it he quotes a verse about a man, a woman and a wedding. The logic only works if Genesis 2:24 was about Christ and the church all along, which he says outright in the next verse. Marriage is not a human arrangement to which the church later attached a religious illustration. It was built, in the week the world was made, as a working model of something that had not yet happened.

Genesis 2:24. The foundational text on marriage, spoken before the fall, and quoted by Jesus when asked about divorce (Matthew 19:4–6). And look who first heard it. Adam had no father and no mother; he is the one man in history with nothing to leave. So this is not a description of his circumstances but law for everyone after him, given before there was a single marriage to regulate, and before there was any sin to correct. Marriage is not a repair issued after things went wrong. It is original equipment, delivered with its instructions.

Leave his father and mother. A new primary loyalty. Parents are still honoured, but the marriage now comes first. It is not mainly about distance. A man can live four hundred miles from his mother and still be run by her, and the wife always knows: a decision made together on Tuesday quietly reopened on the phone on Wednesday; eleven years of Christmases arranged by someone else; a man who defends his wife to nobody and explains her to everybody. And it runs the other way: parents can refuse to release as firmly as sons refuse to leave.

Hold fast. Literally to be glued (proskollaō). Glue two boards properly and leave them overnight, then try to separate them. They do not come apart at the join; the join is now the strongest part. The wood tears, and each board comes away carrying fibre from the other. That explains what a contractual view of marriage never can: why the ending of a marriage does not feel like the ending of an agreement. To anyone who has been through divorce or been left, this is not another sentence passed on you. It explains the shape of the wound. You were not weak when it went on hurting long after everyone assumed you should have recovered. Something God joins had been pulled apart, and it tore. Where the fault was yours, there is complete forgiveness in Christ; where it was done to you, God himself calls such tearing apart violence (Malachi 2:16). Neither his love for you nor his use of you is reduced by one degree.

The two shall become one flesh. A union of the whole life, physical, relational, covenantal and exclusive, sealed in sexual union. Physical: which is why even union with a prostitute makes one flesh (1 Corinthians 6:16), and does damage because it signs what is not there. Relational: two lives intertwined, so that his failure touches her and her suffering is his. Covenantal: a bond witnessed by God (Malachi 2:14), not dissolved by distance or fading feeling. Exclusive: one man and one woman, a union that cannot be shared without being destroyed. Yet the two do not cease to be two; each keeps his or her own gifts and walk with God, and a marriage in which one swallows the other distorts the union. And it is not achieved instantly: the covenant is made at the wedding, but the deep knowing is built over years of choosing each other.

Fulfilled before it was obeyed. Once Paul has told us who it is about, every clause has a second face. A man shall leave his father: and the Son of God did, not ceasing to be one with the Father, but leaving the glory he had before the world existed: I came from the Father and have come into the world (John 16:28; 17:5). And hold fast to his wife: he has held fast to a bride who has let go of him a thousand times, and never once loosened his grip. And the two shall become one flesh: he took flesh to do it. That is why Christian marriage is not finally an achievement to be measured. It is a picture, and the original is holding even in the weeks when the copy is not.

May a marriage ever be ended? God designed it for life: what therefore God has joined together, let not man separate (Matthew 19:6). But Jesus himself allows divorce for sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9), and Paul allows it when an unbelieving spouse deserts (1 Corinthians 7:15). Verdict: in cases of adultery or desertion the innocent party is free to divorce and remarry (Westminster Confession 24.5–6), though reconciliation is better wherever it is possible.

I divorced and remarried on grounds that were not biblical. Should I now leave my present marriage? No. The sin lay in how the earlier marriage was ended, and that sin is to be confessed, and is fully forgiven in Christ (1 John 1:9). But your present marriage is a real marriage, made with vows before God, and breaking it would add a second wrong to the first, not undo it. The law of Moses even forbade a divorced woman who had married again from returning to her first husband (Deuteronomy 24:1–4). So repent honestly of what was wrong, seek to make peace where you can, perhaps with a former spouse or with children who were hurt, and then give yourself wholeheartedly to the marriage you are in. Take any particular questions to your elders. God’s grace was never only for people whose histories are tidy; it was sent for the rest of us.

Where Christians differ: the definition of marriage. Some churches now affirm same-sex marriage. Verdict: the historic Christian view, held with compassion: Scripture defines marriage as the union of one man and one woman, and that pattern is part of its meaning, since it pictures Christ and his church.

In a sentence. That is why a man will leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two will become one flesh.

On a Tuesday. When you and your spouse have decided something and it disappoints your parents, whose disappointment do you actually feel more? And when something happens to you in the middle of a Thursday, who do you tell first? Every spouse knows the answer about their own marriage.

For worship. Before the first wedding was ever held, God had his Son and his church in view. Marvel at the wisdom of a God who wrote the gospel into the week of creation. And adore the Son who left his Father’s glory, without ceasing to be one with him, to come and claim his bride; who took our flesh so that he might be one with us; and who holds fast to his people even when they let go of him. For the divorced and the deserted, here is a Husband who will never tear himself away.

parallels.desc: a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife

verseByVerse.quote: This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.

Mystery. Not a puzzle still unsolved, which is nearly the opposite of Paul’s meaning. He has defined it already: something hidden for ages and now made known (3:3–5), a secret God has decided to tell. And there is an edge to using the word in this city, where the mystery cults sold their secrets to initiates and kept them from everyone else. Paul’s mystery is not whispered to a qualified few in the dark; it is read aloud to a room of ordinary people, and its point is that outsiders have been let in.

It refers to Christ and the church. Paul is saying something remarkable. God did not first invent marriage and then find it a useful illustration. He designed marriage from creation to point to the greater marriage. And that reframes the whole Bible. He wedded himself to Israel: your Maker is your husband (Isaiah 54:5). He wooed her back through Hosea’s scandalous love (Hosea 2:19–20), and grieved her unfaithfulness as a wounded husband. Scripture opens with a wedding in a garden (Genesis 2:24) and closes with a wedding at the end of history, the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9). Everything between is, in one sense, the long story of a Bridegroom coming for his bride. God made man and woman for one flesh so that the world would never be without a living picture of the love that would one day empty heaven to win us.

Why this matters. It explains the commands. Husbands are to love like Christ, and wives to follow like the church, because their marriage is meant to display the gospel to the watching world.

Where Christians differ: a sacrament? The Latin Vulgate translated “mystery” as sacramentum, one ground on which the Roman Catholic Church counts marriage among seven sacraments. The instinct is not contemptible: it wants to say marriage is holy, and it is. The Reformers held that marriage is a holy creation ordinance for all people, not a sacrament of grace for the church. Verdict: marriage is honourable and holy, a living parable of the gospel, but not a sacrament. It points to the gospel; it does not dispense it.

For the single. Twelve verses on marriage, rising to a claim this magnificent: what of the reader who has no marriage? The man of forty who assumed he would be married by now; the widow; the woman whose husband left. Start with the two people best placed to answer. The Lord Jesus never married, and Paul, writing this sentence, was unmarried (1 Corinthians 7:7–8). The two people in the New Testament who understood the mystery of marriage most deeply had no experience of it, and neither thought himself impoverished. The most complete human life ever lived was a single one. And if marriage is the sign, the union of Christ and his church is the reality, and the single Christian already has the reality in full: the same Bridegroom, the same love, on exactly the same terms. In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage (Matthew 22:30), not because something good is taken away, but because signs come down when you arrive. Nobody keeps reading the road sign once he is standing in the city. Every marriage on earth ends, by its own vows, at a graveside; the marriage it pointed to never does. And God said it first to the very people the ancient world pitied most. To the eunuch, who could never marry or have children, he says: I will give in my house and within my walls a monument and a name better than sons and daughters (Isaiah 56:3–5). Better than sons and daughters: a promise of more, made to the one with least.

What it does not mean. If every faithful marriage pictures the gospel, what does a bad marriage say about the gospel? Nothing at all. A sign knocked flat in a ditch does not move the city it pointed to, and no failure of yours has altered the love this verse describes by one degree. Your marriage is not the gospel; it is a picture of it, and pictures may be poor without the original being any less.

In a sentence. This is a profound mystery, but I am talking about Christ and the church.

For worship. From the garden to the wedding supper of the Lamb, the whole Bible is the story of a Bridegroom coming for his bride, and he came, and paid, and holds her still. Some are given the picture for a while. All of us are given the reality for ever.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

parallels.desc: your Maker is your husband

verseByVerse.quote: However, let each one of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
However, let each one of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.

However. After the great mystery of Christ and the church, Paul comes back down, in one word, to a husband and a wife who have to get through Tuesday. The glory is not an alternative to the practicalities; it is the reason for them, and Paul will not let anyone use the mystery to avoid the marriage.

Each one of you. Personal responsibility. Paul does not address the couple; he addresses two individuals, separately, and gives each one command, and neither command has a condition attached. He does not write, love your wife once she has begun to respect you, or respect your husband as soon as he loves you like Christ. That would have been reasonable, and it is the standard deadlock most struggling marriages sit in. She is waiting for him to love her as verse 25 describes, and she is not wrong to want it. He is waiting for her to respect him, and he is not wrong to want it either. Both are sincerely willing to move. Both are waiting for evidence of movement before they move. They can hold that position for eleven years, each convinced they are being reasonable. Paul cuts through it with two words. You cannot obey your half of this verse jointly. You can only obey it first.

Love his wife as himself. Self-giving care, as in vv. 25–29. For a man of few emotional words it means learning to ask and stay: not “are you okay?” but “tell me how you are really doing”, and then sitting with the answer instead of fixing it; reaching for her before she has to signal; naming what he notices: you seem heavy today; what is going on?

And let the wife see that she respects her husband. Literally “fears”: reverent honour, shown in trust, gratitude and support of his leadership, in how she speaks about him as well as to him. In practice: catching the correction before it reaches her lips in front of the children and keeping it for a private moment; letting him make a decision she thinks slightly wrong, when the stakes are low, and not reopening it; saying something genuinely admiring of him where he can hear it. A man, like anyone, tends to become more of what he is told he is.

What it does not mean. Not terror or blind agreement. Respect is not pretending, not agreeing with everything, not staying quiet while something wrong goes unaddressed, and not absorbing harm; the limits of v. 22 stand. What it governs is chiefly manner. The hardest sentence in a marriage can be said with honour or with contempt, in nearly the same words, and only one is obedience. A wife married to a man who has given her little to admire is not asked to manufacture admiration she does not feel. She is asked to refuse contempt, which is possible on a bad day and is very often the last thing standing between a marriage and its end. And the pairing of love for him to give and respect for her to give is a wise observation, not a law of nature: wives need respect and husbands need love too. Ask your spouse which they are short of, and believe the answer.

In a sentence. Still, each one of you must love his wife as he loves himself, and the wife must respect her husband.

On a Tuesday. Of the two halves of this verse, which have you thought about more this year? A husband who can quote “let the wife see that she respects her husband” and could not say, without looking, what he was told in the same breath is not studying Scripture; he is arming himself. The half you were given is the only half you were given. So the chapter that reached as far as Christ and his church ends with two people who each have one thing to do tomorrow: a man who asks a second question at dinner and stays for the answer, and a woman who declines to say the sharp thing in front of the children. Neither will feel cosmic at the time. Both are, and the God who drew the picture in the garden is watching it being drawn again.

For worship. In Christ and his church both halves of this verse are perfectly fulfilled: a Husband who loves without condition and goes first, and a bride who will one day honour him with unclouded joy. Praise the Lord who did not wait for us to move before he moved, but came to us while we were still sinners (Romans 5:8). Every faltering step a husband or wife takes towards the other is lit by that prior love. Adore him, the faithful Bridegroom: whatever the state of our marriages, his marriage to his church will not fail.

5.overview:
Paul continues to describe the new life. God’s beloved children must imitate their Father and walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up as a fragrant sacrifice. That rules out sexual immorality, impurity and greed, crude talk and joking, all of which exclude people from Christ’s kingdom and bring God’s wrath. Once they were darkness; now they are light in the Lord, so they must live as children of light, producing goodness, righteousness and truth, exposing the works of darkness rather than sharing in them. Wise living makes the most of the time in evil days, understands the Lord’s will, and refuses drunkenness in favour of being filled with the Spirit, which shows itself in singing, thanksgiving and mutual submission out of reverence for Christ.

The household code that follows (5:22–6:9) applies this to marriage, family and work. Wives are to submit to their own husbands as to the Lord, because the husband is head of the wife as Christ is head of the church. Husbands must love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself for her, to make her holy and present her glorious; they must love their wives as their own bodies, nourishing and cherishing them as Christ does the church. Genesis 2:24 speaks of the one flesh of marriage, and Paul reveals its deepest meaning: it is a picture of the union of Christ and the church. Each husband must love his wife, and each wife respect her husband.

6.title: Household Duties and the Armour of God
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. <sup>2</sup>“Honor your father and mother” (this is the first commandment with a promise), <sup>3</sup>“that it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land.” <sup>4</sup>Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. <sup>5</sup>Bondservants, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, with a sincere heart, as you would Christ, <sup>6</sup>not by the way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but as bondservants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, <sup>7</sup>rendering service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man, <sup>8</sup>knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord, whether he is a bondservant or is free. <sup>9</sup>Masters, do the same to them, and stop your threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him. <sup>10</sup>Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might. <sup>11</sup>Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil. <sup>12</sup>For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places. <sup>13</sup>Therefore take up the whole armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand firm. <sup>14</sup>Stand therefore, having fastened on the belt of truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, <sup>15</sup>and, as shoes for your feet, having put on the readiness given by the gospel of peace. <sup>16</sup>In all circumstances take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one; <sup>17</sup>and take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, <sup>18</sup>praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication. To that end, keep alert with all perseverance, making supplication for all the saints, <sup>19</sup>and also for me, that words may be given to me in opening my mouth boldly to proclaim the mystery of the gospel, <sup>20</sup>for which I am an ambassador in chains, that I may declare it boldly, as I ought to speak. <sup>21</sup>So that you also may know how I am and what I am doing, Tychicus the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord will tell you everything. <sup>22</sup>I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are, and that he may encourage your hearts. <sup>23</sup>Peace be to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>24</sup>Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with love incorruptible.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Children are to obey their parents in the Lord, for this is right. Honouring father and mother is the first commandment with a promise: that it may go well with them and they may live long. Fathers must not exasperate their children, but raise them in the Lord’s training and instruction. Slaves must obey earthly masters with respect and sincerity, as they would Christ, not only to win favour when watched, but as Christ’s servants doing God’s will from the heart, serving wholeheartedly as to the Lord, knowing the Lord will reward everyone for good done, slave or free. Masters must treat their slaves the same way, without threatening, knowing that their own Master and theirs is in heaven and shows no favouritism.
verseByVerse.theology:
Authority, Service, and the Lordship of Christ

The household codes of Ephesians 5:22–6:9 have sometimes been misread as Paul's accommodation to Roman social structures — a domestication of the gospel that reinforces existing hierarchies. The opposite is true. Paul takes every relationship in the household and transforms it from within by the same double principle: both parties have obligations, and both parties are accountable to Christ. This is not the endorsement of hierarchy for its own sake; it is the sanctification of ordered relationships by the presence of a Lord who stands above every human ordering.

The instruction to servants (vv.5–8) is particularly searching. “Obey... as you would Christ,” “doing the will of God from the heart,” “rendering service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man, knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord.” Paul is not telling slaves that their situation is just; he is telling them that no situation, however unjust, is outside the reach of Christ's transforming presence. The servant who works faithfully for an unworthy master, doing it as for the Lord, is engaged in genuine worship — and will receive the Lord's commendation at the last day, whatever commendation or condemnation the human master gave or withheld.

The warning to masters — “do the same to them, and stop your threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him” (v.9) — is one of the most socially radical statements in the New Testament. The master has a Master. The one with authority is under authority. Before the throne of the impartial God, all distinctions of status dissolve. This truth, fully believed and consistently applied, has done more to dismantle unjust social structures than any legal or political programme. It was ultimately the logic of this verse, applied over centuries, that made slavery in the Christian world an untenable contradiction.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Roman paterfamilias held virtually absolute authority over his household — his wife, his children, and his slaves were all, in various degrees, subject to his legal control. Children had no independent legal standing; slaves were property. Paul's household code addresses children and slaves first, and addresses them as moral agents capable of genuine obedience to God — not as objects to be managed. This is itself a dignity-claim that the Roman household code did not make. And the commands to fathers (don't exasperate) and masters (treat them justly) placed obligations on the powerful toward the powerless that Roman law did not require. The Christian household was different — visibly, consistently, counter-culturally different.

Now: “Children, obey your parents in the Lord” and “Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger” — both imperatives are needed in every age, and our age tends to violate both simultaneously. We live in a culture that simultaneously refuses to discipline children (producing entitled, poorly-bounded young people) and fails to give them the patient, encouraging, Christ-centred nurture that Ephesians 6:4 envisions. The Christian home where authority is exercised in love, where children are both appropriately disciplined and genuinely encouraged in the Lord, where the name of Christ is spoken and the word of God is read — this home is a counterculture, a community of formation in a world that has largely forgotten what formation is for.

verseByVerse.quote: Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.

Meaning first. Ephesians 6 completes the household instructions and then lifts our eyes to the spiritual battle behind all of life. Children obey and honour their parents, as the fifth commandment says, and fathers nurture their children in the Lord’s discipline instead of exasperating them (vv. 1–4). Slaves serve sincerely, as to Christ, who rewards every good deed, and masters stop threatening, because both answer to one impartial Master in heaven (vv. 5–9). Then believers are to be strong in the Lord and put on the whole armour of God, because the real enemy is the devil, not people: truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation and the word of God, all worn in watchful prayer for all the saints and for Paul, Christ’s ambassador in chains (vv. 10–20). The letter closes with news through Tychicus and a blessing of grace on all who love the Lord Jesus with undying love (vv. 21–24).

The setting. Paul is in the middle of the household codes (5:21–6:9). Greek and Roman moralists wrote similar codes, but they spoke only to the person with power: the husband, father and master. Paul speaks first to the weaker party in each pair, as full members of the church with their own calling before God. All of it flows from being filled with the Spirit (5:18) and submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ (5:21).

Children. Picture the letter being read aloud in a crowded room in Ephesus, the children at the edge of it, half listening. Then the reader says: Children. Heads come up. In a world where a child had no legal standing and would never be addressed by a public document, an apostle speaks to them directly. He does not say, fathers, make your children obey, which is what every household code of the time would have said. He speaks to the child, gives the child a reason, and expects the child to answer for himself, as a member of the church who can hear Christ and respond. The word covers children still living under their parents’ authority, not adults.

Obey. Hypakouō: literally to listen under, to listen and do what is said. And notice that Paul does not reuse the word from the marriage passage. Wives were told to arrange themselves under (hypotassō); children are told to obey. A wife is not a child, and a husband who reads his wife’s role from this verse instead of chapter 5 has taken the wrong word from the wrong paragraph. What is asked of a child is straightforward obedience, because a child does not yet know enough to run his own life, which is a temporary condition and is treated as one. And it is parents, both father and mother: in the Roman world the father held legal power, but Paul gives the mother equal standing as one to be obeyed.

In the Lord. Two meanings. First, as an act of service to Christ: a child’s obedience to parents is obedience to the Lord (Colossians 3:20 says this pleases the Lord). Second, within the Lord’s will: this is obedience as a Christian, and that sets its limit.

For this is right. Paul gives three reasons in three verses, each of a different kind. It is right (dikaion): fitting, built into the moral shape of the world, so that someone who had never seen the commandment would sense it (v. 1). It is commanded, written into the law at Sinai (v. 2). And it is blessed: it carries a promise (v. 3). Conscience, Scripture and consequence. Paul does not rely on the parent’s volume.

The child who obeyed. There has been exactly one child in history who had every right to disregard his parents. He had made them. At twelve he astonished the teachers in the temple (Luke 2:46–47). And Luke ends that story: he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them (Luke 2:51). Then eighteen years of silence. The Son of God spent most of two decades doing what he was told in a small town by a carpenter and his wife, and Scripture says he learned obedience (Hebrews 5:8). A child who obeys is not doing something beneath the dignity of heaven. He is doing what the Lord of heaven did first, for longer, with far less reason to.

What it does not mean. Not obedience in sin. “In the Lord” rules out obeying a parent who commands what God forbids; then we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). Nor does it require that children submit to abuse. A parent’s authority is borrowed, never absolute; no parent has the right to injure a child. If you are a young person reading this in a house where you are being hurt, frightened, or asked to keep a secret about what an adult does to you, this verse is not telling you to submit to it. Tell someone, a teacher, a pastor, another adult you trust, and keep telling until somebody acts. That is not disobedience; it is obedience to the Lord in whose name the command was given. And any adult who quotes this verse to keep a child quiet has turned Christ’s words against the very person Christ stopped a letter to address. Nor does it mean that grown children who have left home must obey their parents for life: marriage creates a new household (Genesis 2:24; 5:31). But honour never ends (v. 2).

What if my parents are not Christians and will not let me go to church? Obey them in everything you lawfully can, and honour them even when you disagree; God does not ask you to deceive them or sneak out. Being kept from church is hard, but it is not the same as being commanded to sin. No parent can stop you praying, reading your Bible or trusting Christ, and that is where your faith lives. Ask respectfully whether you may go, or meet a Christian friend, or have the pastor call; a parent who sees a child growing kinder, more honest and more helpful often softens over time. Pray for them by name. Remember that this lasts only while you live under their roof. And if they ever command you to deny Christ or to do what God forbids, then you must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), respectfully and without contempt.

In a sentence. Children, obey your parents as people who belong to the Lord, because this is right.

On a Tuesday. Parents: read this verse with your children and explain it. Children: obeying your parents today, without grumbling, is a way to please Jesus. And for the adult reader: the first authority any of us meets is a human one, in a kitchen. If yours was arbitrary or impossible to please, you may find that submitting to God feels like bracing for something. That is a learned reflex, not a true reading of him.

For worship. The Lord in whose name this command is given is the Son who has always delighted to do his Father’s will: in eternity, in a carpenter’s house, and in a garden where he prayed, not my will but yours. His obedience was never grudging, and it is now counted to every child who has sulked and slammed a door, and to every parent who has failed a child. The same Lord who stopped this letter to speak to children once took them in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16), and he has not changed. In his church no child is overlooked, because the King of heaven was once a child.

verseByVerse.quote: Honor your father and mother (this is the first commandment with a promise), that it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Honor your father and mother (this is the first commandment with a promise), that it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land.

Honour. More than obedience. To honour (timaō) is to treat as weighty, to respect, value and give due regard. Obedience applies to children at home; honour applies for life. For adults it means speaking of parents with respect, not retelling their failures as entertainment even when every word is true; courtesy as they grow slower and more repetitive; listening to their wisdom (Proverbs 23:22); keeping them warmly included instead of quietly sidelined; and practical care when they grow old (1 Timothy 5:4, 8). Jesus condemned religious leaders who used a loophole called Corban, declaring their money dedicated to God, to avoid supporting their parents: making void the word of God by your tradition (Mark 7:9–13). Notice what he thought the commandment required: money, provision, the unglamorous cost of caring for people who can no longer care for themselves.

This is the first commandment with a promise. Paul is quoting the fifth commandment (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16), and by quoting it to Gentile children he shows that the moral law of the Ten Commandments still guides Christians, even though the law as a dividing wall between Jew and Gentile has been broken down in Christ (2:14–15). A careful reader may spot a puzzle: the second commandment already speaks of God’s steadfast love to thousands of those who love him (Exodus 20:6). But that is a statement about God’s character attached to a prohibition; this is the first command with a specific promise attached to keeping it. Some take “first” to mean first in importance, or first in the commandments about our neighbour. Either way, God has singled it out and hung a promise on it.

That it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land. In Exodus the promise ran: in the land that the LORD your God is giving you, a promise about Canaan. Paul quotes it and quietly drops the last clause. A promise about one territory becomes a promise about life anywhere, offered to Greek children in Asia Minor with no stake in Canaan at all. It is the move he has made throughout the letter: the blessings of the covenant opened to the nations.

What it does not mean. Not a guarantee that every obedient child will live long, or that early death proves disobedience. Godly children die young; honouring your parents does not protect you from a drunk driver or a diagnosis. Like the Proverbs, it states how God normally works, not a mechanical rule, and it is observably true at the level it is pitched: a person who learns to honour rightful authority and receive correction generally lives a longer, less damaged life, and a society where the generations honour one another holds together. The promise finds its final fulfilment in eternal life. Nor does honouring parents mean pretending their faults do not exist, or placing them above a spouse.

And if my parents did not deserve it? Paul attaches no clause about sufficiently good parents, and many readers have a father who was frightening, a mother who was cruel, or a parent who simply left. They read this verse with dread, hearing it demand that they pretend the childhood was something it was not. It demands nothing of the kind. Honour is not approval, and it is not pretending. You can honour a person and tell the truth about them; the Bible records the failures of its own heroes without ceasing to treat them with dignity. Honour is compatible with a boundary: the adult child who limits contact with a destructive parent, calmly and without contempt, for the sake of his own household, has not broken this commandment. It is compatible with grief, and with the long, unfinished work of forgiving. What it rules out is contempt: the sneer, the public mockery, the settled determination to make them pay. At its core the duty is small, and survives almost any history: to refuse to treat the people who gave you life as though they were nothing.

The Son at the cross. Watch Jesus keep this commandment. He is on the cross, bearing the sin of the world, and he sees his mother standing there. With what breath he has, he arranges her care: Woman, behold, your son! Behold, your mother! And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home (John 19:26–27). He was in the act of redeeming the world, and he stopped to make sure his mother would have somewhere to live.

In a sentence. Honour your father and mother, which is the first commandment that comes with a promise: so that things may go well for you and you may enjoy a long life on the earth.

On a Tuesday. Notice how you speak about your parents when they are not there: to your spouse, a friend, your children. Our real assessment lives in the stories we choose to repeat, and we are training the next generation in exactly how they will one day speak about us. Then plan one act of honour this week: a visit, a call, practical help, patience with their slowness.

For worship. The God who wrote this commandment on stone is the Father from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named (3:14–15). He once promised one small land to one nation; in Christ he has widened the promise until the meek inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5), and Greek children in Ephesus could hear it as theirs. His Son kept this commandment perfectly to his last breath, and his righteousness covers every son and daughter who has not. And to those whose earthly parents failed them he is the parent who never leaves: though father and mother forsake them, the LORD takes them in (Psalm 27:10).

parallels.desc: honour your father and your mother
that it may go well with you

verseByVerse.quote: Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.

Fathers. Paul has just spoken to children; the natural counterpart would be “parents”. He says fathers, the one who held the power. In Roman law the father (paterfamilias) had almost absolute power over his children: he could decide whether a newborn lived or was abandoned to die, sell them into slavery, or punish them severely even when grown. Into that world Paul says: limit your power by love. The word can also mean parents (Hebrews 11:23), and the principle applies to mothers too, but fathers bear particular responsibility for the spiritual leadership of the home. And the prohibition comes first: in a relationship that unequal, the damage a man can do without meaning to is the first problem to deal with.

Do not provoke your children to anger. The tense describes a settled pattern, not a bad afternoon. Every father loses his temper; Paul forbids the atmosphere. Colossians names the outcome: lest they become discouraged (Colossians 3:21), lose heart, have the wind go out of them. That is the injury: not an angry child, but a child who has quietly stopped trying, because he has worked out that nothing he does will be enough. And almost none of the provocations is a sin a man would confess. Criticism that only notices what is missing. Expectations that keep moving. Comparison with a sibling. Promises casually broken, because a child’s disappointment is easy to absorb. Sarcasm, which a child cannot answer and does not forget. Inconsistency, punishing one day what was ignored the next. Rules without reasons. Hypocrisy, demanding what he does not do. Absence: the father in the house and behind a screen. And the commonest of all: a man warm when things go well and cold when they do not, so that a child grows up managing his father’s mood and learns, without being told, that love is earned by performance.

Why it matters so much. A child’s first picture of authority is a human one, at a kitchen table; his first working model of a father is the man sitting there. Nobody easily thinks his way out of that model. The father who is arbitrary teaches his children that God is arbitrary; the father who is never satisfied teaches them that God is never satisfied, and they may spend thirty years trying to unlearn it.

But bring them up. The word (ektrephō) means to nourish, to rear, to feed up to full growth, the verb used of a husband nourishing his own body (5:29). Fathers are to nurture their children with warmth and tender care, as a gardener tends a plant.

In the discipline. Paideia: training, including correction, the word used of God disciplining his children in love (Hebrews 12:5–11). Discipline is teaching by action: setting boundaries, correcting wrong, giving consequences, and praising what is right. So this is not permissiveness. The father who never corrects anything fails this verse as surely as the one who crushes. The two errors look opposite and share a root: both are easier than the patient, costly work of shaping a person who will one day not be under your authority at all. Beside discipline stands instruction (nouthesia): literally putting in mind, teaching by word, warning and explaining. Children need not only rules but reasons, and not only correction but understanding.

Of the Lord. This is the goal: not only well-behaved children, but children who know the Lord. The father is not forming the child in his own image, or into the career he wishes he had had. He is bringing up someone else’s child. With young children, it looks like presence, affection, calm and consistent boundaries, God woven into ordinary talk (Deuteronomy 6:6–7): God made that butterfly; let us thank God for our food. With older children, genuine interest in their world (the father who does not know his child’s best friend has not yet earned the right to be heard), and correction that is private and aimed at character. With teenagers, a move from authority to influence: what do you think? and actually listening; and above all letting them see a real father’s walk with God: praying, confessing sin, coming back to Christ after failure. More is caught than taught.

The Lord who trained twelve. The discipline and instruction of the Lord has a living pattern, because the Lord himself spent three years bringing up a band of slow, quarrelsome men. He corrected plainly: Get behind me, Satan, he told Peter (Matthew 16:23). He explained again what they had failed to grasp (Mark 8:17–21). He never moved the bar or withdrew his warmth when they failed: having loved his own, he loved them to the end (John 13:1). And when they argued about who was greatest, he did not humiliate them; he set a child in the middle of them and taught them (Mark 9:36). Correction without exasperation has a face.

What if there is no Christian father in the home? Then God has not left your children without a Father, nor you without help. Timothy was raised in the faith by his mother Eunice and his grandmother Lois, while his father seems to have been an unbelieving Greek (Acts 16:1; 2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15), and he became one of Paul’s most trusted men. A single mother, or a believing mother whose husband is indifferent, can do everything this verse describes: nurture, correct, teach and pray. God calls himself the father of the fatherless and the protector of widows (Psalm 68:5). And the church has its part: godly men in the congregation can befriend, include and show faithfulness to children who have no believing father at home. If you are carrying this alone, ask for that help. It is not a failure; it is the family of God doing its work.

Where Christians differ: physical discipline? Proverbs says, whoever spares the rod hates his son (Proverbs 13:24), and many Christians understand that to allow measured physical correction of young children, given calmly, never in anger, never to injure, and always with love and explanation. Others take the rod as a figure for discipline in general, and some believe physical discipline is unwise in every case. Verdict: whatever a parent decides, this verse rules out anything that provokes, humiliates or harms a child. Discipline that crushes a child’s spirit (Colossians 3:21) is not the Lord’s discipline, and abuse must never hide behind Scripture.

What it does not mean. Not a ban on firm discipline or on telling children no: lack of discipline is itself a failure of love (Proverbs 13:24; Hebrews 12:7–11). Nor does “of the Lord” mean that fathers can make their children Christians: only God gives new life (2:1–5). Fathers sow and water; God gives growth. And the verse does not mean children’s faith or failures are entirely the parents’ fault: children are responsible persons too (Ezekiel 18:20).

Our children have turned away from the faith. Did we fail them? Perhaps in some ways, as every parent does, but their unbelief does not prove it. God himself, the only perfect Father, grieved over children he had reared who rebelled against him (Isaiah 1:2). Faith cannot be handed down; new birth is God’s work, not the parents’ (John 1:13). If you see real failures, confess them to God, and where it would help, apologise to your adult child plainly. Then keep the door open: love them without nagging, keep a place for them at the table, take an interest in their lives, and do not turn every visit into a sermon. Let them see a parent who still walks with Christ and is kind. Above all, keep praying, for years if need be. Many prodigals have come home in their thirties and forties, and the father in the parable was watching the road (Luke 15:20).

In a sentence. Fathers, do not exasperate your children, but raise them with the training and teaching that come from the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Do not ask yourself whether you provoke your children. Ask one of them: is there something I do that makes you feel you can never quite get it right? Then say nothing until they have finished, and do not explain. And to the father whose children are grown, who recognised himself in that list: it is not too late to say so. An apology to an adult child, specific, without excuses, without a single “but you also”, is one of the most powerful things in the world.
