And God has been a Father to your children in ways you never managed, and he is able to repair what you broke.

For worship. At the Jordan, before Jesus had preached a sermon or healed anyone, a voice came from heaven: this is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased (Matthew 3:17). The approval came first, out loud, before there was any record to earn it. That is the Father who has adopted us in the Beloved (1:5–6). His delight in his children does not wait for their record, because it rests on his Son’s. He disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness (Hebrews 12:10), and he has never once disciplined in a temper. Every earthly father is a faint copy of him, and he does not tire of his children.

verseByVerse.quote: Bondservants, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, with a sincere heart, as you would Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bondservants, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, with a sincere heart, as you would Christ,

Bondservants. Douloi: slaves. Perhaps a third of the people of a city like Ephesus were slaves, and many of the first Christians were slaves (1 Corinthians 1:26; 7:21), while some were masters. Roman slavery was not based on race: people became slaves through war, debt, crime or birth. Some were household servants, teachers, doctors or managers; others laboured in mines and fields in terrible conditions. Release was common enough that many could hope for freedom. But a slave was legally property, without rights, and it was still bondage and an assault on human dignity.

Speaking to the property. Every household code of the period spoke to the owner about managing his property. Paul speaks to the property, as a person with a conscience, a Lord, and choices to make about his work. A man with no legal standing is told that his ordinary labour is offered to Jesus Christ and will be assessed by him. Nobody in that world spoke to slaves like that.

Obey your earthly masters. Literally masters according to the flesh: their human masters. The phrase hints at a contrast: they have another Master in heaven (v. 9). The earthly master’s authority is real but limited.

With fear and trembling. Not cringing terror of the master. Paul uses the same phrase of arriving at Corinth (1 Corinthians 2:3), and of the Christian life itself: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you (Philippians 2:12–13). It is the seriousness of someone who knows God is watching. The trembling has been redirected upward, over the master’s head.

With a sincere heart. “Sincere” (haplotēs) means single, undivided: without hidden motives, without one face for the master and another behind his back. For a slave, whose whole existence invited a double life, that was a startling thing to ask and a great gift: you may be owned, but you need not be divided.

As you would Christ. The motive that transforms everything. The slave is not told his master deserves this; he is told to look past him. There is another figure standing behind the man who owns him, and the work is really being handed to that one. Christ dignified the work of the lowest.

A Lord who took the slave’s name. The word for slave here is doulos, and it is the word Paul uses for what the Son of God did: though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (doulos), and became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:6–8). So when a slave in Ephesus heard this read aloud and was told to serve as to Christ, he was addressed by a Lord who had taken his job title, and who had been raised and seated in the heavenly places, exactly where chapter 2 says this slave has been seated too (2:6).

What it does not mean. Not that Paul approves of slavery or thinks it good. He addresses believers within a social system they could not change, and tells them how to live as Christians in it. He never says their situation is just, and he tells slaves who can gain their freedom to take it (1 Corinthians 7:21). Nor does it mean obeying a master who commands sin: obedience is “as to Christ”, and Christ never commands sin.

Where Christians differ: does the Bible endorse slavery? In the nineteenth century, slave-owners in the American South quoted texts like this to defend slavery. Paul does not endorse the institution. He regulates it while undermining it from within. He lists slave-traders, “enslavers”, among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10), which alone condemns the Atlantic slave trade at its root; he urges slaves to gain their freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21); he tells masters that they and their slaves have the same Master who shows no favouritism (v. 9); and he asks Philemon to receive his runaway slave Onesimus no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother (Philemon 16). In the church, slave and free were equals at the Lord’s Table (Galatians 3:28). Why not call for revolt? A slave revolt in the first century would have been drowned in blood, as the thousands crucified after Spartacus showed, and would have branded the young church as sedition. Verdict: the gospel undermined slavery from within, and Christians such as William Wilberforce rightly led its abolition. Modern slavery and human trafficking are evils Christians must oppose.

Today. We do not have slavery in this form, and an employee is not owned; the New Testament is emphatic about the wickedness of withholding wages and exploiting the weak. But the principle reaches everyone who works under conditions they did not choose and cannot change: the manager who will never be fair, the industry that rewards the wrong things, the job taken because the mortgage exists. Paul’s answer is neither resignation nor resentment. It is a change of employer at the level that matters.

In a sentence. Slaves, obey your earthly masters with deep respect and an undivided heart, just as you would obey Christ,

On a Tuesday. Think of the part of your work no one senior will ever inspect. What governs the quality of it? If the honest answer is whether it is likely to be noticed, your real employer is the person who signs the form. If it is because this is the work I have been given, something has already changed hands. Do today’s dullest task as if he had asked you to do it, because he has.

For worship. Every slave who heard this letter had a price, written down by the man who owned him. And every one who belonged to Christ had already been bought at another price, not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18–19), and was in the Lord’s reckoning his freedman (1 Corinthians 7:22). Here is a Master who pays for his servants with his own life, who will one day dress himself for service and wait on them at his own table (Luke 12:37), and whose reign will break every chain.
verseByVerse.note: Slavery was part of everyday life in the Roman world; many early believers were slaves or owned slaves.

verseByVerse.quote: not by the way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but as bondservants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, rendering service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man,
verseByVerse.commentary:
not by the way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but as bondservants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, rendering service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man,

Not by the way of eye-service. Ophthalmodoulia, a word that appears nowhere before Paul, and a man does not invent vocabulary unless nothing else will do: eye-slavery, work that exists only while it is being looked at. The servant who slacks off when the supervisor leaves the room. And it is not the same as laziness; eye-service can be very energetic. It is a matter of where the effort is aimed: the report polished because the right person will read it, the visible task done first. It produces a person who is never quite the same twice, always adjusting to an audience, which is exhausting in a way hard work never is. Its companion is the people-pleaser (anthrōpareskos), working to win human approval rather than God’s: the motive is image, not integrity.

But as bondservants of Christ. The deepest identity of a Christian slave was not “slave of a master” but “slave of Christ” (Paul uses the same title of himself, Romans 1:1). Every Christian, slave or free, belongs to Christ.

Doing the will of God from the heart. Literally from the soul. Look at who this is said to and what he does all day: cleaning, carrying, cooking, accounting, minding someone else’s children. Nothing religious about any of it. And Paul says that when he does it well, he is doing the will of God. That demolishes the division most of us carry without examining: sacred activities, prayer, church, evangelism, and then everything else, which is at best neutral. We are God’s workmanship, created for good works (2:10), and here is what a good work looks like on a Tuesday: a floor properly swept by a man nobody is watching. The Reformers called this the doctrine of vocation: every lawful calling can be done for God’s glory (1 Corinthians 10:31), and Luther said the milkmaid and the farmer serve God as truly as the priest. The nurse on the night shift, the mother whose day’s work will be undone by bedtime, the man who drives a van: none is doing something less spiritual than the one leading the service on Sunday. Ordinary work was never the waiting room for real ministry.

I delight to do your will. Only one person has ever done the will of God from the heart without a divided moment. Hebrews hears Christ speaking Psalm 40 as he comes into the world: Behold, I have come to do your will, O God (Hebrews 10:7), and the psalm adds, your law is within my heart (Psalm 40:8). His food was to do the will of him who sent him (John 4:34), in the unrecorded years at the bench as much as at the cross, and by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all (Hebrews 10:10). The slave sweeping an unwatched floor from the heart walks in the footsteps of the Servant whose obedience saved him.

Rendering service with a good will. Not grudgingly, with resentment, but wanting the person you serve to do well. That is a great thing to ask of a slave about the man who owns him, or of an employee about a manager who took credit for her work. And Paul gives the reason: as to the Lord and not to man, and the Lord repays every good deed (v. 8). Goodwill towards an undeserving employer is not manufactured by trying to like him. It becomes possible when the transaction has been re-routed, so that he is no longer the one paying for it.

As to the Lord and not to man. The audience has changed. The worker serves the human employer, but ultimately works for Christ (Colossians 3:23). Christ was in the meeting where an employee’s credit was taken, saw the extra hour no one noticed, and will miss nothing (v. 8). That changes not her circumstances but her inner life: the quality of her work is no longer hostage to her employer’s fairness.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians must accept unjust treatment without protest, stay in an exploitative job, or never speak up for fair conditions. Paul told slaves to take freedom if they could (1 Corinthians 7:21); James condemns employers who withhold wages (James 5:4); and Paul himself used his Roman rights (Acts 16:37; 22:25). Working heartily for the Lord and standing up for yourself are not in competition. What is forbidden is the divided heart that gives a man its hours and withholds its integrity.

Does this mean I should not care what my boss thinks of me? No. It is right to want your employer to be pleased with your work, and good to be glad when it is noticed; Joseph and Daniel both won the trust of those over them (Genesis 39:4; Daniel 6:3). The fault Paul names is letting human approval become your master: working well only when it will be seen, bending your conscience to the mood of the office, or being flattened for a week by one cool remark. The cure is not to stop caring but to change whose opinion weighs most. When the work is done for Christ, a manager’s praise becomes a pleasant extra instead of oxygen, and criticism becomes useful information instead of a verdict on your worth. You can receive both calmly, because you already know whose well done matters most (Matthew 25:21).

In a sentence. not only to win their favour when they are watching, but as slaves of Christ, doing God’s will from the heart; serve wholeheartedly and willingly, as if you were serving the Lord and not people,

On a Tuesday. Notice what changes in your work when the person who assesses you leaves the building: the pace, the care, the attention to the part nobody sees. The gap between those two versions of you is the exact measure of how much of your working life is being done for God and how much for an audience.

For worship. God sees the swept floor that nobody inspects. His eyes run to and fro throughout the whole earth (2 Chronicles 16:9), and nothing done for him in a back room is too small for them. The Lord whom every hidden worker serves is no distant proprietor. He is the Christ who never once worked for an audience, who did not receive glory from people (John 5:41), and who takes every unseen task done in his name as a gift handed to him in person. You are serving the Lord Christ (Colossians 3:24): the master of the house is the King of glory, and he is pleased with small things done for love.

verseByVerse.quote: knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord, whether he is a bondservant or is free.
verseByVerse.commentary:
knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord, whether he is a bondservant or is free.

Knowing. Not hoping, or trusting that somehow it will come right. The whole sentence rests on something known: a fact about how God has arranged reality, as certain on the worst Thursday of your working life as on the best. Feelings are not asked to carry this. You are handed something to know, and then sent back to work on the strength of it.

Whatever good anyone does. No threshold, no category excluded. In the first setting, a man sweeping a floor his owner would never inspect. In yours, the meal cooked for a family who did not think to say thank you, the shift quietly covered, the expense claim filled in honestly, patience held with the same difficult relative for the ninth year running. Jesus set the bar at exactly this height: a cup of cold water given to a disciple, and the giver will by no means lose his reward (Matthew 10:42). And Hebrews makes it a statement about God’s character: God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name (Hebrews 6:10). If God let one of these drop, he would not be merely forgetful. He would be unjust.

This he will receive back from the Lord. The verb (komizō) means to receive back what is yours, to collect what was deposited, the word Paul uses of the judgement seat (2 Corinthians 5:10). Every unnoticed good thing you have done has been deposited. Feel that for the person it was first written to. A slave’s work did not bear his name: whatever he built, grew, mended or managed was credited to the man who owned him. Paul tells that man that a complete and accurate record exists, kept by the only one who was actually watching, and that it will be read back to him in person. The visible accounting of this world is the inaccurate one.

Whether he is a bondservant or is free. Before the Lord’s judgement, social status makes no difference. A slave’s faithful work will be rewarded as fully as a free person’s, each good thing entered under the name of the one who actually did it.

What it does not mean. Not that we earn salvation by good works: salvation is by grace through faith (2:8–9). What is promised is not wages earned but reward given: not the ground of your acceptance, but the Father’s pleasure in what his own Spirit produced in you (2:10). Augustine said that when God crowns our merits, he crowns his own gifts. Salvation is not what is handed back on that day; salvation is why you are standing there at all. Nor are the rewards necessarily material, or in this life. Paul does not say the credit stolen from you will be publicly restored here, or that the family will eventually notice. Most of it will not be settled here. But nothing is pending for ever. The wait is real; the loss is not.

The Servant who seemed to labour in vain. This promise holds because it has already been kept once, for Christ. The Servant of Isaiah, whose songs the New Testament sees fulfilled in Jesus (Acts 8:32–35), says: I have laboured in vain; I have spent my strength for nothing; yet surely my right is with the LORD, and my recompense with my God (Isaiah 49:4). From outside, his life looked like that: a village carpenter, a short ministry, the crowds gone, his friends scattered, his body in another man’s tomb. Then God highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name (Philippians 2:9). The Lord who will hand back your hidden work had his own handed back to him on the third day.

In a sentence. because you know that the Lord will reward everyone for whatever good they do, whether they are slave or free.

For worship. The woman who has cared for a parent with dementia for six years; the father whose ordinary life is a series of things nobody thanks him for; the believer who served one small church for thirty years and whose name is in no history: none of it was thrown away. It was banked, by a Lord who does not lose things. He who has numbered the hairs of your head (Matthew 10:30) keeps a fuller record of your love than you do, and on that day he will read it back to you with joy.

verseByVerse.quote: Masters, do the same to them, and stop your threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Masters, do the same to them, and stop your threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him.

Masters, do the same to them. The most startling words in the household code. Paul has spent four verses telling slaves how to work: with fear and trembling, a sincere heart, as to Christ, from the heart, with goodwill. He turns to the owners and says: the same. Not a parallel standard adapted for masters. The same. The codes of the moralists explained to a master how to get the best from his household; they did not place him under the same obligation as his property.

And stop your threatening. Not stop punishing, but stop threatening. The master’s usual instrument was not so much the whip as the constant possibility of it: beatings, being sold away from family, harder work. A household can be run for years on fear without a blow landing. The modern equivalent is rarely a threat spoken aloud: it is the reminder of how competitive the job market is, the review used as leverage, the public dressing-down aimed at everyone else in the room, the displeasure never stated and always available. It reliably produces compliance. Paul forbids it, not because it does not work, but because it does to a person what God does not do to you.

Knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven. One word, kyrios, used once, governing both men. Not their master and your Lord, as though there were two arrangements. The same Master, over both. Before that throne, the slave and the slaveholder are colleagues. The master will answer to Christ for how he treated his slaves. Colossians 4:1 adds: treat them justly and fairly.

The Master who did not threaten. Peter, writing to slaves with harsh masters, points to the one Master who had every right to threaten and never did: when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). Legions of angels were a word away (Matthew 26:53), and he used none of them to frighten anyone into compliance. He ruled by laying his life down. That is the Master in heaven to whom every earthly master answers, and a man who rules by fear rules in the way his own Lord refused to rule.

And that there is no partiality with him. The word (prosōpolēmpsia) comes from the Hebrew picture of lifting the face: a judge raising a man’s face to see who he is before deciding his case. God does not lift the face. The LORD your God … is not partial and takes no bribe (Deuteronomy 10:17); Peter, in a Gentile house against every instinct of his upbringing: Truly I understand that God shows no partiality (Acts 10:34); and James treats seating the rich visitor well and the poor one badly as a denial of the faith (James 2:1–9). So a master used to status deciding outcomes is told that in the only court that finally sits, his advantages do not exist. That is why this short verse had consequences out of all proportion to its length. Once two men believe they have one Lord and one impartial Judge, and sit at one table and call each other brother, slavery has lost its foundation. It took far too long, and Christians defended the indefensible for generations, but when it came down, it came down to arguments built from verses like this.

What it does not mean. Not that authority itself is wrong. The master is not told to stop being a master, nor the employer an employer. But all authority is held under Christ, accountable to him, and must be used for the good of those under it: treating people as persons, not resources; giving credit where it is due instead of absorbing it upward; paying fairly and promptly (Leviticus 19:13; James 5:4).

In a sentence. And masters, treat your slaves in the same way; stop threatening them, because you know that both you and they have the same Master in heaven, and he has no favourites.

On a Tuesday. Almost everyone has power over someone: a parent over a child, an elder over a church, a customer over the person serving him, a healthy adult over an ageing relative. So ask: how do you speak to someone who cannot answer back, and has no way of making it cost you anything? That is the one situation in which nothing but character is at work.

For worship. Before this Master no one is admitted on the strength of his rank, and no one is turned away for the lack of it. The LORD looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7), and then he does what no impartial judge in any court has done: he bears the sentence of the guilty himself. The master and the slave of Ephesus came to his table as debtors forgiven by the same blood, and they will rise to the same inheritance. He who washed his servants’ feet (John 13:5) is enthroned in heaven, and before his throne the powerful and the powerless stand equally low and are equally loved.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Finally, they must be strong in the Lord and his mighty power, and put on God’s full armour to stand against the devil’s schemes, for the struggle is not against human enemies but against the rulers, authorities and spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms. So they must take up the whole armour, to stand firm in the day of evil: truth as a belt, righteousness as a breastplate, readiness from the gospel of peace on their feet, faith as a shield to extinguish the evil one’s flaming arrows, salvation as a helmet, and the Spirit’s sword, God’s word. They must pray in the Spirit on all occasions, with every kind of prayer, staying alert and praying for all God’s people, and for Paul, that he may be given words to make known the gospel’s mystery fearlessly, as an ambassador in chains.
verseByVerse.theology:
Spiritual Warfare and the Victory of Christ

The passage grounds the doctrine of spiritual warfare in the victory already achieved by Christ. The Reformers consistently insisted that the Christian fights from victory, not toward it. At the cross and resurrection, Christ decisively defeated the powers: “He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15). The “rulers and authorities” of Ephesians 6:12 are already defeated enemies — real, malevolent, and active, but operating under the authority of One who has conquered them. The Christian's warfare is not the decisive battle; it is the mopping-up operation conducted in light of a victory already won.

This context — victory already achieved — is what makes “standing” the characteristic posture of the Christian warrior rather than “advancing.” Paul does not say “take more territory.” He says “stand.” Hold what Christ has secured. Don't give ground to a defeated enemy. Don't abandon the position that grace has placed you in. This is not a passive posture; it requires every piece of armour, every act of faith, every prayer offered in the Spirit. But it is a posture of confidence, not of uncertainty — the confidence of those who know how the battle ends and who are fighting in the strength of its Victor.

Prayer (vv.18–20) is the atmosphere in which the armoured Christian stands. It is “at all times in the Spirit” — not occasional, not formal, but the constant, Spirit-sustained reaching toward the Commander. Paul's request for prayer for himself (vv.19–20) is among the most searching things in the letter. The apostle who has written the most magnificent theological letter in the New Testament asks his readers to pray that he would have the boldness to speak the gospel clearly. He is acutely aware that the proclamation of the gospel is itself a spiritual warfare activity, requiring not merely intellectual preparation but Spirit-given courage and divine enablement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ephesus was a city saturated with occult practice. The book of Acts records that when the gospel came to Ephesus, it confronted demonic powers directly — the sons of Sceva, the burning of the magic books, the riot engineered by Demetrius the silversmith whose trade in Artemis-shrines was threatened (Acts 19). The Ephesian Christians knew, from personal experience, that spiritual warfare was real. When Paul tells them to stand against “the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places,” he is not speaking metaphorically to a congregation that has only ever faced theoretical opposition. He is arming people who have already been in the fight.

Now: The tendency in contemporary Christianity is to spiritualise spiritual warfare into invisibility (it's just a metaphor for human sin and social structures) or to sensationalise it into obsession (seeing demonic activity behind every difficulty). Paul's teaching steers between both errors. The powers are real — personal, intelligent, malevolent.

But they are defeated — operating under the authority of the risen Christ who has already triumphed over them. The Christian response is neither to ignore them nor to be paralyzed by them, but to stand — in the truth, in righteousness, in the gospel, in faith, in salvation, in the word of God, and in unceasing prayer. This is neither the naivety of the denier nor the anxiety of the obsessed. It is the steady, armoured confidence of those who know their Commander.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might.

Finally. The last section of the letter (vv. 10–20) gathers everything up. The church, God’s new people (chapter 2), called to unity (chapter 4) and holiness (chapters 4–5), living the gospel at home and at work (5:21–6:9), is in a spiritual war. And look at what Paul has just been talking about: telling the truth, anger, honest work, words, husbands and wives, parents and children, employers and workers. Then: finally, be strong. The armour is not issued for a separate arena of spiritual specialists. It is issued for that one. The war is fought over whether a man speaks kindly to his wife on a Thursday evening.

Be strong in the Lord. The verb is passive: be strengthened, go on being made strong. It is the second great passive command in a few paragraphs: be filled with the Spirit (5:18), be strengthened in the Lord (6:10). And nobody says “be strong” to a strong person. The command assumes weakness; if you felt you do not have what it asks for, you have understood it. The strength is issued, not mustered. And it is “in the Lord”: not a substance poured into you that runs low, but a position, the phrase this letter has used more than any other. Strength here is a matter of where you are standing, which is why the chapter’s whole demand will be that you do not move.

And in the strength of his might. Paul uses three words for power that he used in 1:19–20, of the power that raised Christ from the dead and seated him above all powers. So the strength on offer is not a general assurance that God will help you cope. It is measured, and the measure is a resurrection. The power that brought a dead man out of a sealed tomb is named here, and its direction is towards us who believe.

What it does not mean. Not “try harder” or “be strong in yourself”. Self-confidence is the first thing to fall in spiritual battle (1 Corinthians 10:12). The command is to rely on the Lord’s strength, which is made perfect in our weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9–10; Isaiah 40:29–31).

In a sentence. Finally, be strengthened by the Lord and by his mighty power.

On a Tuesday. When the hard thing arrives this week, the dreaded conversation, the old temptation, the unexpected news, watch where your mind goes in the first three seconds: to your own competence and record, or to him? Most of us supply ourselves first and pray afterwards. Paul’s order is the other way round, and it is a relief: the strength was never going to come from where you keep looking first.

For worship. The Lord in whom we are told to be strong was himself crucified in weakness, and lives by the power of God (2 Corinthians 13:4). He went down into the weakest place there is and came up holding all authority, and he does not stand back to watch his people struggle. He gives the order and supplies what it requires, lending his own risen strength to hands that shake. Paul, who had every natural reason to trust his own, could only say: I thank him who has given me strength, Christ Jesus our Lord (1 Timothy 1:12). Every Christian still standing at the end will say the same.

verseByVerse.quote: Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil. For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil. For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places.

Put on. The clothing picture again (4:22–24): putting on the new self, and now the armour. The armour is not an extra added to the Christian life; it is the Christian life itself, lived in Christ.

The whole armour of God. Panoplia: the full equipment of a heavily armed soldier, from which comes our word panoply. Not selected pieces, but the whole kit. Paul may have looked at the Roman soldier chained to him (Acts 28:16, 20) as he wrote. But the picture comes first from Isaiah, where the LORD saw that there was no one to intercede, and put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head (Isaiah 59:16–17), and where the Messiah wears righteousness and faithfulness as his belt (Isaiah 11:5). The armour of God is God’s own armour, worn first by Christ and now given to his people.

That you may be able to stand. The aim is to stand, to hold one’s ground, not to advance and conquer new territory. Christ has already won (1:20–22; Colossians 2:15). The church holds the ground he has won.

Against the schemes of the devil. “Schemes” (methodeia, our methods) are strategies, patient cunning (4:14). The devil rarely attacks head-on. He accuses: the accuser of our brothers (Revelation 12:10), whose verdict, God could not love someone who did what you did, leaves believers going over sins the cross has already settled. He deceives with near-truths, beginning as in Eden with a question: did God actually say? (Genesis 3:1). He distracts, filling a life with good and neutral things until there is no room for prayer and Scripture. And he discourages, as with Elijah under the broom tree after his greatest victory (1 Kings 19). None of it is dramatic. A new believer, ashamed of a returning sin, stops telling anyone, reads his Bible less because he feels unclean, and drifts from his group: accused into silence. A committed professional keeps her rhythms the first year in a demanding job, misses church the second, and by the third lives as if God were absent: no attack anyone noticed, just the sum of reasonable compromises.

For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood. “Wrestle” (palē) is hand-to-hand combat, the Greek sport of wrestling: close, personal and exhausting. And the opponent is not flesh and blood, not human beings. Our real enemies are not the people who oppose us: the persecutor, the critic, the false teacher, the hostile government. They are captives of the enemy, people to be won (2 Timothy 2:25–26). Paul himself had been a persecutor.

But against the rulers, against the authorities. The same words as in 1:21 and 3:10: ranks of spiritual beings. In plain terms, what the Bible elsewhere calls the devil and his angels: personal, intelligent, organised in rank and command, whose hatred is aimed at God, at Christ and at his people. Not mere figures of speech for human evil or political systems, though they work through those.

Against the cosmic powers over this present darkness. Literally world-rulers of this darkness: evil spirits who influence this fallen world (2:2; John 12:31; 1 John 5:19). The Ephesians did not need persuading. They had seen the sons of Sceva, who tried to use the name of Jesus as a technique and were overpowered by the man they meant to help (Acts 19:13–16); converts burning their magic books in public; and a riot, stirred up by a silversmith whose trade in Artemis shrines was collapsing, that filled the theatre for two hours (Acts 19:23–41). These readers had watched the powers behave like something with a will.

Against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places. The heavenly places (see 1:3) are the unseen realm. Evil powers operate there, but Christ is seated far above them (1:20–21), and believers are seated with him (2:6). The battle is real, but it is fought from a throne already won.

What it does not mean. Not that every problem is directly caused by a demon, or that we are not responsible for our sins. The world, the flesh and the devil work together (2:1–3). There are two ways to go wrong. One is to empty the passage, treating the powers as a first-century way of talking about social pressures, so that nothing is really there and the armour is a metaphor for trying harder. The other is to become preoccupied: detecting a demon behind every difficulty, treating depression, illness, marital strain or plain sin as an attack requiring deliverance instead of a doctor, repentance or a hard conversation. Both take the soldier off his feet. C. S. Lewis warned of the same two errors: disbelieving in devils, and taking an excessive and unhealthy interest in them. Notice that Paul does not tell anyone to hunt these beings, address them, name them or bind them. He says put your armour on and stand.

Where Christians differ: spiritual warfare. Some deliverance ministries focus on identifying, naming and binding territorial spirits over cities, or casting demons out of believers. Others, influenced by modern scepticism, neglect the battle altogether. Verdict: the battle is real, but the weapons Paul names are not special techniques. They are the ordinary means of grace: truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, salvation, the word and prayer. A Christian doing those seven things is fully equipped whether or not he ever identifies one of his attackers. Can a Christian be possessed? No. A believer is indwelt by the Holy Spirit and sealed as God’s own (1:13–14); God has delivered us from the domain of darkness (Colossians 1:13); and he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4). A Christian can be tempted, deceived and attacked, and must resist; he cannot be owned or inhabited by a demon. And territorial spirits? Daniel shows that spiritual powers are bound up with earthly kingdoms (Daniel 10:13), but Daniel did not name or bind them; he prayed and fasted, and an angel did the fighting. Scripture never commands believers to map or address such spirits.

Should I speak to the devil, or rebuke him by name? Scripture gives little encouragement to it. Even the archangel Michael would not pronounce judgement on the devil himself, but said, The Lord rebuke you (Jude 1:9). Jesus did speak to Satan in the wilderness, briefly, and only with Scripture (Matthew 4:10). The New Testament’s instruction is not to address the enemy but to resist him: submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you (James 4:7). Notice the order: submitting to God comes first. So when you sense an attack, turn and talk to your Father, not to your accuser. Confess any sin, take hold of a promise, say it aloud, and get on with the next act of obedience. The devil is not moved by the volume of our commands, but he cannot stand against Christ, in whom you stand.

In a sentence. Put on the full armour God gives, so that you can stand firm against the devil’s schemes; for our fight is not against human beings, but against the rulers, the authorities, the powers of this dark world and the evil spiritual forces in the heavenly realms.

On a Tuesday. The colleague who opposes you, the family member who mocks your faith, is not your enemy. Pray for them, and resist the one behind the scenes.

For worship. Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, and yet the victory over the powers was won in flesh and blood. Since the children share in flesh and blood, the Son of God took the same nature, so that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil (Hebrews 2:14). The Divine Warrior who once put on righteousness as a breastplate put on a human body, met the tempter in the wilderness with nothing but the word of God, and at the cross broke the grip of the rulers and authorities. Every power in the heavenly places now lies beneath the feet of a man with nail-scars, and he will not lose one of those the Father has given him (John 6:39).
verseByVerse.note: Paul may have written with a Roman soldier guarding him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore take up the whole armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand firm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore take up the whole armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand firm.

Therefore. Because the enemy is real and powerful (v. 12). A soldier told he faces a trained, organised, heavily armed enemy does not debate whether to put on his armour.

Take up. Paul changes the verb. In verse 11 it was put on, the word for getting dressed. Here it is take up (analabete): a soldier shouldering his equipment at the call to battle. The first is about how you live; the second about what you do when you realise you are in it. And the purpose is that you may be able to withstand (antistēnai), to stand against the attack, the root of resist the devil (James 4:7; 1 Peter 5:9).

The whole armour of God. And it is of God, which answers the anxiety this chapter always raises. Every piece, followed back, is a description of God himself before it is a description of you: his truth, his righteousness, his gospel, his salvation, his word. You are not asked to manufacture six spiritual qualities and hope they are strong enough. You are handed his.

In the evil day. Two senses. The whole present age is evil (5:16; Galatians 1:4): we are always at war. But within it come particular days, and they rarely announce themselves. Sometimes it is the obvious thing: the phone call at an odd hour, the scan, the sentence from a spouse that reorganises everything. Quite as often it is not a catastrophe at all: the afternoon a temptation arrives with a force it has never had; the week God goes silent and prayer feels like talking to the ceiling. Jesus himself faced such hours (Luke 4:13; 22:53). And note the order: take up the armour that you may be able to withstand in that day. Nobody has ever put on armour during an assault. So the weight of this verse falls on ordinary days. What holds a Christian upright in a crisis is the reading done in unremarkable weeks, the praying that became a habit before it was needed, the confession kept short, the friends who already had permission to ask hard questions.

And having done all, to stand firm. Having done everything needed, having put on the armour and fought, the aim is to stand. Consider how modest that is. Paul has described a cosmic war and issued a full set of divine armour, and the objective, stated four times in this paragraph and never upgraded, is that you should still be on your feet at the end. Not that you should have won or seen results; that you should not have fallen over. There are years in which nothing gets better: the marriage is still hard, the depression has not lifted, the prayer is still unanswered. Paul’s word for a man in that condition, if he is still there, still believing, still coming back, is victory. Standing is not a consolation prize. It is the objective.

The hour of darkness. There was one evil day above all others. In Gethsemane Jesus said to those who came for him, this is your hour, and the power of darkness (Luke 22:53). Every power this passage names was given its moment and spent it on him: betrayal, desertion, false witness, mockery and the cross. He had prayed while his friends slept, he went into that day equipped, and he stood. When it was over he had not fallen; he had finished (John 19:30). Our evil days are small beside his, and they are fought on ground he has already held.

What it does not mean. Not that believers can lose their salvation if they fail to stand. God keeps his people (1:13–14; John 10:28–29), and he keeps them precisely by giving them this armour and the will to wear it. But neither may believers be careless: God’s keeping works through our watchful perseverance, not apart from it.

Should I pray on the armour, piece by piece, every morning? You may, and many Christians find it a helpful pattern, so long as it never becomes a charm, as though forgetting the words left you unprotected. The armour is not put on by naming it but by doing what each piece means. So ten quiet minutes in the morning might look like this: read a passage of Scripture and carry one verse into the day (the sword); confess anything specific, and thank God that you stand in Christ’s righteousness, not your own (the breastplate); resolve to be honest in everything today (the belt); remind yourself of the gospel in a sentence (the shoes and the helmet); and ask for help with the temptation or worry you can already see coming (the shield). Then on Monday at eleven, when the email lands, you will have something in your hand. Armour is worn by being used.

In a sentence. So take up the full armour of God, so that when the day of evil comes you can hold your ground, and when you have done everything, still be standing.

On a Tuesday. Think of the last truly hard thing that happened to you. What did you actually reach for on the first day: distraction, someone to agree with you, the same three thoughts on a loop? That is not a verdict on your faith. It is a report on your ordinary weeks, and you can change it starting this one.

For worship. You are not asked to take ground; it was taken, and you are asked only to stand on it. The armour is God’s own, and so is the standing: the one who stood in the hour of darkness now keeps those who stand in him. He is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy (Jude 24). When the last evil day is over, every one of his soldiers will be found on their feet, not because they held on well but because he held them, and the glory of every one still standing is his.

verseByVerse.quote: Stand therefore, having fastened on the belt of truth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stand therefore, having fastened on the belt of truth,

Stand therefore. The fourth “stand” (see v. 13). In the Greek it is the main verb, and what follows, having fastened, having put on, having shod, taking up, hangs from it. So the armour is not a row of tasks to complete before you are allowed to stand; it describes what standing consists of. A man wearing these things is a man standing.

Having fastened on the belt. Literally having girded your loins. A Roman soldier wore a tunic under his armour. Before fighting he gathered it up and tucked it into a strong leather belt, so it would not catch, and the belt also held the sword and the lower armour in place. Without it, everything else hung loose. In the Bible, girding the loins means getting ready for action (Exodus 12:11; 1 Peter 1:13).

Of truth. Isaiah says the Messiah will wear faithfulness as the belt of his loins (Isaiah 11:5). Two sides: the truth of God’s word, the gospel (1:13; 4:21), and personal truthfulness, integrity, an undivided life (4:25). And truth here has a face: the truth is in Jesus (4:21), who said, I am the truth (John 14:6). So fastening this belt is not chiefly an intellectual achievement. It is staying close to a Person, and letting his account of things overrule yours.

Why first? Because of who the enemy is. Jesus named his native language: he is a liar and the father of lies (John 8:44). Deception is almost his whole armoury. Accusation is a lie about your standing; temptation a lie about what will satisfy you; discouragement a lie about what God is doing. So the first piece answers the first thing thrown at you. A man who cannot tell what is true will not know he is being attacked at all.

The relief of one story. Integrity is a demand, but it is first a relief. A man maintaining two versions of himself is running two systems at once: remembering which account he gave to whom, steering conversations away from certain subjects, never fully present with people who love him. He is tired in a way sleep does not touch. David, having lived a lie for most of a year, said his bones wasted away (Psalm 32:3). A man with one story has nothing to maintain. And the belt carried the scabbard: the sword, the word of God (v. 17), hangs from it. A man whose life is not true will find Scripture will not come to hand when he needs it, because he cannot draw with conviction on a word he is not living in. The enemy has nothing to say to a man with nothing to hide.

What it does not mean. Not that we must have every theological question answered before we can stand. The belt is the central truth of the gospel, held firmly, and an honest life. Nor is it cold intellectualism: truth is held in love (4:15). And you cannot tighten what you cannot see. Self-deception is the one lie that arrives already believed (Jeremiah 17:9), which is why David asks God to teach him wisdom in the secret heart (Psalm 51:6), and why in practice the belt usually needs another person: someone in your life with permission to tell you what they see.

In a sentence. Stand firm, then, with the belt of truth fastened round your waist,

On a Tuesday. Almost nobody reading this tells outright lies. Watch instead for shading over the next seven days: the figure rounded in your favour, the false impression you noticed forming and did not correct, “I never got your message”, the story of the meeting in which you come out slightly better than you did. Count them instead of defending them. The belt loosens a notch at a time, and every notch is deniable.

For worship. When Pilate asked, What is truth? (John 18:38), the Truth was standing in front of him, bound, accused by false witnesses and silent before them. He who could not lie let lies be told about him until they had nailed him to a cross, and he did not bend one word to save himself. So the belt we fasten is woven from his faithfulness, not ours. He has never deceived anyone and never will. He knows every story we have told about ourselves, the true one and the shaded ones, and he has not withdrawn his love; and in him liars are given one true story to live in, which is his.
verseByVerse.note: The soldier’s belt held his tunic and sword in place.

parallels.desc: righteousness shall be the belt of his waist

verseByVerse.quote: and having put on the breastplate of righteousness,
verseByVerse.commentary:
and having put on the breastplate of righteousness,

The breastplate. Not a decorative plate but twenty to thirty pounds of iron on the torso, with one job: keeping iron out of the heart and lungs. A soldier could fight on with most wounds; what no soldier survived was a blade through the chest. So the piece tells you where Paul thinks the serious blows land: not on your comfort or reputation, but on the heart, the centre from which the whole life is run: keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life (Proverbs 4:23).

Of righteousness. Again from Isaiah 59:17, where the LORD puts on righteousness as a breastplate when he comes to save. Righteousness means being right with God and doing what is right. Which does Paul mean?

1. Imputed righteousness. The righteousness of Christ credited to believers by faith (Romans 3:21–26; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). And here is why it matters. The shield (v. 16) is for darts, and darts are lies. But not every accusation against a Christian is a lie. The charge that undoes people is very rarely a fabrication. It is a fact, correctly dated, brought up at the worst moment: you did that; you know you did. There is nothing in it to refute, which is exactly why it works. A defence that depends on the charge being untrue fails the first time the charge is true. This is what the breastplate is for. Watch how Paul handles the same moment: who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died (Romans 8:33–34). He does not say nobody has anything on you. He names who is on the bench and who is at the right hand. The breastplate does not argue about the charge sheet; it stands between the charge sheet and your heart, and it is made of somebody else’s obedience.

2. Practical righteousness. A life of holiness and integrity (4:24; 5:9). If the plate is Christ’s, what does my own holiness protect? Not your standing; that never rested on it. What deliberate, unconfessed sin costs you is your confidence, the thing that keeps a man on his feet: the foothold of 4:27, given and then occupied. The plate is his; the straps are yours, and a man in excellent armour can still leave a buckle undone. And notice that the Roman kit had nothing for the back. Every piece faces forward. There is no provision anywhere for a man who turns and runs.

Verdict: both. Imputed righteousness is the foundation: our standing before God rests on Christ alone. Practical righteousness flows from it and protects us in the daily fight. One answers the accuser; the other gives him no opening.

What it does not mean. Not that we must achieve a perfect life before we can resist the devil. The breastplate is first Christ’s righteousness, given as a gift. When we fail, the remedy is not to give up but to confess and stand again in Christ’s righteousness (1 John 1:9; 2:1–2). And armour is not a feeling. Iron does not feel like anything; you find out it was there when the blow lands and you are still standing. The accused man who keeps returning to the God he has offended is demonstrating the breastplate, not lacking it. But the reverse guard holds too: a man who reasons that the plate is Christ’s and so the buckles do not matter has misread the sentence. What is denied is that your record covers you, not that your conduct matters.

In a sentence. with the breastplate of righteousness in place,

On a Tuesday. Write down the worst true thing about yourself. Now ask what you would want said in your defence if it were read aloud before God. Every answer that begins “but I also gave, served, stayed, tried” is cardboard, and will go through like paper. The only answer that holds does not mention you at all.

For worship. At the decisive battle, the Divine Warrior of Isaiah 59 went out wearing none of it: no breastplate, nothing over the chest. And a soldier put a spear into his side (John 19:34), at exactly the height the plate would have covered. He went unarmoured at the one point Paul tells you never to leave open. That is where your breastplate came from. He had nothing over his heart, so that you would.

parallels.desc: he put on righteousness as a breastplate

verseByVerse.ref: v. 15 — The Shoes of the Gospel of Peace
verseByVerse.quote: and, as shoes for your feet, having put on the readiness given by the gospel of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and, as shoes for your feet, having put on the readiness given by the gospel of peace.

As shoes for your feet. Roman soldiers wore the caliga, a heavy sandal-boot with thick leather soles studded with nails, for grip on rough or slippery ground. In close combat the enemy is first trying not to wound you but to knock you off balance, because a man who has lost his footing can be finished at leisure; and in a Roman line, one man who slipped opened a gap, and gaps are where lines break. That is how the attacks of this chapter work. They rarely come as an argument you cannot answer. They come as a shove: an accusation, a disappointment, a fear.

Having put on the readiness. “Readiness” (hetoimasia) can mean preparedness to move, or a prepared base, a firm footing. Two readings: (1) the stability the gospel gives, so that we stand without slipping; or (2) readiness to go and share the gospel. Verdict: the context of standing (vv. 11–14) favours firm footing first; but those who stand firm on the gospel of peace are also ready to share it. A man with no footing cannot go anywhere, and a man going nowhere did not need boots.

Given by the gospel of peace. Isaiah supplies the picture: how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace … who says to Zion, Your God reigns (Isaiah 52:7). A city waits on the outcome of a battle fought out of sight, and then a runner comes over the ridge, and long before he can be heard the watchmen can tell from the way he runs what he carries. The herald is not proposing terms; he is reporting a result, settled before he set off. That is what gospel means. And this letter has already named the first herald: Christ himself came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near (2:17), on feet that would be nailed to a cross to make the peace he announced. When Christians lose their footing in evangelism, it is often because they think they are arguing a case that might be lost, instead of running with a report that is already true. The gospel announces peace with God through Christ’s death (2:14–17; Romans 5:1), and peace between people once divided. The paradox: we fight wearing shoes made of peace. We do not fight to win peace; we fight because our own war is over and we stand on the settlement.

Peace with God, and feeling peaceful. A believer unsure of his standing has no footing, and an anxious reader may hear: if you do not feel peaceful, you do not have the shoes on. That is not Paul’s meaning. Peace with God (Romans 5:1) is not a mood but a state of affairs: the ending of a war, declared from the other side, on the basis of what Christ did. The peace of God (Philippians 4:7) is a felt thing, and it comes and goes with sleep, health and circumstance. You can have the first at full strength while feeling almost none of the second. A treaty ends a war whether or not the soldiers feel calm that morning, and a Christian lying awake at three in the morning with a tight chest is standing on ground not one inch less solid. And note the verb: we have peace with God. Signed, and not by you.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians are aggressive towards people: the gospel we carry is a gospel of peace, and our war is against the devil, not human beings (v. 12). And “readiness” is not a rebuke telling you to hunt conversations. Peter says, always being prepared to make a defence to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you (1 Peter 3:15). Asks: the initiative may well not be yours.

In a sentence. and with your feet fitted with the readiness that comes from the gospel of peace.

On a Tuesday. Watch how your sense of God’s attitude towards you moves across two weeks: after a good week, does he seem nearer? After a week of the usual failure, further off? If his disposition seems to move with your performance, you are not standing on the treaty but on your record, the one surface that will not hold you when you most need it. And test your readiness: could you say in three sentences, without church vocabulary, what the good news is and what it has done to you?

For worship. The oldest promise in the Bible is about feet: the woman’s offspring would crush the serpent’s head, though his own heel would be struck (Genesis 3:15). Christ took that wound at the cross and struck that blow, and Paul tells the church at Rome that the God of peace will soon share the victory with them, putting Satan beneath their feet as well (Romans 16:20). So the feet the enemy keeps trying to sweep from under us, shod with the gospel of peace, are the very feet God means to set on his head. Our Captain has won the war, and he does not keep the triumph to himself.
verseByVerse.note: Roman soldiers wore sturdy studded sandals for a firm footing.

parallels.desc: the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace

verseByVerse.quote: In all circumstances take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In all circumstances take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one.

In all circumstances. Or “in addition to all these”, “over all these”. The physical picture supports the second. The great shield was not strapped to the body; it was held out in front, and everything else was behind it. Faith is not the fourth item of six; it is the piece held in front of all the others. And the verb changes. The first three pieces are put on, worn even in camp; from now on they are taken up. A soldier off duty kept his belt and boots on, but his shield was stacked and had to be seized when the alarm went.

The shield. Not a small round shield, but the Roman scutum: a large rectangular shield, about four feet tall and two and a half feet wide, wood covered with leather, covering the whole body. Soldiers could lock their shields side by side and overhead into a wall, the “tortoise” formation, protecting the whole unit. Faith is not only individual: believers protect one another.

Of faith. Faith is trust in God: in his character, his promises and his Son. Not faith in faith, or confidence in ourselves, but trust in God himself (Psalm 18:30; 1 John 5:4).

With which you can extinguish. Before battle, soldiers soaked the leather in water, so that burning arrows were put out when they struck. And this letter has already named the soaking: the washing of water with the word (5:26). The hide is soaked in Scripture over time, so that when the fire arrow lands there is already something in the leather that puts it out. Nobody soaks a shield while arrows are in the air, and that is the honest reason many Christians find their faith apparently useless at two in the morning. The shield was fine. It was dry.

All the flaming darts of the evil one. Arrows tipped with cloth soaked in pitch and set alight. A fire arrow does not need to hit anything vital. It only has to lodge somewhere and start something, and then the fire does what the arrow could not. That is how the thought at two in the morning works: one suggestion catches another until you lie there with a whole case built against yourself, or against God, that you would never have accepted as a single sentence. The darts are doubts about God’s goodness (Genesis 3:1), accusations that you are beyond forgiveness, sudden temptations, fears, despair, blasphemous thoughts. And “all”: there is no dart faith cannot put out.

How faith extinguishes. By answering the lie with God’s truth. When the dart says, God does not love you, faith answers: he loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20). When it says, you are too sinful, faith answers: there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1).

What it does not mean. Not that a believer who has fiery thoughts is failing. The arrival of the thought is not your sin; you did not fire it. A dart that has struck the shield has not entered you, and the blasphemous, filthy or despairing thing that lands out of nowhere is not evidence of what you secretly are. It becomes yours only when you agree with it and give it a place to burn (see 5:3). The horror you feel at it is not the sound of a man being exposed. It is the sound of the shield. Nor must faith be strong to work. A door of oak and hide stops an arrow because of what it is made of, not because of how confidently it is held. Faith has never saved anyone; it is the empty hand that takes hold of Christ, and its whole strength is on loan from what it holds. Weak faith in a strong Christ is safe. That is why Jesus spoke of faith like a grain of mustard seed (Matthew 17:20), and why the most useful prayer in the Gospels came from a father whose faith was failing in public: I believe; help my unbelief! (Mark 9:24). Jesus did not send him away to work on his conviction. He healed the boy.

In a sentence. In every situation take up the shield of faith, with which you can put out all the burning arrows of the evil one.

On a Tuesday. Most Christians are not shot at randomly; they are hit by the same two or three arrows for thirty years: you are a fraud; God is disappointed in you; nothing will ever change; you have already ruined it. Write down the one sentence that lands most often, in the words it uses on you. Unnamed, it feels like the truth; written down, it looks like what it is. Then find the verse that answers it and learn it before the next time. And do not carry it alone. There will be a stretch of your life when you cannot lift your shield at all. Be somewhere other people are holding theirs.

For worship. On the night Satan demanded to have the disciples, to sift them like wheat, Jesus told Peter: I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail (Luke 22:31–32). Peter’s shield dropped that night, and still his faith did not finally fail, because it was held from the other side. The same Lord always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). The hand that lifts the shield is weak; the hand that holds that hand is not. Every fiery dart ever put out in a believer’s life has been put out under the prayers of Christ.
verseByVerse.note: The Roman shield was large, about four feet tall, wood covered with leather; soldiers could lock shields into a wall.

parallels.desc: he is a shield for all those who take refuge in him

verseByVerse.quote: and take the helmet of salvation,
verseByVerse.commentary:
and take the helmet of salvation,

And take. The verb (dexasthe) means receive, accept what is being handed to you. You do not forge a helmet. It is issued, and the soldier’s whole responsibility is to put out his hands and take it. Salvation is God’s gift (2:8).

The helmet. Bronze or iron, with cheek-pieces, protecting the head, the seat of thought and decision. A blow that did not kill could still stun a soldier and leave him helpless. Despair is a head wound. It rarely kills a Christian outright; it persuades him that standing is pointless, and a man who believes that will put his shield down himself.

Of salvation. Again from Isaiah 59:17. Paul takes the armour off the Divine Warrior himself, who armed himself because there was no one else to fight, and buckles it onto ordinary Christians in Ephesus. In 1 Thessalonians 5:8 he calls it the hope of salvation. Salvation has three tenses: we have been saved (2:5, 8), are being kept, and will be saved at the day of redemption (4:30). The helmet covers the mind with all three: he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6).

Why the mind? The devil attacks the mind with doubt: are you really saved? Will you really make it? Is any of this true? The helmet guards the mind with the knowledge that salvation is God’s work, not ours, and is secure. A soldier who knows the outcome of the war is already settled fights differently from one who fears defeat.

Salvation has a name. In the end the helmet is not a doctrine but a Person. The angel told Joseph, you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21), and old Simeon, holding the baby in the temple, said, my eyes have seen your salvation (Luke 2:30). So the helmet guards the head with what Christ has done, is doing and will do: he died and rose, he keeps his people now, and he will appear a second time to save those who are eagerly waiting for him (Hebrews 9:28). A believer whose thoughts are reeling needs, before any argument, to lift his eyes to the one whose name means the LORD saves.

Where assurance comes from. God intends you to have it. John wrote a letter so that you may know that you have eternal life (1 John 5:13). Assurance is not over-confidence to be discouraged in case it makes people careless; it is normal Christian health. It comes from three places, and anxious believers usually have the order backwards. First and chiefly, the promise of God, which stands outside you and does not move: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37). Second, the witness of the Spirit, who bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God (Romans 8:16): not usually a voice, but the settled instinct that makes a frightened person say Father. Third, the evidences of grace in a changed life. That third is genuine and Scripture uses it (2 Peter 1:10), but it is the only one that looks inward, and the least readable when you are lowest, and it is the one a troubled Christian spends all night on. A man who keeps digging up the seed to see whether it has sprouted ends with no plant and no assurance. Look at Christ first and yourself third.

When assurance has gone. Ask honestly which of two things has happened. Sometimes there is something specific, done, or left undone, or being quietly kept, and the conscience is doing its proper work. The answer is not more introspection but confession, and the relief is often immediate. But sometimes there is nothing specific, only fog. Then remember that the soul is attached to a body. Grief, exhaustion, illness and depression all lie, in your own voice, about God’s attitude towards you. A Christian who has not slept properly for a fortnight should be very slow to trust his own assessment of his standing before God. God sent an angel to Elijah under the broom tree with food and a second sleep before one word of correction (1 Kings 19:5–8).

What it does not mean. Not presumption, the careless assumption that nothing matters because God will sort it out. Assurance is held by faith and confirmed by a changed life. Nor does it mean believers never struggle with doubt: the helmet is given precisely because they will.

In a sentence. Take the helmet of salvation,

On a Tuesday. Finish this sentence honestly, with the first thing that comes: when ______ happens, I will be all right. When the scan is clear; when he calls; when the money is in place. Whatever fills the blank is what is actually on your head, and every one of those can be taken by a phone call. The helmet Paul gives is the one piece whose content lies entirely in the future and entirely beyond the reach of anything that can happen to you this week. My salvation does not depend on my grip on God, but on his grip on me (John 10:28–29).

For worship. Salvation belongs to the LORD (Jonah 2:9), from first to last. He chose us before the foundation of the world, he holds us now, and he will finish what he began, and nothing that happens to the one wearing his helmet can dent it. When our heads are bowed with fear and fog, he is our glory and the lifter of our heads (Psalm 3:3), and he lifts them gently, for he knows our frame and remembers that we are dust (Psalm 103:14). The day of redemption is fixed, and on it he will crown the heads he has guarded all along.

parallels.desc: a helmet of salvation on his head

verseByVerse.ref: v. 17b — The Sword of the Spirit
verseByVerse.quote: and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God,

The sword. Machaira: the Roman short sword, about the length of your forearm, made for close combat. It is the only offensive weapon in the list. And its size tells you where it is meant to be used: not chiefly as a missile fired at the culture from a safe distance, but in the fight eighteen inches from your face: the lie that has just arrived in your own head, the conversation you are actually in, the thing you are about to talk yourself into. God has issued a weapon of exactly that reach.

Of the Spirit. The sword is the Spirit’s. He breathed out the word (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21) and makes it effective in hearts: it is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword (Hebrews 4:12). The hand on your arm and the blade in your hand come from the same Person, which is why the sword cannot be used against him: the man who uses Scripture to justify what grieves the Spirit finds the blade has an edge on both sides. The word without the Spirit is a sword in an untrained hand; the Spirit without the word is feeling cut loose from truth.

Which is the word of God. This is the only piece Paul stops to explain. He uses rhēma, often a word spoken, a particular saying: Scripture applied to a particular attack. Jesus showed how in the wilderness. Three times he was tempted, and three times he answered, It is written (Matthew 4:1–11), and all three answers come from Deuteronomy 6–8, Moses’ sermon about Israel’s forty years in the wilderness: hunger, testing, and how Israel failed at exactly those points. So here is the Son of God, in a wilderness, forty days hungry, tempted where Israel collapsed, answering from the very passage that records the collapse. He fought that lost battle again on the same ground, and won. And he won the most concentrated assault in history with about three chapters of one book. You do not need to have mastered sixty-six books before the sword is any use. You need to truly possess some of it.

Scripture corrected by Scripture. In the second temptation the devil quotes Scripture too, Psalm 91, torn from its setting. Jesus does not say the psalm is wrong; he says, Again it is written (Matthew 4:7), and gives another text. A promise lifted out of context and turned into a lever to make God serve your plans is answered by the rest of the Bible. That is why the whole of it must be read, and why a Christian who knows only his favourite verses carries a weapon that can be taken from him.

Defensive and offensive. The sword parries attacks, as Jesus did. But it also advances: through the preaching of the word, captives are set free (Acts 26:18). Every time the gospel is preached and someone believes, the sword has struck. It does not always bring instant results, but it does not return empty (Isaiah 55:11).

What it does not mean. Not a magic formula, as if quoting verses works automatically. The sword must be understood and used rightly, in the Spirit, with faith. Nor may Christians use the Bible as a club against people, to wound or win arguments. The enemy is the devil, not flesh and blood (v. 12).

In a sentence. and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

On a Tuesday. Jesus said the Spirit will bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you (John 14:26). He brings to remembrance; he does not bring to first acquaintance. He can hand you at two in the morning only what was put in by daylight. So take the verse that answers the dart you named at verse 16, and carry it until it is yours; one verse truly learned in a month is worth fifty attempted in January and dropped by February. And say it aloud when the attack comes. Jesus did not think his answers; he spoke them. A lie answered silently is just two thoughts meeting in one tired head. A word of God spoken aloud is something entering the room from outside you. It feels absurd for about four seconds, and then it does not.

For worship. Of the six pieces, five are silent: they simply hold. The last thing God puts in your hand is the only one that speaks, and it is his own voice: the voice that said, Let there be light, and has spoken to us in these last days by his Son (Hebrews 1:2). The Word who became flesh answered the liar with it in the wilderness, and he will at last slay the lawless one with the breath of his mouth (2 Thessalonians 2:8). The enemy’s whole method is speech, and God has answered him with a better word, and put it in a trembling believer’s hand.
verseByVerse.note: The Roman sword was a short blade for close combat.

parallels.desc: he made my mouth like a sharp sword

verseByVerse.quote: praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication. To that end, keep alert with all perseverance, making supplication for all the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication. To that end, keep alert with all perseverance, making supplication for all the saints,

Praying at all times. The grammar ties prayer to the whole armour: the soldier stands, armed, praying. Prayer is not a seventh piece; it is the air the armoured soldier breathes, how he stays in touch with his commander and draws on reinforcements he cannot produce in the field. Paul says “all” four times: all times, all prayer, all perseverance, all the saints. No moment is outside prayer, no form excluded, no believer beyond its reach (1 Thessalonians 5:17; Luke 18:1). The believer who prays only under pressure has already lost the battle of the ordinary days.

In the Spirit. Some take this to mean praying in tongues, and there are verses that lend themselves to that reading (Jude 20; 1 Corinthians 14:15). But this letter has already shown what Paul means: through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father (2:18). Prayer is to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit: the whole Trinity involved in one person saying one sentence in his kitchen. To pray in the Spirit is to pray as someone given access by the Spirit and helped by him while he prays: we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us (Romans 8:26–27). Halting prayer is therefore not second-rate prayer; it is prayer in which the weakness has already been allowed for.

With all prayer and supplication. Every kind of prayer: praise, thanks, confession. And “supplication” (deēsis) is the particular request arising from a particular need. That is the warrant for praying specifically. Name the person, the job, the scan, the son, the sum of money. God is not honoured by vagueness, and prayer that risks nothing specific can never be seen to be answered, which may be part of its appeal.

To that end, keep alert. Stay awake, like a sentry at night (agrypnountes). And what does a praying sentry watch? The ground he has been given. Which friend has gone quiet in the last two months. Which marriage in your church has changed its tone. Which man has stopped coming and has not been asked why. Which of your children answered a question this week in a way not quite like him. Most of this never becomes a conversation; it becomes prayer. The person you pray for may not know what he is in the middle of, and your prayer may be the shield he does not know he is standing behind.

The one who stayed awake. In Gethsemane only one person kept watch. Jesus asked three friends to stay awake with him, and three times he found them sleeping (Mark 14:37–41). He prayed alone, with honest request and with surrender: remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will (Mark 14:36). And his prayer for all the saints did not wait for his friends to wake: earlier that night he had prayed for them, and for all who would believe in him through their word (John 17:20). The church keeps watch in prayer because it was saved by the one who stayed awake.

With all perseverance. Do not give up. Jesus told a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart (Luke 18:1–8): a widow with no money and no standing, against a judge who neither feared God nor respected man, and her one asset was that she would not go away. And she won. Jesus is not saying God must be worn down. He argues from worse to better: if persistence achieves that with a corrupt official, what will it do with a Father who is neither corrupt nor indifferent? The widow persists because the judge is unwilling; you persist because the Father is not. And the danger Jesus names is not that God will fail to answer, but that we will lose heart, that the praying will quietly stop in the third or fourth year. Perseverance is the refusal to conclude from a decade of silence that he is not listening, even for the name that has been on your list for eleven years.

Making supplication for all the saints. The battle is fought together. Each believer prays for others and is prayed for; a soldier who fights alone is easily picked off. Paul has modelled this in his own prayers (1:15–23; 3:14–21).

What it does not mean. Not that “praying in the Spirit” means only praying in tongues; every believer is called to pray in the Spirit. Nor does “at all times” mean continuous words. It means a heart turned towards God through the day, and regular, persevering times of prayer. And it is not a vending machine: Scripture deals honestly with the prayer that receives a no (2 Corinthians 12:8–9).

What does praying at all times look like for a busy parent? Mostly short, honest prayers woven through the day, held together by a little time set apart. With small children you may never get an unbroken half-hour, and God knows it. So pray as you go: a sentence during the nappy change, thanks over the washing-up, a cry for patience on the stairs, a blessing over a sleeping child. Nehemiah prayed in the moment between a king’s question and his own answer (Nehemiah 2:4–5). Tie prayer to things that happen anyway: the school run, the kettle, bath time. Then guard one small regular time, even five minutes before the house wakes or after it sleeps, with a Bible open. Pray aloud with your children too; they learn more from hearing you pray than from being told to. A tired parent’s scattered prayers are not second-class prayer; they are exactly what Paul means.
