In a sentence. Pray in the Spirit on every occasion, with every kind of prayer and request; with this in mind, stay alert and keep on praying for all the Lord’s people.

On a Tuesday. Most of us pray for a circle of people we like and people we are related to. Name three Christians you find difficult, the one who wearies you, the one who was unfair to you, the one whose views you find hard to sit near, and pray for their good by name this week. You will find it very hard to go on resenting someone you are asking God to bless.

For worship. The armour never made anyone self-sufficient, and God never meant it to. He has made his children a praying people, given access in one Spirit to the Father, so that the halting sentences of a tired believer are received in the throne room for the sake of the Son in whose name they are offered. And we are on the other side of this verse too: somebody prayed for you today, by name, and you will not know who in this life. The Father heard every one of those prayers, and some of what you call your own standing has been his answer to them all along.

verseByVerse.quote: and also for me, that words may be given to me in opening my mouth boldly to proclaim the mystery of the gospel, for which I am an ambassador in chains, that I may declare it boldly, as I ought to speak.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and also for me, that words may be given to me in opening my mouth boldly to proclaim the mystery of the gospel, for which I am an ambassador in chains, that I may declare it boldly, as I ought to speak.

And also for me. The great apostle asks ordinary believers to pray for him. He did not see himself as above needing their prayers, and every gospel worker needs the prayers of the church.

That words may be given to me. Even Paul needed help to speak. This is the man who was stoned at Lystra and left for dead (Acts 14:19), flogged five times and shipwrecked three times (2 Corinthians 11:24–25), who wanted to walk into a rioting theatre in Ephesus until his friends held him back (Acts 19:30–31). He asks a church to pray that he will not lose his nerve. Courage was not a feature of his temperament; it was supplied in answer to prayer. I was with you in weakness and in fear and much trembling, he told Corinth (1 Corinthians 2:3), and one night the Lord said to him there, Do not be afraid, but go on speaking (Acts 18:9), which no one says to a man who is not afraid. So if your mouth goes dry when the conversation turns, nerves are not the absence of the Spirit. The best-prepared man in the New Testament still needed the words given (Matthew 10:19).

In opening my mouth boldly. “Boldly” (en parrēsia, see 3:12): with freedom, frankness, courage. Paul was facing trial before Caesar (Acts 25:11–12; 28:16–31). He might have been tempted to soften the message to protect himself. He asks for courage to speak plainly.

To proclaim the mystery of the gospel. The mystery has a fixed meaning in this letter: that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, sharers in the promise (3:6). And that sentence is the reason he is in chains. The riot that ended his freedom began with the accusation that he had brought a Greek into the temple (Acts 21:27–29), and the crowd listened in silence until he reached the word Gentiles, and then demanded his death (Acts 22:21–22). He asks the church to pray that he will keep saying, boldly, the exact sentence that cost him his liberty and would soon cost him his life. Not that the chain would come off; that the mouth would stay open.

Openly, like his Lord. When Jesus stood before the high priest, he said, I have spoken openly to the world; I have said nothing in secret (John 18:20), and the word for openly is Paul’s word here, parrēsia. The Lord whom Paul represents faced his own trial without softening a sentence, and made the good confession before Pontius Pilate (1 Timothy 6:13). An ambassador says what his King says, in the way his King said it. And the mystery he announces is a Person: the mystery of Christ (3:4), crucified and risen, in whom Jew and Gentile are one body.

For which I am an ambassador in chains. A deliberate scandal. An ambassador was inviolable: to lay hands on another nation’s envoy was not a crime but an act of war. So “ambassador in chains” is a legal absurdity said aloud: the empire has manacled the representative of the King of kings, and so declared what it thinks of his King (2 Corinthians 5:20). The word for chain (halysis) was sometimes used of the ornamental chains ambassadors wore as a badge of office; Paul’s iron chain was his. It fastened him by the wrist to a soldier of the guard, in shifts, round the clock, and Paul says the result was that it became known throughout the whole imperial guard that his imprisonment was for Christ (Philippians 1:13). The chain meant to take him out of circulation delivered him a rotating audience of elite soldiers, one at a time, for years. It was not an interruption of the mission; it was a posting.

That I may declare it boldly, as I ought to speak. He repeats the request: it is what he most needs. “As I ought” is the language of obligation: necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel! (1 Corinthians 9:16). The boldness he wants is not bravado, but faithfulness to a commission he did not give himself and cannot resign.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul did not care about his release, or that praying for it is wrong (Philippians 1:19; Philemon 22). It is not a fault to ask for relief; it is a poverty to ask for nothing else. And God answered: Paul preached in Rome with all boldness and without hindrance (Acts 28:30–31).

In a sentence. Pray also for me, that whenever I open my mouth I will be given the words to make known boldly the mystery of the gospel, for which I am an ambassador in chains; pray that I may speak it fearlessly, as I should.

On a Tuesday. Write down the prayer requests you have actually given people in the last year. Sort them into two columns: things you wanted changed, and things you wanted to become or do inside what was not changing. For most of us the first column is nearly everything. Paul, facing a capital charge, asked for the second. And pray this for your pastor and for missionaries you know, by name: for words, for boldness, for clarity.

For worship. The King who sends ambassadors in chains once wore them himself: they bound Jesus and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate (Mark 15:1). The world laid hands on the one envoy whose person was truly sacred, and through that outrage God was reconciling the world to himself, and now sends his ambassadors to plead with it to be reconciled (2 Corinthians 5:19–20). No wonder his servants could ask for boldness in chains before release from them. The message was bought at such a cost that no prison can make it cheap, and the King who sent it is worth more than the message.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Tychicus, a dear brother and faithful servant, will tell them all Paul’s news and encourage them; that is why Paul is sending him. Paul ends with peace to the brothers and sisters, and love with faith from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, and grace to all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with undying love.
verseByVerse.theology:
Grace as the Alpha and Omega of the Christian Life

Ephesians begins with grace (1:2: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ”) and ends with grace (6:24: “Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ”). The entire letter is enclosed within this grace — and this is not merely a rhetorical device. It is a theological statement: the Christian life from first to last, from election before time began to the consummation of all things, is entirely an affair of grace. There is no moment in the Christian's experience that is not sustained by grace, no achievement that is not the fruit of grace, no prayer that is answered by anything other than grace.

The Reformed tradition has consistently defined grace as God's undeserved favour — not merely his assistance added to human effort, but his sovereign initiative in the face of human helplessness. Ephesians 2:8–9 defines salvation by grace through faith, with the explicit denial that this is our own doing. But grace is not only the initial gift; it is the sustaining reality of the entire Christian life. “I am what I am by the grace of God,” Paul writes to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 15:10). The letter to the Ephesians is the fullest exposition of what that grace is, what it has done, and what it looks like in the life of those who have received it.

Tychicus — the letter-carrier, the beloved brother, the faithful minister — is himself a theological figure in the ending of the letter. He represents the ordinary, faithful, unglamorous work of ministry that keeps the church alive between the apostolic moments: the friend who carries the letter, who brings the news, who comforts the worried flock. Every church is sustained by Tychicuses — people whose names are not famous, whose ministry is not spectacular, who are simply faithful. The letter that contains the most magnificent theology in the New Testament is delivered by one such person. Grace works through the ordinary.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul is in a Roman prison when he writes these final words. He may never see the Ephesians again. His benediction — “peace... love... faith... grace be with you” — is spoken over people he cannot reach with his hands or his presence, people he is releasing into the care of the God about whom he has been writing for six chapters.

This is what pastoral love looks like at its most costly and most beautiful: the shepherd who cannot be with his flock entrusting them to the Chief Shepherd, speaking blessing over them, sending them a trusted friend, and then releasing them in faith. Paul's imprisonment did not imprison his hope. The chains on his wrists did not chain the word of God (2 Timothy 2:9). The letter reached Ephesus. The grace it describes reached its readers. It reaches us still.

Now: “Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with love incorruptible.” The word translated “incorruptible” (aphtharsia) is the same word used for the resurrection body — imperishable, undying, not subject to decay. The love of the true believer for Christ is not a passing emotion or a seasonal feeling; it is something that has been planted by God in a soul that has been made alive in Christ, and it partakes of the imperishable quality of its Object.

This love will outlast every earthly thing. It will survive death, outlast time, and find its perfect and eternal fulfilment at the Marriage Supper of the Lamb. The letter ends with this love — and this love, in its countless expressions across the centuries, has carried the gospel from Rome to Ephesus to the ends of the earth, and to us. Grace to you. And peace. And love incorruptible.

verseByVerse.quote: So that you also may know how I am and what I am doing, Tychicus the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord will tell you everything. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are, and that he may encourage your hearts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So that you also may know how I am and what I am doing, Tychicus the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord will tell you everything. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are, and that he may encourage your hearts.

So that you also may know how I am. Read this as the Ephesians would. Their apostle, who had spent three years with them and wept with them at Miletus (Acts 20:31, 36–38), was in custody in Rome awaiting Nero’s judgement, and they had no way of finding out whether he was alive. No post, no messenger service, only rumour and distance and silence, and anyone who has waited for news of someone they love knows what that silence does at two in the morning. So Paul, the one in chains, spends his letter-carrier on their peace of mind.

Tychicus. A believer from the province of Asia (Acts 20:4), the region around Ephesus. He is named five times in the New Testament, and always he is going somewhere for somebody else. He travelled with Paul carrying the collection for Jerusalem; he carried this letter and Colossians (Colossians 4:7–8), probably with Onesimus and the letter to Philemon; later Paul sent him to Ephesus again (2 Timothy 4:12) and possibly to Crete (Titus 3:12). Not one sentence he wrote survives. And consider what he was holding on that road: the only copy in existence of the letter you have just read. If Tychicus had lost the bag or turned back, we would not have Ephesians. The most magnificent theology in the New Testament travelled to us in the hands of a man we know almost nothing about, and it arrived because he was reliable.

The beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord. Beloved: the language of family, not employment. A brother. And a faithful servant (diakonos), where the adjective matters most. Not gifted, impressive or eloquent: faithful, the quality of a man who does what he said he would, on the day he said, whether or not anyone is watching. It is the least glamorous word in the Christian vocabulary, and the one Scripture reaches for most when it wants to say a life counted.

Will tell you everything. Some news was better carried by word of mouth than written, especially for a prisoner whose letters might be read. But Tychicus is sent not only to inform them but to encourage your hearts: the verb (parakaleō) means to comfort, to come alongside, from the same family as the Spirit’s title, the Helper (John 14:16). He comes to steady them.

The Faithful One behind the faithful man. Tychicus is faithful in the Lord, and the phrase points past him to Christ, who was faithful to him who appointed him (Hebrews 3:2) and is called the faithful witness (Revelation 1:5). Tychicus would tell the church everything about Paul; Jesus said to his anxious friends, I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you (John 15:15). The church has never been left in the dark about its Lord. He sends news and messengers, and he came himself as the message.

What it does not mean. Not that these closing personal notes are unimportant because they contain no doctrine. They show that the great truths of chapters 1–3 are lived among real people, with names, journeys and concerns. God’s eternal purpose is enormous, and it moves at the speed of an ordinary man keeping his word.

In a sentence. Tychicus, our dear brother and faithful servant in the Lord, will tell you everything, so that you also may know how I am and what I am doing; I am sending him to you for this very purpose, so that you may know how we are and so that he may encourage you.

On a Tuesday. If you have quietly decided your part in the church is decorative, look at how this letter ends: the eternal purpose of God handed to an ordinary man for a journey. Every church is held up by people like Tychicus: the woman who has opened the building on Sunday mornings for nineteen years, the man who drives two elderly members to church and back and has never mentioned it. And most anxiety about those we love is caused not by bad news but by no news. Someone is quietly wondering about you and will not ask: tell them how you are. Someone else has gone silent: go and find out.

For worship. The God who planned salvation before the ages was pleased to send the letter of it in a travelling bag on a Roman road, in the hands of a brother we would otherwise never have heard of. He does his greatest work through the reliable and the unremarkable, and loses none of it on the way. And he has not left his anxious people waiting for news: Christ promised not to leave us as orphans, and sent the Helper to come alongside us (John 14:16–18), so that no believer in any century is without word from the throne.
verseByVerse.note: Tychicus came from the province of Asia and carried this letter and Colossians.

verseByVerse.quote: Peace be to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with love incorruptible.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peace be to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with love incorruptible.

Peace be to the brothers. “Brothers” includes sisters: the whole church family. And peace is not calm feelings; it has an address in this letter: the war ended at 2:14–17, where Christ himself is our peace, and the ground the soldier stood on eight verses ago (v. 15).

And love with faith. Faith and love together, as on the first page: your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints (1:15), and in the middle: that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, rooted and grounded in love (3:17). Beginning, centre and end. Paul is not adding a new thought at the door; he asks God to keep giving them what he thanked God for at the start. Faith works through love (Galatians 5:6).

From God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. The same two persons named in the opening greeting (1:2), as the single source of every blessing. The letter begins and ends with the Father and the Son.

Grace be with all. The last word of the letter, as of most of Paul’s letters, is grace. Grace began it (1:2), was lavished upon us (1:7–8), saved us (2:5, 8), was given even to the least of all the saints (3:8) and measured to each of us (4:7), and grace ends it. In four words Paul hands back everything six chapters have unfolded. And for six chapters he has said “you”; here he speaks about them: peace be to the brothers, grace be with all who love our Lord. Probably the letter was carried from church to church and read aloud in each; some of the oldest manuscripts lack the words in Ephesus at 1:1. The last blessing is pronounced over whoever is in the room when it is read. You are in the room.

Who love our Lord Jesus Christ. Paul could have described the people grace rests on in many ways, and says only one. Not all who have understood this letter, which after three chapters on election and the heavenly places would be a fair worry. Not those with their doctrine straight or their household in order or their armour buckled. All who love our Lord Jesus Christ. It is the lowest bar in the letter and the most searching: a man can pass a doctrine exam he does not mean, and behave well for a season out of fear or habit, but nobody sustains love for a person he does not actually love (1 Corinthians 16:22; 1 Peter 1:8).

How do I know whether I love him? Scripture answers with a scene. On a beach in Galilee, a man who had three times denied knowing Jesus is asked three times whether he loves him. Peter does not appeal to his feelings, and certainly not to his record, which he has just wrecked. He appeals over his own head to the one asking: Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you (John 21:17). That is love for Christ on a bad day, and it is available to you. So do not ask, do I feel warmly towards him? That will mostly tell you about your sleep. Ask about direction. In your worst week this year, did some part of you still want him, even while you were avoiding him? Does it still gladden you, under the numbness, to hear him spoken well of? Would you rather be near him than not? If you can say yes, however faintly, this verse describes you, and the blessing at the end of Ephesians has your name in it.

With love incorruptible. “Incorruptible” (aphtharsia) means imperishable, undying: a resurrection word, used of the body sown perishable and raised imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:42, 53–54). It may describe the love itself, a love for Jesus that does not fade, or the sphere of the grace, “grace in immortality”. Verdict: the ESV’s reading, an undying love for Jesus, is most natural. So a Christian’s love for Christ, which today may feel thin and distracted, is made of the same material as the resurrection body: it will not be left in the grave with everything that perishes. Yet Ephesus later received a warning from the risen Christ that it had abandoned the love it had at first (Revelation 2:4). Undying love must be guarded.

My love for Christ has grown cold. How do I get it back? Do what the risen Christ told the Ephesians when their love had cooled: remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first (Revelation 2:5). Remember: go back to what first moved you, the cross, his patience with you, the forgiveness you were given, and look at it again, slowly. Repent: name whatever has crowded him out, a sin kept, a busyness, a screen, and turn from it. Do the first works: return to the simple things, reading the Gospels, praying honestly, being with his people, telling someone about him. Love is seldom restored by trying to feel it; it is rekindled by looking again at the one who loved you. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). The fire is lit again from his, not yours.

What it does not mean. Not that grace is earned by love. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). The blessing describes those to whom grace has come: they love the one who gave it. The last sentence of Ephesians is not the place where the letter changes its mind and puts something back on your account.

In a sentence. Peace to the brothers and sisters, and love together with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ; grace to all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with a love that never dies.

For worship. The last word Paul writes to these churches, in the Greek, is that one: imperishable. A letter that opened before the foundation of the world closes beyond the reach of decay, and everything between, the choosing, the raising, the wall pulled down, the household, the armour, is held between those two points. Nothing in it started with you, and nothing in it can rot. All of it is the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, who will present his church to himself without spot or wrinkle (5:27), and whose love for her, unlike ours, has never once grown thin.

6.overview:
The household code continues. Children are to obey their parents in the Lord, honouring father and mother as the commandment with a promise requires, and fathers must not provoke their children but bring them up in the Lord’s discipline and instruction. Slaves are to serve their masters sincerely, as serving Christ, knowing the Lord will reward every good deed, and masters must treat them likewise, without threats, for both have the same Master in heaven, who shows no favouritism. Paul does not endorse slavery here; he puts master and slave under one Lord, and plants the truth that would later undo the institution.

Then comes the famous call to spiritual warfare (vv. 10–20). Believers must be strong in the Lord’s might and put on the whole armour of God, because the real enemy is not flesh and blood but the devil and the spiritual powers of evil. The armour is God’s own (Isaiah 11:5; 59:17): the belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, shoes ready with the gospel of peace, the shield of faith that quenches the evil one’s fiery arrows, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, the word of God, all taken up in constant prayer in the Spirit for all the saints, and for Paul, an ambassador in chains, to speak boldly. The letter ends with news through Tychicus and a blessing of peace, love, faith and grace on all who love the Lord Jesus with undying love.
